q: In the anatomical position, which way do the palms face?
acc: forward / forwards / anterior / anteriorly / supinated / supination / front
model: Forwards (supinated), standing upright with the arms by the sides.
hint: The forearm position in which the radius and ulna lie parallel.
why: The anatomical position is one fixed reference posture, so terms like medial and lateral mean the same whatever position the patient is really in; with the forearms supinated the radius and ulna lie side by side.

q: Which plane divides the body into right and left halves in the midline?
hint: A front-to-back plane exactly in the middle.
why: Sagittal planes run front to back; the one exactly in the midline is the median plane. Coronal planes separate front from back and transverse planes upper from lower.

q: Which vertebral level is the transpyloric plane?
hint: The top of the lumbar spine.
why: It lies halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis and crosses the pylorus, the 9th costal cartilage tips, the neck of the pancreas, the renal hila and the origin of the SMA.

q: Which vertebral level do the highest points of the iliac crests mark?
hint: The landmark used to find the space for a lumbar puncture.
why: The supracristal (Tuffier's) line crosses L4 or the L4/5 space, well below the end of the spinal cord at L1/2, which is why lumbar puncture is done at L3/4 or L4/5.

q: McBurney's point lies one third of the way from which bony landmark to the umbilicus?
hint: The front end of the iliac crest.
why: McBurney's point roughly overlies the base of the appendix; tenderness here suggests appendicitis once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

q: The lowest point of the costal margin (10th cartilage) marks which plane and vertebral level?
hint: The plane "under the ribs", two levels below the transpyloric plane.
why: The subcostal plane runs through the lowest point of the costal margin and, with the intertubercular plane, divides the abdomen into the 9 regions.

q: What is the opening between the greater and lesser sacs called?
hint: Named after a Danish anatomist; it sits behind the portal triad.
why: It lies behind the free edge of the lesser omentum with the IVC behind it and is the only communication between the lesser sac and the rest of the peritoneal cavity.

q: Which three structures run in the free edge of the lesser omentum?
model: Common bile duct, hepatic artery proper and portal vein (the portal triad).
hint: The same triad found at the corner of every liver lobule.
why: The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the free edge; clamping it (Pringle manoeuvre) stops hepatic inflow during liver bleeding.

q: Why is pain from the parietal peritoneum well localised?
acc: somatic / intercostal / spinal nerve / body wall / same nerves
model: It has somatic innervation from the same nerves as the overlying abdominal wall.
hint: Which type of nerve also supplies the skin of the abdominal wall?
why: Parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves (T7–L1), so pain maps precisely; visceral peritoneum has only autonomic afferents, giving vague midline pain.

q: Where does peritoneal fluid collect in a patient lying supine?
hint: Between the liver and the right kidney.
why: It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when supine, so it is the first place checked for free fluid on a FAST scan.

q: What is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in an upright woman?
hint: The space between the uterus and the rectum.
why: Pus and blood gather here when upright; it can be reached through the posterior vaginal fornix. In men the equivalent is the rectovesical pouch.

q: Which peritoneal fold contains the ligamentum teres (remnant of the umbilical vein)?
hint: Sickle-shaped fold joining liver to anterior abdominal wall.
why: It attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall; its free lower edge carries the ligamentum teres, which can recanalise in portal hypertension (caput medusae).

q: In which abdominal region does the spleen lie?
acc: left hypochondri / luq / left upper quadrant
hint: Under the lower ribs on one side.
why: The spleen lies along the 10th rib and only becomes palpable when enlarged about three times, growing down towards the right iliac fossa.

q: The fundus of the gallbladder lies where the right midclavicular line meets which costal cartilage?
hint: The same costal cartilage the transpyloric plane runs through.
why: This is where Murphy's sign is tested: pain stops inspiration as the inflamed gallbladder meets the examining hand.

q: Which incision is used for an open appendicectomy?
model: A Lanz (or gridiron) incision in the right iliac fossa.
hint: Named incisions in the right iliac fossa.
why: Both are centred near McBurney's point; Lanz is transverse along skin creases for a better scar, gridiron is oblique and splits the muscles in the line of their fibres.

q: Which transverse suprapubic incision is used for caesarean section?
hint: The "bikini line" incision, named after a German gynaecologist.
why: It runs just above the pubic symphysis in a skin crease, then separates the rectus muscles in the midline; it heals well and hides under clothing.

q: Which right subcostal incision gives access to the gallbladder?
hint: Named after a Swiss surgeon with a duodenal manoeuvre.
why: It follows the right costal margin over the gallbladder and liver; the same surgeon gave his name to the manoeuvre for mobilising the duodenum.

q: Through which structure does a midline laparotomy pass?
hint: The white line between the two recti.
why: It is the relatively avascular fibrous midline where the rectus sheaths fuse, so it gives quick access with little bleeding.

q: Name a feature of the large intestine that the small intestine lacks.
model: Taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae.
hint: Longitudinal muscle bands, sacculations or fatty tags.
why: The colon's longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands (taeniae coli) that pucker the wall into haustra, and fat tags hang from it.

q: Jejunum or ileum: which has long vasa recta and few arterial arcades?
hint: The more proximal of the two.
why: The jejunum is wider and redder with long vasa recta and 1–2 arcades; the ileum has short vasa recta, many arcades and more mesenteric fat.

q: Where in the gut are Peyer's patches most numerous?
why: Peyer's patches are lymphoid follicles in the ileal wall that sample gut antigens through M cells.

q: Which part of the duodenum receives the major duodenal papilla?
hint: The part running vertically down beside the head of the pancreas.
why: The bile duct and main pancreatic duct open together at the major papilla (ampulla of Vater) in the descending part, beside the head of the pancreas.

q: On X-ray, how do small bowel folds differ from colonic haustra?
model: Small bowel folds (valvulae conniventes) cross the whole width; haustral folds only part-way.
hint: Compare how far each kind of fold spans the bowel.
why: Plicae circulares are complete circular folds, while haustral folds are made by the taeniae and don't span the lumen.

q: Above what diameter is the small bowel dilated on an abdominal X-ray?
model: More than 3 cm (3-6-9 rule: small bowel 3, colon 6, caecum 9 cm).
hint: The smallest number of a three-number rule for bowel diameters.
why: These thresholds flag obstruction or ileus; the caecum tolerates the most dilatation before it risks perforating.

q: Which sign on an abdominal X-ray shows both sides of the bowel wall because of free gas?
hint: Gas on both sides of the bowel wall.
why: Free intraperitoneal gas outlines the outer surface of the bowel wall as well as the gas inside, so the whole wall becomes visible; it means perforation.

q: What shape does a sigmoid volvulus make on an abdominal X-ray?
model: A large "coffee bean" loop pointing to the right upper quadrant.
hint: The shape of a breakfast drink's seed.
why: The twisted sigmoid becomes a hugely dilated closed loop whose two limbs press together, making the bean's central cleft.

q: Which X-ray best shows a pneumoperitoneum?
model: An erect chest X-ray: free air under the diaphragm.
hint: Patient sitting up, film of the thorax.
why: Free gas rises to the highest point, under the domes of the diaphragm, when the patient sits up; it needs a few minutes upright to collect.

q: Which plane separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum?
model: The plane through the sternal angle (T4/5).
hint: The ridge between manubrium and body of the sternum.
why: The sternal angle lies at the 2nd costal cartilage and level with T4/5, where the carina, the start and end of the aortic arch and the azygos–SVC junction all lie.

q: Which subdivision of the mediastinum contains the heart?
hint: Between the anterior and posterior parts.
why: The inferior mediastinum is split by the pericardium into anterior (in front), middle (heart and pericardium) and posterior (behind) parts.

q: Name two structures in the posterior mediastinum.
acc: aorta / oesophagus / esophagus / thoracic duct / azygos / vagus
model: Descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos veins, vagus nerves.
hint: Think of tubes and vessels running between neck and abdomen behind the heart.
why: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and in front of T5–T12, a pathway for structures running between neck and abdomen.

q: Which ribs are "floating"?
why: Their cartilages end in the abdominal wall muscles with no anterior attachment to the sternum or other cartilages.

q: What type of joint is the manubriosternal joint?
hint: The same joint type as the intervertebral discs.
why: Fibrocartilage between hyaline-covered bones allows slight movement as the ribs rise, the same joint type as the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

q: What type of joint is the 1st sternocostal joint?
hint: Hyaline cartilage only, no joint cavity.
why: The 1st costal cartilage joins the manubrium directly with hyaline cartilage and no joint cavity, unlike the synovial 2nd–7th sternocostal joints.

q: On which border of a rib does the costal groove lie?
model: The inferior (lower) border, on its inner surface.
hint: The side away from the head.
why: The groove shelters the intercostal vein, artery and nerve, which is why needles go just above a rib.

q: Name the bony boundaries of the superior thoracic aperture.
acc: t1 + first rib / 1st rib / ribs + manubrium / jugular notch
model: T1 vertebra, the first ribs and their cartilages, and the upper border of the manubrium.
hint: One vertebra, a pair of curved bones and the top of the breastbone.
why: The inlet slopes down anteriorly; the lung apices and cervical pleura bulge up through it above the clavicle.

q: At which vertebral level does the aorta pass through the diaphragm?
hint: The lowest of the three main openings.
why: "I 8 10 Eggs At 12": IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12. The aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament rather than through muscle.

q: At which vertebral level does the IVC pass through the diaphragm?
model: T8 (caval opening, in the central tendon).
hint: The highest of the three main openings.
why: Because it sits in the central tendon, the caval opening is pulled open on inspiration, helping venous return.

q: Which structure, when present in the neck, can compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus?
hint: An extra bone above the first rib.
why: An extra rib from C7 narrows the space over the first rib, stretching the lower trunk (C8–T1) and the subclavian artery: thoracic outlet syndrome.

q: Which facets on a thoracic vertebral body articulate with the heads of ribs?
hint: Half-sized facets on the vertebral body.
why: Most rib heads articulate with two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them, so each body carries half-facets above and below.

q: Which costal cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle?
hint: The rib after the one hidden under the clavicle.
why: The sternal angle is the reliable starting point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces because the 1st rib is hidden behind the clavicle.

q: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right main bronchus?
model: It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
hint: Compare the width and angle of the two main bronchi.
why: The left main bronchus angles away more sharply under the aortic arch, so the right is the straighter path down from the trachea.

q: Where does the conducting zone of the airway end?
hint: The last airway with no alveoli in its wall.
why: Everything up to the terminal bronchioles only conducts air (anatomical dead space); gas exchange starts at the respiratory bronchioles.

q: How many bronchopulmonary segments does the right lung have?
why: Right upper 3, middle 2, lower 5. Each segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery, so it can be resected alone.

q: What supplies the centre of a bronchopulmonary segment, and what drains it?
model: A segmental bronchus and pulmonary artery branch centrally; pulmonary veins run between segments.
hint: One airway and one vessel in the middle; the other vessel runs in the boundaries.
why: Because the veins lie in the intersegmental septa, surgeons use them to find the planes between segments.

q: Above which structure does thermal injury from hot gases mainly occur?
acc: vocal cord / vocal fold / cords / larynx / glottis
hint: The structures that close to protect the airway reflexively.
why: The upper airway cools inhaled gas very efficiently, so thermal burns cause supraglottic oedema and stridor; lower airways suffer chemical injury from smoke.

q: What lies directly in front of the trachea at rings 2–4?
model: The isthmus of the thyroid gland.
hint: The bridge of a butterfly-shaped gland.
why: This is why a tracheostomy may need the isthmus divided or retracted; inferior thyroid veins also lie in front lower down.

q: Which nerves lie in the grooves between trachea and oesophagus?
hint: Branches of the vagus that loop back up to the larynx.
why: They run up in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves to supply the larynx, so thyroid and oesophageal surgery risks hoarseness.

q: Which vein arches over the right side of the trachea to join the SVC?
hint: An unpaired vein draining the posterior thoracic wall.
why: It arches over the root of the right lung at T4 to enter the SVC; the left side has the aortic arch in the equivalent position.

q: How many lobes does the left lung have?
model: Two (upper, with the lingula, and lower).
why: The left lung has only an oblique fissure; the lingula of the upper lobe is the equivalent of the right middle lobe.

q: Which fissure is found only in the right lung?
hint: It runs flat, along the 4th costal cartilage.
why: It separates the right upper and middle lobes; both lungs have an oblique fissure.

q: What tongue-like part of the left upper lobe corresponds to the right middle lobe?
why: It lies below the cardiac notch and has its own superior and inferior lingular segments.

q: At which rib does the lower edge of the lung cross the midaxillary line?
why: Rule of 6-8-10 for the lung (midclavicular, midaxillary, paravertebral) and 8-10-12 for the parietal pleura; the gap is the costodiaphragmatic recess.

q: At which rib does the parietal pleura cross the midaxillary line?
hint: Two ribs below the lung edge.
why: The pleura reaches two ribs lower than the lung, leaving the costodiaphragmatic recess where effusions collect.

q: Where does fluid from a pleural effusion collect first?
hint: The angle between ribs and diaphragm.
why: It is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, below the lung edge, which is why blunting of the costophrenic angle is an early sign.

q: Along which rib does the oblique fissure run?
model: Along the 5th rib (from T2/3 behind to the 6th costal cartilage in front).
why: This matches the medial border of the scapula with the arm fully raised; below it lies the lower lobe, mostly heard from the back.

q: From which side of the chest are the lower lobes best auscultated?
hint: Follow the slope of the oblique fissure.
why: The oblique fissures run down and forward, so the lower lobes occupy most of the posterior chest while the upper and middle lobes lie in front.

q: Which heart chamber makes the deep impression on the left lung?
why: The heart lies more to the left, so the left lung has a deep cardiac impression and a notch on its anterior border; the right lung's impression is from the right atrium.

q: What structure grooves the left lung above and behind its hilum?
model: The aorta (arch above, descending aorta behind).
hint: The great artery that arches to the left.
why: The arch passes over the left root and the descending aorta runs down behind it, leaving a continuous aortic groove.

q: Which structures in the lung root lie most anterior and inferior?
why: From front to back the root is veins, artery, bronchus, and the inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure.

q: On which side is the upper lobe bronchus above the pulmonary artery at the hilum?
why: The right upper lobe bronchus leaves the main bronchus before the artery crosses; on the left the pulmonary artery is the highest structure (RALS).

q: What is the fold of pleura hanging down from the lung root called?
hint: Not a true ligament; a sleeve of pleura.
why: It is the empty lower part of the pleural sleeve around the root, giving room for the root to move during breathing.

q: Which nerve passes in front of the lung root, and which behind?
hint: The diaphragm's nerve and the wandering nerve.
why: The phrenic descends anterior to the root to the diaphragm; the vagus passes posterior to it to form the pulmonary and oesophageal plexuses.

q: Which nodes receive lymph first from the lung tissue?
why: Lymph then flows to the tracheobronchial (carinal) and paratracheal nodes; this is the route of lung cancer spread used in N staging.

q: Which lobe's lymph drains partly to the opposite side?
hint: A lower lobe on the side with two lobes.
why: Some of its lymph crosses to right-sided nodes, so a left lower lobe tumour can involve contralateral nodes (N3).

q: Which nerve carries pain from the mediastinal pleura, referring it to the shoulder tip?
hint: The nerve that keeps the diaphragm alive.
why: The phrenic nerve supplies mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura; C4 also supplies the skin over the shoulder, so pain is referred there.

q: What effect does vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation have on the bronchi?
hint: The opposite of what salbutamol does.
why: Acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors in airway smooth muscle; inhaled antimuscarinics block this. Sympathetic β2 stimulation dilates.

q: Is the visceral pleura sensitive to pain?
model: No: it has only autonomic innervation.
hint: Think about which pleural layer has somatic nerves.
why: Pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura (intercostal and phrenic nerves), which is why lung tumours can grow painlessly until they reach the chest wall.

q: Which hilum normally sits higher on a chest X-ray?
hint: The side where the pulmonary artery climbs over the bronchus.
why: The left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus, lifting the left hilar shadow above the right.

q: Which hemidiaphragm is normally higher on a chest X-ray?
why: The liver sits under the right dome and pushes it up; the gastric bubble lies under the left.

q: How many anterior ribs should be visible above the diaphragm on a well-inspired chest X-ray?
why: Fewer means poor inspiration, which crowds the lung bases and makes the heart look bigger.

q: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus begin?
hint: The level of the cricoid cartilage.
why: It continues from the laryngopharynx at the cricopharyngeus, the narrowest point of the oesophagus.

q: Which artery supplies the abdominal oesophagus?
model: The left gastric artery (from the coeliac trunk).
hint: A branch of the coeliac trunk running along the lesser curvature.
why: Cervical = inferior thyroid, thoracic = aortic branches, abdominal = left gastric; the left gastric vein drains to the portal system.

q: Why do oesophageal varices form in portal hypertension?
model: The lower oesophagus is a portosystemic anastomosis (left gastric to azygos veins).
why: Raised portal pressure diverts blood through the left gastric vein into oesophageal veins draining to the azygos system, which dilate into fragile varices.

q: Which heart chamber lies directly in front of the lower oesophagus?
hint: The chamber receiving the pulmonary veins.
why: An enlarged left atrium indents a barium swallow, and transoesophageal echo views the heart through it.

q: Which muscle relaxes to let the bolus enter the oesophagus?
hint: The lowest part of the inferior constrictor.
why: It is the lowest part of the inferior constrictor; failure to relax pushes mucosa out above it (pharyngeal pouch).

q: Which phase of swallowing is voluntary?
why: Chewing and pushing the bolus back are under conscious control; once the bolus touches the pharynx, a brainstem reflex takes over.

q: Which way does the larynx move during the pharyngeal phase?
hint: Feel your Adam's apple when you swallow.
why: Elevation tucks the larynx under the tongue base so the epiglottis tips over the inlet, and opens the upper oesophageal sphincter.

q: Which cranial nerves give sensation and motor supply to the pharynx during swallowing?
why: IX carries sensation from the oropharynx that triggers the reflex; X supplies the constrictors, palate and larynx.

q: At which vertebral level does the pylorus lie?
model: L1 (transpyloric plane), just right of midline.
why: The transpyloric plane is named after it; the pylorus moves with posture and stomach filling.

q: Which arteries supply the lesser curvature of the stomach?
model: The left and right gastric arteries.
hint: A pair named for opposite sides, one straight off the coeliac trunk.
why: The left gastric comes straight off the coeliac trunk and the right gastric from the hepatic artery; they anastomose along the lesser curvature.

q: Which arteries supply the fundus of the stomach?
model: The short gastric arteries (from the splenic artery).
hint: Small branches of the splenic artery.
why: They run in the gastrosplenic ligament; the fundus is a watershed area.

q: What is the innermost muscle layer of the stomach wall?
hint: The stomach's extra layer compared with the rest of the gut.
why: The stomach has three layers (outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique) for churning food.

q: Which organ lies behind the stomach across the lesser sac and can be eroded by a posterior ulcer?
hint: A gland that lies across the posterior abdominal wall.
why: The stomach bed includes the pancreas, spleen, left kidney and adrenal, splenic artery and transverse mesocolon; posterior ulcers can penetrate the pancreas.

q: Which nerve carries parasympathetic supply to the stomach?
model: The vagus nerve (anterior and posterior vagal trunks).
why: Vagal fibres increase acid secretion and motility; vagotomy was once used for ulcers.

q: Which splanchnic nerve carries sympathetic fibres to the coeliac ganglion?
hint: The largest of the thoracic splanchnic nerves.
why: Preganglionic fibres pass through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing and synapse in the coeliac ganglion around the coeliac trunk.

q: At which vertebral level does the coeliac trunk arise?
hint: The same level as the aortic hiatus.
why: The coeliac plexus surrounds it on the front of the aorta; a coeliac plexus block here treats pancreatic cancer pain.

q: Which nerves give parasympathetic supply to the hindgut?
why: The vagus reaches only about two-thirds along the transverse colon; beyond that, sacral parasympathetic fibres take over.

q: Do preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the gut synapse in the sympathetic trunk?
model: No: they pass through and synapse in prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
hint: Splanchnic nerves carry the fibres onward.
why: Splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic fibres to ganglia in front of the aorta; postganglionic fibres then follow the arteries.

q: Where is pain from a midgut organ such as the appendix first felt?
why: Midgut visceral afferents enter at T10, the dermatome of the umbilicus; pain shifts to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

q: Where is foregut pain felt?
why: Foregut afferents enter at T5–9; stomach, duodenal, biliary and pancreatic pain all start here.

q: Why can gallbladder pain be felt at the shoulder?
model: Irritation of the diaphragm is carried by the phrenic nerve (C3–5), sharing C4 with the shoulder skin.
why: The brain projects pain from the C4 segment onto the dermatome it usually serves, the top of the shoulder.

q: Where is hindgut pain felt?
hint: Below the umbilicus, in the midline.
why: Hindgut afferents enter at T12–L1, so pain from the distal colon is felt low in the midline.

q: Lymph from the gut drains to nodes named after what?
model: The arteries supplying that part of the gut (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
why: Lymphatics travel alongside the arteries, so cancer resections remove the arterial pedicle with its nodes.

q: Into which vessel does the cisterna chyli drain?
hint: The largest lymphatic vessel in the body.
why: The cisterna chyli at L1–2 collects intestinal and lumbar lymph; the thoracic duct carries it up through the aortic hiatus to the left venous angle.

q: To which nodes does testicular cancer spread first?
hint: Nodes beside the aorta at the level the testis started from.
why: The testis develops near the kidneys and its lymphatics follow the testicular vessels back up; scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to the inguinal nodes.

q: Which node is enlarged in Troisier's sign?
hint: Above the clavicle, near where the thoracic duct ends.
why: It sits near the end of the thoracic duct, so abdominal cancers, classically gastric, can spread there.

q: Which investigation is used with speech and language therapists to look for aspiration during swallowing?
hint: A moving X-ray study of swallowing.
why: It records the oral and pharyngeal phases in real time and shows contrast entering the airway, guiding safe food textures.

q: What is the classic barium swallow appearance of achalasia?
model: A "bird's beak" taper at the lower oesophagus.
hint: The narrowing looks like part of an animal's head.
why: The lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax, so the oesophagus dilates above a smooth narrowing.

q: Which contrast is used if oesophageal perforation is suspected?
why: Barium leaking into the mediastinum causes severe inflammation, so a water-soluble agent is used first.

q: In which organ do T cells mature?
hint: An organ in the anterior mediastinum that shrinks after puberty.
why: Thymocytes undergo positive selection (MHC recognition) and negative selection (removing self-reactive cells); the thymus shrinks after puberty.

q: Where do B cells mature?
hint: Where all blood cells are made.
why: Bone marrow and thymus are the primary lymphoid organs; lymph nodes, spleen and MALT are secondary organs where responses happen.

q: Which part of the spleen removes old red cells?
hint: The colour of the cells it removes.
why: Red pulp cords and sinuses filter blood; white pulp contains lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne antigens.

q: Which infections are most dangerous after splenectomy?
why: The spleen clears these and makes the IgM that opsonises them, so asplenic patients need vaccines and prophylactic antibiotics.

q: Where in the lymph node do T cells mainly lie?
hint: Between the cortex and the medulla.
why: B cells form follicles and germinal centres in the outer cortex, T cells sit in the paracortex, and plasma cells in the medulla.

q: Which lymphoid aggregates in the ileum sample gut antigens?
hint: Named after a Swiss anatomist; found in the distal small bowel.
why: Specialised M cells transport antigens across the epithelium to underlying lymphoid follicles, priming IgA responses.

q: Which ring of lymphoid tissue guards the entrance to the pharynx?
model: Waldeyer's ring (adenoids, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsils).
why: It sits where inhaled and swallowed antigens first meet mucosa.

q: Which primary lymphoid organ shrinks after puberty?
why: Its T-cell education is largely complete after childhood, so it is replaced by fat; remnants lie in the anterior mediastinum.

q: What do lymph nodes filter?
hint: The fluid in the vessels that drain tissue spaces.
why: Afferent lymphatics bring tissue fluid with antigens and dendritic cells to the node, where lymphocytes meet them; efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum.

q: Which immunoglobulin is mainly made at mucosal surfaces?
hint: The antibody found in tears, saliva and breast milk.
why: MALT plasma cells produce dimeric IgA, which is transported across epithelium into secretions.

q: Where is the apex beat normally felt?
hint: One space below the male nipple, in the same vertical line.
why: The apex is formed by the left ventricle; displacement laterally or downward suggests LV enlargement or mediastinal shift.

q: At which vertebral level is the inferior angle of the scapula (arms by sides)?
hint: The spine of the scapula is at T3; this is four levels lower.
why: It gives a quick posterior landmark for counting ribs and finding the lower lung lobes.

q: Which intercostal space is the male nipple usually in?
why: It is a rough landmark only (variable, especially in women) but marks the lower edge of the chest drain safe triangle.

q: Which muscle does most of the work in quiet inspiration?
hint: A dome-shaped sheet supplied by C3–5.
why: Its descent increases the vertical size of the thorax and accounts for about three-quarters of tidal volume; quiet expiration is passive.

q: Is quiet expiration active or passive?
model: Passive (elastic recoil of lungs and chest wall).
hint: Think of a stretched spring returning.
why: Muscles are only recruited for forced expiration: abdominal wall muscles and internal intercostals.

q: Which movement of the upper ribs increases the front-to-back diameter of the chest?
why: Upper ribs swing up and forward like a pump handle, pushing the sternum forwards; lower ribs swing outwards like a bucket handle, widening the chest.

q: Name the muscles that power forced expiration.
acc: abdominal / rectus / oblique / transversus / internal intercostal
model: Abdominal wall muscles (rectus abdominis, obliques, transversus), helped by internal intercostals.
hint: The muscles you tense to cough hard.
why: Raising intra-abdominal pressure pushes the diaphragm up, and the internal intercostals pull the ribs down.

q: Name an accessory muscle of inspiration in the neck.
hint: Look for them straining in a breathless patient's neck.
why: They lift the sternum and first ribs; visible use signals respiratory distress.

q: Which intercostal layer runs down and forward, like hands in pockets?
why: They lift the ribs in inspiration; the internal and innermost layers run at right angles, down and back.

q: Between which two intercostal layers does the neurovascular bundle run?
model: Between the internal and innermost intercostals.
why: The bundle lies in the costal groove deep to the internal intercostals, so a needle above the rib below avoids it.

q: Which artery gives the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces?
hint: A branch of the subclavian running down beside the sternum.
why: It runs about 1 cm lateral to the sternum behind the costal cartilages and is used as the LIMA graft in CABG.

q: Where do posterior intercostal arteries 3–11 come from?
hint: The largest artery in the posterior mediastinum.
why: The first two spaces are supplied from the superior intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk instead.

q: Which X-ray sign of coarctation is caused by enlarged intercostal arteries?
hint: Small bites out of the underside of the ribs.
why: Blood bypasses the narrowing via internal thoracic → intercostal → aorta collaterals, and the enlarged tortuous intercostals erode the rib undersurfaces.

q: List the order of the neurovascular bundle from top to bottom.
hint: A three-letter word for a vehicle.
why: The vein sits highest in the costal groove and the nerve lowest, so the nerve is least protected by the rib.

q: Should a chest drain go above or below a rib?
model: Just above the rib below (upper border of the lower rib).
hint: Think about where the costal groove is.
why: The main neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove under the rib above, so keeping close to the top of the lower rib avoids it.

q: Which intercostal nerves continue on to supply the abdominal wall?
why: They leave the intercostal spaces and run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis to supply abdominal muscles, skin and parietal peritoneum.

q: Intercostal nerves are branches of which part of the thoracic spinal nerves?
hint: The front branch after the spinal nerve splits.
why: Dorsal rami supply the back; ventral rami supply the front and sides of the trunk and, in the limbs, form the plexuses.

q: What do grey rami communicantes carry to the intercostal nerves?
hint: The fibres that make you sweat, after their synapse.
why: These reach sweat glands, skin vessels and hair muscles in each dermatome; white rami (T1–L2 only) carry preganglionic fibres into the trunk.

q: Which nerve from T2 supplies skin of the axilla and medial arm?
hint: Its name combines "between the ribs" and "arm".
why: It explains cardiac pain referred down the inner arm and is at risk in axillary surgery.

q: On which film type is a small pneumothorax sometimes easier to see?
why: The lung gets smaller on expiration but the air in the pleural space doesn't, so it takes up relatively more of the chest.

q: Which way is the trachea pulled in lobar collapse?
why: Lost volume pulls the mediastinum in; a large effusion or tension pneumothorax pushes it away.

q: What is the earliest X-ray sign of a pleural effusion?
hint: The sharp corner where diaphragm meets ribs.
why: Fluid collects first in the costodiaphragmatic recess; about 200 mL is needed on an erect PA film.

q: What is the normal intrapleural pressure relative to atmosphere?
why: Lungs recoil inwards and the chest wall outwards; the sealed fluid layer between them holds the pressure below atmospheric, keeping the lungs open.

q: What is the pleural cavity?
model: A potential space between visceral and parietal pleura with a thin film of fluid.
hint: Normally almost empty: only a film of fluid.
why: It only becomes a real space when air, fluid, blood or pus collects in it.

q: Which pleural layer covers the lung surface and dips into the fissures?
hint: The layer stuck to the organ.
why: Parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum; the two are continuous at the lung root.

q: Name the anterior border of the safe triangle for chest drains.
model: The lateral border of pectoralis major.
hint: The muscle forming the front fold of the armpit.
why: The triangle avoids the internal thoracic vessels in front and the long thoracic nerve behind.

q: Name the posterior border of the safe triangle.
model: The lateral (anterior) border of latissimus dorsi.
hint: The broad back muscle forming the back fold of the armpit.
why: Going behind it risks the long thoracic nerve and thick back muscles.

q: At which intercostal space is the lower border of the safe triangle?
why: Going lower risks the diaphragm, liver or spleen, which rise in expiration.

q: How do you tell the lateral end of the clavicle from the medial end?
model: The lateral end is flat; the medial end is rounded.
hint: Compare the shape of the two ends.
why: The flat acromial end meets the acromion and carries trapezius and deltoid; the rounded sternal end sits in the sternoclavicular joint.

q: Which ligament attaches to the conoid tubercle on the clavicle?
hint: It runs down to a hook-like process on the scapula.
why: It suspends the scapula and arm from the clavicle and is key to acromioclavicular stability.

q: Which part of the clavicle is most often fractured?
why: It is the thinnest part, at the junction of the two curves, and lacks muscle and ligament support.

q: Which muscle attaches to the groove on the underside of the clavicle?
why: It anchors the clavicle and cushions the subclavian vessels below during fractures.

q: Which process of the scapula gives attachment to pectoralis minor?
why: Short head of biceps and coracobrachialis attach here too; it is palpable below the lateral clavicle.

q: Which muscle attaches to the infraglenoid tubercle?
hint: The main extensor of the elbow.
why: The supraglenoid tubercle takes the long head of biceps, which runs inside the shoulder joint.

q: Which nerve passes through the suprascapular notch?
hint: Named after the region above the scapula.
why: It passes under the transverse scapular ligament to supply supraspinatus and infraspinatus; the suprascapular artery passes over the ligament.

q: Why are the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints called atypical?
model: Their articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
hint: The surface cartilage is a different type from most synovial joints.
why: The clavicle ossifies in membrane, so its joint surfaces are fibrocartilaginous.

q: What divides the sternoclavicular joint into two cavities?
hint: A fibrocartilage plate inside the joint.
why: The disc acts as a shock absorber and strong check ligament, making the joint very stable despite its shallow surfaces.

q: Which is the strongest ligament stabilising the sternoclavicular joint?
hint: It joins the clavicle to the first rib.
why: It ties the clavicle down to the 1st rib; because of it the clavicle fractures rather than dislocates.

q: Which way is the medial fragment of a fractured clavicle pulled?
hint: Think about the neck muscle attached to it.
why: The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the arm, so the shoulder droops.

q: Which ligament mainly holds the acromioclavicular joint together?
hint: It links the clavicle to a process on the front of the scapula.
why: When it tears along with the AC ligament the clavicle rides up, giving a step deformity.

q: Which two muscles form the posterior axillary fold?
hint: A broad back muscle and the larger teres.
why: The anterior fold is pectoralis major; these folds help orient you when examining the axilla.

q: Which muscle runs from ribs 1–8 to the medial border of the scapula?
hint: Its digitations look like a saw.
why: It holds the scapula against the chest wall and protracts it, hence "boxer's muscle".

q: Which muscle lies deep to pectoralis major, from ribs 3–5 to the coracoid?
why: It divides the axillary artery into three parts and is a landmark for the brachial plexus cords.

q: Which nerve supplies trapezius?
hint: A cranial nerve that leaves the skull and supplies two neck muscles.
why: C3–4 add proprioception; damage in the posterior triangle stops shrugging and causes drooping.

q: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior?
hint: A long nerve running down the side of the chest.
why: It runs on the outer surface of serratus anterior, so axillary surgery can damage it, causing winging.

q: Which nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae?
hint: A branch from the C5 root to the back of the scapula.
why: It comes straight off the C5 root and runs along the medial border of the scapula.

q: Which two muscles together rotate the scapula upwards to raise the arm above the head?
hint: A big back muscle and the boxer's muscle.
why: Upper and lower trapezius with serratus turn the glenoid upwards for abduction above 90°.

q: Injury to which nerve causes a winged scapula?
why: Without serratus anterior the medial border lifts off the chest wall, worst when pushing against a wall.

q: Which nerve wraps round the surgical neck of the humerus?
why: It passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and is at risk in neck fractures and dislocations.

q: Which nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus?
hint: The nerve to the forearm extensors.
why: Midshaft fractures can damage it, causing wrist drop.

q: Which rotator cuff muscle attaches to the lesser tubercle?
hint: The only cuff muscle on the front of the scapula.
why: The other three (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) attach to the greater tubercle.

q: Which tendon runs in the intertubercular groove?
hint: An elbow flexor with two heads.
why: Pectoralis major attaches to the lateral lip, latissimus to the floor and teres major to the medial lip ("lady between two majors").

q: Which nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle?
why: It is the "funny bone" and is at risk in medial epicondyle fractures and cubital tunnel syndrome.

q: Which rotator cuff muscle starts abduction?
hint: The cuff muscle above the spine of the scapula.
why: Deltoid takes over from about 15–90°, then scapular rotation by trapezius and serratus.

q: Which two rotator cuff muscles laterally rotate the shoulder?
hint: The two cuff muscles on the back below the spine.
why: Subscapularis is the medial rotator; supraspinatus abducts.

q: Which fibrocartilage ring deepens the glenoid cavity?
why: The glenoid covers only about a third of the head; the labrum deepens it but the joint still trades stability for movement.

q: Which tendon runs inside the shoulder joint capsule?
hint: It starts from the supraglenoid tubercle.
why: It arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and is wrapped in a synovial sheath as it crosses the joint.

q: Which muscle abducts the shoulder from about 15° to 90°?
hint: The muscle forming the cap of the shoulder.
why: Its middle fibres are the main abductor once supraspinatus has started the movement.

q: In which direction does the humeral head usually dislocate?
model: Anteriorly (about 95%), after escaping inferiorly through the weak lower capsule.
why: The inferior capsule has no cuff support, so the head comes out below and is then pulled forwards to sit under the coracoid.

q: Which nerve should be checked before and after reducing a shoulder dislocation?
why: It wraps round the surgical neck right next to the dislocating head; test sensation over the regimental badge area.

q: What is a Hill–Sachs lesion?
model: An impaction fracture (dent) in the posterolateral humeral head.
hint: Damage to the ball, not the socket.
why: The head is driven against the anterior glenoid rim as it dislocates; a matching anterior labral tear is a Bankart lesion.

q: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the axilla?
why: The long thoracic nerve runs on it, which is why it is at risk in axillary surgery.

q: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
hint: A small chest muscle from ribs to coracoid.
why: Part 1 is above it, part 2 behind it and part 3 below it; the cords of the plexus are named relative to the second part.

q: Roughly what proportion of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes?
why: That's why axillary nodes are sampled (sentinel node biopsy) in breast cancer.

q: Which spinal nerve roots form the brachial plexus?
hint: Lower four cervical plus the first thoracic.
why: Their ventral rami pass between the anterior and middle scalenes.

q: Which trunk is formed by C8 and T1?
hint: The one nearest the first rib.
why: Upper = C5–6, middle = C7, lower = C8–T1.

q: From which cord does the ulnar nerve arise?
hint: The cord nearest the chest wall.
why: The medial cord takes the anterior division of the lower trunk (C8–T1), which also matches the ulnar nerve's roots.

q: From which cord do the axillary and radial nerves arise?
why: It is made of all three posterior divisions and supplies the posterior (extensor) muscles.

q: Which two cords contribute to the median nerve?
why: Their contributions join in front of the axillary artery in an M-shape with the musculocutaneous and ulnar nerves.

q: What are the cords of the brachial plexus named after?
model: Their position relative to the axillary artery.
why: Behind pectoralis minor the lateral, medial and posterior cords lie on those sides of the second part of the axillary artery.

q: Which roots are damaged in Erb's palsy?
hint: The roots of the upper trunk.
why: Head and shoulder forced apart stretch the upper trunk, giving the "waiter's tip" posture.

q: Describe the arm posture in Erb's palsy.
acc: waiter / adducted / internally rotated / medially rotated
model: "Waiter's tip": arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated.
hint: Think of someone asking discreetly for a tip.
why: Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis are lost, so unopposed muscles pull the limb that way.

q: Which roots are damaged in Klumpke's palsy?
hint: The roots of the lower trunk.
why: Upward traction on the arm stretches the lower trunk, paralysing small hand muscles (claw hand), sometimes with Horner's syndrome.

q: Why can Klumpke's palsy cause Horner's syndrome?
model: The T1 root carries sympathetic fibres to the head.
hint: Which root carries the autonomic supply to the eye?
why: Preganglionic fibres to the eye leave via T1; damaging it gives ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

q: Through which space does the axillary nerve pass?
why: It is bounded by teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the humerus; the posterior circumflex humeral artery runs with it.

q: Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis?
hint: It supplies the anterior arm muscles.
why: It then runs between biceps and brachialis and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

q: Through which canal does the ulnar nerve enter the hand?
why: It passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

q: Through which tunnel does the median nerve enter the hand?
hint: The tunnel under the flexor retinaculum.
why: It runs deep to the flexor retinaculum with the long flexor tendons, so compression causes thenar weakness and numb lateral fingers.

q: Does the median nerve give any branches in the arm?
model: No: it gives no branches above the elbow.
hint: Think of the musculocutaneous nerve doing that job.
why: It travels with the brachial artery and only starts branching in the forearm.

q: Which nerve supplies biceps?
hint: The nerve of the anterior arm compartment.
why: It supplies all three anterior arm muscles: coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis.

q: What does LOAF stand for?
model: Lateral two Lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis.
hint: Median nerve muscles in the hand.
why: These are the median nerve's hand muscles; nearly all others are ulnar.

q: Which nerve supplies adductor pollicis?
why: Adductor pollicis is the basis of Froment's sign for ulnar nerve palsy.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the palmar skin of the lateral three and a half fingers?
hint: The nerve through the carpal tunnel.
why: The ulnar supplies the medial one and a half; the radial supplies the back of the lateral hand.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the dorsal first web space?
hint: The nerve injured in Saturday night palsy.
why: It is the purest autonomous area for testing radial sensation.

q: Which nerve injury causes wrist drop?
hint: The nerve in the spiral groove.
why: It supplies all the wrist and finger extensors, so damage in the spiral groove lets the wrist flop.

q: What is Froment's sign testing?
hint: Paper gripped between thumb and index finger.
why: Holding paper between thumb and index, the patient flexes the thumb tip (FPL, median) to compensate for weak adductor pollicis.

q: Which nerve lesion gives a "hand of benediction" when making a fist?
why: Index and middle FDS/FDP (median) can't flex while ring and little (ulnar FDP) can.

q: Why is ulnar claw hand worse with a wrist lesion than an elbow lesion?
model: A wrist lesion spares FDP, which flexes the fingertips and exaggerates the claw (ulnar paradox).
hint: Which long flexor is still working with a distal lesion?
why: An elbow lesion also paralyses the ulnar half of FDP, so the IP joints flex less and the claw is milder.

q: How would you test the axillary nerve's sensation?
model: Sensation over the lower deltoid ("regimental badge" area).
hint: Where a soldier's sleeve badge sits.
why: This patch is supplied only by the axillary nerve's superior lateral cutaneous branch.

q: Which chamber forms most of the sternocostal (anterior) surface of the heart?
why: The heart is rotated so the RV faces forward; the LV forms the apex and left border, the LA the base.

q: What separates the smooth and rough parts of the right atrium?
hint: A muscular ridge whose top holds the pacemaker.
why: It marks the junction of the smooth sinus venarum and the rough pectinate muscle part; the SA node lies at its upper end.

q: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
hint: A fetal hole between the atria.
why: In the fetus it shunts blood from right to left atrium; it closes at birth when left atrial pressure rises.

q: Which structure in the right ventricle carries the right bundle branch?
hint: A muscular bridge across the RV cavity.
why: It runs from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle, letting it contract in time with the rest of the ventricle.

q: Where do blood clots most often form in atrial fibrillation?
acc: left auricle / left atrial appendage / laa / appendage
hint: An ear-shaped pouch off the left atrium.
why: Blood stagnates in this blind pouch when the atria stop contracting; LAA occlusion devices target it.

q: What electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles?
model: The fibrous skeleton of the heart.
hint: Dense connective tissue rings around the valves.
why: Its rings support the valves and block conduction, so the AV node and bundle are the only route.

q: Where is the aortic valve best heard?
model: The 2nd right intercostal space beside the sternum.
hint: The space just below the right clavicle by the sternum.
why: Sound carries along the ascending aorta, which comes closest to the chest wall there.

q: Where is the mitral valve best heard?
model: At the apex: 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line.
hint: Where you feel the heart's beat on the chest wall.
why: The valve lies behind the sternum but sound carries into the LV towards the apex.

q: Where is the tricuspid valve best heard?
acc: lower left sternal / left sternal edge / 4th / 5th
why: Its sound carries into the right ventricle, which lies behind the lower sternum.

q: What stops the AV valve cusps everting in systole?
model: Chordae tendineae pulled taut by papillary muscles.
hint: Heart strings and the muscles holding them.
why: Papillary muscles contract with the ventricle, tightening the chordae; rupture after MI causes acute regurgitation.

q: Which is the highest of the four heart valves?
model: The pulmonary valve (behind the left 3rd costal cartilage).
hint: The valve leading to the lungs.
why: The pulmonary trunk sits highest and furthest forward of the outflow tracts.

q: Where is the SA node?
model: In the right atrial wall where the SVC meets the top of the crista terminalis.
hint: Near where the superior vena cava enters.
why: Its cells have the fastest spontaneous depolarisation, so they set the rate.

q: Where is the AV node?
model: In the interatrial septum near the opening of the coronary sinus (triangle of Koch).
hint: Near the opening of the main cardiac vein.
why: It sits just above the tricuspid valve; surgery or ablation here risks heart block.

q: Which coronary artery usually supplies the AV node?
why: That's why inferior MI (RCA territory) often causes bradycardia and AV block.

q: Why does the AV node delay conduction?
model: To give the ventricles time to fill after atrial contraction.
hint: What happens to the ventricles while the atria contract?
why: The ~0.1 s delay (PR interval) separates atrial and ventricular systole.

q: In which direction do the ventricles contract?
hint: Like squeezing toothpaste from the closed end.
why: Purkinje fibres reach the apex first, so contraction squeezes blood up towards the outflow valves.

q: What is the intrinsic rate of the AV junction?
hint: Slower than the SA node, faster than the ventricles.
why: If the SA node fails the AV junction takes over (junctional rhythm); ventricular escape is slower, 20–40.

q: Where is ECG lead V1 placed?
hint: Same space as V2, other side of the sternum.
why: V2 is the mirror position on the left; misplacing them high changes the trace.

q: Where is ECG lead V4 placed?
why: V5 and V6 go on the same horizontal line at the anterior and mid-axillary lines.

q: What forms the right border of the heart on the surface?
model: The right atrium (3rd–6th right costal cartilages beside the sternum).
hint: The chamber receiving the vena cavae.
why: The SVC continues it upwards; the same chamber forms the right heart border on CXR.

q: What effect does the vagus have on heart rate?
model: It slows it (via M2 receptors on the SA node).
hint: Think of the effect of atropine, which blocks it.
why: Resting rate (60–80) is below the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100) because of vagal tone.

q: Which receptor mediates the sympathetic increase in contractility?
hint: The receptor that cardioselective beta-blockers target.
why: β1 stimulation raises cAMP, increasing calcium entry and contractility; beta-blockers act here.

q: Does the vagus significantly affect ventricular contractility?
model: No: its effect on contractility is mainly in the atria.
hint: Think about where parasympathetic fibres actually reach.
why: Parasympathetic fibres richly supply the nodes and atria but sparsely the ventricles.

q: Which two kinds of autonomic fibres does the cardiac plexus contain?
hint: Both arms of the autonomic system.
why: Sympathetic cardiac nerves come from the cervical and upper thoracic ganglia; parasympathetic from vagal cardiac branches.

q: Where does the deep part of the cardiac plexus lie?
model: In front of the tracheal bifurcation, behind the aortic arch.
hint: In front of where the windpipe divides.
why: The superficial part lies below the arch; fibres spread along the coronary arteries.

q: Through which spinal segments do cardiac pain fibres enter?
why: They travel with sympathetic nerves; somatic fibres from the chest wall and inner arm enter the same segments.

q: Why is cardiac pain felt in the medial arm?
acc: t1 / t2 / intercostobrachial / dermatome / same segment
model: Cardiac afferents share the T1–T2 segments that supply the inner arm.
hint: Which spinal segments supply the skin of the inner arm?
why: The brain can't separate visceral from somatic input at the same segment and projects it to the familiar skin area.

q: Why may diabetics have a silent MI?
model: Autonomic neuropathy damages the visceral pain fibres.
why: Without the afferents travelling with sympathetic nerves, ischaemic pain isn't felt.

q: Around which structure does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hook?
acc: arch of the aorta / aortic arch / aorta / ligamentum arteriosum
model: The arch of the aorta (beside the ligamentum arteriosum).
hint: The great vessel arching to the left.
why: Its long thoracic course explains hoarseness with lung cancer, aortic aneurysm or mediastinal nodes.

q: Around which artery does the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hook?
hint: An artery heading to the arm.
why: It loops up much higher than the left, so it has a shorter course.

q: Which laryngeal muscle is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
hint: It tilts the thyroid cartilage to tense the cords.
why: All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

q: Which chamber forms the right heart border on a chest X-ray?
hint: The chamber the vena cavae open into.
why: The SVC forms the upper part; the silhouette is lost when the right middle lobe is consolidated.

q: Loss of the right heart border on CXR suggests disease in which lobe?
hint: The lobe only the right lung has.
why: The middle lobe touches the right atrium; consolidation removes the air–soft tissue interface (silhouette sign).

q: Which chamber forms most of the left heart border on CXR?
hint: The chamber with the thickest wall.
why: Above it lie the left atrial appendage, pulmonary trunk and aortic knuckle.

q: Why can't heart size be judged on an AP chest film?
model: The heart is further from the detector, so it is magnified.
hint: Think about how far the heart is from the detector.
why: In a PA film the heart is against the detector; AP films are usually taken on unwell patients at the bedside.

q: In a PA film, where does the X-ray beam enter?
hint: Read the letters of PA in order.
why: The detector sits against the front of the chest, close to the heart.

q: What is the normal upper limit of the cardiothoracic ratio?
why: Heart width ÷ internal thoracic width on a PA film; above 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.

q: How is the heart width measured for the cardiothoracic ratio?
model: Widest horizontal heart diameter: midline to right border plus midline to left border.
hint: Add two measurements from the centre line.
why: The two sides are measured separately from the midline because the heart lies asymmetrically.

q: In the spinal cord, what does "dorsal" mean?
why: In the cord and brainstem dorsal = posterior, but in the cerebrum it means superior because of the bend at the midbrain.

q: In the cerebrum, what does "rostral" mean?
why: The neuraxis bends about 90° at the midbrain–diencephalon junction, so rostral points forwards in the forebrain but upwards in the cord.

q: Where is grey matter in the spinal cord?
model: In the centre (H-shaped), with white matter around it.
why: In the brain it is the opposite: cortex outside, white matter inside.

q: What makes white matter white?
why: Myelin is lipid-rich, so tracts of myelinated axons look pale; grey matter is mainly cell bodies and synapses.

q: Which spinal cord horn contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons?
why: That's why sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar.

q: Which structure connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
hint: A thick white band in the midline.
why: It is the largest commissure; cutting it produces split-brain effects.

q: What relays all sensations except smell to the cortex?
hint: Paired nuclei either side of the third ventricle.
why: Smell reaches the olfactory cortex directly; all other sensory pathways synapse in the thalamus.

q: Which brain region controls temperature, thirst and the pituitary?
why: It sits below the thalamus in the floor of the third ventricle, connected to the pituitary by the infundibulum.

q: Which part of the brainstem contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centres and the pyramids?
hint: The lowest part of the brainstem.
why: It also holds the nuclei of IX–XII and is continuous with the cord at the foramen magnum.

q: Which channel connects the 3rd and 4th ventricles?
hint: A narrow channel through the midbrain.
why: It runs through the midbrain; blockage causes obstructive hydrocephalus.

q: Where is CSF made?
hint: Tufts of capillaries in the ventricles.
why: About 500 mL a day is produced, mainly in the lateral ventricles, and absorbed into the venous sinuses via arachnoid granulations.

q: Where are the cell bodies of sensory neurons in a spinal nerve?
hint: A swelling on the back root.
why: They are pseudounipolar: one process to the periphery, one into the dorsal horn.

q: Which ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve becomes the intercostal nerve?
why: The dorsal ramus supplies the back muscles and skin.

q: Which rami communicantes exist only from T1 to L2?
why: They carry preganglionic sympathetic fibres from the lateral horn; grey rami return postganglionic fibres to every spinal nerve.

q: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
why: There are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae because C1–7 exit above their vertebrae.

q: What induces the ectoderm to form the neural plate?
hint: A rod of mesoderm along the embryo's axis.
why: It signals (e.g. sonic hedgehog) to the overlying ectoderm; this is induction.

q: Name two derivatives of the neural crest.
acc: dorsal root / schwann / adrenal medulla / melanocyte / autonomic ganglia / enteric
model: Dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, enteric neurons.
hint: Think of peripheral nervous structures and pigment cells.
why: Neural crest cells leave the edges of the neural folds and migrate widely; Hirschsprung's disease is a failure of their migration to the gut.

q: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close causes what?
why: The caudal neuropore closes around day 28; folic acid before conception lowers the risk.

q: Which secondary brain vesicle becomes the thalamus and hypothalamus?
why: The telencephalon makes the hemispheres; the diencephalon also gives the retina and optic nerve.

q: Which secondary vesicle becomes the pons and cerebellum?
hint: The front part of the hindbrain.
why: The rhombencephalon splits into metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla).

q: Which lobe contains the primary motor cortex?
hint: In front of the central sulcus.
why: The precentral gyrus lies just in front of the central sulcus.

q: Which lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
model: The occipital lobe (around the calcarine sulcus).
why: Damage gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

q: Where is Broca's area?
model: The inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) frontal lobe.
hint: Low down, just in front of the motor cortex for the face.
why: Damage gives expressive aphasia: halting speech with relatively good comprehension.

q: Where is Wernicke's area?
model: The superior temporal gyrus of the dominant temporal lobe.
why: Damage gives receptive aphasia: fluent speech without sense and poor comprehension.

q: Which sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes?
why: Motor cortex lies in front of it and somatosensory cortex behind.

q: Which cells myelinate axons in the CNS?
why: One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many axons; Schwann cells do this in the PNS (one per segment).

q: Which spinal levels give sympathetic outflow?
why: Preganglionic neurons sit in the lateral horn only at these levels.

q: Name the four cranial nerves with parasympathetic outflow.
acc: iii / 3 / oculomotor + vii / 7 / facial + ix / 9 / glossopharyngeal + x / 10 / vagus
model: III, VII, IX and X (plus S2–4 from the sacral cord).
why: Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral.

q: Is the knee-jerk reflex monosynaptic or polysynaptic?
why: The Ia afferent from the muscle spindle synapses directly on the α motor neuron of the same muscle.

q: Brisk reflexes suggest an upper or lower motor neuron lesion?
why: Loss of descending inhibition makes the reflex arc overactive; LMN lesions reduce or abolish reflexes.

q: Name the receptor that starts the stretch reflex.
hint: An encapsulated sensor within the muscle belly.
why: Stretching it fires Ia afferents, which excite the α motor neurons of the same muscle.

q: What is the root value of the biceps reflex?
why: "5, 6 pick up sticks". Brachioradialis is also C5–6.

q: What is the root value of the triceps reflex?
why: "7, 8 lay them straight".

q: What is the root value of the knee reflex?
why: "3, 4 kick the door". The femoral nerve carries it to quadriceps.

q: What is the root value of the ankle reflex?
why: "1, 2 buckle my shoe". An S1 disc prolapse often abolishes it.

q: Where does fertilisation usually happen?
model: In the ampulla of the uterine tube.
hint: The widest part of the uterine tube.
why: It is the widest, longest part of the tube; implantation elsewhere in the tube causes ectopic pregnancy.

q: Which part of the blastocyst becomes the embryo?
why: The trophoblast forms the placenta and membranes.

q: Which trophoblast layer invades the endometrium and makes hCG?
hint: The layer with no cell boundaries.
why: It is a multinucleated layer without cell borders; hCG maintains the corpus luteum and is detected by pregnancy tests.

q: On which day does the primitive streak appear?
why: It marks the start of gastrulation and the body axis; epiblast cells move through it to form mesoderm and endoderm.

q: Which week is called the "week of twos"?
hint: Count what there are two of.
why: Two germ layers (epiblast, hypoblast), two cavities (amniotic, yolk sac) and two trophoblast layers.

q: What are the three germ layers formed in gastrulation?
why: All tissues derive from them; the epiblast gives rise to all three.

q: Which germ layer forms the nervous system?
why: The notochord induces it to become the neural plate around day 18.

q: Which weeks after fertilisation are the embryonic period?
hint: Starts with gastrulation, ends with all organs present.
why: All major organs form then, so teratogens cause major malformations.

q: How does gestational age differ from fertilisation age?
model: Gestational age is about 2 weeks more (counted from the last menstrual period).
hint: Think of when ovulation happens in the cycle.
why: The LMP is a date patients know; ovulation and fertilisation happen about 2 weeks later.

q: What does "all or none" refer to in early development?
acc: first two weeks / 2 weeks / weeks 1 / pre embryonic / preembryonic
model: Teratogen exposure in the first 2 weeks either kills the embryo or has no effect.
why: Cells are still interchangeable, so surviving cells can replace damaged ones.

q: What is induction in development?
model: One tissue signalling to another to change its fate.
hint: Think of the notochord and the neural plate.
why: The notochord inducing the neural plate is the classic example.

q: Which process separates the fingers?
why: Cells between the digit rays die; failure causes syndactyly.

q: Which renal anomaly has fused lower poles held low by the inferior mesenteric artery?
why: The fused lower poles catch under the IMA during ascent; it is prone to stones, infection and PUJ obstruction.

q: Bilateral renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios and which sequence?
hint: Named after the pathologist who described the flat face and small lungs.
why: No fetal urine means little amniotic fluid, so the lungs fail to grow and the face and limbs are compressed.

q: In a duplex kidney, which pole's ureter opens lower and more medially in the bladder?
why: It tends to obstruct or form a ureterocele; the lower-pole ureter opens higher and more laterally with a short tunnel, so it refluxes.

q: Urine leaking from a newborn's umbilicus suggests a patent remnant of which structure?
hint: It normally becomes the median umbilical ligament.
why: The urachus joins the bladder apex to the umbilicus and normally becomes the median umbilical ligament.

q: Name the three narrowings of the ureter where stones lodge.
acc: pelviureteric / pelvi ureteric / puj + brim + vesicoureteric / vesico ureteric / vuj
model: The pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the vesicoureteric junction.
hint: Top, middle and bottom of the ureter.
why: The VUJ is the narrowest; on X-ray the ureter runs over the transverse processes, the sacroiliac joint and the ischial spine.

q: Beside the cervix, the ureter passes under which artery?
model: The uterine artery ("water under the bridge").
why: The ureter can be clamped or tied with the uterine artery at hysterectomy.

q: In a man, which tube crosses over the ureter just before it enters the bladder?
hint: It carries sperm from the epididymis.
why: It plays the same role as the uterine artery in women, crossing above the ureter near the bladder.

q: Ureteric colic spreads from the loin towards where?
acc: groin / scrotum / testis / testicle / labia / labium
why: Ureteric afferents enter at T11–L2; the genitofemoral nerve (L1–2) shares those segments, so the pain spreads to the genitals.

q: What is the standard imaging test for suspected renal colic?
hint: A low-dose scan of kidneys, ureters and bladder, no dye.
why: Almost all stones show on low-dose CT; ultrasound is used in pregnancy and children.

q: What is the emergency when infection builds up above an obstructing ureteric stone?
hint: It needs urgent nephrostomy or a stent.
why: Antibiotics can't clear trapped pus, so it needs urgent drainage by nephrostomy or ureteric stent.

q: Which zone of the prostate enlarges in BPH?
hint: The zone around the urethra, not the peripheral zone.
why: It surrounds the prostatic urethra, so growth obstructs flow; cancer usually arises in the peripheral zone, which is felt on DRE.

q: Painless retention with overflow incontinence and bilateral hydronephrosis: acute or chronic retention?
why: The bladder stretches slowly, so it doesn't hurt, and the back pressure damages both kidneys.

q: Give a voiding symptom of bladder outlet obstruction.
acc: hesitan / poor stream / weak stream / poor flow / weak flow / straining / strain / dribbl / incomplete / intermitten / terminal
model: Hesitancy, poor stream, straining, terminal dribbling or incomplete emptying.
hint: A problem with starting, flow or finishing.
why: Storage symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia) come from the irritable, thickened detrusor rather than the obstruction itself.

q: Where do collecting ducts empty urine into a minor calyx?
why: Urine then passes minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.

q: What stops urine refluxing from the bladder into the ureter?
model: The ureter's oblique path through the bladder wall acts as a flap valve.
hint: Think about the angle the ureter takes through the bladder wall.
why: Bladder pressure squashes the ureter shut as it fills; a short tunnel causes vesicoureteric reflux.

q: On a plain X-ray, the abdominal ureter runs over the tips of which bony features?
hint: Bony projections sticking out sideways from the lumbar vertebrae.
why: It then crosses the sacroiliac joint and heads to the ischial spine, which is where stones are looked for.

q: What is the smooth triangular area inside the base of the bladder called?
why: Its corners are the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; unlike the rest of the lining, it doesn't fold or stretch.

q: Which openings form the three corners of the trigone?
model: The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
why: Inflammation here (trigonitis) gives intense urgency.

q: Which surface of the bladder is covered by peritoneum?
why: A filling bladder rises above the pubis and peels peritoneum off the anterior abdominal wall, so a suprapubic catheter can avoid the peritoneal cavity.

q: Rupture of the bladder dome after a blow to a full bladder is intraperitoneal or extraperitoneal?
why: The dome is covered by peritoneum, so urine leaks into the peritoneal cavity; pelvic fractures usually tear the bladder extraperitoneally.

q: Which nerves carry parasympathetic supply to the detrusor?
hint: They arise from the sacral cord.
why: They contract the detrusor via M3 receptors and relax the internal sphincter, causing voiding.

q: Which nerve supplies the external urethral sphincter?
hint: It also supplies the perineum and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
why: It gives voluntary control; stretching it in childbirth contributes to stress incontinence.

q: Sympathetic fibres relax the detrusor during filling through which receptor?
why: Mirabegron, a β3 agonist, treats overactive bladder; α1 receptors contract the bladder neck.

q: Where is the centre that coordinates detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation?
why: Spinal cord lesions above the sacral cord cut it off, giving detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia.

q: What sort of bladder does a cauda equina lesion cause?
acc: atonic / flaccid / painless retention / overflow / areflexi
model: An atonic bladder with painless retention and overflow incontinence.
hint: The sacral reflex arc is cut.
why: The sacral reflex arc is broken, so the detrusor can't contract.

q: Which part of the male urethra is shortest and least distensible?
hint: The part passing through the deep perineal pouch.
why: It passes through the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch and is easily torn in pelvic fractures.

q: Which part of the male urethra is the longest?
why: It runs in the corpus spongiosum to the external meatus; the bulbourethral glands open into it.

q: Which way should the penis be held during male catheterisation?
hint: Straighten the bend in the urethra.
why: This straightens the urethra's curve; resistance is expected at the external sphincter and prostate, and the balloon is inflated only once urine drains.

q: Why are UTIs more common in women?
model: The female urethra is short (about 4 cm).
hint: Compare its length with the male urethra.
why: Bacteria from the perineum have less distance to travel to the bladder.

q: Which artery supplies the embryonic midgut?
hint: It arises from the aorta at L1.
why: The midgut runs from the major duodenal papilla to two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.

q: Pain from midgut organs is felt in which region?
why: Visceral afferents follow the SMA's sympathetic supply into T10, the dermatome of the umbilicus; early appendicitis pain starts here.

q: Through how many degrees does the midgut rotate around the SMA?
hint: Three quarters of a full turn.
why: 90° while herniated and 180° on returning; incomplete rotation (malrotation) predisposes to volvulus.

q: In which week does the midgut herniate into the umbilical cord?
why: It grows faster than the abdominal cavity and returns by week 10.

q: The stomach rotates 90° around its long axis. Where does the left vagus end up?
hint: The left side of the stomach turns to face this way.
why: The rotation also creates the lesser sac behind the stomach.

q: Failure of duodenal recanalisation gives which X-ray sign?
why: Gas fills the stomach and proximal duodenum only; duodenal atresia is linked with Down syndrome.

q: Which pancreatic bud forms the uncinate process?
hint: The bud that travels with the bile duct.
why: It swings behind the duodenum with the bile duct to fuse with the dorsal bud; if it encircles the duodenum it forms an annular pancreas.

q: Failure of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse gives what?
why: Most secretion then drains through the small minor papilla, which may predispose to pancreatitis.

q: Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of which embryonic duct?
hint: It joins the midgut to the yolk sac.
why: Rule of 2s: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 tissue types; ectopic gastric mucosa can bleed.

q: What divides the cloaca into the urogenital sinus and anorectal canal?
hint: A partition between the urinary and rectal parts.
why: Problems with it cause anorectal malformations such as imperforate anus and fistulas.

q: Which line in the anal canal marks where hindgut endoderm meets ectoderm?
why: Above it: IMA, portal drainage and painless visceral nerves; below it: pudendal vessels and painful somatic nerves.

q: Which abdominal wall defect has the gut covered by a membranous sac?
why: The midgut fails to return through the umbilical ring and other anomalies are common; gastroschisis has no sac and lies beside the umbilicus.

q: Which embryonic mesentery forms the lesser omentum and falciform ligament?
why: Only the foregut has one, and the liver grows into it; the dorsal mesentery forms the greater omentum.

q: Malrotation puts a newborn at risk of what surgical emergency?
why: A narrow mesenteric base lets the bowel twist around the SMA; bilious vomiting in a newborn needs an urgent contrast study.

q: Which ligament holds the radial head against the ulna?
why: It forms a ring with the radial notch; in toddlers the head can slip out of it ("pulled elbow").

q: Which structure binds the distal radius and ulna and keeps the ulna off the carpus?
hint: A disc of fibrocartilage on the ulnar side.
why: Tears cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and an unstable distal radioulnar joint.

q: What type of synovial joint are the radioulnar joints?
why: The radius rotates around the ulna on an axis through both heads in pronation and supination.

q: Which is the strongest supinator of the forearm?
why: It works best with the elbow flexed (screwdriver action), so supination is stronger than pronation.

q: Name the two pronator muscles.
why: Pronator teres is supplied by the median nerve, pronator quadratus by its anterior interosseous branch.

q: Which nerve supplies supinator?
model: The deep branch of the radial nerve (posterior interosseous).
why: It passes through supinator, where it can be compressed.

q: What type of synovial joint is the radiocarpal (wrist) joint?
why: It allows flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation but no rotation.

q: Which nerve supplies all the wrist extensors?
hint: Damaged in a midshaft humerus fracture.
why: Radial palsy gives wrist drop and a weak grip.

q: Which two muscles produce ulnar deviation at the wrist?
acc: fcu / flexor carpi ulnaris + ecu / extensor carpi ulnaris
hint: A flexor and an extensor on the medial side.
why: A flexor and an extensor on the same side work together; ulnar deviation has the greater range.

q: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
why: Compression gives tingling in the lateral 3½ digits, thenar wasting and weak abductor pollicis brevis.

q: How many tendons pass through the carpal tunnel?
why: FCR runs in its own split in the retinaculum.

q: Why is palm sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
acc: palmar cutaneous / palmar branch / superficial / outside / before / above / proximal
model: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves above the wrist and runs superficial to the retinaculum.
hint: The branch to the palm skin takes a different route.
why: Numb palm skin points to a lesion higher up the median nerve.

q: Which tendons are inflamed in de Quervain's tenosynovitis?
acc: apl / abductor pollicis longus + epb / extensor pollicis brevis
why: Finkelstein's test (ulnar deviation with the thumb tucked in) is painful.

q: Infection in which digit's flexor sheath can spread into the ulnar bursa?
hint: The thumb's sheath joins the radial bursa instead.
why: Its sheath joins the ulnar bursa, while the thumb's joins the radial bursa; the two bursae can connect (horseshoe abscess).

q: The blood supply of which carpal bone enters distally, putting its proximal pole at risk of avascular necrosis?
hint: Tender in the snuffbox after a fall.
why: A waist fracture cuts off the proximal pole, causing non-union and arthritis.

q: Which nerve is at risk when the lunate dislocates forwards?
hint: It runs through the carpal tunnel.
why: The lunate is pushed into the carpal tunnel, causing acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

q: A supracondylar humerus fracture in a child can compress which artery?
hint: The continuation of the axillary artery.
why: Ischaemia of the forearm flexors leads to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

q: Which tendon can rupture weeks after a distal radius fracture?
why: It turns round Lister's tubercle and frays at the fracture, so the thumb can't be extended.

q: Which dermatome covers the middle finger?
hint: Between the thumb and little finger roots.
why: Thumb C6, middle finger C7, little finger C8.

q: Which dermatome covers the thumb?
hint: The root also tested by the brachioradialis reflex.
why: A C6 root lesion also weakens elbow flexion and reduces the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes.

q: Which dermatome covers the little finger?
why: Ulnar nerve lesions also affect the little finger, but C8 extends up the medial forearm.

q: Which dermatome covers the medial side of the elbow and forearm?
why: T2 covers the axilla and upper medial arm.

q: Which root is tested by finger abduction?
hint: The lowest root of the brachial plexus.
why: The interossei are supplied by the ulnar nerve from T1 (C8).

q: Opposition of the thumb combines which three movements?
hint: Bring the thumb pulp to the little finger pulp.
