why: It brings the thumb pulp onto the finger pulps, needed for a precision grip.

q: At which joint does most thumb movement happen?
hint: Between the trapezium and the 1st metacarpal.
why: Its saddle shape allows movement in two planes plus opposition; it is a common site of osteoarthritis.

q: Thumb abduction moves the thumb in which direction relative to the palm?
acc: right angle / perpendicular / 90 / forward / anterior / away from the palm
model: At right angles to the palm (forwards).
hint: The thumbnail faces sideways, so its planes are rotated.
why: The thumb's movement planes are rotated 90° compared with the fingers'.

q: Which muscle is the only flexor of the DIP joints?
why: Test it by holding the PIP straight and asking the patient to bend the fingertip.

q: Which muscle flexes the PIP joints and is tested by holding the other fingers straight?
hint: Its tendons split around the deeper tendons.
why: Holding the other fingers straight blocks FDP, which shares a muscle belly.

q: Which muscles flex the MCP joints while extending the IP joints?
hint: Worm-shaped muscles arising from the FDP tendons.
why: They insert into the extensor expansions; loss gives the claw hand.

q: Which nerve supplies the thenar muscles (APB, FPB, opponens pollicis)?
model: The recurrent branch of the median nerve.
why: It is superficial at the base of the thenar eminence, so it is easily cut.

q: Which muscle is weak when Froment's sign is positive?
hint: The thumb muscle supplied by the deep ulnar nerve.
why: With ulnar palsy the patient grips paper by flexing the thumb IP joint with FPL (median nerve) instead of adducting.

q: Dorsal interossei abduct the fingers. What do the palmar interossei do?
why: PAD (palmar adduct) and DAB (dorsal abduct); both are ulnar-supplied.

q: Which grip clamps an object between the flexed fingers and palm, with the thumb wrapped over?
why: Long flexors and interossei grip while the wrist extensors hold the wrist extended.

q: Which grip is lost most in median nerve palsy?
why: The median nerve supplies opponens pollicis, APB and FPB, so pulp-to-pulp opposition fails.

q: Which grip uses fingers flexed at the IP joints without the thumb, as in carrying a bag?
why: Only FDS and FDP are needed, so it survives some nerve lesions.

q: Which arterial arch in the palm lies just deep to the palmar aponeurosis?
hint: The more distal of the two arches.
why: It lies over the flexor tendons; the deep arch is about 1 cm more proximal, on the metacarpal bases.

q: Thickening and contracture of the palmar aponeurosis is called what?
hint: It usually pulls the ring and little fingers bent.
why: It usually pulls the ring and little fingers into flexion at the MCP and PIP joints.

q: Which pulleys of the fibrous flexor sheath must be kept to prevent bowstringing?
why: They lie over the shafts of the proximal and middle phalanges.

q: Trigger finger occurs where the tendon catches at which pulley?
why: A nodule on the flexor tendon catches at the pulley's edge; a steroid injection or release of the pulley treats it.

q: Rupture of the extensor tendon at the DIP joint gives which deformity?
why: The fingertip droops and can't be straightened; treat with a splint holding the DIP extended.

q: Rupture of the central slip of the extensor expansion gives which deformity?
hint: The PIP pokes through the lateral bands.
why: The PIP pushes through between the lateral bands, which slip forwards.

q: Where does the central slip of the extensor expansion insert?
model: The base of the middle phalanx.
hint: The lateral bands go one bone further.
why: The lateral bands continue to the base of the distal phalanx.

q: Which muscle wastes visibly in the first web space on the back of the hand in ulnar palsy?
why: All the interossei are ulnar-supplied; the first is the most visible.

q: At the wrist, the radial pulse lies lateral to which tendon?
hint: A wrist flexor on the thumb side.
why: The artery lies on the distal radius here, so it is used for pulses and ABGs.

q: Where does the radial artery pass from the front of the wrist to the back?
hint: A hollow seen when the thumb is extended.
why: It then passes between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous to form the deep palmar arch.

q: Is the superficial branch of the radial nerve sensory, motor or mixed?
hint: It supplies the skin of the first web space only.
why: It supplies skin over the lateral dorsum of the hand and first web space; a tight cast causes numbness without weakness.

q: Which two carpal bones border Guyon's canal?
model: The pisiform and the hook of the hamate.
hint: A pea-shaped bone and the bone with a hook-like process.
why: The canal lies superficial to the flexor retinaculum and carries the ulnar nerve and artery into the hand.

q: At the wrist, on which side of the ulnar artery does the ulnar nerve lie?
why: The nerve lies nearest the pisiform and the FCU tendon.

q: Why is sensation on the back of the hand spared in an ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist?
acc: dorsal cutaneous / dorsal branch / above / proximal / before / higher
model: The dorsal cutaneous branch leaves about 5 cm above the wrist.
hint: Where does that branch come off the nerve?
why: So a lesion in Guyon's canal spares it, while one at the elbow does not.

q: Which branch of the ulnar nerve winds round the hook of hamate to supply the interossei?
why: It also supplies the hypothenar muscles, medial lumbricals and adductor pollicis.

q: Name the proximal row of carpal bones from lateral to medial.
why: Only the scaphoid and lunate articulate with the radius.

q: Name the distal row of carpal bones from lateral to medial.
why: The trapezium carries the thumb's saddle joint; the hamate's hook forms part of Guyon's canal.

q: Which carpal bone is fractured most often?
hint: It lies in the floor of the snuffbox.
why: Falls on the outstretched hand fracture its waist; early X-rays can miss it, so treat tenderness as a fracture.

q: A 5th metacarpal neck fracture from punching is called what?
why: Check for rotation: the fingers cross when flexed.

q: An intra-articular fracture of the base of the 1st metacarpal is called what?
why: APL pulls the shaft away, making it unstable.

q: Which carpal bone is a sesamoid in the FCU tendon?
why: It anchors the flexor retinaculum and borders Guyon's canal.

q: Which carpal bone has a hook?
why: The hook anchors the flexor retinaculum; fractures (golf, racquet sports) can injure the ulnar nerve.

q: Which is the largest carpal bone?
why: It sits centrally, articulates with the 3rd metacarpal and is the first to ossify.

q: Which carpal bone forms a saddle joint with the thumb metacarpal?
why: Osteoarthritis here is common and causes pain at the base of the thumb.

q: How many phalanges are in one hand?
why: The thumb has 2 and each finger has 3.

q: Which artery mainly forms the superficial palmar arch?
hint: It enters the hand through Guyon's canal.
why: The radial artery adds a small superficial branch.

q: Which artery mainly forms the deep palmar arch?
hint: It passes through the anatomical snuffbox first.
why: It enters the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous.

q: Which test checks collateral flow through the palmar arches before radial artery puncture?
hint: Compress both arteries and release one.
why: Compress both arteries, let the hand blanch, then release the ulnar; colour should return within about 10 seconds.

q: Which tendons form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox?
acc: apl / abductor pollicis longus + epb / extensor pollicis brevis
hint: The tendons of the first extensor compartment.
why: These are the same tendons inflamed in de Quervain's tenosynovitis.

q: Which tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox?
why: It hooks round Lister's tubercle on the back of the radius.

q: Which bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
hint: A boat-shaped bone and the bone the thumb sits on.
why: Tenderness here after a fall suggests a scaphoid fracture.

q: Which artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
hint: The pulse felt at the wrist.
why: It winds round the back of the wrist to reach the first web space.

q: Which glands opening posterolateral to the vaginal orifice can form cysts and abscesses?
hint: The female equivalent of the bulbourethral glands.
why: They lubricate the vestibule; a blocked duct forms a cyst at about 5 or 7 o'clock.

q: To which nodes does lymph from the vulva drain?
why: Vulval cancer spreads to the groin nodes first.

q: Which ligament passes through the inguinal canal to end in the labium majus?
model: The round ligament of the uterus.
why: It is a remnant of the gubernaculum and can cause groin pain in pregnancy as it stretches.

q: Which organ lies in front of the uterus, separated by a shallow pouch?
hint: It sits behind the pubic symphysis.
why: The vesicouterine pouch lies between them; the deep rectouterine pouch lies behind the uterus.

q: Describe the usual position of the uterus.
why: The cervix tilts forward on the vagina and the body bends forward on the cervix; about 20% are retroverted.

q: Which part of the uterine tube is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy?
hint: The widest part of the tube.
why: It is where fertilisation usually happens; a ruptured tubal ectopic is a surgical emergency.

q: Pain from the ovary can be referred to the medial thigh through which nerve?
hint: It runs along the pelvic side wall beside the ovary.
why: It runs on the lateral pelvic wall right beside the ovarian fossa.

q: Which part of the uterine tube carries the fimbriae?
why: The fimbriae sweep over the ovary to catch the oocyte.

q: From which vessel does the ovarian artery arise?
model: The abdominal aorta at about L2.
why: The ovary develops near the kidney, then descends, bringing its vessels in the suspensory ligament.

q: Into which vein does the left ovarian vein drain?
hint: Same as the left testicular vein.
why: The right ovarian vein drains straight into the IVC.

q: To which nodes does ovarian lymph drain?
hint: They follow the ovarian vessels back to their origin.
why: Lymph follows the ovarian vessels back to their origin near the kidneys, not to the pelvic nodes.

q: From which artery does the uterine artery arise?
model: The anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
hint: The main artery of the pelvis.
why: It crosses the ureter beside the cervix and joins the ovarian artery near the tube.

q: The uterine artery crosses over which structure about 2 cm lateral to the cervix?
why: The ureter can be clamped or tied with the uterine artery at hysterectomy.

q: Which double fold of peritoneum runs from the side of the uterus to the pelvic wall?
why: It contains the tube, the round ligament, the ligament of the ovary and the uterine vessels, with the ureter at its base.

q: The round ligament and the ligament of the ovary are remnants of which embryonic structure?
hint: In males it guides the testis down.
why: In males it guides the testis into the scrotum.

q: Name the three cervical ligaments formed from endopelvic fascia.
acc: cardinal / transverse cervical + uterosacral / utero sacral + pubocervical / pubo cervical
model: Cardinal (transverse cervical), uterosacral and pubocervical ligaments.
hint: A lateral, a posterior and an anterior one.
why: Together with levator ani they hold the cervix and upper vagina up.

q: What are the most important supports of the uterus?
acc: levator / pelvic floor / pelvic diaphragm + fascia / cardinal / uterosacral
model: Levator ani and the endopelvic fascia (cardinal and uterosacral ligaments).
hint: A muscle sheet and condensed connective tissue.
why: Damage to these in childbirth leads to prolapse.

q: Which two ligaments are NOT important supports of the uterus?
hint: One named after a shape, one after a width.
why: The round ligament helps keep the uterus anteverted but bears little load.

q: Give a consequence of pelvic floor damage in childbirth.
model: Uterovaginal prolapse, cystocele, rectocele or stress incontinence.
why: Levator ani tears, pudendal nerve stretch and fascial damage weaken support; menopause makes it worse.

q: Which part of the uterus forms in the 3rd trimester and is the usual site of a caesarean incision?
why: It forms from the isthmus, is thin and less vascular, and heals with a lower risk of rupture in later pregnancies.

q: Where in the cervix do CIN and cervical cancer arise?
hint: The area sampled at a smear test.
why: HPV infects the metaplastic cells there; screening samples this area.

q: At about how many weeks is the uterine fundus level with the umbilicus?
why: It reaches the pubic symphysis at ~12 weeks and the xiphisternum at ~36 weeks.

q: Which vaginal fornix is the deepest?
hint: It lies next to the pouch of Douglas.
why: It lies next to the rectouterine pouch, which can be reached through it.

q: To which nodes does lymph from the upper vagina drain?
model: The internal and external iliac nodes.
why: Below the hymen, lymph goes to the superficial inguinal nodes.

q: To which nodes does lymph from the vagina below the hymen drain?
hint: The same nodes as the vulva.
why: The upper vagina drains to the iliac nodes instead.

q: Which nerve gives somatic sensation to the lower vagina?
why: The upper vagina has visceral nerves only and is relatively insensitive to touch.

q: The glans clitoridis and glans penis both develop from which embryonic structure?
hint: The midline swelling in front of the cloacal membrane.
why: DHT drives it to form the penis; without it, it forms the clitoris.

q: Which female structure corresponds to the bulb of the penis?
hint: Erectile tissue on either side of the vestibule.
why: Both are covered by bulbospongiosus; the clitoris itself has no corpus spongiosum or urethra.

q: Which female structure corresponds to the scrotum?
why: Both come from the labioscrotal swellings.

q: The superficial perineal pouch lies between which two layers?
acc: perineal membrane + colles / superficial perineal fascia
model: Between the perineal membrane and the superficial perineal (Colles') fascia.
hint: A membrane above and a fascia below.
why: The deep pouch lies above the perineal membrane and holds the external urethral sphincter.

q: Which muscle covers the crura of the clitoris?
hint: Named after a bone and the erectile tissue.
why: It holds blood in the erectile tissue; bulbospongiosus covers the vestibular bulbs.

q: Which glands lie in the female superficial perineal pouch?
hint: They sit at the back of the vestibular bulbs.
why: They sit at the back of the vestibular bulbs and open into the vestibule.

q: Which nerves make the clitoris and vestibular bulbs engorge?
model: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4), via the cavernous nerves.
why: They release nitric oxide, relaxing the smooth muscle so the erectile tissue fills with blood.

q: Which signalling molecule relaxes the smooth muscle of erectile tissue?
why: It raises cGMP; sildenafil blocks PDE5, which breaks cGMP down.

q: Which nerve carries sensation from the clitoris?
model: The dorsal nerve of the clitoris, a branch of the pudendal nerve.
hint: Its parent nerve comes from S2–4 and supplies the external sphincters.
why: It carries the afferent side of the arousal reflex; the pudendal nerve also supplies bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus.

q: Which tibial landmark receives the patellar ligament?
why: Repeated pulling in adolescents causes Osgood–Schlatter disease.

q: Which surface of the tibia lies directly under the skin?
model: The medial surface (with the anterior border).
why: With no muscle cover, tibial fractures are often open and heal slowly.

q: Which prominence on the lateral tibial condyle receives the iliotibial tract?
why: Iliotibial band syndrome causes pain on the lateral knee near it.

q: Which nerve winds round the neck of the fibula?
why: Fractures, tight casts or crossing the legs can damage it, causing foot drop.

q: Which malleolus extends further down?
why: It forms the outer wall of the ankle mortise and blocks eversion, so inversion sprains are more common.

q: The Weber classification grades ankle fractures by the level of which bone's fracture?
model: The fibula, relative to the syndesmosis.
hint: The lateral malleolus belongs to this bone.
why: A below, B at, C above the syndesmosis; higher fractures are more likely to be unstable.

q: What type of joint is the inferior tibiofibular joint?
hint: Bones held by ligament and membrane, with slight movement.
why: It holds the ankle mortise together; injury is a "high ankle sprain".

q: The patella is the largest example of which type of bone?
why: It develops in the quadriceps tendon and lengthens the quadriceps lever arm.

q: Which patellar facet is larger?
hint: It matches the more prominent femoral condyle.
why: It matches the more prominent lateral femoral condyle, which helps stop the patella dislocating laterally.

q: Which muscle resists lateral dislocation of the patella?
hint: The lowest fibres of one part of quadriceps.
why: Its lowest fibres pull the patella medially; it wastes quickly after knee injury.

q: In the last degrees of knee extension, which way does the femur rotate on the fixed tibia?
why: The medial condyle's surface is longer, so the femur turns as it finishes extending; the ligaments tighten and the knee locks.

q: Which muscle unlocks the knee?
hint: It lies in the floor of the popliteal fossa.
why: It laterally rotates the femur on the tibia so flexion can begin.

q: What type of synovial joint is the knee?
hint: Mainly bends one way, with a little rotation.
why: It mainly flexes and extends but allows some rotation when flexed.

q: Which ligament stops the tibia sliding forwards on the femur?
why: It is tested with Lachman's and the anterior drawer test.

q: Which ligament is tested with the posterior sag sign?
why: It is torn in dashboard injuries, where the tibia is pushed backwards.

q: Which meniscus is torn more often?
hint: Attached to the tibial collateral ligament.
why: It is attached to the MCL, so it can't move out of the way when twisted.

q: Which collateral ligament resists a valgus force?
hint: A blow to the outside of the knee stretches it.
why: A blow to the outside of the knee opens the medial side.

q: Name the "unhappy triad" of knee injury.
acc: acl / anterior cruciate + mcl / medial collateral / tibial collateral + medial meniscus
hint: A cruciate, a collateral and a meniscus.
why: A valgus and rotational blow to the planted leg (e.g. a tackle) tears all three.

q: Which nerve supplies quadriceps femoris?
why: Femoral nerve damage stops knee extension and abolishes the knee jerk.

q: Which nerve supplies the hamstrings?
model: The sciatic nerve (mainly its tibial part).
hint: The largest nerve in the body.
why: Only the short head of biceps femoris is from the common fibular part.

q: Which three muscles insert at the pes anserinus?
why: Each is from a different compartment and nerve (femoral, obturator, sciatic); bursitis here causes medial knee pain.

q: Which hamstring is the only lateral rotator of the flexed knee?
hint: It inserts on the fibular head.
why: The other hamstrings insert medially and rotate the knee medially.

q: Which part of quadriceps also flexes the hip?
hint: The only part arising from the AIIS.
why: It arises from the AIIS, so it crosses both the hip and the knee.

q: Which muscle group is the most important dynamic stabiliser of the knee?
why: Rehabilitation after knee injury focuses on strengthening it.

q: Why does the knee rely on soft tissues for stability?
acc: flat / shallow / poor bony / incongruent / congruen
model: The tibial plateaus are flat, so the bones fit together poorly.
hint: Look at the shape of the tibial plateaus.
why: Ligaments, menisci and muscles make up for the poor bony fit.

q: A knee dislocation is limb-threatening because of injury to which artery?
hint: Tethered above and below the knee.
why: It is tethered above and below the knee, so check pulses and ABPI in every dislocation.

q: A Baker's cyst arises from the bursa between which two muscles?
hint: A hamstring and a calf muscle.
why: It connects with the joint, so an effusion fills it; rupture mimics DVT.

q: Swelling of which bursa causes "housemaid's knee"?
why: Repeated kneeling irritates it; the superficial infrapatellar bursa gives "clergyman's knee".

q: Which bursa communicates with the knee joint and fills with an effusion?
why: Fluid pushed down from it lifts the patella (patellar tap).

q: What is bleeding into the knee joint after injury called?
why: Swelling within ~2 hours suggests an ACL tear or a fracture; slower swelling suggests a meniscal tear.

q: Which is the deepest of the main structures in the popliteal fossa?
hint: Felt deep with the knee flexed.
why: It lies on the femur and capsule, so its pulse is felt deeply with the knee flexed.

q: Which is the most superficial of the main neurovascular structures in the popliteal fossa?
hint: The larger branch of the sciatic nerve.
why: From superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.

q: Which muscle forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa?
hint: Its tendon runs to the fibular head.
why: Semimembranosus and semitendinosus form the superomedial boundary; the gastrocnemius heads form the inferior boundaries.

q: Which is the commonest peripheral arterial aneurysm?
hint: A pulsatile mass behind the knee.
why: It is often bilateral and linked with abdominal aortic aneurysm; it can thrombose and threaten the leg.

q: Which is more mobile but less stable: the shoulder or the hip?
hint: The one with the shallow socket.
why: Its shallow glenoid gives a large range but little bony stability, so it dislocates more often.

q: Give an example of a primary cartilaginous joint.
acc: growth plate / epiphyseal / sternocostal / synchondrosis / spheno occipital
model: A growth plate (or the 1st sternocostal joint).
hint: Temporary hyaline cartilage joints in growing bones.
why: Primary cartilaginous joints use hyaline cartilage and are usually temporary.

q: What type of joint is the pubic symphysis?
hint: The same type as an intervertebral disc.
why: Secondary cartilaginous joints are midline and allow slight movement, like the intervertebral discs.

q: A tooth in its socket is which type of fibrous joint?
why: The periodontal ligament holds the tooth.

q: Give an example of a synovial pivot joint.
acc: atlantoaxial / atlanto axial / radioulnar / radio ulnar
model: The atlantoaxial or proximal radioulnar joint.
hint: One bone rotates within a ring.
why: One bone rotates within a ring of bone and ligament.

q: Which law says the nerves to the muscles moving a joint also supply the joint and its overlying skin?
why: It explains referred joint pain, e.g. hip disease felt in the knee.

q: What type of cartilage covers synovial joint surfaces?
why: It is smooth and low-friction but avascular and slow to heal.

q: How is articular cartilage nourished?
why: It has no blood vessels, so it heals poorly; joint movement helps pump nutrients in.

q: Why can hip disease cause knee pain?
acc: obturator / femoral / shared / same nerve / both
model: The obturator and femoral nerves supply both joints.
hint: Think about which nerves supply each joint.
why: Always examine the hip in a child with knee pain (e.g. slipped capital femoral epiphysis).

q: What is a bursa?
model: A closed, synovial-lined sac of fluid that reduces friction.
hint: A cushion where tendon rubs over bone.
why: Bursae sit where tendon, muscle or skin moves over bone; overuse or infection causes bursitis.

q: What type of tissue makes up ligaments?
model: Dense regular connective tissue (type I collagen).
why: Parallel collagen fibres resist tension in one direction.

q: Why do ligaments heal slowly?
model: They have a poor blood supply.
why: Few cells and vessels mean slow repair, and healed ligaments may stay lax.

q: Which synoviocytes make hyaluronan and lubricin?
why: Type A cells are macrophage-like and remove debris.

q: Which molecule gives synovial fluid its viscosity?
hint: A glycosaminoglycan injected into osteoarthritic knees.
why: Lubricin gives boundary lubrication; both are made by type B synoviocytes.

q: Why can bacteria enter a joint through the synovium easily?
model: The synovium has no basement membrane and its capillaries are fenestrated.
hint: Look at what's missing beneath the lining cells.
why: This allows fast exchange to nourish cartilage but also lets bacteria and inflammatory cells in.

q: Which growth plate zone is responsible for lengthening the bone?
why: Chondrocytes divide there in columns, then enlarge, calcify and are replaced by bone.

q: In which type of ossification is a hyaline cartilage model replaced by bone?
hint: Long bones form this way, not the skull vault.
why: Long bones form this way; the skull vault and clavicle form by intramembranous ossification.

q: What tissue forms the soft callus in fracture healing?
hint: Laid down by chondroblasts after the haematoma.
why: It is replaced by woven bone (hard callus), then remodelled into lamellar bone.

q: Which hormone closes the growth plates after puberty?
hint: Even in males, it comes from aromatised testosterone.
why: This is why precocious puberty causes short adult height, in both sexes.

q: Which gene is mutated in achondroplasia?
why: Overactive FGFR3 slows chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate, causing short limbs.

q: On an axial CT brain viewed in the standard way, the patient's left is on which side of the screen?
hint: Images are viewed as if from the feet.
why: Axial images are viewed from the patient's feet, so left and right are reversed; check the L/R marker.

q: On an axial MRI of the spinal cord, is the top of the image dorsal or ventral?
hint: The top of the image is the front of the patient.
why: In the cord and brainstem dorsal means posterior; only in the forebrain does dorsal mean superior because of the cephalic flexure.

q: Is CSF bright or dark on a T2-weighted MRI?
why: "World War 2": water is white on T2; on T1 and CT CSF is dark.

q: Is fresh blood bright or dark on CT?
hint: Why CT is used first in a suspected bleed.
why: That is why CT is first-line for suspected haemorrhage and head injury.

q: Through which foramen does the mandibular nerve (V3) leave the skull?
hint: An oval opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid.
why: V1 leaves through the superior orbital fissure and V2 through the foramen rotundum.

q: Which cranial nerve leaves the back of the brainstem?
why: It is the only nerve to leave dorsally and the only one to cross before leaving; its long thin course makes it vulnerable to head injury.

q: An eye that is "down and out" with ptosis and a dilated pupil suggests a lesion of which nerve?
hint: It supplies most of the eye muscles.
why: Only lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) still work; a dilated pupil suggests compression, e.g. a PCom aneurysm.

q: Which way does the tongue deviate with a hypoglossal nerve lesion?
model: Towards the side of the lesion.
hint: The healthy side pushes it across.
why: The working genioglossus pushes the tongue across to the weak side.

q: Which way does the uvula deviate with a vagus nerve lesion?
acc: away / opposite / contralateral / healthy / normal side
model: Away from the side of the lesion.
hint: The working muscles on the other side win.
why: The working palatal muscles pull it towards the healthy side.

q: Through which foramen do IX, X and XI leave the skull?
hint: The sigmoid sinus leaves the skull here too.
why: A tumour here (jugular foramen syndrome) affects all three together.

q: Through which opening does the facial nerve leave the skull?
hint: Between the styloid and mastoid processes.
why: It enters through the internal acoustic meatus and runs in the facial canal before exiting to the parotid.

q: Which nerve palsy is a "false localising sign" of raised intracranial pressure?
why: Its long intracranial course means pressure anywhere can stretch it, so it doesn't point to where the lesion is.

q: Which part of the brainstem contains the substantia nigra and the cerebral aqueduct?
hint: The top part of the brainstem.
why: Loss of substantia nigra dopamine neurons causes Parkinson's disease.

q: Where do the corticospinal tracts decussate?
model: In the pyramids of the lower medulla.
hint: The lower end of the brainstem.
why: About 85–90% cross here to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

q: Occlusion of which artery causes the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome?
model: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (or vertebral artery).
hint: A cerebellar branch of the vertebral artery.
why: It gives same-side face and opposite-side body pain/temperature loss, Horner's, dysphagia, ataxia and vertigo.

q: A patient is conscious but can only move their eyes vertically and blink. Where is the lesion?
model: The ventral pons (basilar artery occlusion): locked-in syndrome.
hint: The bulging middle part of the brainstem.
why: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres are cut but the reticular activating system and vertical gaze centres in the midbrain are spared.

q: Herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum compresses which structure?
hint: The lowest part of the brainstem.
why: Its respiratory and cardiac centres fail, causing respiratory arrest ("coning").

q: Which cerebellar peduncle carries the main output of the cerebellum?
why: Output from the dentate nucleus goes to the opposite thalamus and red nucleus.

q: Which cerebellar peduncle carries input from the cerebral cortex via the pontine nuclei?
why: It is the largest peduncle; fibres cross in the pons to reach the opposite hemisphere.

q: Which is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus?
why: Lateral to medial: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial ("Don't Eat Greasy Food").

q: A cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes limb ataxia on which side?
why: The pathways cross twice, so each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body.

q: Truncal ataxia with a wide-based gait points to damage of which part of the cerebellum?
why: Alcohol classically damages the anterior vermis; hemisphere damage gives limb ataxia instead.

q: Which part of the internal capsule carries corticospinal fibres to the limbs?
why: A small lacunar infarct here causes a dense hemiplegia on the opposite side.

q: Which arteries supply the internal capsule and cause lacunar strokes?
model: The lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.
hint: Small deep branches of the MCA.
why: Small, deep end-arteries damaged by hypertension.

q: Which gyrus contains the primary motor cortex?
hint: Just in front of the central sulcus.
why: It lies in front of the central sulcus; the leg area is on the medial surface (ACA territory).

q: Which nucleus lies lateral to the internal capsule?
model: The lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus).
why: The caudate and thalamus lie medial to the internal capsule.

q: Which three bones fuse to form the acetabulum?
hint: The three parts of the hip bone.
why: They meet at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage, which fuses at about 15–17 years.

q: What type of synovial joint is the hip?
why: It moves in three planes, but the deep acetabulum makes it very stable.

q: What fibrocartilage rim deepens the acetabulum?
why: Tears cause groin pain and clicking, often with hip impingement.

q: Which is the strongest hip flexor?
hint: It inserts on the lesser trochanter.
why: It inserts on the lesser trochanter; the psoas sign (pain on hip extension) suggests retrocaecal appendicitis or psoas abscess.

q: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus?
hint: It leaves the pelvis above piriformis.
why: Damage gives a Trendelenburg gait.

q: Which nerve supplies gluteus maximus?
hint: It leaves the pelvis below piriformis.
why: Gluteus maximus is used for powerful extension, e.g. climbing stairs and rising from a chair.

q: Which nerve supplies the hip adductors?
hint: Named after the foramen it passes through.
why: The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve.

q: Name a lateral rotator of the hip.
acc: piriformis / obturator / gemell / quadratus femoris / gluteus maximus / maximus
model: Piriformis, obturator internus or externus, the gemelli, quadratus femoris or gluteus maximus.
hint: The short muscles deep in the buttock.
why: The short lateral rotators sit deep to gluteus maximus.

q: Which is the strongest ligament of the hip?
model: The iliofemoral ligament (Y ligament of Bigelow).
why: It runs from the AIIS to the intertrochanteric line and stops hyperextension.

q: When standing, the line of gravity falls in front of or behind the hip joint?
hint: Which way would the trunk fall without the ligaments?
why: Body weight pushes the hip into extension, so the iliofemoral ligament takes the load with little muscle work.

q: In which position is the hip most easily dislocated?
hint: Sitting in a car with the knees together.
why: A knee hitting the dashboard drives the femoral head out backwards, putting the sciatic nerve at risk.

q: Which artery is the main supply to the femoral head in adults?
why: Its retinacular branches run along the neck, so displaced intracapsular fractures cause avascular necrosis.

q: Where is the great saphenous vein found for a cut-down at the ankle?
model: About 1 cm in front of and above the medial malleolus.
hint: On the inner side of the ankle.
why: Its position there is constant even when the patient is shocked and veins are collapsed; the saphenous nerve lies with it.

q: Where is the femoral vein relative to the femoral artery?
why: Lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, Y-fronts (NAVY).

q: Where is the femoral artery pulse felt?
hint: Halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis.
why: Halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament.

q: Which nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis?
model: The superior gluteal nerve (with its vessels).
hint: It supplies gluteus medius and minimus.
why: Everything else passing through the greater sciatic foramen leaves below piriformis.

q: Which quadrant of the buttock is safe for intramuscular injection?
why: The sciatic nerve lies below a line from the PSIS to the greater trochanter.

q: The sciatic nerve runs midway between which two bony landmarks?
model: The greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity.
hint: One on the femur, one you sit on.
why: It lies deep to gluteus maximus before entering the back of the thigh.

q: What are the root values of the femoral and obturator nerves?
hint: The same three lumbar roots for both.
why: The femoral comes from the posterior divisions, the obturator from the anterior divisions.

q: What are the root values of the sciatic nerve?
hint: From the lower lumbar to the third sacral root.
why: It comes from the sacral plexus, which forms on piriformis.

q: In which muscle does the lumbar plexus form?
hint: A hip flexor on the posterior abdominal wall.
why: The femoral nerve emerges lateral to it and the obturator nerve medial to it.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the medial leg and foot?
hint: A branch of the femoral nerve.
why: It runs with the great saphenous vein and is at risk during vein harvest.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the 1st web space of the foot?
hint: A branch of the common fibular nerve.
why: It also supplies the anterior compartment (dorsiflexors).

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the lateral side of the foot?
why: It runs with the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus; it is used for nerve grafts and biopsies.

q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg (evertors)?
hint: A branch of the common fibular nerve.
why: It supplies fibularis longus and brevis and the skin of the dorsum of the foot.

q: Which nerve passes behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel?
why: It divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves to the sole.

q: Standing on the right leg, the left side of the pelvis drops. Which nerve is damaged?
why: Gluteus medius and minimus of the standing leg normally hold the pelvis level; this is a positive Trendelenburg sign.

q: Foot drop after a fracture of the fibular neck is due to injury of which nerve?
acc: common fibular / common peroneal / fibular / peroneal
hint: It winds round the neck of the fibula.
why: Dorsiflexion and eversion are lost, with numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

q: A patient can't stand on tiptoe and has a numb sole. Which nerve is injured?
why: It supplies the plantarflexors and the skin of the sole.

q: Which dermatome covers the big toe and dorsum of the foot?
why: An L4/5 disc prolapse affects L5, causing weak big toe extension.

q: Which dermatome covers the little toe and lateral foot?
why: An S1 lesion also reduces the ankle jerk.

q: Which dermatome covers the medial malleolus?
hint: The root also tested by the knee jerk.
why: L3 covers the knee and L5 the dorsum of the foot.

q: Which dermatomes give saddle anaesthesia when lost?
why: Saddle anaesthesia with urinary retention suggests cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency.

q: What is the root value of hip flexion?
why: Hip extension is L4–5; knee extension L3–4.

q: What is the root value of ankle plantarflexion?
why: Same as the ankle jerk.

q: What is the root value of ankle dorsiflexion?
why: L5 alone is tested by big toe extension.

q: Which line on an AP pelvis X-ray is broken in a neck of femur fracture?
why: It runs smoothly along the underside of the femoral neck and the top of the obturator foramen.

q: How does the leg lie in a displaced neck of femur fracture?
hint: Look at the length and the foot position.
why: The muscles pull the distal fragment up and iliopsoas rotates it outwards.

q: Which bone holds the pituitary gland?
hint: The bone with the sella turcica.
why: Surgery reaches the gland through the nose and sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal).

q: What is the bony fossa containing the pituitary called?
why: An enlarged sella on imaging suggests a pituitary adenoma.

q: Which part of the pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin?
hint: The part made of neural tissue.
why: The hormones are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and travel down axons.

q: Which part of the anterior pituitary wraps around the stalk?
why: The pars distalis makes most hormones; the pars intermedia is rudimentary in humans.

q: How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary?
hint: Like the hepatic system, two capillary beds in series.
why: They are released at the median eminence and carried down the stalk.

q: Which structure lies directly above the pituitary (above the diaphragma sellae)?
hint: Where the nasal retinal fibres cross.
why: A macroadenoma presses on its crossing fibres, causing bitemporal hemianopia.

q: Which visual field defect does a pituitary macroadenoma cause?
why: It compresses the crossing nasal fibres, which see the temporal fields.

q: Which cranial nerve runs free in the cavernous sinus and is often the first affected by lateral spread?
why: III, IV, V1 and V2 are in the wall of the sinus; VI lies beside the ICA in the middle.

q: Which artery lies behind the dorsum sellae on the front of the pons?
hint: Formed by the two vertebral arteries.
why: It is formed by the two vertebral arteries.

q: Which nerve runs close to the inferior thyroid artery?
hint: It supplies most of the laryngeal muscles.
why: The artery is tied away from the gland to avoid it; injury causes hoarseness.

q: Which nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery?
acc: external laryngeal / external branch / superior laryngeal
model: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
why: The artery is tied close to the gland to protect it; injury affects cricothyroid and voice pitch.

q: Which artery gives rise to the superior thyroid artery?
model: The external carotid artery (its first branch).
hint: The carotid branch that supplies the face.
why: The inferior thyroid comes from the thyrocervical trunk.

q: Which artery gives rise to the inferior thyroid artery?
model: The thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.
hint: A trunk from the subclavian artery.
why: It also supplies the parathyroids.

q: Why does the thyroid move upwards on swallowing?
model: It is enclosed in pretracheal fascia attached to the larynx.
why: Neck lumps that move on swallowing are thyroid (or thyroglossal cysts, which also move on tongue protrusion).

q: Into which veins do the superior and middle thyroid veins drain?
hint: The large vein in the carotid sheath.
why: The inferior thyroid veins drain to the brachiocephalic veins.

q: Why should the strap muscles be cut high during thyroid surgery?
model: Their nerve supply (ansa cervicalis) enters them low.
hint: Think about where their motor branches reach them.
why: Cutting high avoids denervating them.

q: Which embryonic structure forms the anterior pituitary?
hint: An outpouching of the roof of the primitive mouth.
why: It grows up from the roof of the primitive mouth (ectoderm); remnants can form a craniopharyngioma.

q: Where does the thyroid gland start to develop?
model: At the foramen caecum of the tongue.
hint: A pit where the front two-thirds and back third of an oral structure meet.
why: It descends via the thyroglossal duct in front of the hyoid.

q: Which neck lump moves up when the tongue is stuck out?
hint: A remnant of the thyroid's descent.
why: It stays attached to the tongue by the remains of the duct; it is removed with the middle of the hyoid (Sistrunk).

q: From which pharyngeal pouch do the inferior parathyroids develop?
why: They migrate down with the thymus, past the superior parathyroids from the 4th pouch, so their position varies more.

q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal medulla?
hint: The same origin as sympathetic ganglia.
why: Its chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic neurons; tumours are phaeochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.

q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal cortex?
why: The medulla is from neural crest.

q: What does the pineal gland secrete?
why: It is released in the dark and regulates circadian rhythm.

q: Why is the pineal gland useful on imaging?
model: It calcifies with age and marks the midline.
why: A shifted pineal suggests a mass pushing the brain across.

q: A pineal tumour causing inability to look up is which syndrome?
why: The tumour presses on the superior colliculi and tectum; it can also block the aqueduct.

q: At which vertebral level is the cricoid cartilage?
hint: Where the trachea and oesophagus begin.
why: The larynx becomes the trachea and the pharynx becomes the oesophagus here.

q: At which vertebral level is the hyoid bone?
why: The thyroid cartilage lies at C4–5.

q: Name the lower bony boundaries of the neck.
acc: jugular notch / suprasternal / manubrium / sternum + clavicle
model: The jugular notch of the manubrium and the clavicles (to the acromion and C7).
hint: The top of the breastbone and the collarbones.
why: The upper boundary is the mandible, mastoid process and superior nuchal line.

q: Which space between the pharynx and prevertebral fascia can become infected in children?
why: Retropharyngeal abscess causes neck stiffness, drooling and stridor.

q: Infection in the "danger space" can spread down to where?
why: It lies between the alar and prevertebral fascia and runs from the skull base to the diaphragm, causing mediastinitis.

q: Which fascial layer encloses the brachial plexus roots and continues as the axillary sheath?
hint: The layer in front of the vertebrae.
why: It also covers the scalenes and the floor of the posterior triangle.

q: Which layer of fascia splits round SCM and trapezius?
model: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
why: It forms the roof of both neck triangles.

q: What are the three boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck?
acc: sternocleidomastoid / scm + midline / middle + mandible / jaw
model: Anterior border of SCM, midline of the neck, lower border of the mandible.
hint: A muscle, an imaginary vertical line and a bone.
why: It contains the carotid sheath, thyroid, larynx and submandibular gland.

q: Name the three main contents of the carotid sheath.
model: The common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve.
hint: An artery, a vein and a cranial nerve.
why: The sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, not in it.

q: Where is the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath?
model: Between and behind the artery and the vein.
hint: Think of the artery and vein first.
why: The artery is medial, the IJV lateral.

q: Which nerve chain lies behind the carotid sheath, not inside it?
why: Damage causes Horner's syndrome.

q: Where is the needle inserted for an internal jugular line using landmarks?
model: At the apex of the triangle between the sternal and clavicular heads of SCM, lateral to the carotid pulse.
hint: Between the two heads of a neck muscle.
why: Aim towards the same-side nipple; ultrasound guidance is standard.

q: Why is the right internal jugular vein preferred for central lines?
acc: straight / direct / svc / thoracic duct / pleura
model: It runs straight down to the SVC, and the thoracic duct and higher pleural dome are on the left.
hint: Think about the path to the heart.
why: This lowers the risk of malposition, chylothorax and pneumothorax.

q: Why is the patient tipped head-down for a neck central line?
model: To fill the vein and prevent air embolism.
hint: Two reasons: the vein, and the risk of something entering it.
why: Negative pressure in the veins when sitting up can suck air in.

q: At what level does the common carotid artery divide?
acc: upper border of the thyroid / thyroid cartilage / c4 / 4
model: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4).
hint: Level with the top of the Adam's apple.
why: Atheroma at the bifurcation causes TIAs and strokes.

q: Which carotid artery has no branches in the neck?
hint: It enters the skull through the carotid canal.
why: Its first branch is the ophthalmic artery inside the skull.

q: What are the two terminal branches of the external carotid artery?
model: The maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
hint: The last two in "Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students".
why: They split behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland.

q: From which vessel does the right common carotid artery arise?
hint: The first branch of the aortic arch.
why: The left common carotid arises directly from the aortic arch.

q: Which baroreceptor lies at the origin of the internal carotid artery?
hint: Not the carotid body, which senses oxygen.
why: It is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; massage slows the heart.

q: Where is the carotid pulse felt?
model: At the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, in front of SCM.
why: Never press both sides together, and avoid firm pressure in older people (carotid sinus).

q: Which nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially to supply trapezius?
why: It is easily cut during lymph node biopsy, so the patient can't shrug.

q: Which nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta?
hint: A branch of the left vagus.
why: It can be compressed by lung cancer or an aneurysm, causing hoarseness.

q: Which nerve crosses superficial to the internal and external carotid arteries above the hyoid?
why: It is at risk in carotid endarterectomy, causing tongue deviation.

q: Which laryngeal muscle is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
hint: It tilts the thyroid cartilage forward.
why: It is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and tenses the vocal cords.

q: Which jugular vein is used to assess the JVP?
hint: The deep one in the carotid sheath.
why: It has no valves above the heart and is directly in line with the right atrium; its pulsation is seen, not felt.

q: Which jugular vein crosses superficial to SCM?
why: It runs under platysma and drains into the subclavian vein.

q: Into which vein does the external jugular vein drain?
why: It pierces the deep fascia just above the clavicle.

q: What are the boundaries of the posterior triangle?
model: Posterior border of SCM, anterior border of trapezius and the middle third of the clavicle.
why: Its floor is prevertebral fascia over the scalenes, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.

q: Which muscle divides the posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular parts?
why: The brachial plexus trunks and subclavian artery lie in the supraclavicular part.

q: Which nerve runs down the front of scalenus anterior?
why: It runs from lateral to medial under the prevertebral fascia; interscalene blocks often paralyse it.

q: Which vessel passes behind scalenus anterior?
why: The subclavian vein passes in front of the muscle on the 1st rib.

q: Where does scalenus anterior insert?
model: The scalene tubercle of the 1st rib.
why: It separates the subclavian vein (in front) from the subclavian artery (behind).

q: Which structures emerge between scalenus anterior and medius?
model: The brachial plexus roots and the subclavian artery.
hint: A nerve network and a major artery.
why: A cervical rib can compress them here (thoracic outlet syndrome).

q: Where is the subclavian artery pulse felt?
model: Behind the middle of the clavicle, pressing down onto the 1st rib.
hint: Above the middle of the collarbone.
why: Pressing here can control bleeding from the upper limb.

q: What part of the brachial plexus lies in the posterior triangle?
hint: The first two parts of the plexus, from the spine outwards.
why: Divisions and cords lie behind the clavicle and in the axilla.

q: Turning the head to the left against resistance tests which sternocleidomastoid?
hint: Each SCM turns the face away from itself.
why: Each SCM turns the face to the opposite side.

q: Which nerve supplies the motor fibres of SCM and trapezius?
hint: A cranial nerve with a spinal root.
why: C2–4 branches carry proprioception from these muscles.

q: Which part of trapezius elevates the scapula?
why: Shrugging against resistance tests the accessory nerve.

q: Which roots form the cervical plexus?
why: It lies deep to SCM and gives the phrenic nerve and ansa cervicalis.

q: Where do the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge?
model: At the nerve point (Erb's point), the midpoint of SCM's posterior border.
hint: The middle of the posterior border of SCM.
why: This is where a superficial cervical plexus block is given.

q: Which cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus supplies the skin over the parotid and earlobe?
why: It winds round SCM just below where the accessory nerve emerges.

q: Which nerve loop supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles?
why: It lies on the carotid sheath.

q: Which muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter at C6?
hint: Part of the inferior constrictor attached to the cricoid.
why: It is the narrowest point of the oesophagus, about 15 cm from the teeth; a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's) forms just above it.

q: Which artery supplies the cervical oesophagus and trachea?
hint: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk.
why: The thoracic oesophagus gets aortic branches; the abdominal part gets the left gastric artery.

q: Which side is the cervical oesophagus approached from surgically?
hint: Which way does it bulge from behind the trachea?
why: The oesophagus lies slightly to the left of the trachea in the neck.

q: Venous drainage of which part of the oesophagus links the portal and systemic circulations?
why: The left gastric vein (portal) meets oesophageal veins (azygos), forming varices in portal hypertension.

q: Name the three branches of the arch of the aorta.
acc: brachiocephalic + left common carotid + left subclavian
model: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.
hint: Right to left: one trunk, then two arteries on the left.
why: The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid.

q: An aberrant right subclavian artery passing behind the oesophagus causes what?
why: It arises from the end of the arch and compresses the oesophagus.

q: At which level does the arch of the aorta begin and end?
acc: sternal angle / t4 / 4 / angle of louis
hint: Where the 2nd costal cartilage meets the sternum.
why: The trachea also bifurcates around this level.

q: Which two veins join to form each brachiocephalic vein?
model: The internal jugular and subclavian veins.
hint: One from the head, one from the arm.
why: They join behind each sternoclavicular joint.

q: Which venous junction receives the thoracic duct?
acc: left venous angle / left internal jugular / left subclavian / junction
model: Into the left venous angle (junction of the left IJV and subclavian vein).
hint: On the left, where two big veins meet.
why: Damage in left neck surgery causes a chyle leak.

q: Which brachiocephalic vein is longer?
hint: The SVC lies on the right.
why: It crosses behind the manubrium to join the right one behind the right 1st costal cartilage, forming the SVC.

q: Name a tributary of the brachiocephalic vein.
acc: vertebral / internal thoracic / inferior thyroid / superior intercostal / thymic / pericardiophrenic
model: Vertebral, internal thoracic, inferior thyroid, left superior intercostal, thymic or pericardiophrenic veins.
hint: Veins from the vertebrae, chest wall and thyroid.
why: The EJV drains into the subclavian vein instead.

q: Which node at the angle of the mandible drains the tonsil?
hint: Where the IJV crosses the posterior belly of a muscle.
why: It enlarges in tonsillitis.

q: An enlarged left supraclavicular node suggests cancer where?
why: Virchow's node receives lymph via the thoracic duct (Troisier's sign).

q: Where does all lymph from the head and neck end up before reaching the veins?
model: The deep cervical nodes along the IJV.
why: They then drain via the jugular trunks into the thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct.

q: Which nodes drain the tip of the tongue?
why: The side of the tongue drains to submandibular nodes; the back drains to deep cervical nodes on both sides.

q: What are the root values of the phrenic nerve?
why: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"; mainly C4.

q: Why can diaphragmatic irritation cause shoulder-tip pain?
model: The phrenic nerve (C4) shares its roots with the skin over the shoulder.
hint: Compare the diaphragm's nerve roots with the shoulder dermatome.
why: Blood under the diaphragm (e.g. ruptured spleen, Kehr's sign) is felt at the shoulder.

q: What does a unilateral phrenic nerve palsy look like on a chest X-ray?
why: The paralysed side moves up paradoxically on a sniff test.

q: Which regional anaesthetic block almost always paralyses the phrenic nerve on that side?
hint: Given between two neck muscles for shoulder surgery.
why: The phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior, right next to the injection site.

q: In which week does the lung bud appear?
hint: The same week the heart starts beating.
why: It grows from the ventral wall of the foregut.

q: Which germ layer forms the epithelium of the airways and alveoli?
hint: The lining of the gut tube.
why: Cartilage, smooth muscle and vessels come from splanchnic mesoderm.

q: What separates the developing trachea from the oesophagus?
acc: tracheooesophageal septum / tracheo oesophageal septum / tracheoesophageal / septum
why: Incomplete separation causes a tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

q: A newborn with frothy saliva, choking on feeds and an NG tube that won't pass most likely has what?
why: Polyhydramnios in pregnancy is a clue; check for other VACTERL anomalies.

q: In which stage of lung development do capillaries grow in and type I and II cells appear?
why: Survival becomes possible from about 24 weeks.

q: Which stage of lung development reaches the terminal bronchioles but allows no gas exchange?
why: The lung looks like a gland at this stage.

q: Which alveolar cells secrete surfactant in the fetal lung?
why: Production starts at ~20–24 weeks and is adequate by ~34–35 weeks.

q: What is given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery to speed up lung maturation?
why: They increase surfactant production and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

q: Most alveoli form during which period?
why: The alveolar stage begins late in pregnancy and continues through childhood.

q: Why does renal agenesis cause pulmonary hypoplasia?
hint: Fetal urine makes up most of what surrounds the fetus.
why: Fetal breathing of amniotic fluid and room in the chest are needed for lung growth.

q: Which side is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia usually on?
hint: The liver protects the other side.
why: The pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close; gut in the chest causes pulmonary hypoplasia.

q: Which structure forms the central tendon of the diaphragm?
why: It forms in the neck region, so the diaphragm keeps its C3–5 phrenic nerve supply.

q: How many lobar bronchi does the right lung bud form?
why: The bronchial buds appear in week 5.

q: In which part of the gallbladder do stones often lodge?
hint: An eponymous pouch near the cystic duct.
why: A stone impacted here blocks the cystic duct, causing biliary colic or cholecystitis; a large one can compress the common hepatic duct (Mirizzi).

q: Where is the fundus of the gallbladder on the surface?
model: At the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage.
hint: Where the midclavicular line meets the costal margin.
why: Where the midclavicular line meets the costal margin; Murphy's sign is tested here.

q: A gallstone eroding into the duodenum and blocking the terminal ileum causes what?
why: The gallbladder lies against the duodenum, so a fistula can form; the stone impacts at the ileocaecal valve.

q: Which triangle contains the cystic artery?
hint: An eponymous triangle dissected at cholecystectomy.
why: It is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and inferior border of the liver; the artery is identified and tied at cholecystectomy.

q: The cystic artery usually arises from which artery?
hint: A branch of the hepatic artery proper.
why: It runs in Calot's triangle.

q: Which hormone makes the gallbladder contract?
why: Fat in the duodenum releases it; it also relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so fatty meals trigger biliary colic.

q: Which two ducts join to form the common bile duct?
model: The cystic duct and the common hepatic duct.
hint: One from the gallbladder, one from the liver.
why: The right and left hepatic ducts first join to form the common hepatic duct.

q: Into which part of the duodenum does bile enter?
hint: The part that runs down beside the head of the pancreas.
why: At the major duodenal papilla, about 10 cm from the pylorus.

q: Which sphincter controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum?
why: It is cut during ERCP (sphincterotomy) to remove bile duct stones.

q: Which part of the pancreas hooks behind the superior mesenteric vessels?
why: It comes from the ventral pancreatic bud.

q: Which part of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament?
hint: The end next to the spleen.
why: It is the only intraperitoneal part and can be damaged during splenectomy.

q: Which part of the pancreas lies in front of the portal vein at L1?
hint: Between the head and the body.
why: The SMV and splenic vein join behind it to form the portal vein.

q: What separates the pancreas from the stomach?
why: Inflammatory fluid from pancreatitis collects here to form a pseudocyst.

q: Which vein runs along the back of the body of the pancreas?
why: Pancreatitis can cause splenic vein thrombosis and gastric varices.

q: Which duct passes through or behind the head of the pancreas?
hint: It carries bile from the liver.
why: Cancer of the pancreatic head blocks it, causing painless obstructive jaundice.

q: Which large vessels lie directly behind the pancreas?
acc: ivc / inferior vena cava / aorta / sma / superior mesenteric / portal
model: The IVC, aorta, SMA/SMV and portal vein.
hint: The great vessels of the posterior abdominal wall.
why: Invasion of these vessels decides whether a pancreatic cancer can be removed.

q: What is the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis in the UK?
hint: The other common cause is alcohol.
why: A stone blocks the ampulla, where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet; alcohol is the second commonest cause.

q: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests what?
acc: pancreatic / pancreas / head / malignan / cancer / tumour
model: Cancer of the head of the pancreas (or other malignant obstruction).
why: Courvoisier's law: a stone-scarred gallbladder rarely distends, so a palpable one points to malignancy.

q: Why does pancreatic pain radiate to the back?
model: The pancreas is retroperitoneal, on the posterior abdominal wall and coeliac plexus.
why: Patients often sit forward for relief.

q: Bruising in the flanks in severe pancreatitis is called what?
hint: An eponymous sign; Cullen's is the umbilical one.
why: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracks to the flanks; Cullen's sign is periumbilical bruising.

q: Where does the main pancreatic duct begin?
hint: The end next to the spleen.
why: It runs the full length of the gland to the head, then joins the bile duct.

q: What is the name of the junction of the bile duct and main pancreatic duct?
why: It opens at the major duodenal papilla; tumours here (ampullary carcinoma) cause early jaundice.

q: Through which papilla does the accessory pancreatic duct drain?
why: It lies about 2 cm above the major papilla; in pancreas divisum most juice drains this way.

q: Which two arteries form the anastomosis supplying the head of the pancreas?
acc: superior pancreaticoduodenal / gastroduodenal + inferior pancreaticoduodenal / sma / superior mesenteric
model: The superior pancreaticoduodenal (from the gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (from the SMA).
hint: One from the coeliac side, one from the midgut artery.
why: The head sits where foregut and midgut supplies meet, so it gets both.

q: Which artery supplies the body and tail of the pancreas?
hint: It runs along the top of the pancreas.
why: Its branches include the dorsal and great pancreatic arteries.

q: Into which venous system does the pancreas drain?
hint: The system carrying gut blood to the liver.
why: Insulin and glucagon reach the liver first.

q: What is the first-line imaging test for gallstones?
why: Stones are bright with an acoustic shadow; it also shows wall thickening and dilated ducts.

q: What proportion of gallstones show on a plain X-ray?
why: Most are cholesterol stones, which are radiolucent, unlike most kidney stones.

q: Which test shows the bile ducts using MRI without instruments?
hint: An MRI of the biliary and pancreatic ducts.
why: It finds duct stones; ERCP is used when treatment is needed.

q: Which procedure both shows and removes common bile duct stones?
why: An endoscope passed to the papilla allows sphincterotomy and stone extraction; pancreatitis is its main complication.

q: Where do the dorsal columns decussate?
hint: The lowest part of the brainstem.
why: So a cord lesion causes loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception on the same side.

q: Where does the spinothalamic tract cross?
acc: spinal cord / cord / within / segment / anterior white commissure / entry
model: In the spinal cord, within 1–2 segments of entry.
hint: Close to where the fibres enter.
why: So a cord lesion causes loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.

q: Which sensations are lost on the opposite side in Brown-Séquard syndrome?
why: The spinothalamic tract has already crossed; weakness and loss of proprioception are on the same side.

q: Anterior spinal artery occlusion spares which sensations?
acc: proprioception / vibration / fine touch / dorsal column
hint: The tracts at the back of the cord.
why: The dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.

q: Which cord syndrome gives cape-like loss of pain and temperature?
hint: A fluid-filled cavity in the middle of the cord.
why: Crossing spinothalamic fibres in the centre are damaged first.

q: Where are the cell bodies of sensory neurons in spinal nerves?
hint: A swelling on the dorsal root.
why: It lies in the intervertebral foramen.

q: How many cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae are there?
why: Plus 5 fused sacral and 3–5 coccygeal.

q: Which curves of the spine are primary curves present at birth?
hint: The curves that are concave forwards.
why: The cervical and lumbar lordoses develop with head holding and walking.

q: Which vertebra has no body and no spinous process?
why: Its body has fused with the axis to form the dens.

q: Which feature is unique to cervical vertebrae?
acc: foramen transversarium / transverse foramen / foramina transversaria
hint: A hole for the vertebral artery.
why: The vertebral artery runs through it from C6 upwards.

q: Which feature identifies a thoracic vertebra?
why: On the bodies and transverse processes.

q: What is the projection on top of the axis called?
why: It forms a pivot joint with the atlas.

q: Through which opening is a caudal epidural given?
hint: A gap at the lower end of the sacrum.
why: It is the gap at the lower end of the sacral canal where the laminae of S5 fail to fuse.

q: Which part of the vertebra is the "neck of the Scottie dog" on an oblique lumbar X-ray?
hint: The part between the articular processes.
why: A defect (spondylolysis) looks like a collar and can lead to spondylolisthesis.

q: Which vertebra must be seen on a lateral cervical X-ray for it to be adequate?
why: Injuries here are missed if the film stops short; use a swimmer's view or CT.

q: Which X-ray view shows the dens and the lateral masses of C1?
why: Used for Jefferson and dens fractures (CT is now preferred).

q: What type of joint is an intervertebral disc?
hint: Same type of joint that joins the two pubic bones.
why: Facet joints are synovial plane joints.

q: Name the gel-like centre of an intervertebral disc.
why: It spreads load onto the annulus fibrosus; it dries out with age.

q: Between which vertebrae are there no intervertebral discs?
model: Between the skull and C1, and between C1 and C2.
why: The atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints are synovial.

q: Why do intervertebral discs heal poorly?
hint: Think about how they get nutrients.
why: They are nourished by diffusion through the vertebral endplates.

q: In which direction do disc prolapses usually occur?
hint: The posterior longitudinal ligament protects the midline.
why: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and strongest in the midline.

q: An L4/5 disc prolapse usually compresses which nerve root?
hint: The root that traverses that disc.
why: A posterolateral prolapse hits the root passing down to the next foramen.

q: Which reflex is lost with an S1 root compression?
hint: Tested by tapping the Achilles tendon.
why: An L5/S1 disc prolapse causes it with weak plantarflexion and numbness of the lateral foot.

q: A C5/6 disc prolapse affects which root?
hint: Cervical roots exit above their vertebra.
why: Cervical roots exit above their numbered vertebra; the patient has a numb thumb and weak biceps.

q: What are the key features of cauda equina syndrome?
model: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, bilateral leg symptoms.
why: It needs emergency MRI and decompression.

q: Which test stretches the L5 and S1 roots?
hint: Lift the straight leg with the patient lying down.
why: Leg pain between 30° and 70° suggests root irritation.

q: Which joint allows nodding ("yes")?
why: Rotation ("no") happens at the atlanto-axial joint.

q: About half of all neck rotation occurs at which joint?
why: The dens pivots in a ring formed by the anterior arch and the transverse ligament.

q: Which ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas?
model: The transverse ligament of the atlas.
why: Laxity in rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome lets the dens compress the cord.

q: Which region of the spine allows the least rotation?
hint: The facets face medially and laterally.
why: Its facets lie in the sagittal plane, locking rotation; most flexion happens at L4–S1.

q: Why is thoracic flexion limited?
model: The ribs and sternum, thin discs and overlapping spinous processes.
hint: What is attached to each thoracic vertebra?
why: Rotation is relatively free because the facets lie in a coronal plane.

q: Which test measures lumbar flexion?
hint: Mark 10 cm above and 5 cm below the dimples of Venus.
why: Reduced in ankylosing spondylitis.

q: Which nerves supply the erector spinae?
acc: posterior rami / dorsal rami / posterior primary
model: The posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.
why: The superficial back muscles are upper limb muscles supplied by anterior rami.

q: Name the three columns of erector spinae from lateral to medial.
why: "I Love Spine".

q: Which elastic ligament joins adjacent laminae?
why: It is felt as a "give" during lumbar puncture; thickening causes spinal stenosis.

q: Which spinous process marks the level of the inferior angle of the scapula?
why: The root of the scapular spine is T3 and the iliac crests are L4.

q: The dimples of Venus mark which vertebral level?
why: They overlie the posterior superior iliac spines and the end of the dural sac.

q: What causes neurogenic claudication eased by leaning forward?
why: Flexion widens the canal; disc, facet and ligamentum flavum changes narrow it.

q: Which nerve supplies the outer annulus and posterior longitudinal ligament?
hint: It re-enters the canal through the intervertebral foramen.
why: Annular tears can cause back pain without root signs.

q: Which abdominal muscle helps stabilise the spine by raising intra-abdominal pressure?
why: Core stability training targets it with multifidus.

q: A wedge compression fracture of the anterior vertebral body involves how many columns?
hint: Only the front of the body.
why: It is stable; typical in osteoporosis.

q: Is a burst fracture with retropulsion stable or unstable?
hint: How many columns does it involve?
why: It involves the anterior and middle columns, and bone pushed backwards can damage the cord.

q: What is a burst fracture of C1 called?
hint: An eponymous fracture from axial loading.
why: Axial loading (diving) splits the ring of the atlas.

q: What is a fracture through the pars of C2 called?
hint: Named after a form of execution.
why: It results from hyperextension, as in judicial hanging.

q: At which vertebral level does the spinal cord end in adults?
why: It ends at about L3 at birth; below it lies the cauda equina.

q: At which levels is a lumbar puncture performed in adults?
hint: Below the end of the spinal cord.
why: Below the end of the cord; Tuffier's line across the iliac crests marks L4.

q: Name the ligament felt as a "give" just before the epidural space during lumbar puncture.
why: The needle then passes the epidural space, dura and arachnoid into the subarachnoid space.

q: Which spinal nerve exits below C7?
hint: There is one more cervical nerve than cervical vertebrae.
why: C1–7 exit above their vertebrae; from T1 onwards each exits below its vertebra.

q: What is the large reinforcing artery of the lower spinal cord called?
why: It arises at T9–L2 and is at risk in aortic surgery, causing paraplegia.

q: At which level does the dural sac end?
hint: Level with the dimples of Venus.
why: The cord ends at L1/2 but the dural sac continues with the cauda equina.

q: What are the only branches of the ascending aorta?
model: The right and left coronary arteries.
why: They arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve cusps.

q: Through which diaphragmatic opening does the aorta pass, and at what level?
hint: The lowest of the three big openings.
why: It passes behind the diaphragm between the crura, so breathing doesn't squeeze it.

q: Name a branch of the descending thoracic aorta.
acc: intercostal / bronchial / oesophageal / esophageal / pericardial / mediastinal / phrenic / subcostal
model: Posterior intercostal, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal, superior phrenic or subcostal arteries.
hint: Think of the chest wall and the organs behind the heart.
why: It supplies the chest wall and posterior mediastinal organs.

q: Coarctation of the aorta usually occurs just after the origin of which artery?
model: The left subclavian artery (near the ligamentum arteriosum).
hint: The last branch of the arch.
why: It causes radiofemoral delay, upper limb hypertension and rib notching from enlarged intercostal collaterals.

q: Which coronary artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove?
acc: lad / left anterior descending / anterior interventricular
model: The left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) artery.
hint: A branch of the left main stem.
why: It supplies the anterior LV wall and anterior 2/3 of the septum; blockage is the "widow-maker".

q: Why do inferior MIs often cause bradycardia and heart block?
acc: av node / atrioventricular node / av nodal / sa node / sinoatrial / node
model: The RCA usually supplies the AV node (~80%) and SA node (~60%).
hint: Which conducting tissue does the RCA supply?
why: Ischaemia of the nodes slows conduction; it usually recovers after reperfusion.

q: Coronary dominance is decided by which artery gives which branch?
model: The artery that gives the posterior descending (interventricular) artery.
hint: A branch running down the back of the heart between the ventricles.
why: About 70% are right-dominant.

q: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF suggests blockage of which artery?
why: It supplies the inferior LV wall; check right-sided leads for RV infarction.

q: ST elevation in V1–V4 suggests blockage of which artery?
acc: lad / left anterior descending / anterior interventricular
model: The left anterior descending artery (anterior MI).
why: It supplies the anterior wall and septum.

q: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 suggests blockage of which artery?
hint: It runs in the left atrioventricular groove.
why: It runs in the left AV groove to the lateral and posterior LV.

q: During which part of the cardiac cycle do the coronary arteries mainly fill?
why: The contracting LV squeezes its vessels in systole, so tachycardia shortens filling time.

q: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain?
hint: The chamber that receives the venae cavae.
why: It opens between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve.

q: Which cardiac vein runs with the LAD artery?
why: It runs up the anterior interventricular groove then round the left AV groove to the coronary sinus.

q: Which veins drain the right ventricle straight into the right atrium?
hint: They lie on the front of the heart.
why: They bypass the coronary sinus.

q: Which cardiac vein runs with the posterior descending artery?
hint: Between the great and the small.
why: It drains into the coronary sinus.

q: What is an anastomosis?
model: A connection between blood vessels so blood can reach an area by more than one route.
hint: Think of the circle of Willis.
why: It protects tissue when one vessel is blocked, e.g. the circle of Willis.

q: Why does sudden coronary occlusion cause infarction despite anastomoses?
acc: end arter / functional / small / inadequate / insufficient / too few
model: Coronary arteries are functional end arteries: their anastomoses are too small to open quickly.
hint: The connections exist but can't carry enough blood quickly.
why: Slow narrowing gives time for collaterals to grow, so chronic disease may cause angina without infarction.

q: Name an example of a true end artery.
model: The central artery of the retina (or renal/splenic segmental arteries).
why: Blockage causes infarction because no other vessel reaches the area.

q: Name a function of the pericardium.
acc: fix / anchor / prevent / overdistension / over distension / lubricat / friction / barrier / infection
model: Fixes the heart, prevents over-distension, lubricates movement and acts as a barrier to infection.
hint: Think of what a tough sac with slippery lining does.
why: The tough fibrous layer limits acute dilatation.

q: To which structure is the fibrous pericardium fused below?
model: The central tendon of the diaphragm.
why: So the heart moves with the diaphragm during breathing.

q: Which pericardial sinus lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk?
why: Surgeons pass a clamp through it to clamp the great arteries during bypass.

q: Which pericardial sinus lies behind the left atrium?
why: It is a blind pocket bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC.

q: What is Beck's triad in cardiac tamponade?
acc: hypotension / low bp / low blood pressure + jvp / jugular / distended neck + muffled / quiet / soft
model: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds.
hint: Pressure, neck veins and heart sounds.
why: The heart can't fill because the fibrous pericardium can't stretch.

q: Why can a small rapid effusion cause tamponade while a large slow one may not?
model: The fibrous pericardium can't stretch quickly, but stretches slowly over time.
why: As little as 100–200 mL can compress the heart if it collects fast.

q: Where is the needle inserted for pericardiocentesis?
model: Below the xiphisternum at the left xiphocostal angle, aiming towards the left shoulder.
hint: Below the tip of the sternum.
why: This avoids the pleura and the internal thoracic artery.

q: What is meant by a potential space?
acc: potential / no space / touch / film / only when / normally empty / collapsed
model: A space whose layers normally touch, separated only by a thin film of fluid; it opens up only when fluid, blood or air collects.
hint: The layers are normally in contact.
why: The pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities are all potential spaces.

q: What is blood in the pericardial cavity called?
why: Causes include trauma, aortic dissection and rupture after MI.

q: Which nerves carry pain sensation from the pericardium?
why: They supply the fibrous and parietal layers; the visceral layer is insensitive.

q: Do the phrenic nerves pass in front of or behind the lung roots?
hint: The vagus takes the opposite route.
why: The vagus nerves pass behind the lung roots.

q: Why can pericarditis cause shoulder-tip pain?
acc: c3 / c4 / c5 / phrenic / same / shared
model: The phrenic nerve (C3–5) shares spinal segments with the skin of the shoulder.
hint: Compare the roots of the nerve supplying the pericardium with the shoulder dermatomes.
why: The brain misattributes the pain to the shoulder (referred pain).

q: How does pericarditis pain change with position?
acc: sitting forward / leaning forward / lean forward / sit forward / forward
model: It is worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward.
hint: Which posture lifts the heart off the inflamed back of the sac?
why: Sitting forward reduces contact between the inflamed layers; MI pain doesn't change with position.

q: Name the three structures at the renal hilum from front to back.
model: Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis (VAP).
why: Useful for orienting a kidney and in nephrectomy.

q: Which layer of fascia encloses the kidney and suprarenal gland?
why: It contains perirenal fat and limits the spread of perinephric collections.

q: Name a hormone the kidney makes.
acc: renin / erythropoietin / epo / calcitriol / vitamin d
model: Renin, erythropoietin or calcitriol (active vitamin D).
hint: Think about anaemia and bone disease in chronic kidney disease.
why: Chronic kidney disease causes anaemia and bone disease for this reason.

q: What are the projections of cortex between the pyramids called?
why: Interlobar vessels run through them.

q: Into which structure does each renal papilla open?
why: Minor calyces join to form 2–3 major calyces, which form the renal pelvis.

q: What are the triangular structures in the renal medulla called?
