why: They contain loops of Henle and collecting ducts, with their apex (papilla) pointing to the sinus.

q: Which way does the renal hilum face in a transverse section?
why: The kidney lies on psoas, which angles it so the hilum faces forwards and inwards.

q: Which part of the duodenum lies in front of the right renal hilum?
hint: The part beside the head of the pancreas.
why: It can be injured during right nephrectomy.

q: Which organ covers most of the front of the right kidney?
hint: The reason the right kidney is lower.
why: The hepatorenal pouch (Morison's) separates them.

q: Name an anterior relation of the left kidney.
acc: stomach / spleen / pancreas / splenic / colon / flexure / jejunum / suprarenal / adrenal
model: The stomach, spleen, pancreas, splenic flexure of the colon, jejunum and suprarenal gland.
hint: Think of the organs in the left upper quadrant.
why: The tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels cross its hilum.

q: At what level do the renal arteries arise?
why: Just below the SMA.

q: Which renal vein is longer, and why?
model: The left, because it has to cross in front of the aorta to reach the IVC.
hint: The IVC lies on the right.
why: It can be compressed between the aorta and SMA (nutcracker syndrome).

q: Which renal artery passes behind the IVC?
hint: The IVC is on that side.
why: The IVC lies on the right of the aorta.

q: Which veins drain into the left renal vein but not the right?
model: The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins.
hint: One from the gonad, one from the gland above the kidney.
why: On the right they drain straight into the IVC; a left renal tumour can cause a left varicocele.

q: To which nodes does the kidney drain lymph?
why: They lie along the aorta at the level of the renal vessels.

q: Why are segmental renal arteries important in surgery?
model: They are end arteries, so blocking one infarcts that segment.
hint: They don't connect with each other.
why: This allows partial nephrectomy along segment boundaries.

q: What shape is the right suprarenal gland?
why: The left is crescent-shaped.

q: Which hormone does the zona glomerulosa make?
why: "Salt, sugar, sex": glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis.

q: Which hormone does the zona fasciculata make?
why: It is the middle and thickest layer of the cortex.

q: Which large vein lies directly in front of the right suprarenal gland?
hint: The largest vein in the abdomen.
why: The right suprarenal vein is very short and drains straight into it.

q: Into which vein does the left suprarenal vein drain?
hint: Same as the left gonadal vein.
why: The right drains straight into the IVC.

q: How many arteries supply each suprarenal gland?
model: Three: superior, middle and inferior suprarenal arteries.
why: From the inferior phrenic artery, the aorta and the renal artery.

q: Why do sympathetic fibres to the adrenal medulla not synapse in a ganglion?
acc: chromaffin / postganglionic / act as / neural crest / modified
model: The chromaffin cells act as the postganglionic neurons.
hint: What are the medullary cells derived from?
why: They are modified sympathetic neurons from the neural crest that release adrenaline into the blood.

q: What is the first-line imaging test for the kidneys?
why: It shows size, hydronephrosis, cysts and masses without radiation.

q: Which nuclear medicine scan shows renal scarring?
why: Used in children after UTIs; MAG3 shows drainage.

q: Which test shows vesicoureteric reflux?
hint: Contrast is filmed while passing urine.
why: Contrast is put into the bladder and watched during voiding.

q: Where does psoas major insert?
why: Iliopsoas is the strongest hip flexor.

q: What is the main action of quadratus lumborum?
acc: lateral flexion / side flexion / lateral bend / fix / 12th rib
model: Lateral flexion of the trunk (and fixing the 12th rib in breathing).
hint: It runs from the iliac crest to the lowest rib.
why: It runs from the iliac crest to the 12th rib.

q: Which sign suggests a retrocaecal appendix irritating psoas?
model: The psoas sign: pain on extending the right hip.
why: The inflamed appendix lies on psoas.

q: At which level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?
why: About the level of the umbilicus and iliac crests.

q: Name the three unpaired gut branches of the abdominal aorta with their levels.
acc: coeliac / celiac + superior mesenteric / sma + inferior mesenteric / ima
hint: One for each part of the gut.
why: They supply the foregut, midgut and hindgut.

q: At what level do the gonadal arteries arise?
why: The gonads start near the kidneys and bring their arteries with them as they descend.

q: Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are above or below the renal arteries?
hint: Compare their position with the renal artery origins.
why: Men are screened at 65; repair is considered at 5.5 cm or more.

q: At what level is the IVC formed?
why: The common iliac veins join behind the right common iliac artery.

q: At what level does the IVC pass through the diaphragm?
hint: The highest of the three big openings.
why: It passes through the central tendon, so inspiration helps venous return.

q: Which venous system connects the IVC and SVC if the IVC is blocked?
model: The azygos system (via the ascending lumbar veins).
hint: It runs up the back of the thorax.
why: Superficial epigastric–thoracoepigastric veins also dilate.

q: Which valveless venous plexus lets prostate cancer spread to the spine?
hint: An eponymous plexus around the spine.
why: It connects pelvic veins with the vertebral veins without valves.

q: What is the surface marking of the aortic bifurcation?
model: Just below and left of the umbilicus, at the level of the iliac crests (L4).
why: An expansile mass above it suggests AAA.

q: On which side of the aorta does the IVC lie?
why: That is why the left renal vein is longer.

q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys lie?
hint: From the last thoracic to the 3rd lumbar.
why: The right is a little lower because of the liver.

q: Which kidney lies lower?
why: The liver pushes it down.

q: What is the renal angle?
model: The angle between the 12th rib and the lateral border of erector spinae.
hint: Between a rib and a back muscle.
why: Tenderness there suggests pyelonephritis.

q: Which is the hardest tissue in the body?
hint: The outer covering of the crown.
why: It is acellular, so it can't repair itself once lost to decay.

q: Which tissue makes up the bulk of a tooth?
why: Its tubules make it sensitive when exposed.

q: What covers the root of a tooth?
why: The periodontal ligament anchors into it.

q: What holds a tooth in its socket?
why: This fibrous joint is a gomphosis.

q: How many deciduous teeth are there?
why: 5 in each quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars.

q: At about what age do the first deciduous teeth erupt?
why: Usually the lower central incisors.

q: Which permanent teeth erupt first, at about 6 years?
hint: Large grinding teeth at the back.
why: They erupt behind the deciduous teeth, so they don't replace any.

q: At about what age do the second permanent molars erupt?
hint: Around the start of secondary school.
why: Third molars (wisdom teeth) follow at 17–25 years.

q: How many permanent teeth are there?
why: 8 per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars.

q: Which permanent teeth replace the deciduous molars?
hint: The teeth just in front of the molars.
why: The permanent molars erupt behind them with no deciduous predecessors.

q: What is the dental formula of the permanent teeth in one quadrant?
why: Deciduous is 2-1-0-2.

q: Which nerve enters the mandibular foramen?
hint: A branch of V3 supplying the lower teeth.
why: It supplies the lower teeth; it is blocked here for dental anaesthesia.

q: Which muscle attaches to the coronoid process?
why: It elevates and retracts the mandible.

q: Which muscle attaches to the neck of the mandible?
why: It also attaches to the TMJ disc and pulls the condyle forward to open the jaw.

q: Under which tooth is the mental foramen found?
hint: Between the canine and first molar.
why: The mental nerve exits here to supply the chin and lower lip.

q: Why does the mandible often fracture in two places?
model: It forms a ring with the skull.
hint: Think of breaking a polo mint.
why: A blow to one side often fractures the opposite condylar neck or angle too.

q: What forms the lower boundary of the temporal fossa?
why: Below it the temporal fossa continues into the infratemporal fossa.

q: Which four bones meet at the pterion?
hint: The H-shaped junction on the side of the skull.
why: It is the thinnest part of the skull.

q: Which artery lies under the pterion?
model: The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
hint: It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
why: A fracture here can tear it, causing an extradural haematoma with a lucid interval.

q: Which artery is biopsied in suspected giant cell arteritis?
hint: Felt in front of the ear.
why: Its pulse is felt just in front of the tragus.

q: Which nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland?
model: The auriculotemporal nerve (from IX via the otic ganglion).
hint: Its name links the ear and the temple.
why: Damage in parotid surgery can cause gustatory sweating (Frey's syndrome).

q: What does temporalis do to the mandible?
model: Elevates (closes) the jaw; posterior fibres retract it.
hint: Clench your teeth and feel your temple.
why: It inserts on the coronoid process.

q: Which structure divides the TMJ into two compartments?
why: Gliding happens in the upper compartment, hinge rotation in the lower.

q: Which ligament is the main stabiliser of the TMJ?
hint: It is on the outer side of the capsule.
why: The sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory.

q: Which accessory ligament attaches to the lingula?
why: It runs from the spine of the sphenoid; the inferior alveolar nerve passes between it and the ramus.

q: What type of cartilage covers the TMJ articular surfaces?
why: The joint develops from membrane bone, not a cartilage model.

q: Which muscle starts opening the jaw?
why: It pulls the condyle and disc forward onto the articular eminence; gravity and the suprahyoids help.

q: Which muscle retracts the mandible?
hint: Its fibres fan out over the side of the head.
why: Its horizontal posterior fibres pull the coronoid backwards.

q: Which three muscles close the jaw?
hint: All muscles of mastication except one.
why: All are supplied by V3.

q: In grinding, the right pterygoids move the chin to which side?
hint: The chin moves away from the working muscles.
why: They pull the right condyle forward, swinging the chin to the opposite side.

q: In anterior TMJ dislocation, where does the head of the mandible get stuck?
acc: in front of the articular eminence / anterior / front / eminence
model: In front of the articular eminence.
why: Spasm of the elevators holds it there, so the mouth is stuck open.

q: How is an anterior TMJ dislocation reduced?
model: Press down on the lower molars, then push back.
why: Downwards clears the articular eminence; backwards guides the head into the fossa.

q: Which nerve supplies all the muscles of mastication?
hint: The third division of the trigeminal.
why: They all develop from the 1st pharyngeal arch.

q: Where does masseter originate?
why: It inserts on the lateral surface of the ramus and angle.

q: Which muscle of mastication opens rather than closes the jaw?
hint: The odd one out of the four.
why: The others (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close it.

q: With a right V3 lesion, which way does the jaw deviate on opening?
why: The working left lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw across.

q: What forms the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa?
hint: The vertical part of the lower jaw.
why: The medial wall is the lateral pterygoid plate.

q: What forms the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa?
why: Both pterygoid muscles arise from it.

q: Which major artery runs through the infratemporal fossa?
hint: A terminal branch of the ECA.
why: It gives the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries.

q: Which nerve joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa?
hint: A branch of the facial nerve that crosses the eardrum.
why: It carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

q: Which bone contains the cribriform plate?
why: Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia.

q: Which bone contains the sella turcica?
why: The pituitary sits in it.

q: Which bone contains the mastoid process?
hint: It also contains the inner ear.
why: Its air cells connect to the middle ear, so otitis media can spread (mastoiditis).

q: Which bone forms the front of the hard palate?
why: The palatine bones form the back third.

q: Which suture lies between the frontal and parietal bones?
hint: It runs like a crown across the head.
why: It meets the sagittal suture at the bregma.

q: Which suture lies between the parietal and occipital bones?
why: Named after the Greek letter lambda (λ).

q: When does the anterior fontanelle usually close?
hint: About a year and a half.
why: It bulges with raised ICP (e.g. meningitis) and is sunken in dehydration.

q: When does the posterior fontanelle usually close?
why: It is triangular and lies at the lambda.

q: Early fusion of skull sutures is called what?
why: The skull grows parallel to the fused suture, giving an abnormal head shape.

q: What passes through the foramen spinosum?
why: Damage causes an extradural haematoma.

q: What passes through the foramen rotundum?
why: V1 uses the superior orbital fissure and V3 the foramen ovale.

q: Which cranial nerves pass through the internal acoustic meatus?
hint: The nerve of expression and the nerve of hearing and balance.
why: A vestibular schwannoma here can affect both.

q: What passes through the optic canal?
model: The optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery.
hint: A nerve and an artery to the eye.
why: The ophthalmic veins pass through the superior orbital fissure instead.

q: What passes through the hypoglossal canal?
hint: The nerve to the tongue muscles.
why: It lies just above the occipital condyle.

q: Through which opening does the internal carotid artery enter the skull?
why: It then runs over the foramen lacerum into the cavernous sinus.

q: Which nerve supplies the lower teeth?
why: Blocking it at the mandibular foramen numbs all the lower teeth on one side and the lower lip.

q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the upper teeth?
model: The maxillary nerve (V2), via the superior alveolar nerves.
why: Upper teeth can be numbed by local infiltration because the maxilla is thin.

q: Why can maxillary sinusitis cause upper toothache?
model: The upper molar roots and superior alveolar nerves lie in the sinus floor.
hint: Think about what lies in the floor of the maxillary air space.
why: Inflammation in the sinus irritates the nerves to the teeth.

q: Which artery supplies the teeth?
model: The maxillary artery, via the superior and inferior alveolar arteries.
hint: A terminal branch of the ECA.
why: The inferior alveolar artery runs with its nerve in the mandibular canal.

q: Which nerve supplies the gums on the lingual side of the lower teeth?
hint: It also carries general sensation from the front of the tongue.
why: It is often numbed with an inferior alveolar block because it lies nearby.

q: Which bones form the hard palate?
model: The palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones.
hint: The upper jaw bone and a bone named after the palate.
why: The maxillae form the front two-thirds, the palatine bones the back third.

q: What does the soft palate do in swallowing?
model: It rises to seal off the nasopharynx.
hint: It stops food going up into the nose.
why: Failure (e.g. vagal palsy, cleft palate) causes nasal regurgitation.

q: Which nerve supplies tensor veli palatini?
hint: The odd one out among the palate muscles.
why: It is the only palate muscle not supplied by the vagus.

q: Which nerve supplies levator veli palatini?
hint: Most palate and pharynx muscles share it.
why: It elevates the soft palate.

q: Which palate muscle opens the auditory tube on swallowing?
why: In cleft palate it can't work properly, so middle ear effusions are common.

q: With a left vagus nerve lesion, which way does the uvula deviate?
model: To the right (away from the lesion).
hint: The healthy side pulls it across.
why: The working right levator veli palatini pulls it over.

q: Which nerve supplies most of the hard palate?
hint: It exits through a foramen at the back of the hard palate.
why: It emerges through the greater palatine foramen near the 3rd molar.

q: Which nerve supplies the hard palate behind the incisors?
hint: It runs along the nasal septum first.
why: It passes through the incisive foramen.

q: Which nerves give sensation to the soft palate?
why: The glossopharyngeal supplies the back of it too.

q: Which nerve is the afferent limb of the gag reflex?
hint: It supplies the posterior third of the tongue.
why: It carries sensation from the back of the tongue and oropharynx.

q: Which nerve is the efferent limb of the gag reflex?
why: It contracts the pharyngeal constrictors and palate muscles.

q: At what vertebral level does the pharynx become the oesophagus?
why: The larynx becomes the trachea at the same level.

q: Which part of the pharynx contains the piriform fossae?
why: They lie either side of the laryngeal inlet; fish bones lodge there.

q: Which part of the pharynx lies behind the mouth?
why: It extends from the soft palate to the tip of the epiglottis and contains the palatine tonsils.

q: In which recess does nasopharyngeal cancer often start?
hint: An eponymous fossa behind the torus tubarius.
why: It lies behind the auditory tube opening, so a one-sided middle ear effusion in an adult needs it checked.

q: Where does the auditory tube open?
model: On the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
hint: The top part of the pharynx.
why: It is surrounded by the torus tubarius, about 1 cm behind the inferior concha.

q: Why do children get more middle ear infections?
model: Their auditory tubes are shorter and more horizontal.
hint: Compare the tube's length and angle with adults.
why: Enlarged adenoids can also block the tube.

q: Name the three pharyngeal constrictor muscles.
why: They overlap like stacked cups and insert into the pharyngeal raphe.

q: Where do the pharyngeal constrictors insert?
model: The pharyngeal raphe at the back.
hint: A midline seam at the back.
why: It runs down the midline from the skull base.

q: Which part of the inferior constrictor forms the upper oesophageal sphincter?
why: Its fibres run horizontally from one side of the cricoid to the other.

q: Which longitudinal pharyngeal muscle is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
hint: It arises from the styloid process.
why: It is the only pharyngeal muscle not supplied by the vagus.

q: What is quinsy?
why: Pus collects between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor after tonsillitis.

q: Name a sign of quinsy.
acc: trismus / hot potato / uvula / drool / deviat
model: Trismus, "hot potato" voice, uvula pushed to the opposite side, drooling.
hint: Think of opening the mouth and the voice.
why: Trismus is from irritation of the medial pterygoid.

q: What type of epithelium lines the oropharynx?
why: It withstands friction from swallowed food; the nasopharynx has respiratory epithelium.

q: Which nerves form the pharyngeal plexus?
model: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves (plus sympathetic fibres).
hint: Two cranial nerves leaving through the jugular foramen.
why: IX is mainly sensory and X motor.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx?
hint: It also supplies the back third of the tongue.
why: It is the afferent of the gag reflex.

q: Why can tonsillitis cause earache?
acc: glossopharyngeal / ix / referred / tympanic / same nerve
model: Referred pain via the glossopharyngeal nerve, which also supplies the middle ear.
hint: One nerve supplies both the tonsil and the middle ear.
why: The vagus also has an auricular branch, so throat cancers can present with otalgia.

q: Which nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane?
model: The internal laryngeal nerve (with the superior laryngeal vessels).
hint: A sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
why: It passes through the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors.

q: Which structures pass above the superior constrictor?
model: The auditory tube and levator veli palatini.
hint: A tube and a palate muscle.
why: The superior constrictor stops short of the skull base.

q: Which nerve passes between the superior and middle constrictors?
why: It runs to the back of the tongue and tonsil.

q: Which nerve passes below the inferior constrictor into the larynx?
hint: It loops round a great vessel first.
why: It enters behind the cricothyroid joint.

q: What is the weak area between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus called?
why: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) herniates through it.

q: What is the main function of cricopharyngeus at rest?
acc: prevent / stop / air / reflux / closed / contracted
model: It stays contracted to stop air entering the oesophagus and reflux into the pharynx.
why: It relaxes only briefly during swallowing.

q: How far from the incisor teeth is the upper oesophageal sphincter?
hint: About the length of a pencil.
why: Useful for endoscopy; the lower sphincter is about 40 cm from the teeth.

q: Name the four parts of Waldeyer's ring.
model: Pharyngeal (adenoids), tubal, palatine and lingual tonsils.
hint: Nasopharynx roof, tube openings, oropharynx, tongue.
why: The ring guards the entrance to the airway and gut.

q: Enlarged adenoids cause which ear problem in children?
why: They block the auditory tube openings.

q: Which vein usually causes bleeding after tonsillectomy?
hint: A vein running beside the tonsil.
why: It lies in the tonsil bed; the tonsillar branch of the facial artery can also bleed.

q: Which node drains the palatine tonsil?
hint: At the angle of the mandible.
why: It enlarges in tonsillitis.

q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only complete ring?
why: It is shaped like a signet ring, taller at the back.

q: Which type of cartilage forms the epiglottis?
hint: It needs to bend back and forth.
why: The thyroid, cricoid and most of the arytenoids are hyaline and can calcify with age.

q: Which ligament forms the basis of the vocal cord?
model: The vocal ligament (upper edge of the conus elasticus).
hint: Part of the cricothyroid membrane's upper free edge.
why: It runs from the thyroid cartilage to the vocal process of the arytenoid.

q: At which joint does the thyroid cartilage tilt to tense the vocal cords?
hint: Between the two largest laryngeal cartilages.
why: The cricothyroid muscle tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, lengthening the cords.

q: Where is an emergency surgical airway made?
hint: The soft dip between two cartilages.
why: It lies below the vocal cords, is superficial and has few vessels.

q: At which vertebral level is the cricoid cartilage felt?
hint: The firm ring below the dip.
why: It marks the start of the trachea and oesophagus.

q: Which muscles close the laryngeal inlet?
model: The aryepiglottic and oblique arytenoid muscles (sphincter of the inlet).
hint: They run in the folds from the arytenoids to the epiglottis.
why: They draw the aryepiglottic folds together in swallowing.

q: Name a group of muscles that elevates the larynx in swallowing.
acc: suprahyoid / mylohyoid / digastric / geniohyoid / stylohyoid / thyrohyoid / stylopharyngeus / palatopharyngeus
model: The suprahyoid muscles (and thyrohyoid and longitudinal pharyngeal muscles).
why: Raising the larynx tucks it under the tongue base and tips the epiglottis over the inlet.

q: Which is the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords?
hint: It lies on the back of the cricoid.
why: Paralysis of both (bilateral RLN injury) leaves the cords near the midline, causing stridor.

q: Which muscle tenses the vocal cords to raise pitch?
hint: The only intrinsic muscle outside the larynx.
why: It is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, so injury gives a monotonous voice.

q: Which muscle shortens and relaxes the vocal cords?
hint: It runs from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid.
why: It lowers pitch and fine-tunes tension.

q: Why does the larynx close during heavy lifting?
acc: intrathoracic / intra abdominal / pressure / valsalva / fix
model: To raise intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure and fix the chest.
hint: Think of straining against a closed airway.
why: The same effort closure helps coughing, defecation and childbirth.

q: Name the three chambers of the larynx.
acc: vestibule / supraglottis + ventricle / sinus + infraglottic / subglottis
hint: Above, between and below the folds.
why: They are divided by the vestibular folds and vocal folds.

q: What is the gap between the vocal folds called?
why: It is the narrowest part of the adult airway.

q: What are the vestibular folds also called?
why: They lie above the true cords and help close the larynx.

q: What is the most important function of the larynx?
hint: Keeping food out of the lungs.
why: It acts as a sphincter in swallowing and triggers coughing.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation above the vocal cords?
why: It carries the afferent limb of the cough reflex.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation below the vocal cords?
hint: It loops round a great vessel.
why: It also supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid.

q: Which recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer and more often damaged?
hint: It goes further into the chest.
why: It loops under the aortic arch, so lung cancer and aortic aneurysms can compress it.

q: What happens if both recurrent laryngeal nerves are cut?
model: Both cords sit near the midline, causing stridor and airway obstruction.
why: It may need a tracheostomy.

q: Which nerve is at risk when tying the superior thyroid artery?
why: Injury weakens cricothyroid, causing a monotonous voice.

q: Which artery supplies the larynx above the vocal cords?
why: It comes from the superior thyroid artery (ECA).

q: Why do glottic cancers have a good prognosis?
model: The vocal folds have very little lymphatic drainage, and hoarseness makes them present early.
hint: Think about drainage and how soon symptoms appear.
why: Supraglottic cancers spread to nodes early.

q: During quiet breathing, are the vocal cords abducted or adducted?
why: In speech they are adducted (nearly closed) and vibrate.

q: During whispering, where does the glottis stay open?
model: A small gap at the back between the arytenoids.
why: The front of the cords close but air passes through the posterior gap without vibrating the cords.

q: Which part of the penis is the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum?
why: It carries the external urethral meatus and is very sensitive (dorsal nerve).

q: Which smooth muscle in the scrotum wrinkles the skin in the cold?
hint: It lies just under the scrotal skin.
why: Together with cremaster it pulls the testes closer to the body to keep them warm.

q: Which gland makes most of the volume of semen?
why: Their fluid is rich in fructose; the prostate adds ~30%.

q: Pain from the testis is often referred to which region?
hint: Think about where the testis develops.
why: The testis develops at the T10 level and its nerves come with the testicular artery; torsion can present as abdominal pain.

q: Which organ lies directly behind the prostate?
why: That's why the prostate is examined by DRE; Denonvilliers' fascia separates them.

q: The vas deferens crosses over which structure behind the bladder?
hint: It carries urine from the kidney.
why: The vas then widens into the ampulla behind the bladder.

q: What tissue surrounds the urethra in the penis?
why: It stays soft in erection so the urethra stays open for ejaculation.

q: Which arteries run in the centre of each corpus cavernosum?
why: Their helicine branches fill the erectile tissue during erection.

q: Which tough layer surrounds the corpora cavernosa?
why: Veins are squashed against it in erection; it tears in penile fracture.

q: Which fascia surrounds all three erectile bodies together?
why: The deep dorsal vein, dorsal arteries and nerves lie inside it.

q: Which vein runs in the midline on the dorsum of the penis inside Buck's fascia?
hint: The deeper of the two midline veins.
why: It drains under the pubic symphysis into the prostatic venous plexus.

q: On the dorsum of the penis, which structure is most lateral?
hint: Vein in the middle, then artery, then...
why: From the midline out: deep dorsal vein, dorsal artery, dorsal nerve.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the penis?
model: The dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal, S2–4).
hint: A branch of the nerve to the perineum.
why: It is blocked for circumcision (penile block).

q: From which artery do the arteries of the penis arise?
hint: A branch of the internal iliac artery.
why: It gives the dorsal, deep and bulbar arteries.

q: To which nodes does the skin of the penis drain?
why: The glans and erectile tissue drain to deep inguinal and internal iliac nodes.

q: Urine from a ruptured spongy urethra can spread into which areas?
model: The scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall.
hint: Think about where the superficial fascia continues.
why: It spreads under Colles' fascia, which is continuous with dartos and Scarpa's fascia.

q: Why does extravasated urine from the superficial perineal pouch not reach the thighs?
model: Colles' fascia is attached to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament.
hint: The deep fascia of the thigh.
why: It is also attached to the perineal membrane behind, so urine can't reach the anal triangle.

q: What separates the superficial and deep perineal pouches?
hint: A strong sheet across the urogenital triangle.
why: The superficial pouch lies below it and the deep pouch above it.

q: Blood at the urethral meatus after trauma means you should avoid what?
model: Urethral catheterisation (until urethral injury is excluded).
hint: A common bedside procedure for the bladder.
why: A catheter can turn a partial tear into a complete one.

q: To which nodes does the scrotal skin drain?
why: The testis drains to para-aortic nodes instead.

q: Which nerves supply the front of the scrotum?
model: The ilioinguinal and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerves (L1).
hint: L1 branches of the lumbar plexus.
why: The back is supplied by the pudendal (S3) and posterior femoral cutaneous nerves.

q: How does the pampiniform plexus help sperm production?
acc: cool / temperature / counter current / countercurrent / heat
model: It cools arterial blood going to the testis (counter-current exchange).
hint: Sperm production needs it a few degrees below core.
why: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2–3 °C below core.

q: Which structure in the spermatic cord feels like a firm cord?
why: It is felt at the back of the cord and is cut in vasectomy.

q: Which nerve in the spermatic cord supplies cremaster?
model: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
hint: It also supplies the skin of the front of the scrotum.
why: Stroking the inner thigh raises the testis (cremasteric reflex, L1–2); lost in torsion.

q: Which nerve runs in the inguinal canal outside the spermatic cord?
hint: Named after the ilium and the groin.
why: It is at risk in hernia repair, causing groin and scrotal numbness or pain.

q: Which spermatic fascia comes from the transversalis fascia?
why: External oblique gives the external spermatic fascia; internal oblique gives cremaster.

q: From which embryonic structure does the tunica vaginalis develop?
why: It is peritoneum carried down with the testis; if it stays open, hydroceles and indirect hernias form.

q: What is a collection of fluid in the tunica vaginalis called?
why: It transilluminates and you can get above it.

q: Which anatomical variant predisposes to testicular torsion?
hint: Named after part of a bell.
why: The tunica vaginalis surrounds the whole testis so it hangs free and can twist.

q: Which cells in the testis make testosterone?
why: They lie between the seminiferous tubules; Sertoli cells support sperm development.

q: Which tough capsule surrounds the testis?
why: Septa from it divide the testis into lobules.

q: Where do sperm mature and gain motility?
hint: Along the back of the testis.
why: It is a single coiled duct ~6 m long on the back of the testis.

q: At what level does the testicular artery arise from the aorta?
why: The testis develops near the kidneys and brings its artery down with it.

q: Into which vein does the right testicular vein drain?
hint: The largest vein in the abdomen.
why: The left drains into the left renal vein.

q: Which spinal level gives sympathetic supply to the testis?
why: Pain is therefore referred to the periumbilical region.

q: Why are varicoceles more common on the left?
acc: left renal / renal / right angle / longer
model: The left testicular vein is longer and enters the left renal vein at a right angle.
hint: Where does the left testicular vein end?
why: A new left varicocele in an older man can signal a renal tumour.

q: Why does testicular lymph drain to para-aortic rather than inguinal nodes?
acc: descen / develop / kidney / posterior abdominal / retroperitone / l2 / follow
model: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys and keeps its original lymph drainage when it descends.
hint: Think about where the testis starts in the embryo.
why: Its lymphatics run back up with the testicular vessels to the L1–2 level.

q: Within how many hours must testicular torsion be untwisted to save the testis?
why: Salvage rates fall sharply after this; both testes are fixed at surgery.

q: Why should a testicular tumour not be biopsied through the scrotum?
model: It could spread the tumour to the scrotal skin and its inguinal lymph nodes.
hint: Scrotal skin and testis drain to different nodes.
why: Removal is through an inguinal incision (orchidectomy).

q: Which zone of the prostate gives rise to most cancers?
why: It lies at the back and sides, so cancers are felt on DRE.

q: Which fascia separates the prostate from the rectum?
why: It is a barrier to tumour spread and a surgical plane.

q: Through which valveless venous plexus can prostate cancer reach the spine?
hint: An eponymous plexus around the spine.
why: It connects the prostatic venous plexus with the vertebral veins without valves.

q: Which enzyme from the prostate liquefies semen?
why: It leaks into the blood in prostate disease and is used as a marker.

q: How does a cancerous prostate feel on DRE?
model: Hard, irregular and craggy, often with a lost median sulcus.
hint: Compare with a smooth, rubbery gland.
why: BPH feels smooth, rubbery and enlarged.

q: Which midline feature of the prostate is lost in advanced cancer?
hint: The dip between the two lateral lobes.
why: It lies between the two lateral lobes and is usually still felt in BPH.

q: How does an enlarged prostate in BPH feel on DRE?
hint: Compare with a hard, craggy gland.
why: BPH starts in the transition zone around the urethra, so obstruction can be severe even if the gland feels only mildly enlarged.

q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system causes erection?
why: "Point and shoot": parasympathetic points, sympathetic shoots.

q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system causes emission?
why: It contracts the vas, seminal vesicles and prostate and closes the bladder neck.

q: Which muscle's rhythmic contractions expel semen during ejaculation?
hint: It covers the bulb of the penis.
why: It is supplied by the pudendal nerve (somatic).

q: Why can α-blockers cause retrograde ejaculation?
acc: bladder neck / internal sphincter / internal urethral
model: They relax the bladder neck (internal urethral sphincter).
why: Semen goes back into the bladder instead of out.

q: Which molecule relaxes cavernous smooth muscle to start an erection?
hint: A gas released by the cavernous nerves.
why: It raises cGMP; sildenafil blocks PDE5 so cGMP stays high.

q: Put the path of sperm in order from the testis.
model: Seminiferous tubules → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
why: Mnemonic SEVEN UP.

q: Which two ducts join to form the ejaculatory duct?
model: The vas deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle.
hint: One from the testis, one from a gland behind the bladder.
why: It runs through the prostate to open on the seminal colliculus.

q: Into which part of the urethra do the ejaculatory ducts open?
hint: The part surrounded by the prostate.
why: They open on the seminal colliculus.

q: Which part of the male urethra is the widest and most dilatable?
why: It contains the seminal colliculus.

q: Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter?
why: It passes through the deep perineal pouch and is torn in pelvic fractures.

q: In which pouch is the external urethral sphincter?
why: It lies above the perineal membrane.

q: Where do the bulbourethral glands lie?
why: Their ducts open into the proximal spongy urethra.

q: What do the bulbourethral glands secrete?
model: Mucus (pre-ejaculate) that lubricates and neutralises the urethra.
why: It protects sperm from acidic urine residue.

q: What is the female homologue of the bulbourethral glands?
hint: They can form cysts at the vaginal opening.
why: Both lubricate during arousal.

q: Which bone forms most of the orbital roof?
why: The lesser wing of the sphenoid completes it at the back.

q: Which orbital wall is paper-thin and spreads ethmoid sinusitis to the orbit?
model: The medial wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid).
hint: The wall next to the nose.
why: Orbital cellulitis in children often comes from ethmoid sinusitis.

q: Which orbital wall breaks in a blowout fracture, trapping inferior rectus?
why: It is thin maxilla; the patient can't look up and has a numb cheek (infraorbital nerve).

q: Which bone forms most of the lateral orbital wall?
model: The zygoma (with the greater wing of the sphenoid).
why: The lateral wall is the strongest.

q: Which cranial nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the tendinous ring?
model: The trochlear nerve (IV), with the lacrimal and frontal nerves.
why: Anaesthetic injected inside the cone of muscles may spare it.

q: Which vein passes through the superior orbital fissure?
hint: The upper vein of the orbit.
why: It drains to the cavernous sinus, a route for infection.

q: Between which two parts of the sphenoid is the superior orbital fissure?
model: Between the greater and lesser wings.
why: The optic canal lies in the lesser wing just above it.

q: Which nerve supplies lateral rectus?
why: "LR6 SO4, rest 3".

q: Which nerve supplies superior oblique?
why: "LR6 SO4, rest 3".

q: To test superior oblique, the patient looks in and then in which direction?
hint: Like looking at your nose then your feet.
why: In adduction the superior oblique acts as a pure depressor.

q: Which muscle raises the upper eyelid?
hint: It contains a smooth muscle part with sympathetic supply.
why: It is supplied by III, with a smooth muscle part (superior tarsal) supplied by sympathetics; loss causes ptosis.

q: Which extraocular muscle does not arise from the orbital apex?
why: It arises from the front of the orbital floor.

q: Which branch of V1 supplies the cornea?
model: The nasociliary nerve (via the long ciliary nerves).
hint: It also supplies the tip of the nose.
why: It carries the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

q: What does Hutchinson's sign predict in shingles?
hint: The nasociliary nerve supplies the nose tip and what else?
why: Vesicles on the tip of the nose mean the nasociliary nerve is involved, which also supplies the eye.

q: Which nerve is the efferent limb of the corneal reflex?
why: It closes the eye via orbicularis oculi; the afferent is V1.

q: Which branch of V1 supplies the forehead?
model: The frontal nerve (supraorbital and supratrochlear branches).
why: It runs just under the orbital roof.

q: Which fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
model: The fibres from the nasal half of each retina.
hint: The fibres from the half of the retina nearest the nose.
why: They see the temporal fields, so chiasmal compression gives bitemporal hemianopia.

q: Why does raised intracranial pressure cause papilloedema?
model: The optic nerve is surrounded by meninges and CSF, so the pressure is transmitted to the optic disc.
why: Venous return from the retina is impaired, causing disc swelling.

q: Which type of glial cell myelinates the optic nerve?
why: The optic nerve is really a CNS tract, so it is affected by MS (optic neuritis).

q: From which artery does the ophthalmic artery arise?
hint: It enters the skull through the carotid canal.
why: It is the first intracranial branch.

q: Occlusion of which artery causes sudden painless monocular blindness with a cherry-red spot?
hint: A branch of the ophthalmic artery running in the optic nerve.
why: It is an end artery running in the optic nerve.

q: Why can facial infections spread to the cavernous sinus?
why: Infection in the "danger triangle" of the face can travel back to the cavernous sinus.

q: Which nerve palsy causes a "down and out" eye with ptosis?
hint: It supplies most of the eye muscles.
why: Lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) pull the eye down and out unopposed.

q: Why does a PCom aneurysm cause a dilated pupil with a III palsy?
model: The pupillary (parasympathetic) fibres run on the outside of the nerve.
hint: Where do the parasympathetic fibres sit in the nerve?
why: Compression affects them first; diabetic (ischaemic) III palsy often spares the pupil.

q: Which nerve leaves the back of the brainstem and has the longest intracranial course?
why: Its long thin course makes it vulnerable in head injury.

q: A patient with diplopia going downstairs tilts their head. Which nerve is affected?
why: The superior oblique can't depress the adducted eye; head tilt away compensates.

q: Which nerve runs inside the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery?
why: It is often the first nerve affected by cavernous sinus disease.

q: Name the nerves in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
acc: iii / 3 / oculomotor + iv / 4 / trochlear + v1 / ophthalmic + v2 / maxillary
why: VI and the ICA lie inside the sinus.

q: A carotid–cavernous fistula causes which eye sign?
hint: The eye bulges in time with the pulse.
why: High-pressure arterial blood floods the cavernous sinus and backs up into the ophthalmic veins.

q: Where does the parasympathetic supply to the pupil synapse?
hint: A small ganglion lateral to the optic nerve.
why: Postganglionic fibres travel in the short ciliary nerves to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.

q: What is a tonic (Adie's) pupil?
model: A large pupil reacting slowly to light due to ciliary ganglion damage.
hint: Damage to the ganglion behind the eye.
why: It reacts better to near than to light.

q: Which nerves carry postganglionic fibres from the ciliary ganglion to the eye?
why: The long ciliary nerves carry sensory and sympathetic fibres.

q: A pituitary tumour compressing the chiasm causes which field defect?
why: It damages the crossing nasal fibres.

q: A lesion of the right optic tract causes which field defect?
hint: The same half of the field in both eyes.
why: The right tract carries the left visual field from both eyes.

q: A temporal lobe lesion affecting Meyer's loop causes which defect?
acc: upper quadrantanopia / superior quadrantanopia / pie in the sky / upper
model: A contralateral upper quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky").
hint: Which half of the field do the lower retinal fibres see?
why: Meyer's loop carries the lower retinal fibres, which see the upper field.

q: Why is the macula often spared in occipital (PCA) strokes?
acc: dual / mca / middle cerebral / two / both
model: The macular cortex has a dual blood supply (PCA and MCA).
hint: Think about the blood supply to the occipital pole.
why: So a PCA stroke gives homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

q: In which nucleus does the optic tract synapse?
why: Fibres then pass in the optic radiations to the visual cortex.

q: Where does aqueous humour drain from the eye?
model: Through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm at the iridocorneal angle.
hint: Where the iris meets the cornea.
why: Blockage raises intraocular pressure (glaucoma).

q: Which structure makes aqueous humour?
hint: It also contains the muscle of accommodation.
why: It flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber.

q: Which part of the retina gives the sharpest vision?
hint: A pit packed with cones only.
why: It has only cones, tightly packed.

q: What happens to the lens when the ciliary muscle contracts?
model: The zonules relax and the lens becomes rounder (for near vision).
why: This is accommodation, driven by parasympathetic fibres from III.

q: Which part of the eye provides most of its focusing power?
hint: The clear front of the eye.
why: The lens provides the adjustable part.

q: Which organelle makes proteins for secretion and is prominent in plasma cells?
why: Its ribosomes make proteins that enter the ER lumen for export; in neurons it appears as Nissl bodies.

q: Which organelle detoxifies drugs and makes steroids?
why: It expands with enzyme-inducing drugs (alcohol, rifampicin) and is abundant in hepatocytes and Leydig cells.

q: Defects in which organelle's enzymes cause Tay–Sachs and Gaucher disease?
why: Missing acid hydrolases let undigested material build up (lysosomal storage diseases).

q: Why are mitochondrial diseases inherited from the mother?
model: Mitochondria in the embryo come from the egg; sperm mitochondria are destroyed.
hint: Which gamete gives the embryo its cytoplasm?
why: Examples include MELAS and Leber's optic neuropathy; severity depends on the proportion of faulty mitochondria (heteroplasmy).

q: Which organelle breaks down very-long-chain fatty acids?
why: Defects cause Zellweger syndrome and adrenoleukodystrophy.

q: Why can antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes without harming human ones?
model: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, human ones are 80S.
why: Aminoglycosides, macrolides and tetracyclines bind the bacterial subunits (selective toxicity).

q: Which organelle adds mannose-6-phosphate to send enzymes to lysosomes?
why: Failure (I-cell disease) means the enzymes are secreted instead.

q: Defective cilia (microtubules) cause which syndrome with sinusitis, infertility and situs inversus?
why: Dynein arm defects stop cilia beating, so mucus isn't cleared and sperm can't swim.

q: Antibodies against desmoglein in desmosomes cause which blistering disease?
why: Cells lose their attachments to each other, giving fragile blisters; antibodies against hemidesmosomes cause bullous pemphigoid.

q: Which membrane channel is faulty in cystic fibrosis?
why: Thick secretions block airways, pancreatic ducts and the vas deferens.

q: Which junctions allow ions to pass directly between cardiac muscle cells?
why: They let the action potential spread so the heart contracts together.

q: Which intermediate filament is a marker of epithelial tumours?
hint: Also found in hair and nails.
why: Vimentin marks mesenchymal tumours, desmin muscle, GFAP glial tumours.

q: Which bacterial structure do penicillins target?
why: Human cells have no cell wall, so penicillins are selectively toxic.

q: How does Mycobacterium tuberculosis survive inside macrophages?
model: It stops the phagosome fusing with lysosomes.
why: So it isn't digested and can persist in granulomas.

q: Which type of diarrhoea stops when the patient fasts?
model: Osmotic diarrhoea stops on fasting; secretory continues.
hint: Something in the gut lumen is pulling water in.
why: Unabsorbed solutes (e.g. lactose, laxatives) hold water in the lumen by osmosis. Remove them by fasting and the diarrhoea stops; secretory diarrhoea is driven by active ion secretion, so it carries on.

q: Name a stool test that helps tell IBD from IBS.
model: Faecal calprotectin is raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
hint: A neutrophil protein measured in faeces.
why: Calprotectin comes from neutrophils, so it rises when the bowel wall is inflamed (IBD, infection) but stays normal in functional IBS.

q: Which channel is driven open by cholera toxin to cause secretory diarrhoea?
model: Cholera toxin keeps Gs on → ↑ cAMP → CFTR Cl⁻ secretion; water follows.
hint: The chloride channel that's faulty in cystic fibrosis.
why: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs so it stays active; cAMP rises and CFTR pumps chloride into the lumen, with sodium and water following.

q: Why is loperamide avoided in bloody diarrhoea with fever?
acc: dysentery / invasive / toxic megacolon / toxin / keeps
model: It slows transit, keeping invasive organisms and toxins in the gut (risk of toxic megacolon).
hint: Think about what the gut is trying to flush out.
why: Antimotility drugs stop the gut flushing out invasive organisms and their toxins, which can worsen colitis and precipitate toxic megacolon.

q: First-line oral treatment for C. difficile?
model: Oral vancomycin; fidaxomicin second line. Stop the culprit antibiotic and PPIs.
hint: An oral glycopeptide that isn't absorbed from the gut.
why: Vancomycin given orally isn't absorbed, so it reaches high concentrations in the colon where C. difficile lives; IV vancomycin doesn't reach the gut lumen.

q: Which electrolyte does the colon secrete, explaining why diarrhoea causes its loss?
model: The colon secretes K⁺, so diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia.
hint: Low levels cause U waves and flat T waves.
why: Colonic cells secrete potassium (more so under aldosterone), so large-volume diarrhoea drains K⁺ and causes hypokalaemia.

q: Where in the gut are vitamin B12 and bile salts absorbed?
hint: The last part of the small bowel.
why: The terminal ileum carries the receptors for the B12–intrinsic factor complex and the transporters that reclaim bile salts, so ileal resection or Crohn's affects both.

q: Which transporter absorbs glucose with sodium in the small intestine?
model: SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled); fructose uses GLUT5; both exit via GLUT2.
hint: The reason oral rehydration solution contains salt and sugar together.
why: SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to pull glucose in; each glucose brings sodium (and water) with it, which is why oral rehydration solution combines the two.

q: Which plasma protein provides most of the oncotic pressure?
hint: Made by the liver; low in nephrotic syndrome.
why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and too large to leave capillaries easily, so it generates most of the colloid osmotic pressure.

q: Name a cause of oedema due to low oncotic pressure.
acc: nephrotic / cirrhosis / liver / malnutrition / protein-losing / hypoalbuminaemia
model: Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy.
hint: Think about where albumin is lost, or not made.
why: Low albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid filters out into tissues: lost in the urine (nephrotic), not made (cirrhosis) or not built (malnutrition).

q: Which glands in the duodenal submucosa identify it histologically?
hint: Alkaline mucus glands named after a Swiss anatomist.
why: Brunner's glands secrete alkaline mucus to neutralise acid arriving from the stomach; their submucosal position is unique to the duodenum.

q: Which spirometry ratio confirms airflow obstruction?
hint: Volume blown out in one second over the total.
why: Obstruction slows how fast air leaves, so FEV1 falls more than FVC and the ratio drops below 0.7; restriction lowers both, keeping the ratio normal.

q: Which pneumocytes produce surfactant?
hint: The cuboidal ones, not the flat gas-exchange cells.
why: Type II cells make surfactant, which lowers surface tension so small alveoli don't collapse; type I cells are thin for gas exchange.

q: Name the enzyme imbalance behind emphysema.
hint: Too much breakdown enzyme, too little inhibitor.
why: Neutrophil elastase from smoke-driven inflammation digests elastin in alveolar walls; α1-antitrypsin normally neutralises it, so the balance tips towards destruction.

q: Which type of emphysema is linked to α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
model: Panacinar, lower lobes (centriacinar, upper lobes, in smokers).
hint: Affects the whole acinus, mainly the lower lobes.
why: Without the inhibitor, damage hits whole acini evenly and is worst where blood flow is greatest (the bases); smoking damage starts centrally in the upper lobes.

q: Which two inhaler classes are combined at step 2 in COPD without asthmatic features?
why: When one long-acting bronchodilator isn't enough and there are no asthmatic features, NICE adds the other class (LABA plus LAMA) rather than a steroid.

q: Which inhaled drug class raises pneumonia risk in COPD?
hint: The anti-inflammatory added for triple therapy.
why: Inhaled steroids suppress local airway immunity, so COPD patients on ICS have more pneumonia; that's why ICS is reserved for asthmatic features or frequent exacerbations.

q: In what form is most CO₂ carried in blood?
model: ~70% as bicarbonate; also carbamino compounds and dissolved.
hint: Carbonic anhydrase makes it inside red cells.
why: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells rapidly turns CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H⁺ (buffered by haemoglobin) and bicarbonate that moves into plasma.

q: What acid–base disorder does vomiting cause?
model: Metabolic alkalosis (loss of HCl), with hypokalaemia.
why: Vomiting loses HCl, leaving bicarbonate unopposed; volume loss then drives aldosterone, which wastes K⁺ and H⁺ and keeps the alkalosis going.

q: Name a cause of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
acc: dka / ketoacidosis / lactic / lactate / uraemia / methanol / ethylene glycol / salicylate / aspirin
model: DKA, lactic acidosis, uraemia, toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates).
why: A high anion gap means an unmeasured acid has been added (ketones, lactate, uraemic acids, toxins), consuming bicarbonate without raising chloride.

q: Name a factor that shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
acc: co2 / carbon dioxide / acid / h+ / temperature / heat / 2,3 / bpg / dpg / exercise
hint: The Bohr effect: conditions in busy tissue.
why: Active tissues are warm, acidic and full of CO₂; these conditions lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it releases more where it's needed.

q: Why does pulse oximetry mislead in carbon monoxide poisoning?
acc: carboxy / cohb / reads / normal / can't distinguish / cannot distinguish
model: It reads COHb as oxyhaemoglobin, so sats look normal. Use co-oximetry.
hint: The probe can't tell oxyhaemoglobin from another bound form.
why: Standard oximeters use two wavelengths and can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ looks normal while oxygen delivery is poor.

q: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which roots?
hint: "Three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive."
why: The diaphragm develops in the neck and descends, taking its nerve supply from C3–5 with it, which is why high cervical injuries stop breathing.

q: How do you calculate alveolar ventilation?
hint: Subtract the air that never reaches the alveoli.
why: Only air reaching the alveoli takes part in gas exchange, so the dead-space portion of each breath is subtracted before multiplying by the rate.

q: Name the three levels of prevention.
hint: Before disease, early detection, limiting harm.
why: Primary prevention stops disease starting (vaccines), secondary finds it early (screening), tertiary limits harm once established (rehab).

q: Name the two main causes of peptic ulcer disease.
hint: One bacterium and one class of painkiller.
why: H. pylori damages the mucosa and raises acid; NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that maintain mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow.

q: Name a non-invasive test for H. pylori.
acc: urea breath / breath / stool antigen / stool
model: Urea breath test or stool antigen test (stop PPI 2 weeks before).
hint: One you blow into a bag after a labelled drink; one is a faecal sample.
why: H. pylori's urease splits labelled urea into labelled CO₂ that you breathe out; the stool test detects bacterial antigen. PPIs suppress the bacteria and cause false negatives.

q: How does H. pylori in the antrum lead to duodenal ulcers?
hint: It damages the antral D cells that act as a brake.
why: Antral infection kills somatostatin-producing D cells, removing the brake on gastrin; more gastrin means more acid pouring into the duodenum.

q: What is UK first-line H. pylori eradication therapy?
model: 7 days of PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole.
why: A PPI raises gastric pH so the antibiotics work better, and two antibiotics reduce resistance; clarithromycin or metronidazole is chosen by allergy and previous use.

q: Which enzyme do PPIs block?
hint: The final step of secretion in parietal cells.
why: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the final common step of acid secretion, so blocking it stops acid whatever the stimulus (histamine, gastrin or vagal).

q: Which area of the brain detects drugs and toxins to trigger vomiting?
hint: Outside the blood–brain barrier, in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
why: The area postrema lies outside the blood–brain barrier, so it can sample blood for toxins and drugs and relay to the vomiting centre via dopamine and 5-HT3.

q: Which gastric cells make acid and intrinsic factor?
hint: Lost in pernicious anaemia; found in the gastric body.
why: Parietal cells make both, which is why autoimmune gastritis against them causes low acid and B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).

q: Which brush-border enzyme activates trypsinogen?
hint: A duodenal enzyme; its older name ends in -kinase.
why: Enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes; activation happens in the gut, not the pancreas.

q: What is the metaplasia seen in Barrett's oesophagus?
model: Squamous → columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).
hint: The squamous lining is replaced by the type lining the bowel.
why: Chronic acid reflux makes the squamous lining change to acid-resistant intestinal-type columnar cells, which can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

q: Name the characteristic cell of diffuse gastric cancer.
hint: Mucin pushes the nucleus to one side.
why: Diffuse gastric cancer cells fill with mucin that pushes the nucleus aside, and they infiltrate the wall to make it rigid (linitis plastica).

q: Which two-level score guides DVT investigation?
model: Two-level Wells score: D-dimer if unlikely, USS if likely.
hint: Also used for PE; named after a Canadian.
why: Wells sorts DVT as likely or unlikely: unlikely gets a D-dimer first (a negative rules it out), likely goes straight to ultrasound.

q: At what point after starting IV antibiotics should they be reviewed?
model: At 48–72 hours (stop, switch IV to oral, narrow, continue).
hint: Start Smart then Focus: after two to three days.
why: By 48–72 hours cultures are back and the patient's course is clearer, so you can stop, switch IV to oral, narrow or continue (Start Smart then Focus).

q: Name a mediator of acute inflammation that causes vasodilation.
acc: histamine / prostaglandin / no / nitric oxide / bradykinin
hint: Released by mast cells, or made from arachidonic acid.
why: Vasodilation increases blood flow (redness, heat); histamine acts immediately, prostaglandins and NO sustain it.

q: Which precautions and mask are needed for suspected TB?
model: Airborne precautions with an FFP3 respirator and negative-pressure room.
hint: Spread by droplet nuclei that hang about for hours.
why: TB spreads on tiny droplet nuclei that stay airborne, so a fitted FFP3 respirator and a negative-pressure room are needed rather than a surgical mask.

q: Why use soap and water rather than alcohol gel for C. difficile?
hint: Alcohol doesn't kill its resistant form.
why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol can't kill; washing with soap and water physically removes them from the hands.

q: Where do T cells mature?
why: T cells are selected in the thymus: positive selection keeps those that recognise self-MHC, negative selection deletes strongly self-reactive ones.

q: Which organism causes most cellulitis and impetigo?
hint: Gram-positive cocci in clusters or chains.
why: Both are skin-colonising Gram-positive cocci; impetigo is often Staph aureus, cellulitis usually Strep pyogenes.

q: What is first-pass metabolism?
model: Metabolism in the gut wall and liver before the drug reaches the systemic circulation.
hint: Oral drugs travel via the portal vein first.
why: Oral drugs pass through the gut wall and then the liver via the portal vein before reaching the circulation, so some is metabolised first (e.g. GTN is given sublingually).

q: Which cells kill virus-infected cells lacking MHC class I?
hint: Innate lymphocytes that check for "missing self".
why: NK cells kill cells that have lost MHC class I ("missing self"), a trick viruses and tumours use to hide from cytotoxic T cells.

q: Where does the thoracic duct drain?
acc: left venous angle / left subclavian / left internal jugular / left
model: Into the left venous angle (left subclavian/internal jugular junction).
hint: The junction of the internal jugular and subclavian, on one side.
why: The thoracic duct carries lymph from most of the body and empties where the left internal jugular joins the left subclavian vein.

q: Which white cell has a bilobed nucleus and red granules?
hint: Raised in allergy and parasite infections.
why: Eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and granules containing major basic protein; they rise in allergy, asthma and parasitic infection.

q: Which cytokine drives CRP production?
hint: The main cytokine acting on the liver in the acute phase.
why: IL-6 from macrophages travels to the liver and switches on acute-phase proteins, including CRP.

q: What complex forms pores in bacterial membranes?
hint: The terminal complement components assemble into it.
why: The terminal components C5b–C9 assemble into a pore that lets water in and lyses the cell; deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infection.

q: Name the three complement pathways.
hint: One antibody-triggered, one sugar-binding, one always ticking over.
why: Classical is triggered by antibody–antigen complexes, lectin by mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars, alternative by spontaneous C3 activation on surfaces.

q: What does the "inverse care law" state?
model: Those most in need of care get the least of it.
hint: Tudor Hart's observation about where good care ends up.
why: Tudor Hart noted that good care tends to be least available where it's most needed (deprived areas), because of market forces.

q: Name the criteria used to call a pleural effusion an exudate.
hint: Compares pleural and serum protein and LDH.
why: Light's criteria call an effusion an exudate if pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >⅔ of the upper normal limit.

q: Immediate treatment of a tension pneumothorax?
model: Needle or finger decompression, then a chest drain.
hint: Second intercostal space, midclavicular, or the fifth space.
why: Tension physiology (rising pressure, falling venous return) kills before an X-ray can be done, so decompress first, then place a definitive drain.

q: How does a competitive antagonist change the dose–response curve?
model: Shifts it to the right with the same maximum (surmountable).
hint: Same maximum effect, but you need more agonist.
why: A competitive antagonist binds the same site reversibly, so enough agonist can outcompete it: the curve moves right but the maximum is unchanged.

q: Which chemoreceptors drive most of the ventilatory response to CO₂?
model: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla (via CSF H⁺).
hint: They sense CSF pH in the brainstem.
why: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and lowers CSF pH, which central chemoreceptors sense; they account for most of the response to CO₂, while peripheral ones sense hypoxia.

q: Name a drug with zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
hint: An antiepileptic, or a common social drug.
why: Zero-order drugs saturate their enzymes, so a fixed amount is cleared per hour and small dose increases can cause big rises in level (phenytoin toxicity).

q: Which pharmacokinetic value determines the loading dose?
hint: The apparent space a drug spreads into.
why: The loading dose has to fill the volume the drug distributes into (dose = target concentration × Vd); clearance sets the maintenance dose.

q: Name the asbestos-related malignancy of the pleura.
hint: Long latency; not a lung carcinoma.
why: Mesothelioma arises from the pleura decades after asbestos exposure; asbestos also raises lung cancer risk, especially with smoking.

q: Name Parsons' model of the obligations of a patient.
hint: The rights and duties of being unwell.
why: Parsons said the sick are excused normal duties but are obliged to want to get well and to seek and cooperate with medical help.

q: Which nerve should you check before and after reducing a shoulder dislocation?
model: The axillary nerve (regimental badge area, deltoid).
hint: Check the "regimental badge" patch of skin.
why: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and is stretched in dislocation; check sensation over the "regimental badge" before and after.

q: Which nerve is at risk in a humeral shaft fracture?
hint: Runs in the spiral groove; injury gives wrist drop.
why: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove against the humeral shaft, so a fracture there can cause wrist drop.

q: Which collagen type is found in hyaline cartilage?
hint: One more than the type in bone.
why: Type II collagen gives hyaline cartilage its tensile framework; bone, tendon and skin are mainly type I.

q: What change in cartilage starts osteoarthritis?
model: Proteoglycan loss and fibrillation of cartilage.
hint: Loss of the water-holding molecules, then surface splitting.
why: Losing proteoglycans means cartilage holds less water and loses its springiness; the surface then splits (fibrillation) and wears down.

q: Name the four stages of fracture healing.
model: Haematoma/inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling.
hint: A blood clot, two kinds of callus, then reshaping.
why: Bleeding forms a haematoma and inflammation, fibrocartilage forms a soft callus, woven bone makes a hard callus, then remodelling restores lamellar bone.

q: Which skin layer contains melanocytes and stem cells?
hint: The deepest layer of the epidermis.
why: The stratum basale is the dividing layer: stem cells (keratinocytes) and melanocytes sit there, on the basement membrane.

q: Name a regional block for forearm fracture reduction.
model: Bier's block (IV regional) or haematoma block.
hint: IV regional anaesthesia with a cuff, named after a surgeon.
why: Bier's block injects local anaesthetic IV below a cuff to numb the whole limb; a haematoma block injects straight into the fracture site.

q: What does PICO stand for?
hint: Who, what, versus what, and what you measure.
why: PICO turns a clinical question into a searchable one: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.

q: What investigation should every patient with syncope have?
why: An ECG can show dangerous causes of syncope, such as heart block, long QT, Brugada, WPW or ischaemia, cheaply and quickly.

q: Name a red flag feature of syncope.
acc: exertion / exercise / lying / supine / ecg / murmur / family history / sudden death / heart failure
model: Exertional or supine syncope, abnormal ECG, new murmur, FHx sudden death, heart failure.
hint: Think of circumstances that point to a cardiac cause.
why: Syncope on exertion or lying down, with palpitations, a murmur, an abnormal ECG or family history of sudden death, suggests a cardiac cause needing urgent assessment.

q: First-line investigation for stable chest pain (NICE)?
acc: ct coronary / ctca / ct angiography / ct
hint: A non-invasive scan of the heart's arteries.
why: NICE uses CT coronary angiography first because it has a very high negative predictive value and shows anatomy directly.

q: Which blood test confirms myocardial infarction?
hint: A cardiac muscle protein, measured high-sensitivity.
why: Troponin is released from damaged myocytes; a rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile with ischaemic features confirms MI.

q: Which heart block has progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat?
acc: mobitz i / mobitz 1 / wenckebach / mobitz type 1
hint: Second-degree, type I, with an eponym.
why: In Mobitz I the AV node tires a little more with each beat until one P wave isn't conducted; it's usually nodal and benign.

q: What ECG pattern defines atrial fibrillation?
model: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves.
hint: Think about rhythm regularity and atrial activity.
why: Chaotic atrial activity replaces organised P waves, and the AV node conducts randomly, so QRS complexes are irregularly irregular.

q: Which coronary artery supplies the AV node in most people?
hint: The reason inferior MIs cause heart block.
why: The AV nodal artery usually comes from the RCA, so inferior MIs (RCA) often cause heart block.

q: Which heart sound marks closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves?
why: S2 is the closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole; splitting widens with inspiration as right-sided filling increases.

q: What generates the pacemaker potential in the SA node?
hint: An oddly named inward current, blocked by ivabradine.
why: HCN channels open at negative voltages and let in a slow inward Na⁺ current, so the membrane drifts up to threshold automatically; ivabradine blocks it.

q: Where are the arterial baroreceptors?
hint: Two places: the carotid bifurcation and the top of the aorta.
why: Carotid sinus receptors signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve and aortic arch receptors via the vagus to the medulla, adjusting heart rate and vascular tone.

q: When do neutrophils first infiltrate after an MI?
why: Neutrophils arrive from about 24 hours and peak at 1–3 days, followed by macrophages; this timeline is used to date infarcts.

q: Nerve conduction in demyelinating neuropathy shows?
model: Slowed conduction velocity and conduction block.
hint: Myelin speeds signals up, so lose it and...
why: Myelin lets impulses jump between nodes; demyelination slows conduction velocity and can block conduction, whereas axonal loss mainly reduces amplitude.

q: Which organism classically triggers Guillain–Barré syndrome?
hint: A curved Gram-negative gut bacterium from undercooked chicken.
why: Campylobacter jejuni carries antigens that mimic gangliosides on peripheral nerves, so antibodies made against it attack myelin (molecular mimicry).

q: What should you monitor to spot respiratory failure in GBS?
hint: A spirometry volume, not oxygen sats.
why: Falling FVC shows diaphragm weakness before oxygen sats drop; an FVC below about 20 mL/kg calls for ICU review.

q: What CSF finding is typical of GBS?
model: High protein with normal cell count.
hint: Cells normal, but something else is raised.
why: Albuminocytological dissociation: protein rises from nerve root inflammation while the cell count stays normal (often only after the first week).

q: Acute treatment for a cluster headache attack?
hint: High-flow gas plus a subcutaneous drug.
why: High-flow 100% oxygen and subcutaneous or nasal triptans work fast enough for short, intense attacks; oral drugs act too slowly.

q: Name a migraine prophylactic drug.
hint: A beta-blocker, an antiepileptic or a tricyclic.
why: Propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline reduce attack frequency; topiramate is teratogenic, so avoid it in women who could become pregnant.

q: Which ion flows in to depolarise a neuron during an action potential?
hint: Its channels are blocked by local anaesthetics.
why: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and sodium rushes in down its gradient, depolarising the membrane; K⁺ outflow then repolarises it.

q: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres?
model: III, VII, IX and X (plus S2–4).
why: Cranial parasympathetic outflow travels in III (pupil), VII (tears, saliva), IX (parotid) and X (thoracic and abdominal organs); sacral outflow is S2–4.

q: Which receptor mediates bronchodilation?
why: β2-adrenoceptors on airway smooth muscle raise cAMP and relax it, which is why β2 agonists treat asthma and non-selective β-blockers can trigger bronchospasm.

q: What neurotransmitter do sympathetic nerves to sweat glands release?
hint: The exception: the same as the parasympathetic transmitter.
why: Sympathetic fibres to sweat glands are the exception: they release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors, which is why anticholinergics stop sweating.

q: Upper age limit for walking independently?
why: Most children walk by 12–15 months; not walking by 18 months is a red flag for motor delay, muscle disease or cerebral palsy.

q: Which hand preference age is a red flag?
why: Handedness normally isn't established until about 18 months to 2 years; an early preference suggests weakness of the other hand (e.g. hemiplegic cerebral palsy).

q: Name a fracture pattern suggestive of non-accidental injury.
hint: Chest wall injuries in infants, or classic injuries at the ends of long bones.
why: Posterior rib fractures come from squeezing the chest, and metaphyseal corner fractures from shaking or twisting; neither fits accidental falls in infants.

q: What does jaundice in the first 24 hours of life suggest?
model: Always pathological: haemolysis (ABO/Rh, G6PD) or sepsis.
why: Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours; jaundice in the first day means bilirubin is rising fast, usually from haemolysis or sepsis.

q: An absent red reflex in a newborn may mean?
hint: A lens opacity, or an eye tumour.
why: The red reflex needs a clear path through the lens and a normal retina; cataract or retinoblastoma blocks it and needs urgent ophthalmology.

q: Name a core principle of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
acc: best interests / non-discrimination / heard / life / survival
model: Best interests, non-discrimination, right to life and development, right to be heard.
hint: One of four general principles, e.g. what's best for the child.
why: The UNCRC's four general principles are non-discrimination, best interests, the right to life and development, and the right to be heard.

q: What forms during gastrulation?
acc: trilaminar / three germ / ectoderm / mesoderm / endoderm
model: The trilaminar disc: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm.
why: Gastrulation turns the bilaminar disc into three germ layers: ectoderm (nervous system, skin), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood) and endoderm (gut lining).

q: Which structure induces neurulation?
why: The notochord signals to the overlying ectoderm (e.g. via sonic hedgehog) to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube.

q: Name an autosomal recessive condition.
acc: cystic fibrosis / cf / sickle / thalassaemia / pku / haemochromatosis
model: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, β-thalassaemia, PKU, haemochromatosis.
hint: Classic examples affect the lungs and pancreas, or haemoglobin.
why: Recessive conditions need two faulty copies, so carriers are healthy and the risk for each child of two carriers is 1 in 4.

q: Paternal deletion at 15q11–13 causes which syndrome?
hint: Hyperphagia and floppiness (maternal deletion gives Angelman).
why: Genes at 15q11–13 are imprinted: losing the paternal copy gives Prader–Willi, losing the maternal copy gives Angelman.

q: What hypothesis explains inherited tumour-suppressor cancers?
hint: Retinoblastoma: one copy inherited, one acquired.
why: Both copies of a tumour-suppressor gene must be lost; inherited cases are born with one hit, so they need only one more, giving earlier and bilateral tumours.

q: Painless visible haematuria in an adult should be treated as what until proven otherwise?
why: Bladder cancer classically presents with painless visible haematuria, so adults are referred on a suspected cancer pathway even if the bleeding stops.

q: Which two investigations make up a haematuria clinic assessment?
model: Flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging (CT urogram).
hint: Look inside the bladder, and image the upper tracts.
why: Cystoscopy inspects the bladder lining directly, and CT urography images the kidneys and ureters for upper-tract tumours or stones.

q: Biggest risk factor for bladder cancer?
hint: The same as for lung cancer.
why: Carcinogens from tobacco are excreted in urine and sit in contact with the bladder lining; smoking roughly triples the risk.

q: Which intravesical treatment is used for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
why: BCG instilled into the bladder stimulates a local immune response that reduces recurrence and progression of high-grade superficial tumours.

q: Gold-standard imaging for renal colic?
why: Non-contrast CT KUB detects almost all stones, gives their size and position, and shows other causes of pain.

q: Emergency treatment for an obstructed, infected kidney?
model: Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or JJ stent) + IV antibiotics.
hint: Drain it urgently, from above or below.
why: Pus behind an obstruction won't clear with antibiotics alone and can cause urosepsis, so the kidney needs draining urgently.

q: Name two hormonal functions of the kidney.
acc: epo / erythropoietin / renin / vitamin d / calcitriol
hint: Think red cells, blood pressure and bones.
why: The kidney makes EPO in response to hypoxia, renin to control blood pressure, and activates vitamin D by 1α-hydroxylation, so CKD causes anaemia, hypertension and bone disease.

q: Where is most sodium and water reabsorbed?
hint: The first segment after the glomerulus.
why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, plus nearly all glucose and amino acids.

q: Which transporter do loop diuretics block?
model: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.
hint: In the thick ascending limb of the loop.
why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, which reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered sodium, making them the most powerful diuretics.

q: Name the three drugs in the "triple whammy" for AKI.
hint: A painkiller, a RAAS blocker and a water tablet.
why: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole, ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent, and diuretics reduce volume, so together they collapse glomerular filtration pressure.

q: Which nerve and roots control the external urethral sphincter?
hint: The same nerve that supplies the perineum.
why: The external sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–4), which is why sacral damage causes incontinence.

q: What is "operant conditioning"?
model: Learning by reinforcement or punishment of behaviour (Skinner).
why: In operant conditioning, behaviour followed by reward becomes more frequent and behaviour followed by punishment less frequent.

q: Waist-to-height ratio that indicates central adiposity?
hint: NICE: keep your waist below a simple fraction of your height.
why: A ratio of 0.5 or more ("keep your waist to less than half your height") signals central fat, which predicts cardiometabolic risk better than BMI.

q: Which gut hormone increases hunger before meals?
hint: Made by the stomach; rises when fasting.
why: Ghrelin from the stomach rises before meals and falls after eating, stimulating appetite via the hypothalamus.

q: Mutation of which receptor is the commonest monogenic cause of obesity?
hint: A hypothalamic receptor in the leptin pathway.
