why: MC4R sits downstream of leptin in the hypothalamus; loss of function removes the satiety signal, causing early-onset hyperphagia and obesity.

q: Name a GLP-1 receptor agonist licensed for weight loss.
why: GLP-1 agonists slow gastric emptying and act on hypothalamic satiety centres; semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (Wegovy) is licensed for weight loss.

q: Which bariatric operation is best for T2DM remission?
hint: The one that diverts food past the duodenum.
why: Bypassing the duodenum and speeding nutrients to the distal gut boosts incretin hormones, improving insulin secretion within days, beyond the effect of weight loss.

q: Name a sign of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
hint: Look at the Achilles, the knuckles and the cornea.
why: LDL receptor mutations cause very high LDL from birth, which deposits in tendons (xanthomata) and the cornea (arcus before 45).

q: How do statins lower LDL?
hint: They block the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
why: Blocking HMG-CoA reductase lowers liver cholesterol, so liver cells make more LDL receptors and pull LDL out of the blood.

q: Main determinant of basal metabolic rate?
hint: What makes up most of your body that isn't fat.
why: Muscle and organs use far more energy at rest than fat, so lean mass explains most of the variation in BMR between people.

q: Through how many degrees does the midgut rotate?
why: The midgut herniates into the cord and rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA before returning; malrotation predisposes to volvulus.

q: What is the "rule of 2s" condition from the vitelline duct?
why: Meckel's diverticulum: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric, pancreatic), often presents before age 2.

q: Name the stages of change model.
hint: From not thinking about it, through preparing, to keeping it up.
why: Prochaska and DiClemente's model: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (and relapse); match the intervention to the stage.

q: Which fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement?
why: A fall on an outstretched hand pushes the distal fragment dorsally, giving the "dinner fork" deformity; volar displacement is a Smith's fracture.

q: Where is tenderness in a scaphoid fracture?
hint: A hollow at the base of the thumb.
why: The scaphoid forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, so tenderness there suggests a fracture even if the first X-ray is normal.

q: Main complication of a scaphoid fracture?
model: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
why: Blood enters the scaphoid distally and flows backwards, so a waist fracture can cut off the proximal pole, causing AVN and non-union.

q: Which collagen dominates early tendon repair?
model: Type III, later replaced by type I.
hint: The type later replaced by type I.
why: Fibroblasts first lay down weaker type III collagen, which is gradually remodelled into stronger type I as the tendon matures.

q: Antibodies against what cause myasthenia gravis?
acc: acetylcholine receptor / achr / ach receptor / musk
hint: Postsynaptic nicotinic receptors at the NMJ.
why: Antibodies block and destroy postsynaptic ACh receptors, so fewer are available and transmission fails with repeated use (fatigable weakness).

q: What does botulinum toxin block?
hint: It acts on the presynaptic nerve terminal.
why: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins needed for vesicles to fuse, so ACh isn't released and muscles become flaccid.

q: Which drug treats malignant hyperthermia?
why: Malignant hyperthermia is uncontrolled calcium release through faulty ryanodine receptors; dantrolene blocks the receptor and stops the hypermetabolic crisis.

q: Which protein does calcium bind to start skeletal muscle contraction?
hint: Part of a complex on the thin filament, with tropomyosin.
why: Calcium binds troponin C, which moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites so myosin heads can attach and cross-bridge cycling begins.

q: What is the nocebo effect?
model: Negative expectations causing real adverse effects.
why: Expecting harm can produce real symptoms; telling patients about side effects can increase how often they're reported.

q: Name the four principles of medical ethics.
why: Beauchamp and Childress's four principles: respect autonomy, do good (beneficence), avoid harm (non-maleficence), and be fair (justice).

q: Which case set the standard for disclosure of material risks?
why: Montgomery (2015) replaced the doctor-centred Bolam standard for consent: doctors must disclose risks a reasonable patient, or this patient, would consider significant.

q: Which test defines breach of duty in negligence?
why: Bolam: a doctor isn't negligent if a responsible body of medical opinion would have acted the same way; Bolitho adds that the opinion must be logical.

q: Which conventions protect medical neutrality in conflict?
hint: A Swiss city, the Red Cross.
why: The Geneva Conventions protect the wounded, health workers and hospitals in armed conflict, and require care regardless of side.

q: Which scan confirms gestational age?
hint: First-trimester scan measuring the fetus from head to rump.
why: Crown–rump length between 10 and 14 weeks varies little between fetuses, so it dates the pregnancy most accurately and sets the due date.

q: First-line antihypertensive in pre-eclampsia?
why: Labetalol is effective and safe in pregnancy; nifedipine is the alternative (e.g. in asthma), and ACE inhibitors are avoided.

q: Treatment for eclampsia seizures?
hint: An electrolyte given IV, also used in severe asthma.
why: Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures better than antiepileptics; monitor reflexes, breathing and urine output for toxicity.

q: Name the "4 Ts" of postpartum haemorrhage.
why: Most PPH is from a uterus that doesn't contract (tone); the others are tears (trauma), retained placenta (tissue) and clotting problems (thrombin).

q: How many doctors must certify a termination under the Abortion Act?
why: The Abortion Act 1967 requires two registered medical practitioners to agree in good faith that the legal grounds are met (one in an emergency).

q: Which part of the brain links the nervous and endocrine systems?
why: The hypothalamus receives neural input and controls the pituitary through releasing hormones and direct nerve fibres, linking the two systems.

q: Where do steroid hormones bind?
hint: They're lipid-soluble, so they cross the membrane.
why: Steroids are lipid-soluble, so they cross the cell membrane and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors, which is why their effects are slower.

q: Which hormones does the posterior pituitary release?
hint: Two peptides made in the hypothalamus.
why: ADH and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic nuclei and transported down axons to the posterior pituitary, which stores and releases them.

q: What does progesterone do to the endometrium?
hint: Prepares it for implantation in the second half of the cycle.
why: After ovulation the corpus luteum's progesterone turns the thickened endometrium secretory, with glands and blood supply ready for implantation.

q: What triggers ovulation?
hint: A surge of a pituitary hormone.
why: Rising oestradiol from the dominant follicle switches from negative to positive feedback, causing an LH surge that triggers ovulation about 36 hours later.

q: Why does BP fall in the second trimester?
hint: Hormonal relaxation of the vessel walls.
why: Progesterone and nitric oxide relax vascular smooth muscle, so SVR falls and blood pressure dips in the second trimester, before returning to normal near term.

q: Which reflex drives the positive feedback of labour?
hint: Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin; an eponym.
why: The fetal head stretching the cervix sends signals that release oxytocin, causing stronger contractions and more stretch: a positive feedback loop.

q: Which joints does rheumatoid arthritis typically spare in the hand?
why: RA targets synovial joints of the MCPs, PIPs and wrists and typically spares the DIPs, which are typical in OA and psoriatic arthritis.

q: Name the X-ray signs of osteoarthritis.
model: LOSS: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts.
why: Cartilage loss narrows the joint space; bone responds with osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts (LOSS).

q: Name the inflamed synovial tissue that erodes joints in RA.
why: Pannus is inflamed, proliferating synovium that spreads over cartilage and erodes bone at the joint margins.

q: Which antibody is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
why: Anti-CCP is about 95% specific for RA and predicts erosive disease; rheumatoid factor is less specific.

q: First-line DMARD for RA?
hint: Weekly, with folic acid on another day.
why: Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD, given once weekly with folic acid on a different day to reduce side effects; monitor FBC and LFTs.

q: Which muscles stop the pelvis dropping in single-leg stance?
why: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip and hold the pelvis level when standing on one leg; weakness causes a Trendelenburg sign.

q: Name the metaplasia in a smoker's bronchus.
hint: The type of epithelium on skin.
why: Smoke irritation replaces ciliated columnar epithelium with tougher squamous epithelium, which loses mucociliary clearance and can progress to squamous carcinoma.

q: Name the CURB-65 criteria.
acc: confusion + urea + respiratory / rr + blood pressure / bp + 65 / age
hint: Each letter is a criterion, plus the number.
why: CURB-65 scores 1 for each: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, Age ≥65; higher scores mean higher mortality.

q: Name two "geriatric giants".
acc: falls / immobility / confusion / delirium / incontinence / iatrogenesis / polypharmacy
why: Isaacs' "giants" (immobility, instability/falls, incontinence, intellectual impairment/delirium, iatrogenesis) are common, have many causes and threaten independence.

q: Name the five Fried frailty criteria.
acc: weight loss + exhaustion + weak / grip + slow / walking + activity
model: Weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking, low activity.
hint: Shrinking, tiredness and three more physical measures.
why: Fried's frailty phenotype: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weak grip, slow walking and low activity; three or more means frail.

q: Which receptor does SARS-CoV-2 bind?
why: The spike protein binds ACE2 on respiratory epithelium, helped by the protease TMPRSS2, to enter cells.

q: Which drug reduced COVID-19 deaths in patients needing oxygen (RECOVERY)?
why: RECOVERY showed dexamethasone cut deaths in patients needing oxygen or ventilation by damping the inflammatory response, but not in those who didn't need oxygen.

q: How does aciclovir become active?
hint: A viral enzyme adds the first phosphate.
why: Aciclovir is phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase, so it's activated mainly in infected cells, then terminates viral DNA chains.

q: Mechanism of oseltamivir?
hint: Stops new virions leaving the cell surface.
why: Neuraminidase cuts new virions free from the host cell; blocking it traps them, which is why it works best started within 48 hours.

q: Which enzyme do retroviruses use to make DNA from RNA?
why: Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA, which then integrates into host DNA; NRTIs and NNRTIs target it.

q: What causes influenza pandemics?
why: Influenza has a segmented genome; when two strains infect the same host, segments swap (shift), producing a new subtype nobody is immune to.

q: Which vaccine is given to children as a nasal spray each year?
why: The live attenuated nasal flu vaccine is offered to children each year; it protects them and reduces spread to older relatives.

q: At what ages is the 6-in-1 vaccine given in infancy?
hint: Three doses a month apart, starting at two months.
why: The 6-in-1 (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Hib, hepatitis B) is given at 8, 12 and 16 weeks to build immunity before maternal antibody wanes.

q: How long must depressive symptoms last for a depressive episode?
why: ICD-11 and DSM need symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks to separate a depressive episode from normal low mood.

q: Name a screening tool for postnatal depression.
why: The EPDS is a 10-item self-report scale designed for the postnatal period; it avoids physical symptoms like tiredness that are normal after birth.

q: First-line drug class for moderate–severe depression?
why: SSRIs are as effective as older drugs, with fewer side effects and much lower toxicity in overdose; sertraline is often first choice.

q: Name a feature of serotonin syndrome.
acc: clonus / hyperthermia / agitation / hyperreflexia / diarrhoea / tremor
why: Excess serotonin causes a triad: mental-state change (agitation), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, sweating, diarrhoea) and neuromuscular excitability (clonus, hyperreflexia).

q: Which antidepressant class is most dangerous in overdose?
hint: The older class; look for a broad QRS.
why: TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, causing a broad QRS, arrhythmias and seizures; a few weeks' supply can be fatal.

q: Loss of dopamine in which pathway causes Parkinson's disease?
why: Dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra project to the striatum; losing them disrupts the basal ganglia loop, causing bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.

q: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory one in the brain?
why: GABA opens chloride channels (GABA-A) that hyperpolarise neurons; benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol enhance it.

q: Prevalence equals incidence multiplied by what?
why: Prevalence counts existing cases, so it depends on how often new cases arise (incidence) and how long they last (duration).

q: Name a non-medical source of support for mental health.
acc: mind / samaritans / social prescribing / peer / charity / self-help / citizens advice / hafal
model: Charities (Mind, Samaritans), social prescribing, peer support, self-help.
why: Non-medical support such as charities, peer groups and social prescribing addresses loneliness, finances and purpose, which drive many mental health problems.

q: How much more common is depression in women than men?
why: Depression is about twice as common in women, reflecting hormonal, psychosocial and reporting differences; men are less likely to seek help and more likely to die by suicide.

q: Which joint is classically affected first in gout?
acc: first mtp / 1st mtp / big toe / metatarsophalangeal
why: Urate crystallises most easily in cooler peripheral joints under stress, so the big toe MTP joint is the classic first site (podagra).

q: Name a drug that raises urate and can trigger gout.
model: Thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin.
why: Diuretics and low-dose aspirin reduce renal urate excretion, raising serum urate; ciclosporin does the same.

q: What crystals are seen in gout under polarised light?
hint: Think shape and the sign of birefringence.
why: Gout shows needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent under polarised light; pseudogout shows rhomboid, weakly positive crystals.

q: When should serum urate be rechecked after a flare?
model: At least 2 weeks after the flare (it can be normal during one).
hint: Levels can be falsely low during a flare.
why: Urate can fall during an acute attack as it's deposited in the joint, so a normal level then doesn't rule gout out; recheck once things settle.

q: Mechanism of allopurinol?
hint: Blocks the enzyme that makes uric acid.
why: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and then uric acid; blocking it lowers urate production.

q: First-line IV antibiotic for septic arthritis?
why: Staph aureus is the commonest cause of septic arthritis, so an anti-staphylococcal penicillin is first line, given after aspirating the joint for culture.

q: Name a technique for repairing cartilage defects.
acc: microfracture / chondrocyte / aci / maci / mosaicplasty / graft
hint: Drill the subchondral bone, or implant cultured cells.
why: Cartilage has no blood supply and heals poorly, so repair techniques either drill subchondral bone to release marrow cells or implant cultured chondrocytes.

q: Name the stress model based on appraisal.
hint: Stress depends on how you judge the threat and your ability to cope.
why: In Lazarus and Folkman's model, stress comes from appraisal: is this a threat (primary) and can I cope (secondary)? The same event stresses people differently.

q: Galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea suggests excess of which hormone?
hint: Normally kept in check by dopamine.
why: Prolactin stimulates milk production and suppresses GnRH, causing amenorrhoea; prolactinomas and dopamine antagonists are common causes.

q: Visual field defect from a pituitary tumour?
why: A pituitary tumour grows up into the optic chiasm and compresses the crossing nasal fibres, which carry the temporal visual fields of both eyes.

q: Commonest cause of hyperthyroidism in the UK?
why: In Graves' disease, antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism, a diffuse goitre and features unique to Graves' such as eye disease.

q: Serious side effect of carbimazole to warn about?
model: Agranulocytosis: report a sore throat or fever urgently.
hint: A sore throat and fever matter.
why: Carbimazole can suddenly stop neutrophil production; a sore throat or fever needs an urgent FBC, and the drug is stopped if neutrophils are low.

q: Screening test for Cushing's syndrome?
acc: dexamethasone suppression / dexamethasone / salivary / urinary free cortisol
model: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (or late-night salivary cortisol).
hint: An overnight test with a potent steroid.
why: Normally dexamethasone suppresses ACTH and cortisol overnight; in Cushing's syndrome cortisol stays high because production is autonomous.

q: Test that confirms adrenal insufficiency?
hint: A short synthetic ACTH stimulation test.
why: Synthetic ACTH (tetracosactide) should make the adrenals release cortisol; a poor rise confirms adrenal insufficiency.

q: Which electrolyte pattern does Addison's cause?
acc: low sodium / hyponatraemia / low na + high potassium / hyperkalaemia / high k
why: Without aldosterone the kidney loses sodium and retains potassium; cortisol deficiency adds hypotension and hypoglycaemia.

q: Two commonest causes of hypercalcaemia?
why: Outpatient hypercalcaemia is usually primary hyperparathyroidism, inpatient usually malignancy (bone metastases or PTH-related peptide).

q: First treatment for severe hypercalcaemia?
why: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and dehydration, which worsens it; saline restores volume and promotes calcium excretion, then bisphosphonates block bone resorption.

q: Where is vitamin D 1α-hydroxylated?
why: The liver makes 25-OH vitamin D, then the kidney adds the 1α hydroxyl to make active calcitriol, under PTH control; this is why CKD causes deficiency.

q: Which thyroid hormone is the active form?
why: The thyroid mainly secretes T4, which tissues convert to T3; T3 binds nuclear receptors with much higher affinity.

q: Which adrenal zone makes aldosterone?
why: The cortex runs glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens) from outside in: "salt, sugar, sex".

q: When is growth hormone mostly released?
why: GH is released in pulses, mostly during slow-wave sleep, which is why random levels are unhelpful and IGF-1 is used instead.

q: Strongest predictor of future suicide?
why: Previous self-harm raises the risk of suicide many times over, especially in the year after an episode.

q: Antidote for paracetamol overdose?
why: Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies NAPQI, the toxic paracetamol metabolite; it works best within 8 hours.

q: Treatment for a broad QRS in TCA overdose?
why: Sodium bicarbonate supplies sodium to overcome TCA blockade of cardiac sodium channels, and alkalinising reduces drug binding, narrowing the QRS.

q: Does NICE recommend risk scales to predict suicide?
model: No: do a needs-based psychosocial assessment instead.
why: Risk scales have poor predictive value and can falsely reassure, so NICE advises a needs-based psychosocial assessment instead.

q: Why can't individual suicide be predicted from risk factors?
acc: base rate / rare / low / predictive value / ppv
model: Low base rate gives poor positive predictive value.
hint: Consider how uncommon it is, even in high-risk groups.
why: Suicide is rare even in high-risk groups, so most people flagged as high risk won't die by suicide and some "low-risk" people will: the positive predictive value is low.

q: Name one of Durkheim's types of suicide.
hint: Too little or too much integration or regulation.
why: Durkheim linked suicide to social forces: egoistic (too little integration), altruistic (too much), anomic (too little regulation), fatalistic (too much).

q: Commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
why: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes most community-acquired pneumonia, which is why amoxicillin is first line.

q: Which atypical pneumonia causes hyponatraemia and deranged LFTs?
why: Legionella, from contaminated water systems, often causes hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, diarrhoea and confusion; test with urinary antigen.

q: Which TB blood test isn't affected by BCG?
hint: Measures T cells releasing a cytokine.
why: IGRAs measure interferon-γ released by T cells exposed to TB-specific antigens that BCG lacks, so vaccination doesn't cause false positives as it can with the Mantoux test.

q: Antibiotic for low-severity CAP?
why: Low-severity CAP (CURB-65 0–1) is usually pneumococcal and treated at home with 5 days of oral amoxicillin; doxycycline or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic.

q: Which TB drug causes optic neuritis?
why: Ethambutol can cause dose-related optic neuritis, so check visual acuity and colour vision (red–green loss first) before and during treatment.

q: What is given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy?
why: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine (B6), causing peripheral neuropathy, so B6 is given with it, especially if there's diabetes, alcohol use or malnutrition.

q: Which TB drug turns body fluids orange?
hint: It is also a strong CYP inducer.
why: Rifampicin colours urine, tears and sweat orange-red (it can stain contact lenses); it also strongly induces liver enzymes.

q: Why is TB treated with several drugs at once?
model: To prevent resistance (monotherapy breeds resistant strains).
why: A TB lesion contains billions of bacilli, some of them already resistant to one drug by chance; combining drugs kills those that would survive monotherapy.

q: When does surfactant production start?
why: Type II pneumocytes start making surfactant in the canalicular stage (around 24 weeks), but there isn't enough until about 34 weeks, so preterm babies get RDS.

q: What part of gram-negative bacteria causes septic shock?
why: Lipid A in the lipopolysaccharide of the outer membrane triggers TLR4 on macrophages, releasing cytokines that cause vasodilation and shock.

q: Which cytokines reset the hypothalamic set point in fever?
acc: il-1 / il1 / il-6 / tnf / pge2 / prostaglandin
why: Pyrogenic cytokines act on the hypothalamus to make prostaglandin E2, which raises the set point; that's why NSAIDs and paracetamol reduce fever.

q: Which antibiotic class causes tendon rupture?
hint: Also prolongs QT; carries MHRA warnings.
why: Fluoroquinolones damage tendon cells, especially the Achilles, more so in older people and those on steroids; the MHRA restricts their use.

q: Which antibiotic reacts with alcohol?
hint: Used for anaerobes and C. difficile.
why: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up with alcohol, causing flushing, vomiting and palpitations.

q: Name a strategy to reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescribing for coughs and colds.
acc: delayed / back-up / back up / safety net / leaflet / crp / explain
model: Delayed (back-up) prescribing, explaining natural history, safety-netting, CRP testing.
hint: A prescription they only collect if they're not better.
why: Most coughs and colds are viral and self-limiting; a delayed prescription with clear safety-netting cuts antibiotic use without worse outcomes.

q: In the chill phase of fever, why does the patient shiver?
acc: set point / below / generate heat / heat production
model: The set point has risen, so the body generates heat to reach it.
hint: The thermostat has just been turned up.
why: When the set point rises, the body is suddenly "too cold", so it shivers and vasoconstricts to generate and conserve heat until it reaches the new target.

q: Name a CYP450 inducer.
acc: rifampicin / carbamazepine / phenytoin / st john / alcohol / barbiturate
model: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort, chronic alcohol.
hint: A TB drug or an antiepileptic.
why: Inducers increase CYP enzyme production, speeding metabolism of other drugs (e.g. the pill, warfarin) and making them less effective.

q: Name a CYP450 inhibitor.
acc: clarithromycin / erythromycin / fluconazole / ketoconazole / ciprofloxacin / omeprazole / valproate / grapefruit / metronidazole
model: Macrolides, azoles, ciprofloxacin, omeprazole, valproate, grapefruit.
hint: Some antibiotics, antifungals and a fruit juice.
why: Inhibitors slow metabolism of drugs cleared by CYP enzymes, raising their levels (e.g. clarithromycin with statins raises myopathy risk).

q: What separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
model: CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma) with core temp >40 °C.
why: Both involve heat stress, but heat stroke means thermoregulation has failed (core above 40 °C) with CNS dysfunction, a medical emergency that needs rapid cooling.

q: Which junctions are attacked in pemphigus?
why: Autoantibodies to desmogleins break the desmosomes holding keratinocytes together, giving fragile blisters that rupture easily (positive Nikolsky sign).

q: Which organisms lack a cell wall and are resistant to β-lactams?
why: β-lactams work by blocking cell-wall synthesis, so organisms without a wall, like Mycoplasma, are naturally resistant; use macrolides or doxycycline.

q: Which organelle makes ATP?
why: Mitochondria make ATP through oxidative phosphorylation; they have their own maternally inherited DNA.

q: Name a bacterial exotoxin.
acc: cholera / tetanus / botulinum / diphtheria / shiga / tsst
model: Cholera, tetanus, botulinum, diphtheria, Shiga, TSST-1.
hint: Think watery diarrhoea, lockjaw or floppy paralysis.
why: Exotoxins are proteins secreted by bacteria with specific actions: cholera (secretory diarrhoea), tetanus (spasms), botulinum (flaccid paralysis), diphtheria (myocarditis).

q: How do encapsulated bacteria avoid immunity?
hint: The capsule stops them being eaten.
why: Polysaccharide capsules stop complement and antibodies binding effectively, so phagocytes can't grab the bacteria; opsonisation and the spleen are key defences.

q: Which E. coli strain causes haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
why: Shiga toxin from E. coli O157 damages endothelium in the gut and kidney, causing haemolytic anaemia, low platelets and AKI; avoid antibiotics.

q: Which skin infection has honey-coloured crusts?
hint: Common in children; caused by Staph or Strep.
why: Superficial infection by Staph aureus or Strep pyogenes makes golden crusts; it's very contagious, so children stay off school until crusted or 48 h on treatment.

q: Which spots are pathognomonic of measles?
hint: White spots on the buccal mucosa.
why: Koplik spots are tiny white spots on the buccal mucosa that appear before the measles rash and are specific to it.

q: Congenital rubella causes which triad?
hint: Three organs: two senses and a pump.
why: Rubella in early pregnancy damages developing organs: deafness, cataracts and heart defects (PDA, pulmonary stenosis), which is why girls and women are vaccinated.

q: Which cells present antigen to CD4 T cells on MHC class II?
model: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells).
why: Professional APCs take up antigen, process it and present it on MHC class II to CD4 helper T cells; dendritic cells are the most potent.

q: Which hypersensitivity type is anaphylaxis?
why: IgE on mast cells cross-links on contact with allergen, releasing histamine and other mediators within minutes.

q: Which hypersensitivity type is contact dermatitis?
acc: type iv / type 4 / delayed / t cell
why: Sensitised T cells react to the allergen and recruit macrophages, so the reaction takes 48–72 hours to appear (as in patch testing).

q: Which antibody class suggests acute infection?
why: IgM is the first antibody made in a primary response, so specific IgM suggests recent infection; IgG comes later and lasts.

q: Name a factor affecting parents' MMR decisions.
acc: trust / misinformation / social media / omission / risk / wakefield / convenience / access / complacency / confidence
model: Trust, misinformation, omission bias, complacency, convenience.
hint: A discredited 1998 paper and what parents read online.
why: MMR uptake is shaped by trust in services, misinformation (the discredited Wakefield claims), omission bias, complacency and access to clinics.

q: Which cells in the paracortex of lymph nodes?
hint: Follicles hold B cells; the paracortex holds the others.
why: Lymph nodes are organised by zone: B cells in cortical follicles, T cells in the paracortex, plasma cells and macrophages in the medulla.

q: Which hormone drives red cell production?
why: Kidney cells sense low oxygen and release erythropoietin, which stimulates red cell production in the marrow.

q: Which antibody crosses the placenta?
why: IgG is actively transported across the placenta via FcRn receptors, giving babies passive immunity for their first months.

q: What does the spleen protect against particularly?
hint: Pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus share this feature.
why: The spleen filters blood and makes antibodies against polysaccharide capsules, so splenectomy patients need vaccines and sometimes antibiotics against pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus.

q: Where do B cells undergo affinity maturation?
why: In germinal centres B cells mutate their antibody genes (somatic hypermutation), and those binding antigen best are selected to survive.

q: Charcot's triad of ascending cholangitis?
hint: Three classic features of an infected bile duct.
why: Obstructed bile becomes infected, causing fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice; add hypotension and confusion for Reynolds' pentad.

q: Two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis?
hint: The first two letters of "I GET SMASHED".
why: Gallstones block the pancreatic duct at the ampulla, and alcohol is directly toxic; together they cause about 80% of cases.

q: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests?
hint: An eponymous law says it isn't stones.
why: Courvoisier's law: a palpable gallbladder with painless jaundice is unlikely to be stones (which scar the gallbladder) and suggests a pancreatic head tumour.

q: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
hint: Released by duodenal S cells in response to acid.
why: Duodenal S cells release secretin when acid arrives; it stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate to neutralise it.

q: Where are bile salts reabsorbed?
hint: The end of the small bowel.
why: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver (enterohepatic circulation), so ileal disease causes bile acid diarrhoea.

q: Commonest type of gallstone?
why: Cholesterol stones form when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile salts; risks include female sex, obesity and pregnancy.

q: Emergency drug for suspected malignant spinal cord compression?
why: High-dose dexamethasone reduces oedema around the compressed cord while urgent MRI and definitive treatment (radiotherapy or surgery) are arranged.

q: Key features of cauda equina syndrome?
model: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms.
hint: Numbness in the perineum and continence problems.
why: Compression of the sacral nerve roots causes saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, reduced anal tone and bilateral sciatica; it needs emergency MRI.

q: Mixed UMN and LMN signs with no sensory loss suggest?
why: MND destroys both upper and lower motor neurons but spares sensory pathways, so you see wasting and fasciculations alongside brisk reflexes, with normal sensation.

q: CSF finding supporting MS?
why: Oligoclonal bands show antibodies being made within the CNS; they're significant when present in CSF but not in serum.

q: Treatment for an MS relapse?
hint: A high-dose short course for 3–5 days.
why: High-dose steroids for 3–5 days speed recovery from a relapse but don't change long-term disability.

q: Where do spinothalamic fibres decussate?
model: In the spinal cord, within 1–2 segments.
hint: Within a segment or two of entry.
why: Spinothalamic fibres cross within a segment or two of entering the cord, while dorsal columns cross in the medulla; this explains Brown-Séquard syndrome.

q: Cerebellar lesions cause signs on which side?
why: Cerebellar pathways cross twice, so the net effect is ipsilateral: a right cerebellar lesion causes right-sided ataxia.

q: Hemiballismus comes from a lesion of which nucleus?
why: The subthalamic nucleus normally restrains movement through the basal ganglia; a lesion (often a small stroke) causes wild flinging of the opposite limbs.

q: Why does cardiac pain radiate to the left arm?
acc: convergence / referred / dermatome / t1 / same spinal / shared
model: Cardiac and arm afferents converge on the same T1–T5 dorsal horn neurons.
hint: Visceral and skin nerves converge on one spinal level.
why: Cardiac and arm afferents enter the same spinal segments (T1–5); the brain can't tell their source apart and interprets cardiac pain as coming from the arm (referred pain).

q: What makes an atherosclerotic plaque vulnerable to rupture?
acc: thin cap / thin fibrous / lipid core / macrophage
model: A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid core with many macrophages.
hint: Think about the cap and the core.
why: Plaques with a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and lots of macrophages (which digest the cap) are the ones that rupture and cause thrombosis, regardless of size.

q: Best long-term CABG conduit?
model: The left internal mammary artery (to LAD).
hint: An artery from the chest wall.
why: The left internal mammary artery grafted to the LAD stays open for over 90% at 10 years, much better than vein grafts.

q: Two drugs that must not be combined in angina because of heart block?
why: Verapamil and diltiazem slow AV conduction, as do beta-blockers; combined they can cause severe bradycardia, heart block and heart failure.

q: How long is dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS?
why: Dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months after ACS cuts recurrent events and stent thrombosis, balanced against bleeding risk.

q: Commonest endocrine cause of secondary hypertension?
hint: An adrenal cause; check the renin ratio.
why: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with low renin and, often, hypokalaemia; screen with the aldosterone:renin ratio.

q: Which test confirms hypertension after a raised clinic reading?
why: A single clinic reading can be inflated by white-coat effect, so ambulatory or home monitoring confirms the diagnosis.

q: First-line antihypertensive for a 60-year-old?
hint: Over 55, so not the ACE inhibitor.
why: Over 55 (or of Black African/Caribbean origin), low-renin hypertension responds better to CCBs than ACE inhibitors.

q: Common side effect of ACE inhibitors caused by bradykinin?
why: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it lets bradykinin build up in the airway, causing a dry cough. Switch to an ARB, which doesn't affect bradykinin.

q: Can genetic test results be shared with relatives without consent?
acc: sometimes / some / exceptional / public interest / yes / can
model: Sometimes: GMC allows disclosure in exceptional cases to prevent serious harm (ABC v St George's).
hint: Only rarely, after weighing the risk of harm to relatives.
why: Confidentiality isn't absolute: if a relative faces serious, preventable harm and the patient won't share, disclosure may be justified after careful discussion.

q: Earliest sign of hypovolaemia?
why: Heart rate rises to maintain cardiac output as volume falls; blood pressure is held up by vasoconstriction until about 30% of volume is lost.

q: Major haemorrhage: which drug within 3 hours of trauma?
why: CRASH-2 showed tranexamic acid reduces death from bleeding in trauma if given within 3 hours; later it may cause harm.

q: Why isn't 5% glucose used for resuscitation?
acc: distribut / all compartments / intravascular / free water / only
model: It distributes across all compartments, so little stays intravascular.
hint: Once the sugar is used up, it's just water.
why: Once the glucose is metabolised it's just free water, which spreads across all body compartments, so only about a twelfth stays in the circulation.

q: A disproportionately raised urea suggests?
acc: dehydration / pre-renal / gi bleed / upper gi / bleed
model: Pre-renal state/dehydration or an upper GI bleed.
hint: A protein load in the gut, or volume depletion.
why: Urea rises more than creatinine when the kidney reabsorbs more urea (dehydration) or more protein is absorbed from the gut (digested blood after an upper GI bleed).

q: Commonest cause of CKD in the UK?
why: Diabetes is the leading cause of CKD in the UK, through glomerular hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion and glomerulosclerosis.

q: Commonest intrinsic cause of AKI?
why: ATN follows prolonged poor perfusion or toxins (contrast, aminoglycosides) damaging tubular cells; it's the commonest intrinsic cause of AKI in hospital.

q: Name the four types of shock.
why: Hypovolaemic (fluid or blood loss), cardiogenic (pump failure), obstructive (tamponade, PE, tension pneumothorax) and distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis).

q: Name a health belief model.
acc: health belief / leventhal / common-sense / planned behaviour
model: Health Belief Model, Leventhal's common-sense model, Theory of Planned Behaviour.
why: The Health Belief Model says people act when they feel susceptible, think the condition is serious, and believe the benefits outweigh the barriers.

q: Faltering growth: crossing how many centile spaces (birthweight 9th–91st)?
why: Crossing two or more centile spaces downwards suggests faltering growth; crossing one can be normal as babies settle to their genetic centile.

q: Commonest cause of delayed puberty?
model: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
hint: Runs in families; a normal variant.
why: Constitutional delay is a normal variant: growth and puberty are late but catch up, often with a family history and a delayed bone age.

q: Rapid catch-up growth away from home suggests?
hint: The home environment was the problem.
why: If a child grows quickly once removed from home, the problem was psychosocial deprivation affecting growth hormone, not a medical cause.

q: Pyloric stenosis causes which acid–base disturbance?
why: Repeated vomiting of gastric acid loses H⁺ and Cl⁻, and dehydration drives aldosterone, which wastes K⁺: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

q: Screening blood test for coeliac disease?
why: tTG-IgA is sensitive and specific; total IgA is checked too because IgA deficiency is commoner in coeliac disease and causes false negatives.

q: Name the framework for breaking bad news.
why: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary.

q: Which two natural anticoagulants inactivate factors Va and VIIIa?
model: Activated protein C with protein S.
why: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin activates protein C, which, with protein S, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa to switch coagulation off.

q: Commonest inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians?
why: Factor V Leiden makes factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, so clotting carries on; it's present in about 5% of Caucasians.

q: Which test is prolonged by warfarin?
why: Warfarin reduces vitamin K–dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X); factor VII has the shortest half-life and is in the extrinsic pathway, so PT/INR rises first.

q: Which test monitors unfractionated heparin?
why: Unfractionated heparin boosts antithrombin against thrombin and Xa, prolonging the intrinsic pathway (APTT); LMWH mainly affects Xa, so it isn't monitored by APTT.

q: Haemophilia A is a deficiency of which factor?
why: X-linked deficiency of factor VIII (haemophilia B is factor IX) causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles with a prolonged APTT.

q: Typical bloods in DIC?
acc: low platelets / platelets + prolonged / pt / aptt + fibrinogen / d-dimer
why: Widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors (low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT/APTT) while fibrinolysis raises D-dimer.

q: Reversal of dabigatran?
why: Idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran tightly and reverses it within minutes; andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors.

q: Mechanism of clopidogrel?
hint: Blocks a platelet receptor; a prodrug activated by CYP2C19.
why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing platelet activation; CYP2C19 variants reduce its effect.

q: Which vitamin is needed for collagen synthesis in healing?
why: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that stabilise collagen; deficiency causes scurvy with poor wound healing and bleeding gums.

q: Name a microvascular complication of diabetes.
why: High glucose damages small vessels in the retina, glomeruli and vasa nervorum, which is why diabetes screening covers eyes, urine ACR and feet.

q: When is HbA1c unreliable for diagnosing diabetes?
acc: haemoglobinopathy / anaemia / pregnancy / children / ckd / transfusion / rapid
model: Haemoglobinopathies, anaemia, pregnancy, children, recent transfusion, rapid onset.
hint: Anything that changes red cell lifespan.
why: HbA1c reflects glucose over red cell lifespan (about 3 months), so anything changing red cell turnover or haemoglobin structure makes it unreliable.

q: Name the "sick day rules" drugs to pause.
acc: metformin / sglt2 / ace / arb / diuretic / nsaid / sulfonylurea
model: SADMANS: sulfonylureas, ACEi, diuretics, metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2i.
why: These drugs can cause AKI, lactic acidosis, hypoglycaemia or ketoacidosis when patients are dehydrated, so they're paused during acute illness.

q: Main cause of death in type 2 diabetes?
why: Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis, so MI and stroke cause most deaths; that's why statins, BP control and SGLT2i/GLP-1 agonists matter.

q: Which transporter does insulin move to the muscle cell surface?
why: Insulin moves GLUT4 vesicles to the membrane of muscle and fat cells to take up glucose; exercise does this independently of insulin.

q: Treatment of hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient?
model: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes.
why: Fast-acting glucose raises blood sugar within minutes; recheck after 15 minutes and repeat, then give longer-acting carbohydrate to prevent a relapse.

q: Which drug class causes euglycaemic DKA?
why: SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose by making it spill into urine, so ketoacidosis can develop with near-normal glucose, especially when ill or fasting.

q: Annual screening test for diabetic nephropathy?
why: Albuminuria appears early in diabetic kidney disease, before eGFR falls; the ACR detects it, prompting ACEi/ARB and SGLT2i.

q: Which T2DM drug class reduces heart failure admissions?
why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause natriuresis and osmotic diuresis, reduce preload and improve cardiac energetics, cutting heart failure admissions.

q: Main side effect of sulfonylureas?
hint: They push insulin out whatever the glucose level.
why: Sulfonylureas close K_ATP channels and make beta cells release insulin whatever the glucose level, so hypoglycaemia is common, especially in older people.

q: Name the reversible causes of cardiac arrest (4 Hs).
acc: hypoxia + hypovolaemia + kalaemia / potassium / metabolic + hypothermia
model: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, Hypothermia.
why: Reversible causes of arrest: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia (and metabolic), Hypothermia; plus the 4 Ts (thrombosis, tension, tamponade, toxins).

q: Name the three "give" steps of the Sepsis Six.
why: Oxygen corrects tissue hypoxia, antibiotics within the hour treat the source, and fluids restore perfusion.

q: Name the three "take" steps of the Sepsis Six.
hint: Bottles, a blood gas marker, output.
why: Cultures before antibiotics identify the organism, lactate measures tissue hypoperfusion, and urine output tracks end-organ perfusion.

q: Where is IM adrenaline given in anaphylaxis?
hint: The lateral muscle of the leg.
why: The anterolateral thigh is a large, well-perfused muscle, giving faster absorption than the deltoid or subcutaneous routes.

q: First-line vasopressor in septic shock?
why: Noradrenaline's α1 effect restores vascular tone in distributive shock with little effect on heart rate; target MAP is 65 or above.

q: Which organ failure causes hyaline membranes in the lungs during shock?
why: In ARDS, inflammatory damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane causes protein-rich fluid to leak into alveoli, forming hyaline membranes and severe hypoxia.

q: Which reflex is absent in testicular torsion?
why: Stroking the inner thigh normally lifts the testis via cremaster; in torsion the reflex is usually absent, though its presence doesn't fully exclude torsion.

q: First investigation after a raised PSA (before biopsy)?
why: Multiparametric MRI can show significant tumours, allows targeted biopsy and can avoid biopsy if normal.

q: What prevents tumour flare when starting an LHRH agonist?
hint: Block the receptor during the initial surge.
why: LHRH agonists first cause a surge in LH and testosterone before down-regulation, which can flare symptoms; an anti-androgen blocks the receptor during that surge.

q: Name an alpha-blocker used for BPH.
why: Alpha-blockers relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, improving flow within days; postural hypotension is the main side effect.

q: How long do 5α-reductase inhibitors take to work?
why: 5α-reductase inhibitors stop testosterone being converted to DHT, so the prostate shrinks slowly, over about 6 months.

q: Tumour markers for testicular cancer?
hint: One is also used in pregnancy tests.
why: Seminomas may raise β-hCG; non-seminomas raise AFP and/or β-hCG; LDH reflects tumour bulk; all are used for diagnosis and follow-up.

q: Surgical approach for removing a testicular cancer?
why: An inguinal approach removes the testis and cord without cutting the scrotum, avoiding spread to the scrotal (inguinal) lymph drainage.

q: Ultrasound sign of torsion?
model: Absent or reduced Doppler flow; whirlpool sign.
hint: Colour imaging of the blood supply.
why: Twisting the cord cuts off arterial flow, so Doppler shows absent or reduced flow and the cord may look like a whirlpool; never delay surgery for a scan.

q: Which zone of the prostate does BPH affect?
why: BPH arises in the transition zone around the urethra, so it causes obstructive symptoms; most cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which you feel on DRE.

q: Which cells make testosterone?
why: LH stimulates Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium to make testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support sperm production.

q: Name a social factor in men's poorer health outcomes.
acc: masculinity / help-seeking / stoic / delay / reluctan / work / deprivation
model: Masculine norms delaying help-seeking, work barriers, deprivation.
why: Norms of toughness and self-reliance make men delay seeking help, so problems present later and with worse outcomes.

q: Sudden painless visual loss with a cherry-red spot?
why: Retinal artery occlusion makes the retina pale and swollen, while the thin fovea lets the choroid show through as a cherry-red spot.

q: Which blood tests if you suspect giant cell arteritis?
why: GCA causes very high ESR and CRP; start high-dose steroids before the biopsy because untreated GCA can cause permanent blindness.

q: First-line drop for open-angle glaucoma?
why: Prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow, need only once-daily dosing and lower pressure well; they can darken the iris and lengthen lashes.

q: IV drug used to lower pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma?
why: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body, reducing aqueous production and lowering pressure quickly.

q: Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and haloes?
hint: An eye emergency with raised pressure.
why: Blocked drainage at the iridocorneal angle makes pressure rise suddenly: a painful red eye, corneal oedema (haloes) and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil.

q: Dendritic ulcer on fluorescein suggests?
why: HSV keratitis makes a branching ulcer that stains with fluorescein; steroids make it worse, so treat with topical antivirals.

q: Treatment for wet AMD?
hint: Intravitreal injections against new vessel growth.
why: Wet AMD is driven by VEGF-stimulated new vessels under the retina; anti-VEGF injections stop them leaking and preserve vision.

q: Which part of the eye provides most refractive power?
hint: The front surface, not the lens.
why: Most refraction happens at the air–cornea interface, where the change in refractive index is biggest; the lens fine-tunes focus.

q: Pituitary tumour causes which field defect?
why: The tumour pushes up on the chiasm, damaging the crossing nasal fibres, which carry the temporal field of each eye.

q: PCA stroke causes which field defect?
model: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
hint: Both eyes, same side, centre spared.
why: The occipital cortex processes the opposite visual field, giving a homonymous hemianopia; the macula is often spared because the MCA also supplies its area.

q: Which photoreceptors give colour vision?
hint: Three types, packed in the fovea.
why: Cones work in bright light and come in three types (red, green, blue sensitivity); they're concentrated in the fovea. Rods give vision in low light.

q: Inflammation from rectum continuing proximally suggests?
why: UC always starts in the rectum and spreads continuously upwards, affecting only the mucosa; Crohn's is patchy and transmural.

q: Toxic megacolon: transverse colon diameter above?
hint: The same as the upper normal colon diameter.
why: A transverse colon wider than 6 cm on X-ray in a systemically unwell patient indicates toxic megacolon, which risks perforation.

q: Commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK?
why: Campylobacter, from undercooked poultry, is the commonest bacterial gastroenteritis in the UK and can trigger Guillain–Barré.

q: Non-caseating granulomas suggest?
why: Non-caseating granulomas are typical of Crohn's (and sarcoidosis); caseating granulomas suggest TB.

q: Smoking has what effect on UC risk?
hint: The opposite of its effect in Crohn's.
why: Smoking lowers the risk and severity of UC (possibly via nicotine) but roughly doubles the risk of Crohn's and worsens it.

q: What must be checked before azathioprine?
why: TPMT breaks down azathioprine; people with low activity build up toxic metabolites and can develop severe marrow suppression.

q: First-line drug for mild UC?
hint: The same drug family as sulfasalazine.
why: 5-ASA drugs act topically on the colonic mucosa to reduce inflammation; rectal plus oral is most effective for mild–moderate UC.

q: Coeliac biopsy shows?
model: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, ↑ intraepithelial lymphocytes.
why: Gluten triggers a T-cell response that flattens villi, deepens crypts and raises intraepithelial lymphocytes, reducing the absorptive surface.

q: Lung cancer type linked to SIADH and ectopic ACTH?
why: Small cell carcinoma arises from neuroendocrine cells, so it can secrete ADH (SIADH) and ACTH (Cushing's); it's central, fast-growing and strongly linked to smoking.

q: Pancoast tumour causes which syndrome?
why: A tumour at the lung apex invades the sympathetic chain, causing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and the brachial plexus, causing arm pain.

q: First-line treatment for an EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma?
why: EGFR-mutant tumours depend on EGFR signalling, so an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor like osimertinib works better than chemotherapy.

q: Name the test that samples mediastinal nodes at bronchoscopy.
why: EBUS-guided needle aspiration samples mediastinal nodes through the airway wall, staging lung cancer without surgery.

q: Name the four anticipatory "just in case" drug groups.
acc: opioid / morphine + midazolam / anxiolytic + antiemetic / levomepromazine / haloperidol + antisecret / secret / glycopyrronium / hyoscine
why: Anticipatory medicines cover the common end-of-life symptoms of pain, agitation, nausea and noisy secretions, so they can be given promptly without waiting.

q: Murmur of aortic stenosis?
model: Ejection systolic, radiating to the carotids.
why: A narrowed aortic valve causes turbulent flow as blood is ejected, a crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates along the flow into the carotids.

q: Murmur of mitral regurgitation?
model: Pansystolic at the apex, radiating to the axilla.
hint: Throughout systole, radiating to the axilla.
why: Blood leaks back into the left atrium throughout systole, giving a pansystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla.

q: Triad of symptoms in aortic stenosis?
acc: syncope + angina + breathless / dyspnoea / heart failure
why: A fixed outflow obstruction means cardiac output can't rise on exertion, causing syncope, angina (thick muscle, low coronary perfusion) and breathlessness.

q: Pulse in aortic regurgitation?
why: Blood flows back into the ventricle in diastole, so a large stroke volume is followed by a rapid fall in pressure: a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse.

q: Main cause of mitral stenosis?
why: Rheumatic fever after streptococcal infection causes inflammation that thickens and fuses the mitral leaflets years later.

q: Commonest organism in infective endocarditis?
why: Staph aureus is the commonest cause, especially in IV drug users and with prosthetic material, and causes aggressive valve destruction.

q: Organism linked to colorectal cancer in endocarditis?
hint: A gut streptococcus; scope the colon.
why: Strep gallolyticus endocarditis is strongly associated with colorectal tumours, so these patients need a colonoscopy.

q: What closes the foramen ovale at birth?
acc: left atrial pressure / pressure / first breath
model: ↑ left atrial pressure after the first breaths.
hint: Lung expansion changes the balance between the atria.
why: The first breaths expand the lungs and lower pulmonary resistance, so more blood returns to the left atrium; its pressure rises above the right and pushes the flap shut.

q: Drug that keeps the ductus arteriosus open?
why: Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open, maintaining blood flow in duct-dependent heart lesions until surgery; NSAIDs close it.

q: Lesion seen in rheumatic carditis?
hint: A granuloma named after a German pathologist.
why: Aschoff bodies are granulomas with Anitschkow cells, characteristic of rheumatic carditis.

q: DALYs are the sum of which two measures?
acc: yll / years of life lost / life lost + yld / years lived with disability / disability
model: Years of life lost (YLL) + years lived with disability (YLD).
hint: One for dying early, one for living with illness.
why: DALYs combine premature death (years of life lost compared with ideal life expectancy) and disability (years lived with a condition, weighted by severity), so one number captures both.

q: Leading global risk factor for death?
why: High blood pressure drives stroke, heart disease and kidney disease and is common and often untreated worldwide, so it tops the global risk factor rankings.

q: Roughly what share of under-5 deaths are in the neonatal period?
hint: The first 28 days carry a big chunk.
why: As infections and malnutrition in older children fall, deaths concentrate in the first 28 days, from prematurity, birth asphyxia and neonatal sepsis.

q: Name the two treatments for childhood diarrhoea in LMICs.
hint: A drink and a mineral supplement.
why: Low-osmolarity ORS replaces fluid and salts using the glucose–sodium cotransporter, and zinc shortens the episode and reduces recurrence.

q: What is used to treat uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition in the community?
why: RUTF is energy-dense, peanut-based, needs no water or cooking and resists contamination, so children without complications can be treated safely at home.

q: Who must you report FGM in a girl under 18 to?
hint: A mandatory duty, not just a social services referral.
why: Health professionals in England and Wales have a legal duty to report FGM that is known (seen or disclosed) in a girl under 18 directly to the police.

q: Which type of FGM narrows the vaginal opening?
why: Type III (infibulation) narrows the vaginal opening by cutting and repositioning the labia to create a seal; it causes the most obstetric and urinary complications.

q: Name a global factor that affects health.
acc: climate / conflict / poverty / migration / trafficking / trade / urbanisation / gender
model: Climate change, conflict, poverty, migration, trafficking.
why: Global determinants such as climate change, conflict, poverty and migration shape health beyond individual choices, through food, water, shelter and access to care.

q: Through which system are suspected trafficking victims referred?
hint: A national framework for modern slavery.
why: The National Referral Mechanism identifies victims of modern slavery and gives them access to support; children are referred without needing consent.

q: Leading direct cause of maternal death worldwide?
hint: After delivery, the uterus doesn't contract.
why: Postpartum haemorrhage, mostly from uterine atony, kills fastest where there's no skilled birth attendant, oxytocin or blood transfusion.

q: Name the "three delays" model.
model: Delays in deciding to seek, reaching, and receiving care.
why: Maternal deaths often stem from delays in deciding to seek care, reaching a facility, and receiving adequate treatment once there; each needs a different fix.

q: Who should you use instead of family members to interpret?
why: Family members may filter, censor or misinterpret what's said and compromise confidentiality, especially with children or in cases of abuse; professional interpreters are trained and impartial.

q: Commonest mental health problem in refugees?
why: Refugees often experience war, persecution and loss, so PTSD, depression and anxiety are much more common than in the host population.

q: Do patients need ID or proof of address to register with a GP?
why: NHS England guidance says practices shouldn't refuse registration for lack of ID, proof of address or immigration status, to protect access for vulnerable groups.

q: Name a WHO "Triple Billion" target.
acc: universal health coverage / uhc / emergencies / well-being / wellbeing
model: 1 billion more people with UHC, protected from emergencies, enjoying better health.
hint: Three groups of a billion people each.
why: The WHO's 2019–2023 programme aimed for 1 billion more people each with universal health coverage, protection from health emergencies and better health and well-being.

q: Which parasite causes African sleeping sickness?
why: Trypanosoma brucei is spread by tsetse flies and invades the CNS, disturbing sleep (hence "sleeping sickness"); it's fatal without treatment.

q: Which schistosome causes bladder cancer?
hint: Its name hints at blood in the urine.
why: S. haematobium eggs lodge in the bladder wall, causing haematuria and chronic inflammation that can lead to squamous cell carcinoma.

q: Treatment of severe falciparum malaria?
why: IV artesunate clears parasites faster than quinine and reduces mortality in severe falciparum malaria.

q: What must be checked before primaquine?
hint: An enzyme deficiency that causes haemolysis.
why: Primaquine causes oxidative stress in red cells; people with G6PD deficiency can't protect against it and develop haemolysis.

q: How many malaria films are needed to rule it out?
why: Parasitaemia fluctuates, so one negative film doesn't rule out malaria; three negative films over 72 hours (with rapid tests) are needed.

q: Fever in a traveller from a malaria area is what until proven otherwise?
hint: Rule out the deadliest cause first.
why: Falciparum malaria can kill within days and its symptoms are non-specific, so it must be excluded urgently in anyone back from an endemic area.

q: Name the two malaria vaccines used in Africa.
hint: Letters and numbers: one older, one from Oxford.
why: RTS,S and R21 both target the circumsporozoite protein; R21 (from Oxford) is cheaper to produce and can be made at scale.

q: Who should the clinician look at and speak to when using an interpreter?
model: The patient, speaking in the first person.
why: Addressing the patient directly in the first person keeps the consultation patient-centred; the interpreter acts as a voice, not a third party.

q: Name a culturally sensitive question to explore the patient's view.
acc: what do you think / cause / explanatory / worry / ice
model: "What do you think is causing this?" (explanatory model, ICE).
hint: Ask about their ideas and concerns.
why: Asking about the patient's own explanation (ideas, concerns, expectations) reveals cultural beliefs that affect how they understand illness and accept treatment.

q: What does the "C" before ABCDE stand for in trauma?
why: In major trauma, massive external bleeding kills faster than airway problems, so catastrophic haemorrhage is controlled first (<C>ABCDE).

q: Airway manoeuvre in trauma that protects the cervical spine?
why: A jaw thrust opens the airway without extending the neck, protecting a possibly injured cervical spine.

q: Name a principle of damage control resuscitation.
acc: permissive hypotension / blood products / tranexamic / lethal triad / minimise crystalloid / warm
model: Permissive hypotension, early blood products, TXA, avoiding the lethal triad.
hint: Accept a lower BP; give blood, not saline.
why: Damage control resuscitation accepts a lower BP, gives blood products early in balanced ratios plus TXA, and avoids crystalloid to prevent the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy).

q: What is week 202 about?
model: Puberty and adolescence, prematurity, and ICM skills.
why: Week 202 covers puberty and adolescence (normal, early and delayed puberty, adolescent development) and prematurity (care of preterm infants and their families).

q: First sign of puberty in girls?
why: Breast budding (thelarche) is usually the first sign in girls, followed by pubic hair, the growth spurt and then menarche about 2 years later.

q: First sign of puberty in boys?
why: Testicular volume reaching 4 mL (measured with an orchidometer) marks the start of puberty in boys, driven by rising gonadotrophins.

q: Precocious puberty is defined as signs before what ages?
hint: Girls a year earlier than boys.
why: Signs before 8 in girls or 9 in boys are precocious; girls usually have idiopathic central puberty, while boys more often have a pathological cause.

q: Drug used to treat central precocious puberty?
hint: Continuous stimulation switches the axis off.
why: Continuous GnRH agonist stimulation desensitises pituitary receptors, so LH and FSH fall and puberty pauses (pulsatile GnRH does the opposite).

q: Delayed puberty with anosmia suggests?
why: GnRH neurons migrate from the olfactory placode, so failed migration causes both hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and a poor sense of smell.

q: Karyotype of Turner syndrome?
why: Turner syndrome is loss of one X chromosome (45,X), causing short stature, ovarian failure and heart and kidney anomalies.

q: Which brain area matures last in adolescence?
why: The prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and impulse control, matures into the mid-20s, while reward pathways mature earlier, explaining adolescent risk-taking.

q: Name the adolescent psychosocial screening framework.
why: HEEADSSS covers Home, Education/employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression and Safety, uncovering risks young people may not volunteer.

q: Which structure forms the ureter and collecting system?
hint: Grows out of the mesonephric duct.
why: The ureteric bud grows from the mesonephric duct into the metanephric mesoderm and branches to form the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts.

q: Horseshoe kidney is trapped under which artery?
hint: The midline aortic branch below the renal arteries.
why: The fused lower poles get caught under the inferior mesenteric artery as the kidneys ascend from the pelvis, so they stay low.

q: Which gene starts male gonadal development?
why: SRY on the Y chromosome switches the bipotential gonad towards a testis; without it the gonad becomes an ovary.

q: Which hormone makes the Müllerian ducts regress?
why: Sertoli cells make AMH, which makes the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts regress in males; testosterone from Leydig cells maintains the Wolffian ducts.

q: Name a mental health condition that often starts in adolescence.
hint: Common ones involve mood and worry.
why: About half of adult mental illness starts by age 14 and three-quarters by the mid-20s, so adolescence is when depression, anxiety, eating disorders and self-harm often begin.

q: Why do preterm babies lose so much water?
model: Thin immature skin → high insensible losses.
hint: Through an immature barrier, without sweating.
why: Preterm skin is thin, poorly keratinised and has a large surface area for body weight, so evaporative water loss is very high; incubators with humidity reduce it.

q: Feeding complication of prematurity with bilious aspirates?
hint: Gas in the bowel wall on X-ray.
why: NEC is ischaemic and infective inflammation of an immature bowel; bilious aspirates, distension and bloody stools, with gas in the bowel wall on X-ray, are classic.

q: Gestation at the margins of viability?
why: Survival rises steeply between 22 and 24 weeks; decisions at these gestations are made with parents, balancing chances of survival against major disability.

q: Name a complication of extreme prematurity.
acc: rds / ivh / nec / bpd / rop / sepsis / pda
model: RDS, IVH, NEC, BPD, ROP, sepsis.
why: Every immature organ is at risk: lungs (RDS, BPD), brain (IVH), gut (NEC), eyes (ROP) and immunity (sepsis).

q: Which antenatal drug reduces RDS?
hint: Two IM doses given to the mother.
why: Steroids given to the mother cross the placenta and speed fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, reducing RDS, IVH and death.

q: Commonest cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis?
why: GBS colonises the maternal genital tract and is passed on during birth; intrapartum antibiotics for colonised mothers reduce early-onset infection.

q: Empirical antibiotics for early-onset neonatal sepsis?
why: Benzylpenicillin covers GBS and gentamicin covers E. coli and other Gram-negatives, the main causes of early-onset sepsis.

q: Preterm birth is before how many weeks?
why: Babies born before 37 completed weeks are preterm; risks rise sharply the earlier they're born.

q: Name an effect of prematurity on families.
acc: anxiety / ptsd / depression / bonding / financial / stress / grief / guilt
model: Anxiety, PTSD, depression, bonding difficulties, financial strain.
why: Parents of preterm babies face uncertainty, separation and financial strain, with high rates of anxiety, depression and PTSD and difficulty bonding.

q: What is "family-integrated care" in NICU?
model: Parents act as primary caregivers in the unit.
hint: Mum and dad become part of the care team.
why: In family-integrated care, parents are trained to deliver much of their baby's care, which improves weight gain, breastfeeding and parental confidence.

q: Name a key question in a sexual history.
acc: last sexual / partner / condom / gender / type of sex / sti
model: Last sexual intercourse, partner gender, type of sex, condom use, previous STIs.
why: A focused sexual history assesses risk and guides testing: partners' gender and number, type of sex, condom use, timing and previous STIs.

q: Under what age can a child never legally consent to sex?
why: Under the Sexual Offences Act 2003 a child under 13 can never consent, so any sexual activity is rape and must prompt a safeguarding referral.

q: Guidelines for contraception in under-16s without parents?
why: Fraser guidelines allow contraception for an under-16 who understands the advice, won't tell parents, is likely to have sex anyway, and whose health would otherwise suffer.

q: Test for a relative afferent pupillary defect?
hint: Moving a torch between the eyes.
why: Swinging a light between the eyes shows the affected pupil dilating when lit, because less light signal travels along its damaged optic nerve.

q: Painful red eye, haloes, vomiting: diagnosis?
why: Blocked aqueous drainage raises eye pressure suddenly, causing pain, vomiting, corneal oedema (haloes) and a fixed mid-dilated pupil; it needs urgent pressure lowering.

q: Name part of a paediatric history not in adult histories.
acc: birth / antenatal / development / immunisation / feeding / milestones
why: Paediatric histories add pregnancy and birth, feeding, growth, developmental milestones, immunisations and social situation, because they shape a child's health.

q: In a triadic consultation, who should you engage first?
why: Engaging the child first builds rapport and respects their voice; parents then add detail.

q: Which diagnosis must be excluded in a child with polyuria and weight loss?
why: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in a child are type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise; a same-day finger-prick glucose prevents progression to DKA.

q: Name an inquiry that changed UK child protection law.
acc: climbié / climbie / laming / baby p / connelly
why: The death of Victoria Climbié in 2000 led to the Laming Inquiry, which found failures of communication between agencies and led to the Children Act 2004.

q: Whose responsibility is safeguarding?
why: Abuse is often only spotted by piecing together small concerns, so every professional must recognise and act on them, not just the safeguarding team.

q: Bruising in which infants should raise suspicion of abuse?
model: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant.
hint: Babies who can't move about yet.
why: Babies who aren't yet mobile rarely bruise accidentally ("those who don't cruise rarely bruise"), so any bruise needs a safeguarding assessment.

q: Investigation for suspected physical abuse under 2 years?
why: Young children can have occult fractures with no visible signs, so a full skeletal survey looks for fractures at different stages of healing.

q: What is child sexual exploitation?
acc: exchange / something in return / gifts / money / receives
model: Sexual abuse where the child gets something in return (gifts, money, drugs, affection).
hint: A transaction: the child gets something.
why: In CSE, a child is coerced into sexual activity in exchange for something (gifts, money, drugs, affection or status), often through grooming.

q: Where are children seen for medical assessment after sexual assault?
why: SARCs provide forensic examination, emergency contraception, STI care and support in a child-friendly setting with trained paediatricians.

q: Does a normal examination exclude sexual abuse?
model: No: most CSA leaves no physical signs.
why: Genital tissue heals quickly and much abuse leaves no injury, so a normal examination neither confirms nor excludes abuse; the child's account matters most.

q: Which section of the Children Act covers child protection enquiries?
why: Under Section 47 of the Children Act 1989, the local authority must investigate when there's reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering significant harm.

q: What does FII stand for?
why: In FII a carer fabricates, exaggerates or induces illness in a child, leading to unnecessary tests and treatments.

q: Name the first principle of the Mental Capacity Act.
hint: The starting point for every adult.
why: The MCA starts by assuming every adult has capacity unless it's shown otherwise; an unwise decision doesn't mean someone lacks capacity.

q: Name the four parts of the functional capacity test.
why: A person lacks capacity for a specific decision if, because of an impairment of the mind or brain, they can't understand, retain, use or weigh the information, or communicate a choice.

q: Name a form of child exploitation in the UK.
acc: county lines / criminal / sexual / labour / domestic servitude
model: County lines, sexual, labour, domestic servitude.
why: County lines gangs use children to carry drugs across areas; children can also be exploited sexually, for labour or in domestic servitude.

q: Name a sign of child trafficking.
acc: controlling adult / no documents / id / scripted / missing / school / fear
model: A controlling adult, no ID, scripted story, going missing, not in school.
hint: An adult who speaks for them; no papers.
why: Trafficked children often come with a controlling adult who answers for them, have no documents, give rehearsed stories and go missing.

q: Which ratio does a case–control study calculate?
why: Case–control studies start from outcome, so they can't measure incidence or relative risk; instead they compare the odds of exposure between cases and controls.

q: Which bias is a problem in case–control studies?
why: Cases often think harder about past exposures than controls, so their recall differs systematically (recall bias).

q: Name the "toxic trio".
acc: domestic abuse / violence + mental + substance / alcohol / drug
model: Domestic abuse, parental mental illness, substance misuse.
why: Domestic abuse, parental mental illness and substance misuse together greatly increase the risk of harm to children and appear in many serious case reviews.

q: Which agency leads child protection enquiries?
acc: social services / social care / local authority
hint: Not the police, not the NHS.
why: The local authority's children's social care has the statutory duty to lead Section 47 enquiries, with police, health and education contributing.

q: Which position is the patient in for breast palpation?
model: Lying at 45° with the hand behind the head.
hint: Reclined, with the arm behind the head.
why: Lying at 45° with the hand behind the head spreads the breast tissue thinly over the chest wall, making lumps easier to feel.

q: Name the components of triple assessment.
acc: examination / clinical + imaging / mammogram / ultrasound + biopsy
why: Triple assessment combines clinical examination, imaging (mammogram and/or ultrasound) and core biopsy, which together give high diagnostic accuracy.

q: Age group at highest risk of fatal abuse?
why: Infants under 1 are most vulnerable: small, unable to escape or tell anyone, and easily fatally injured by shaking or impact.

q: Name a burn pattern suggesting abuse.
hint: Think scald patterns and small round marks.
why: Forced immersion causes symmetrical "glove and stocking" scalds with clear tide lines and no splash marks; small round burns suggest cigarettes.

q: What does "Think Family" ask you to do when treating adults?
model: Consider any children they care for.
why: Adults with mental illness, substance misuse or domestic abuse may care for children, so "Think Family" prompts you to ask who's at home and whether they're safe.

q: Name a red flag in a carer's history of an injury.
acc: delay / inconsistent / changing / doesn't fit / no explanation
model: Delayed presentation, inconsistent or changing story, doesn't fit development.
hint: Timing and consistency of the story.
why: Delayed presentation, an explanation that changes or doesn't fit the injury or the child's development, and inconsistent accounts are warning signs.

q: Why is multi-agency working vital in safeguarding?
model: Each agency holds part of the picture; sharing information protects children.
why: Each agency (health, school, social care, police) holds a piece of the picture; inquiries repeatedly show children harmed because information wasn't shared.

q: Name a category of the Child Protection Register.
why: Children on a child protection plan are registered under physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse or neglect, the four statutory categories.

q: Name a typical trigger for asthma.
acc: virus / viral / allergen / exercise / cold / smoke / pollen / dust / nsaid / beta
model: Viral infections, allergens, exercise, cold air, smoke.
why: Triggers inflame already hyperresponsive airways: viral infections, allergens (dust mite, pollen, pets), cold air, exercise and smoke.

q: First test in adult asthma diagnosis (2024)?
why: The 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guidance uses FeNO or blood eosinophils first because they show type 2 airway inflammation, which supports asthma and predicts steroid response.

q: Preferred reliever in people with asthma aged 12+?
hint: An inhaled steroid combined with a fast-acting LABA.
why: ICS/formoterol relieves symptoms quickly while giving a dose of steroid with each use, cutting severe attacks compared with salbutamol alone.

q: Why is SABA-only treatment avoided?
model: Linked to severe attacks and deaths; doesn't treat inflammation.
why: Relying on salbutamol alone treats symptoms but leaves inflammation untouched; heavy SABA use is linked to severe attacks and asthma deaths.

q: Which analysis keeps patients in their randomised groups?
hint: Analyse people as they were allocated.
why: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone in the group they were randomised to, preserving the balance randomisation created and reflecting real-world use.

q: How do you calculate NNT?
hint: The reciprocal of the absolute risk difference.
why: NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: if treatment cuts risk from 10% to 5% (ARR 0.05), you treat 20 people to prevent one event.

q: Commonest cause of wheeze in infants under 1?
why: RSV bronchiolitis infects small airways in winter, causing wheeze, crackles and feeding difficulty in infants.

q: Sudden onset unilateral wheeze after choking suggests?
why: A foreign body usually lodges in one main bronchus (often the right), causing sudden unilateral wheeze after a choking episode; it needs bronchoscopy.

q: Which cytokine drives eosinophilia in asthma?
why: Th2 cells release IL-5, which drives eosinophil production and survival; mepolizumab and benralizumab target this pathway in severe asthma.

q: A normal or rising PaCO₂ in acute asthma means?
hint: They should be blowing it off.
why: In acute asthma patients hyperventilate, so CO₂ should be low; a normal or rising PaCO₂ means they're tiring and may need ventilation.

q: Why must LABAs never be used without ICS in asthma?
why: LABAs relieve bronchospasm but not inflammation, so used alone they can mask worsening asthma; trials showed more asthma deaths.

q: Side effect of inhaled steroids to prevent with rinsing?
hint: A fungal infection in the mouth.
why: Steroid deposited in the mouth suppresses local immunity, allowing Candida to grow; rinsing after use and using a spacer reduce it.

q: Name a feature of life-threatening asthma.
acc: silent chest / cyanosis / sats <92 / 92 / exhaustion / pef <33 / 33 / hypotension / arrhythmia / confusion
model: Silent chest, sats <92%, PEF <33%, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion.
hint: The CHEST mnemonic plus two numbers.
