why: Life-threatening features include PEF <33%, sats <92%, a silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, hypotension or arrhythmia.

q: Name an occupational cause of asthma.
acc: isocyanate / flour / baker / latex / wood / paint
model: Isocyanates (paint sprayers), flour (bakers), latex, wood dust.
hint: Think car body shops, bread-making and hospitals.
why: Isocyanates in spray paints, flour dust in bakeries, latex and wood dust can sensitise airways; symptoms improve on days away from work.

q: What is a type I error?
model: A false positive (rejecting a true null hypothesis).
hint: Finding an effect that isn't there.
why: A type I error means concluding there's an effect when there isn't (a false positive); its probability is alpha, usually set at 0.05.

q: Which two leads determine the axis?
hint: One limb lead and one augmented lead.
why: Lead I looks at the heart's left–right axis and aVF its up–down axis; both positive means normal axis.

q: ST elevation in II, III and aVF suggests which territory?
why: Leads II, III and aVF face the inferior surface of the heart, which the right coronary artery usually supplies.

q: Sawtooth baseline with ventricular rate ~150?
why: Atrial flutter runs at about 300/min, and the AV node usually conducts every second beat, giving a ventricular rate of about 150.

q: What is checked in the hands during a respiratory exam?
acc: clubbing / flap / asterixis / tar / cyanosis / tremor
model: Clubbing, tar staining, CO₂ retention flap, tremor.
hint: Fingernails, staining and a CO₂ sign.
why: The hands show chronic hypoxia (clubbing), smoking (tar staining), CO₂ retention (flap, bounding pulse) and beta-agonist use (fine tremor).

q: Stony dull percussion suggests?
why: Fluid transmits sound poorly, so a pleural effusion is "stony dull" with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance.

q: Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles with clubbing suggest?
why: Fibrosis stiffens the lungs; small airways pop open late in inspiration, giving fine "Velcro" crackles, often with clubbing.

q: How many acceptable spirometry blows are needed?
why: At least three technically acceptable blows, with the best two within 150 mL of each other, ensure the result is reproducible.

q: Name an indication for spirometry.
acc: copd / asthma / restrictive / pre-op / monitoring / neuromuscular
model: Diagnosing COPD/asthma, restrictive disease, monitoring, pre-op assessment.
why: Spirometry confirms obstructive (COPD, asthma) or restrictive disease, monitors progression and assesses fitness for surgery.

q: Restrictive pattern on spirometry?
model: Both reduced, FEV1/FVC normal or high.
why: Restriction reduces total lung volume, so FVC and FEV1 fall together and the ratio stays normal or rises.

q: Name a CXR sign of pulmonary oedema.
acc: bat / kerley / upper lobe / cardiomegaly / effusion
model: Bat's wing shadowing, Kerley B lines, upper lobe diversion, cardiomegaly, effusions.
hint: The ABCDE of heart failure on a film.
why: Raised pulmonary venous pressure diverts blood to the upper lobes, leaks fluid into interstitium (Kerley B lines) and alveoli (bat's wings), often with cardiomegaly.

q: Free air under the diaphragm on an erect CXR suggests?
why: Gas escaping from a perforated bowel rises under the diaphragm on an erect film; it's a surgical emergency.

q: What does the "I" stand for in the RIPE film quality check?
why: Adequate inspiration means about 6 anterior ribs (or 10 posterior) above the diaphragm; poor inspiration crowds the bases and enlarges the heart.

q: Why compare with old films?
model: To tell new from chronic findings and avoid unnecessary tests.
why: Old films show whether a finding is new or long-standing, which changes management and avoids unnecessary scans.

q: Tension or simple pneumothorax: which is a clinical diagnosis treated before the X-ray?
why: Tension pneumothorax causes rapid cardiovascular collapse, so it's diagnosed clinically (tracheal deviation, hypotension, absent breath sounds) and decompressed straight away.

q: Flail chest is how many fractures in how many ribs?
why: Two or more fractures in each of three or more adjacent ribs create a free segment that moves paradoxically, impairing ventilation and indicating serious underlying lung injury.

q: Name a cognitive bias in reading imaging.
acc: anchoring / satisfaction of search / premature closure / confirmation / availability
model: Anchoring, satisfaction of search, premature closure.
why: Satisfaction of search (stopping after one finding), anchoring and premature closure make reporters miss second abnormalities.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
why: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds comes from the lingual nerve (V3), while taste fibres run in it only until they leave as the chorda tympani (VII) to reach the facial nerve.

q: Where does the parotid duct open?
why: The parotid duct crosses masseter, pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar.

q: Which salivary gland gets most stones?
hint: An upward-flowing duct and thicker saliva.
why: The submandibular duct runs uphill against gravity and the saliva is thicker and more alkaline, so stones form there most often.

q: Which nerve passes through the parotid gland?
why: The facial nerve divides into its five branches within the parotid, which is why parotid tumours or surgery can cause facial palsy.

q: Which papillae have no taste buds?
why: Filiform papillae are the most numerous and give the tongue its rough texture; they're mechanical and have no taste buds.

q: Which tongue muscle is supplied by the vagus?
why: All tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus, which comes from the pharyngeal plexus (vagus).

q: Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue to the facial nerve?
why: Taste fibres leave the tongue in the lingual nerve (V3), then branch off it as the chorda tympani, which crosses the middle ear to join the facial nerve (cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion). General sensation stays in the lingual nerve.

q: Which way does the tongue deviate with a left hypoglossal nerve lesion?
why: The working genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and across, so the tongue points towards the weak (lesioned) side.

q: Which nerve supplies the otic ganglion's parasympathetic fibres?
model: Glossopharyngeal (IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve.
hint: Its fibres end up supplying the parotid.
why: Fibres from IX travel in the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion, then via the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid gland.

q: Antibiotic for neutropenic sepsis within 1 hour?
hint: A broad-spectrum penicillin with an inhibitor.
why: Neutropenic sepsis can kill within hours, and Pseudomonas must be covered; piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour is standard.

q: Which organism causes osteomyelitis characteristically in sickle cell disease?
why: Sickle cell causes bone infarcts and splenic dysfunction, and gut ischaemia lets Salmonella into the blood, so it's characteristic (though Staph is still common).

q: What does Candida in a blood culture always need?
model: Treatment: remove the line, start an echinocandin, eye exam and echo.
why: Candida in blood is never a contaminant and can seed the eye and heart valves, so it needs treatment, line removal, eye examination and echo.

q: Commonest organism in line infections?
why: Skin commensals (S. epidermidis) form biofilms on plastic catheters, making them the commonest line infection.

q: Which criteria diagnose infective endocarditis?
why: The Duke criteria combine major criteria (positive cultures, echo evidence) and minor criteria (fever, predisposition, embolic or immune phenomena).

q: First-line drug for candidaemia?
why: Echinocandins are fungicidal against most Candida, including fluconazole-resistant species, and well tolerated.

q: First-line drug for invasive aspergillosis?
hint: A triazole with visual side effects.
why: Voriconazole has the best evidence for invasive aspergillosis; it causes visual disturbance, photosensitivity and many drug interactions.

q: Which antibiotic class do ESBL organisms resist?
why: ESBL enzymes break down penicillins and cephalosporins, so carbapenems are usually needed for serious infections.

q: What does MRSA's mecA gene make it resistant to?
acc: β-lactam / beta-lactam / beta lactam / penicillin / flucloxacillin
why: mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for all β-lactams, so MRSA is resistant to flucloxacillin and the whole class.

q: Which bacterium in prosthetic joint infections forms biofilms and needs rifampicin?
why: Staphylococci form biofilms on prosthetic surfaces, protecting them from antibiotics; rifampicin penetrates biofilm and is added to treatment.

q: Where in the lung do aspirated objects usually go?
model: The right lung (wider, more vertical main bronchus).
hint: The wider, more vertical main bronchus.
why: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects and aspirated material usually go right.

q: Name a CRISPR-based therapy approved in the UK.
model: Exa-cel (Casgevy) for sickle cell and β-thalassaemia.
why: Exa-cel edits patients' own stem cells to switch fetal haemoglobin back on, reducing sickling crises and transfusion needs.

q: Commonest organism causing UTI?
why: E. coli from the gut colonises the periurethral area and ascends; its fimbriae help it adhere to the urothelium.

q: Which organism makes struvite stones?
why: Proteus urease splits urea to ammonia, making urine alkaline so magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) precipitates, sometimes as staghorn stones.

q: Which dipstick result is most specific for UTI?
hint: Bacteria make it from dietary nitrate.
why: Many Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite, so a positive nitrite is quite specific for infection, though not sensitive.

q: Why don't you dipstick urine in over-65s?
hint: Bacteria are often present without infection.
why: Many older people have bacteria in their urine without infection, so dipsticks are unreliable and lead to unnecessary antibiotics; diagnose clinically.

q: Which cells does HIV infect?
why: HIV binds CD4 (with CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptors) on helper T cells; their gradual loss causes immunodeficiency.

q: What does U=U mean?
why: People on effective ART with an undetectable viral load don't pass HIV on sexually, which is powerful against stigma.

q: PEP must start within how many hours?
why: Antiretrovirals started quickly can stop the virus establishing infection; the sooner the better, and not after 72 hours.

q: Usual first-line ART third agent?
why: Integrase inhibitors (e.g. dolutegravir, bictegravir) are potent, well tolerated and have a high barrier to resistance.

q: Test needed before abacavir?
why: HLA-B*57:01 carriers have a high risk of a potentially fatal abacavir hypersensitivity reaction, so they're tested first.

q: Name a source of HIV stigma.
model: Discrimination, fear, homophobia, racism, internalised shame.
why: HIV stigma comes from fear of infection, moral judgements and discrimination (homophobia, racism), and it stops people testing and engaging with care.

q: Formula for volume of diluent with a displacement value?
acc: final volume − displacement / minus displacement / subtract
why: Powder takes up some volume once dissolved, so subtracting the displacement value gives the right volume of diluent for the target concentration.

q: What technique is used when preparing injectables?
why: ANTT protects key parts and key sites from contamination when preparing and giving IV medicines, reducing line infections.

q: Name a criterion for switching IV antibiotics to oral.
acc: improving / afebrile / absorb / oral route / stable
model: Clinically improving, afebrile 24–48 h, can absorb oral drugs.
hint: Getting better and able to swallow.
why: Switching when patients are improving, afebrile and able to absorb oral drugs cuts line complications and hospital stay without worse outcomes.

q: What does D stand for in ABCDE, and what do you check?
why: D is disability: level of consciousness (AVPU or GCS), pupils, and glucose, since hypoglycaemia is a reversible cause of reduced consciousness.

q: Which score triggers escalation of a deteriorating adult?
why: NEWS2 adds scores from six observations plus consciousness; higher totals trigger escalation to doctors or critical care.

q: Ketone threshold for DKA?
why: DKA is defined by ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones ++), plus glucose >11 or known diabetes, and pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15.

q: When is 10% glucose added in DKA?
why: Insulin must continue to clear ketones, so once glucose falls below 14, 10% glucose is added to prevent hypoglycaemia.

q: Name a closed-loop communication technique.
acc: repeat / read back / confirm / closed loop
model: Repeating instructions back to confirm ("1 mg adrenaline given").
why: In closed-loop communication the receiver repeats the instruction and confirms when it's done, preventing errors in emergencies.

q: Which cranial nerve lesion spares the forehead?
model: An upper motor neuron facial palsy.
hint: Bilateral cortical supply to the upper face.
why: The forehead gets cortical input from both hemispheres, so with a UMN lesion (e.g. stroke) the forehead is spared; a LMN lesion (Bell's palsy) affects the whole side.

q: Which nerve root supplies the biceps reflex?
why: The biceps reflex tests C5–6; mnemonic: ankle S1–2, knee L3–4, biceps C5–6, triceps C7–8.

q: Signs of an upper motor neuron lesion?
acc: spastic / increased tone / brisk / upgoing / clonus
model: Increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, clonus.
why: Loss of descending inhibition causes increased tone (spasticity), brisk reflexes, clonus and an upgoing plantar, without wasting.

q: Crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral limbs) suggest a lesion where?
why: Cranial nerve nuclei sit in the brainstem near the long tracts before they cross, so one lesion gives same-side cranial nerve signs and opposite-side limb signs.

q: What should a neuro presentation end with?
hint: Where's the lesion, and what is it?
why: A neuro presentation should end by saying where the lesion is and what it's likely to be, with a plan, because localisation drives the differential.

q: Test for pancreatic insufficiency in malabsorption?
why: Faecal elastase falls when the pancreas makes too little enzyme, so it's a simple non-invasive test for exocrine insufficiency (e.g. in cystic fibrosis).

q: Name a drug that causes constipation.
acc: opioid / codeine / morphine / iron / verapamil / anticholinergic / calcium
why: Opioids and anticholinergics slow gut motility, iron hardens stool, and verapamil relaxes gut smooth muscle.

q: Laxative class for opioid-induced constipation?
why: Opioids reduce peristalsis rather than stool bulk, so stimulants (± softeners) work; bulk-forming laxatives can worsen it; PAMORAs block gut opioid receptors.

q: Mechanism of prucalopride?
why: Prucalopride stimulates 5-HT4 receptors on enteric neurons, promoting peristalsis in chronic constipation that hasn't responded to laxatives.

q: Bowel screening test in Wales?
why: FIT detects human haemoglobin in stool, which is more specific and quantitative than older guaiac tests; a positive result leads to colonoscopy.

q: Where do the taeniae coli converge?
model: At the base of the appendix.
why: The three taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix, a useful way to find it at surgery.

q: IBS diagnostic criteria?
why: Rome IV defines IBS as recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation or changes in stool frequency or form, for 3 months with onset at least 6 months ago.

q: Name an IBS red flag.
acc: weight loss / bleeding / anaemia / nocturnal / age / family history / mass
model: Weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, age >50, FHx.
hint: Signs that point to something sinister.
why: Red flags suggest organic disease such as cancer or IBD: weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, a mass, age over 50 or a family history.

q: Name the diet used second-line in IBS.
why: FODMAPs are poorly absorbed carbohydrates that bacteria ferment, causing gas and fluid shifts; a supervised low-FODMAP diet helps many with IBS.

q: Low-dose drug used for IBS pain as a neuromodulator?
hint: An old antidepressant, taken at night.
why: Low-dose amitriptyline reduces visceral pain signalling and slows transit; it helps IBS pain without being used for depression.

q: Hallmark electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome?
why: Refeeding triggers insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells; phosphate falls fastest, risking heart failure and weakness.

q: Which vitamin is given before refeeding?
why: Carbohydrate metabolism uses thiamine; refeeding a deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine is given first.

q: Name a sign of bulimia on examination.
model: Russell's sign, parotid enlargement, dental erosion.
hint: Look at the knuckles, cheeks and teeth.
why: Self-induced vomiting causes knuckle calluses (Russell's sign), parotid swelling and acid erosion of the teeth.

q: First-line therapy for anorexia in young people?
why: Family therapy for anorexia nervosa (FT-AN) puts parents in charge of re-feeding initially; it has the best evidence in young people.

q: Why is PEG feeding not recommended in advanced dementia?
acc: no benefit / survival / doesn't / does not / aspiration
model: It doesn't improve survival, aspiration or pressure sores.
hint: Look at the evidence on outcomes.
why: Studies show PEG feeding in advanced dementia doesn't prolong life, prevent aspiration or heal pressure sores, and can add burden; careful hand feeding is preferred.

q: Which HLA type is linked to coeliac disease?
why: Nearly all coeliac patients carry HLA-DQ2 or DQ8, which present gluten peptides to T cells; a negative result essentially rules coeliac out.

q: Skin rash linked to coeliac disease?
why: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an itchy blistering rash on elbows, knees and buttocks caused by IgA deposits; it responds to a gluten-free diet.

q: When is parenteral nutrition used?
acc: gut / intestinal failure / not working / non-functional
model: When the gut doesn't work or can't be used.
why: Parenteral nutrition is used when the gut doesn't work or can't be used (e.g. intestinal failure, obstruction); otherwise enteral feeding is safer.

q: Where is iron absorbed?
hint: The first part of the small bowel.
why: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum by DMT1 after reduction to ferrous iron; acid helps and coeliac disease impairs it.

q: Main fuel of colonocytes?
why: Colonic bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids; butyrate is the main energy source for colonocytes.

q: Name a question in a GI symptom history.
acc: blood / weight / bowel / dysphagia / vomiting / pain / jaundice
model: Weight loss, blood, change in bowel habit, dysphagia, vomiting.
why: Alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding, change in bowel habit and dysphagia point to serious pathology and decide urgency.

q: Rule that favours one diagnosis explaining all symptoms?
why: Occam's razor favours one diagnosis explaining everything; Hickam's dictum reminds you that patients can have several diseases at once.

q: What is the core mechanism of fibromyalgia?
hint: The volume knob on pain is turned up.
why: In fibromyalgia the central nervous system amplifies pain signals (central sensitisation), causing widespread pain without tissue damage.

q: Name a drug history item relevant to GI bleeding.
acc: nsaid / aspirin / anticoagulant / warfarin / doac / steroid / ssri
why: NSAIDs, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, SSRIs and steroids raise bleeding risk, so they shape management and whether to stop or reverse drugs.

q: Name a peripheral sign of chronic liver disease.
acc: palmar erythema / spider / clubbing / leuconychia / dupuytren / asterixis / gynaecomastia / jaundice
model: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, clubbing, leuconychia, asterixis.
hint: Look at the hands and chest skin.
why: Chronic liver disease causes peripheral signs from high oestrogen (palmar erythema, spider naevi), low albumin (leuconychia) and encephalopathy (asterixis).

q: Patient position for a digital rectal examination?
why: Left lateral with knees to chest opens the buttocks and is comfortable and dignified; always offer a chaperone and get consent.

q: Framework for urgent handover?
why: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) structures urgent handover so key information isn't missed.

q: Name a mnemonic "surgical sieve" approach.
why: A surgical sieve like VITAMIN CDEF (vascular, infective, traumatic, autoimmune, metabolic, iatrogenic, neoplastic, congenital, degenerative…) helps generate differentials.

q: Name the four AXR densities.
why: On X-ray gas is black, fat dark grey, soft tissue/fluid mid grey and bone white, because each absorbs X-rays differently.

q: Folds that cross the full width of the bowel?
why: Valvulae conniventes cross the full width of the small bowel; colonic haustra cross only partway.

q: Commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in the UK?
why: Adhesions from previous surgery cause most small bowel obstruction in the UK; hernias come next.

q: Sign where both sides of the bowel wall are visible?
hint: A double-wall sign with an eponym.
why: When gas is free in the peritoneum, both sides of the bowel wall are outlined (Rigler's sign), indicating perforation.

q: Large branching renal stone?
why: Staghorn calculi fill the renal pelvis and calyces; they're usually struvite from urease-producing infection.

q: "Coffee bean" sign on AXR?
why: A twisted sigmoid loop fills with gas and looks like a coffee bean pointing towards the right upper quadrant.

q: Rigler's triad indicates?
why: Gallstone ileus gives small bowel obstruction, air in the biliary tree (from a fistula) and an ectopic gallstone, usually in the terminal ileum.

q: Best investigation for most acute abdominal pathology?
why: CT gives detailed images of most acute abdominal pathology quickly; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy, children and biliary problems.

q: Which artery supplies the hindgut?
hint: The third unpaired branch of the aorta.
why: The IMA supplies the hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal.

q: Commonest position of the appendix?
why: The appendix is most often behind the caecum (retrocaecal), so it may not irritate the anterior peritoneum and signs can be atypical.

q: Surface marking of the appendix base?
hint: One-third of the way from ASIS to umbilicus.
why: McBurney's point is one-third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus, over the appendix base; tenderness there suggests appendicitis.

q: What runs in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal?
model: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.
hint: A nerve with its accompanying artery and vein.
why: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels run in Alcock's canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, to supply the perineum.

q: Space between rectum and uterus?
hint: The lowest point of the peritoneal cavity.
why: The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity when upright, so blood or pus collects there.

q: Which muscle forms the anorectal angle?
why: Puborectalis loops around the anorectal junction, pulling it forward to form an angle that helps maintain continence.

q: Which sphincter provides most resting anal pressure?
why: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle under autonomic control and provides most resting anal pressure; the external sphincter adds voluntary squeeze.

q: Where does most of the anal canal lie?
model: In the perineum, below the pelvic floor.
why: Most of the anal canal lies below the pelvic floor in the perineum, surrounded by the ischioanal fossae.

q: Name a portosystemic anastomosis in the rectum.
model: Superior rectal (portal) with middle/inferior rectal (systemic) veins.
hint: Where portal blood meets systemic blood low in the gut.
why: Superior rectal veins drain into the portal system and middle and inferior rectal veins into the systemic system, so portal hypertension can cause rectal varices.

q: Positions of the anal cushions (lithotomy)?
why: The vascular anal cushions sit at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock with the patient in lithotomy, which is where haemorrhoids usually form.

q: Which bowel is peripheral on AXR?
why: The colon frames the abdomen around the edges, while small bowel loops lie centrally.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the skin over the angle of the mandible?
hint: A branch of the cervical plexus named after the ear.
why: The angle of the jaw is not supplied by the trigeminal nerve, so it is spared in trigeminal lesions.

q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the lower lip and chin?
model: The mandibular division (V3), via the mental nerve.
why: The mental nerve leaves through the mental foramen below the second premolar.

q: Which nerve supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek and upper lip?
hint: It exits just below the orbit.
why: It emerges through the infraorbital foramen; numbness here suggests an orbital floor or zygomatic fracture.

q: Which nerve supplies the back of the scalp?
hint: A C2 nerve named after the back of the head.
why: It is blocked for occipital neuralgia and some headaches.

q: What type of fascia is absent from the face?
hint: The face has only superficial fascia.
why: Facial muscles lie in superficial fascia and attach to skin, so swelling and infection spread easily.

q: Why do the eyelids swell so easily?
acc: loose / no deep fascia / superficial / areolar
model: The loose superficial fascia has no deep fascia to contain fluid.
hint: Think about what holds tissue fluid in elsewhere.
why: Allergy, trauma and nephrotic syndrome all show early periorbital swelling.

q: Through which gland does the facial nerve pass after leaving the skull?
why: It divides into its five branches within the gland, superficial to the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery.

q: Which facial nerve branch supplies platysma?
hint: The lowest branch, heading into the neck.
why: It runs down into the neck; injury has little functional effect.

q: Which branch of the facial nerve runs with the parotid duct across masseter?
why: It supplies buccinator and the upper lip muscles.

q: Damage to which facial nerve branch stops the eye closing fully?
hint: It runs along the cheekbone to the eye.
why: It supplies orbicularis oculi; incomplete closure risks exposure keratitis.

q: Which branch of the facial nerve is at risk in submandibular gland surgery?
hint: It runs along the lower border of the jaw.
why: It can loop below the mandible; damage leaves an asymmetric lower lip when smiling.

q: In which type of facial palsy is the forehead spared?
acc: upper motor neuron / umn / upper / central / stroke
model: An upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke).
hint: Compare a cortical lesion with Bell's palsy.
why: The upper face gets input from both hemispheres; a lower motor neuron lesion (Bell's palsy) affects the whole half of the face.

q: Name the two main sphincter muscles of the face.
hint: Ring-shaped muscles round the eye and mouth.
why: They close the eye and mouth; the dilators (e.g. zygomaticus, levators, depressors) open them.

q: Which facial muscle keeps food between the teeth while chewing?
why: It is supplied by the buccal branch of VII, not by V3 like the muscles of mastication.

q: From which pharyngeal arch do the muscles of facial expression develop?
hint: The arch of the facial nerve.
why: That is why they are all supplied by the facial nerve; muscles of mastication come from the 1st arch (V3).

q: Which branch arises from the facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion?
why: It carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland, so a lesion above it gives a dry eye.

q: Where does the facial nerve run in relation to the middle ear?
model: Along the medial wall of the middle ear, above the oval window.
hint: On the inner wall of the tympanic cavity.
why: Its bony covering can be thin, so otitis media and middle ear surgery can damage it.

q: A facial palsy with hyperacusis suggests damage above which branch?
hint: The muscle that damps the stapes.
why: Without stapedius, loud sounds are not damped.

q: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?
acc: zoster / vzv / herpes zoster / shingles / varicella
model: Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion.
hint: A reactivated virus at the geniculate ganglion.
why: It causes a facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal, often with hearing loss and vertigo.

q: Which branch of the facial nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
why: It joins the lingual nerve; it also carries secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

q: Which salivary glands does the facial nerve supply?
why: The parotid is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion.

q: What is the nervus intermedius?
model: The sensory and parasympathetic root of the facial nerve.
hint: The "intermediate" part between VII and VIII.
why: It carries taste and secretomotor fibres alongside the motor root.

q: Where is the facial artery pulse felt?
model: Where it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the front of masseter.
hint: Clench the teeth to find the muscle in front of which it lies.
why: It then runs tortuously to the angle of the mouth and ends as the angular artery.

q: From which artery does the transverse facial artery arise?
hint: A terminal branch of the ECA that runs up in front of the ear.
why: It runs across masseter above the parotid duct.

q: Why do lip lacerations bleed briskly from both cut edges?
acc: anastomos / both sides / across the midline
model: The labial arteries anastomose across the midline.
hint: Think about the arteries from each side.
why: Facial wounds bleed freely but heal well because of the rich blood supply.

q: Into which sinus can facial infection spread via the ophthalmic veins?
why: The facial veins have few valves, so blood can flow backwards; cavernous sinus thrombosis causes proptosis and ophthalmoplegia.

q: What is the "danger triangle" of the face?
model: The area from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose.
hint: A triangle in the middle of the face.
why: Infection here can spread through valveless veins to the cavernous sinus.

q: Which vein connects the facial vein to the pterygoid plexus?
why: It is a second route for infection to reach the cavernous sinus.

q: Which nerve lies superficial to the facial vein near the submandibular gland?
hint: It controls the angle of the mouth.
why: Tying the facial vein low and lifting it protects the nerve (Hayes Martin manoeuvre).

q: Why is a submandibular incision made 2–3 finger-breadths below the mandible?
model: To avoid the marginal mandibular nerve.
hint: Which facial branch can loop below the jaw line?
why: The nerve can loop up to about 2 cm below the jaw.

q: Into which vein does the facial vein drain?
hint: The large vein in the carotid sheath.
why: It joins near the level of the hyoid, close to the upper jugular nodes.

q: Name the five layers of the scalp.
model: Skin, dense connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium.
hint: The letters of the word itself.
why: SCALP; the loose layer is the "danger layer".

q: Which scalp layer is the "danger layer"?
why: Blood and pus spread in it, and emissary veins crossing it carry infection to the dural sinuses.

q: Why does a scalp wound gape?
why: Occipitofrontalis pulls the edges apart when the wound goes through the galea.

q: Why do scalp lacerations bleed heavily?
acc: dense connective / can't retract / cannot retract / held open / septa
model: Vessels in the dense connective tissue are held open and can't retract.
why: Control bleeding with pressure and sutures through the dense layer.

q: Which two scalp arteries come from the internal carotid system?
model: The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (from the ophthalmic).
why: The rest (superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital) come from the external carotid.

q: What does the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis do?
model: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.
why: It is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve; it is spared in UMN facial palsy.

q: What joins the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis?
hint: A sheet of tendon over the vault.
why: It is the third layer of the scalp.

q: Which branch of the maxillary artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum?
why: It is torn in pterion fractures, causing an extradural haematoma.

q: Which terminal branch of the maxillary artery causes posterior nosebleeds?
hint: It passes through a foramen between two bones of the same name.
why: It enters the nose from the pterygopalatine fossa and can be tied endoscopically.

q: The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of which artery?
hint: The other terminal branch is the superficial temporal artery.
why: It begins behind the neck of the mandible in the parotid.

q: Around which muscle does the pterygoid venous plexus lie?
hint: A muscle of mastication that opens the jaw.
why: Chewing squeezes blood out of the plexus.

q: How does the pterygoid plexus connect to the cavernous sinus?
model: Through emissary veins (foramen ovale and lacerum).
why: Dental and facial infection can reach the cavernous sinus this way.

q: What complication can a posterior superior alveolar nerve block cause?
model: A haematoma from puncturing the pterygoid plexus.
hint: The needle enters a venous network.
why: The plexus lies close to the injection site behind the maxilla.

q: What does a "teardrop" sign in the maxillary sinus on a facial X-ray suggest?
hint: The roof of the maxillary sinus is broken.
why: Orbital fat and inferior rectus herniate into the sinus.

q: Which plain film view best shows the facial bones and sinuses?
why: Look for the zygomatic outline, orbital margins and sinus fluid levels; CT is now standard.

q: Name the three articulations within the elbow joint capsule.
acc: humero ulnar / humeroulnar + humero radial / humeroradial + radio ulnar / radioulnar
model: Humero-ulnar, humero-radial and superior radio-ulnar joints.
hint: Humerus with each forearm bone, and the two forearm bones together.
why: All share one capsule and synovial cavity.

q: Which elbow ligament resists valgus stress?
acc: ulnar collateral / medial collateral / ucl / mcl
why: It is torn in throwing athletes.

q: In extension the epicondyles and olecranon form a line; what shape do they form in flexion?
why: The relationship is disturbed in elbow dislocation but not in supracondylar fracture.

q: Which muscle is the main flexor of the elbow?
why: It inserts on the ulna, so it flexes in any forearm position; biceps also supinates.

q: Which nerve supplies triceps?
hint: It supplies all the posterior arm and forearm muscles.
why: A radial nerve lesion in the axilla loses elbow extension; in the radial groove triceps is usually spared.

q: Where does biceps brachii insert?
hint: A bump on the upper radius.
why: Its pull on the radius makes it a powerful supinator.

q: Which nerve supplies brachioradialis?
hint: The odd one out among elbow flexors.
why: Although it flexes the elbow, it develops in the posterior compartment.

q: Name the boundaries of the cubital fossa.
model: A line between the epicondyles, brachioradialis (lateral) and pronator teres (medial).
hint: A line above, then one muscle on each side.
why: The floor is brachialis and supinator; the roof includes the bicipital aponeurosis.

q: List the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial.
model: Radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.
hint: "Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest".
why: "Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest".

q: What protects the brachial artery during venepuncture at the elbow?
why: It separates the median cubital vein from the brachial artery and median nerve.

q: Which nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm?
why: It supplies biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, then becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

q: What separates the anterior and posterior compartments of the arm?
model: The medial and lateral intermuscular septa.
why: Each compartment has one nerve and one main action.

q: Which muscle helps triceps extend the elbow?
hint: A small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow.
why: It runs from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon and is supplied by the radial nerve.

q: At which level does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
model: The lower border of teres major.
hint: A shoulder muscle forming the lower edge of the axilla.
why: The axillary artery itself begins at the lateral border of the 1st rib.

q: Which artery runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove?
hint: The deep artery of the arm.
why: Both are at risk in midshaft humerus fractures.

q: Which artery winds round the surgical neck of the humerus with the axillary nerve?
hint: One of the circumflex humeral arteries.
why: It is injured with the axillary nerve in surgical neck fractures and dislocations.

q: At what level does the brachial artery divide?
acc: neck of the radius / radial neck / cubital fossa
model: At the neck of the radius in the cubital fossa.
why: It gives the radial and ulnar arteries.

q: Why can the axillary artery be tied without the arm losing its blood supply?
model: The scapular anastomosis connects subclavian and axillary branches.
hint: A network of vessels round the scapula.
why: It works if the ligature is between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery.

q: Why can collaterals fail after a sudden arterial blockage?
hint: Think about how quickly collaterals open.
why: Slow occlusion allows them to grow; sudden blockage does not.

q: Where is the brachial pulse felt at the elbow?
model: Medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.
hint: Beside a large tendon you can feel when you bend the elbow.
why: Used for blood pressure and in infants.

q: At the wrist, the ulnar pulse lies lateral to which tendon?
hint: A wrist flexor on the little-finger side.
why: It is harder to feel than the radial pulse.

q: Which superficial vein runs in the deltopectoral groove?
why: It drains into the axillary vein and is used for pacemaker leads.

q: Which vein pierces the deep fascia in the mid-arm to join the brachial veins?
why: Together they form the axillary vein; it is used for PICC lines.

q: What are the deep veins of the forearm that travel in pairs with the arteries called?
why: Arterial pulsation helps push blood along them.

q: Which nerve lies beside the cephalic vein at the wrist?
model: The superficial branch of the radial nerve.
hint: A sensory branch to the back of the thumb.
why: It can be injured during cannulation at the "houseman's vein".

q: Which vessels are joined to make a wrist arteriovenous fistula for dialysis?
model: The radial artery and cephalic vein (Brescia–Cimino).
hint: The thumb-side artery and the thumb-side superficial vein.
why: The arterialised vein enlarges and can be needled repeatedly.

q: Lymph from the medial hand runs with which vein?
why: It drains to the supratrochlear (cubital) nodes, then the axillary nodes.

q: Where do the supratrochlear (cubital) lymph nodes lie?
hint: On the inner side of the elbow.
why: They enlarge with infection of the medial hand and forearm.

q: Where does all lymph from the upper limb end up before the venous angle?
why: Axillary clearance can cause arm lymphoedema.

q: Which landmark on the back of the distal radius does EPL turn around?
why: EPL can rupture there after a distal radius fracture.

q: What is a Colles' fracture?
model: A distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement ("dinner fork").
hint: A wrist fracture from falling on an outstretched hand.
why: Typically from a fall on an outstretched hand in older women.

q: Which muscle attaches to the radial tuberosity?
why: It pulls the radius into supination.

q: Which muscle inserts on the olecranon?
why: An olecranon fracture is pulled apart by triceps, so it usually needs fixation.

q: What is a Monteggia fracture?
model: A fracture of the ulnar shaft with dislocation of the radial head.
hint: Compare with Galeazzi, a fracture of the other forearm bone.
why: The posterior interosseous nerve can be damaged.

q: Which part of the ulna receives brachialis?
hint: The beak-like process at the front.
why: Brachialis flexes the elbow through the ulna.

q: What sign tests for ulnar nerve weakness using a sheet of paper?
why: Adductor pollicis is weak, so the patient flexes the thumb IP joint (FPL, median) to grip.

q: Which muscle is best for testing the median nerve in the hand?
hint: A thenar muscle that lifts the thumb away from the palm.
why: Ask the patient to point the thumb to the ceiling against resistance.

q: Where is sensation tested for the radial nerve in the hand?
acc: first dorsal web / 1st dorsal web / dorsal web / web space / dorsum
model: The dorsum of the first web space.
hint: Between the thumb and index finger, on the back.
why: It is supplied by the superficial branch of the radial nerve.

q: A claw hand affecting the ring and little fingers suggests which nerve lesion?
why: The medial lumbricals and interossei are lost; it is worse with a distal lesion (ulnar paradox).

q: Which ligament is torn in gamekeeper's (skier's) thumb?
model: The ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint.
hint: A collateral ligament on the inner side of the thumb.
why: It weakens pinch grip; a Stener lesion needs surgery.

q: Which way do the fibres of the forearm interosseous membrane run?
acc: down + medial / distal + ulna / radius to ulna
model: Downwards and medially from the radius to the ulna.
hint: From the bone that bears the wrist to the one that forms the elbow.
why: They transfer load from the radius (wrist) to the ulna (elbow).

q: Which nerve is at risk in a medial epicondyle fracture?
why: It runs behind the medial epicondyle.

q: Which nerve is damaged in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
why: It causes weak abduction (deltoid) and a numb "regimental badge" patch.

q: What is "student's elbow"?
hint: Inflammation of a bursa at the back of the elbow.
why: Leaning on the elbow irritates the bursa over the olecranon.

q: What type of joint is the superior radio-ulnar joint?
why: The radial head turns within the annular ligament and radial notch.

q: How much of the ring around the radial head is formed by the annular ligament?
hint: The bony notch forms the smaller part.
why: The radial notch of the ulna forms the remaining fifth.

q: How is a pulled elbow reduced?
model: Supination and flexion of the elbow.
hint: Turn the palm up and bend the elbow.
why: The radial head slips back into the annular ligament with a click.

q: In which space does cerebrospinal fluid circulate?
why: It lies between the arachnoid and pia mater and contains the cerebral arteries.

q: Which vessels tear in a subdural haemorrhage?
hint: Veins crossing from brain to sinus.
why: They cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural sinuses; they stretch with brain atrophy in older people and alcoholics.

q: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
why: Lumbar puncture is done below this at L3/4 or L4/5.

q: Which pia mater extensions anchor the spinal cord laterally?
why: Their tooth-like attachments hold the cord in the middle of the dural sac.

q: Which dural fold separates the cerebral hemispheres?
why: The superior sagittal sinus runs in its attached edge; the cingulate gyrus can herniate under it.

q: Which dural fold lies between the cerebrum and cerebellum?
why: Its free edge forms the tentorial notch; the uncus herniates through it, compressing III.

q: Which dural fold forms a roof over the pituitary fossa?
why: The pituitary stalk passes through it.

q: Between which two layers of dura do the venous sinuses lie?
model: Between the endosteal and meningeal layers.
hint: The bone layer and the brain layer.
why: The layers separate to enclose the sinuses.

q: Which sinus runs in the free edge of the falx cerebri?
hint: The lower of the two sagittal sinuses.
why: It drains into the straight sinus.

q: At what level is a lumbar puncture done in adults?
hint: Below the end of the spinal cord.
why: Below the end of the cord at L1/2; Tuffier's line marks L4.

q: In which space is an epidural injected?
why: It is found by loss of resistance after passing the ligamentum flavum.

q: Why do spinal and epidural blocks cause hypotension?
model: They block sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilation.
hint: Which autonomic outflow leaves the thoracolumbar cord?
why: Treat with fluids and vasopressors.

q: What is the commonest complication of a lumbar puncture?
why: CSF leaks through the dural hole; it is worse sitting up and better lying flat.

q: Why is a CT scan done before LP in a patient with a reduced consciousness level?
acc: cone / coning / herniat / raised icp / mass
model: To exclude a mass or raised pressure that could cause coning.
hint: What could removing CSF from below do to the brainstem?
why: Removing CSF below a mass can pull the brainstem through the foramen magnum.

q: Which serious complication of epidural anaesthesia is linked to anticoagulants?
why: It can compress the cord; anticoagulants are timed around epidural insertion and removal.

q: Which structure produces most cerebrospinal fluid?
hint: A vascular fringe inside the ventricles.
why: Mainly in the lateral ventricles; about 500 mL is made each day.

q: Which narrow channel is the commonest site of obstruction causing congenital hydrocephalus?
why: It joins the 3rd and 4th ventricles through the midbrain and is the narrowest part of the system.

q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid absorbed?
model: Through the arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus.
hint: Projections into the dural venous sinuses.
why: Scarring after meningitis or SAH causes communicating hydrocephalus.

q: What is the triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
model: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and dementia.
why: "Wet, wobbly and wacky"; it can improve with a shunt.

q: Through which foramina does the 4th ventricle drain into the subarachnoid space?
model: The median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka).
hint: One median and two lateral apertures, both eponymous.
why: Blockage (e.g. Dandy–Walker) causes hydrocephalus.

q: Name the layers of the epidermis from deep to superficial.
model: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only) and corneum.
why: "British Soldiers Get Lots of Cash".

q: In which layer of the epidermis do cells divide?
why: Cells take about 4 weeks to reach the surface; melanocytes also lie here.

q: Which cell junction is attacked in pemphigus vulgaris?
why: Cells separate within the epidermis, giving fragile blisters; bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes.

q: Which epidermal layer is found only in thick skin?
why: Thick skin (palms and soles) also has no hair follicles.

q: Which antigen-presenting cells sit in the epidermis?
why: They carry antigens to lymph nodes; involved in contact dermatitis.

q: Which layer of the dermis contains sweat glands and hair follicles?
hint: The deeper of the two dermal layers.
why: It is dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen I, giving strength.

q: Which pressure receptors lie deep in the dermis and hypodermis?
why: They sense vibration and deep pressure; Meissner's corpuscles sense light touch.

q: Which type of epithelium forms the epidermis?
hint: Many layers, flat cells on top, filled with keratin.
why: It is avascular, so it is nourished from the dermis.

q: Between which ribs does the breast lie?
why: It extends from the sternum to the midaxillary line, with an axillary tail.

q: Which ligaments cause skin dimpling when breast cancer pulls on them?
hint: Named after a surgeon; they run from skin to deep fascia.
why: They run from the skin to the deep fascia.

q: Which artery supplies most of the medial breast?
hint: It runs down beside the sternum.
why: The lateral thoracic and intercostal arteries supply the rest.

q: What happens to breast tissue after the menopause?
model: Glandular tissue involutes and is replaced by fat.
hint: Think about what makes mammograms easier in older women.
why: The breast becomes less dense, so mammograms are easier to read.

q: Which dermatome supplies the nipple?
hint: The same level as the sternal angle's neighbour below.
why: The breast is supplied by intercostal nerves T4–6.

q: In which quadrant do most breast cancers arise?
why: It holds the most glandular tissue, including the axillary tail.

q: Approximately what proportion of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes?
hint: Most of it, but not all.
why: Most of the rest drains to the internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes.

q: Which group of axillary nodes receives breast lymph first?
hint: Along the lateral thoracic vessels, under the big chest muscle.
why: They lie along the lateral thoracic vessels.

q: Which axillary nodes lie behind pectoralis minor?
hint: Levels are defined by a small chest muscle.
why: Level I is lateral and level III medial to pectoralis minor.

q: What is the first node to receive lymph from a tumour called?
why: Sentinel node biopsy stages the axilla with less morbidity than clearance.

q: Which nerve injury causes a winged scapula after axillary surgery?
why: It supplies serratus anterior and runs on the medial wall of the axilla.

q: Besides the breast, which regions drain to the axillary nodes?
acc: upper limb / arm + trunk / chest / back
model: The whole upper limb and the skin of the trunk above the umbilicus.
hint: A limb and the skin above the umbilicus.
why: An enlarged axillary node can come from an arm infection or a trunk melanoma.

q: Which imaging is first-line for a breast lump in a woman under 40?
hint: No radiation, good in dense tissue.
why: Young breasts are dense on mammography; ultrasound tells cysts from solid masses.

q: What mammographic finding suggests ductal carcinoma in situ?
why: DCIS often has no mass.

q: At what ages are women screened with mammography in the NHS?
hint: Starts in the early fifties at the latest.
why: The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women from 50 up to their 71st birthday.

q: How does a simple cyst look on breast ultrasound?
hint: Fluid looks this way on ultrasound.
why: Solid suspicious masses are irregular, taller than wide, with posterior shadowing.

q: What are the three parts of triple assessment for a breast lump?
acc: examination / clinical + imaging / mammo / ultrasound + biopsy
hint: Feel it, image it, sample it.
why: All three are done in a one-stop breast clinic.

q: Which women are screened with breast MRI?
acc: high risk / brca / genetic / family history
hint: Women whose lifetime risk is much higher than average.
why: MRI is more sensitive in young dense breasts.

q: What does the free edge of the falciform ligament contain?
model: The ligamentum teres (remnant of the umbilical vein).
hint: A remnant of a fetal vein.
why: Its paraumbilical veins can recanalise in portal hypertension (caput medusae).

q: What is the area of liver not covered by peritoneum called?
why: It is enclosed by the coronary ligaments and lies against the diaphragm.

q: Which way does the liver move during inspiration?
why: The diaphragm descends, so the liver edge is palpated as the patient breathes in.

q: What is the hepatorenal pouch also called?
why: It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when supine, checked first for fluid on a FAST scan.

q: Which structure is most posterior at the porta hepatis?
hint: Ducts in front, artery in the middle.
why: From front to back: bile ducts, hepatic artery, portal vein.

q: Do the hepatic veins leave the liver at the porta hepatis?
why: They drain straight into the IVC on the back of the liver.

q: What is the Pringle manoeuvre?
acc: clamp + hepatoduodenal / lesser omentum / free edge / portal triad
model: Clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament (portal triad) to stop blood flow into the liver.
why: Used to control bleeding in liver trauma or surgery.

q: Which two veins join to form the portal vein?
model: The superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
hint: One from the midgut, one from the spleen.
why: They join behind the neck of the pancreas at L1.

q: Name the portosystemic anastomosis that causes life-threatening bleeding in portal hypertension.
model: Lower oesophagus (left gastric to oesophageal veins).
hint: Where the gullet meets the stomach.
why: Oesophageal varices can bleed massively.

q: Which portosystemic anastomosis gives caput medusae?
model: The paraumbilical veins to the superficial epigastric veins at the umbilicus.
why: Dilated veins radiate from the umbilicus.

q: What proportion of the liver's blood supply comes from the portal vein?
hint: More than half; the hepatic artery gives the rest.
why: The hepatic artery provides the rest, but much of the oxygen.

q: Why does portal hypertension cause a low platelet count?
why: The splenic vein drains into the portal vein, so the spleen congests.

q: Under which ribs does the spleen lie?
why: Its long axis lies along the 10th rib.

q: In which direction does an enlarging spleen grow?
acc: right iliac / rif / umbilicus / down / inferior
model: Downwards and towards the right iliac fossa.
why: You start palpating from the right iliac fossa.

q: Name a feature that distinguishes an enlarged spleen from an enlarged kidney.
acc: notch / can't get above / cannot get above / not ballotable / dull
model: It has a notch, you can't get above it, and it isn't ballotable.
hint: Its edge has a feature, and think about getting above it.
why: A kidney is ballotable and has resonant bowel in front.

q: Which sign describes left shoulder-tip pain from a ruptured spleen?
why: Blood irritates the diaphragm, whose phrenic supply (C4) refers pain to the shoulder.

q: Which vaccinations are needed after splenectomy?
model: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines (plus yearly flu).
why: The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria.

q: Which organ can be damaged during splenectomy because it lies in the splenorenal ligament?
hint: An organ that lies behind the stomach.
why: Injury causes a pancreatic fistula.

q: Why should contact sports be avoided in glandular fever?
hint: Which organ swells in EBV infection?
why: An enlarged spleen leaves the protection of the ribs.

q: The splenic artery arises from which trunk?
why: It is its largest branch and runs tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas.

q: Which vein joins the splenic vein behind the pancreas?
why: The splenic vein then joins the SMV to form the portal vein.

q: Pancreatitis causing splenic vein thrombosis can lead to bleeding from which varices?
why: Blood diverts through the short gastric veins.

q: Which ligament carries the short gastric vessels?
hint: Named after the two organs it joins.
why: It joins the greater curvature of the stomach to the splenic hilum.

q: Which ligament carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas?
hint: Named after the spleen and kidney.
why: It joins the left kidney to the splenic hilum.

q: Is the spleen intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal?
hint: Think about its two peritoneal ligaments.
why: It is covered by peritoneum except at the hilum.

q: At what vertebral level does the IVC pass through the diaphragm?
hint: The highest of the three big openings.
why: "I 8 10 Eggs At 12": IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.

q: Which part of the diaphragm is attached to L1–3?
hint: The longer of the two crura.
why: The left crus attaches to L1–2; the right crus forms the oesophageal sphincter.

q: What does the diaphragm do to the chest on contraction?
model: It flattens and descends, increasing chest volume.
why: Pressure in the chest falls and air flows in.

q: To which level does the right dome of the diaphragm rise in expiration?
hint: The rib below the nipple level in men.
why: The left dome reaches the 5th intercostal space.

q: What passes through the oesophageal hiatus with the oesophagus?
model: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
why: Also oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.

q: Which structures pass through the aortic hiatus?
model: The aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.
hint: An artery, a lymph duct and a vein.
why: It lies behind the median arcuate ligament at T12.

q: Through which gap do the superior epigastric vessels pass?
hint: Between the sternal and costal parts.
why: A congenital hernia can occur here.

q: Which nerve carries pain from the central diaphragm?
why: Pain is referred to the shoulder tip (C4).

q: Pain from the peripheral diaphragm is felt where?
acc: chest wall / abdomen / costal margin / lower chest
model: Over the lower chest wall and upper abdomen.
hint: Its outer parts share nerves with the body wall.
why: The peripheral diaphragm is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves (T6–11).

q: Why does cholecystitis cause right shoulder pain?
model: The inflamed gallbladder irritates the diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C4).
why: C4 also supplies the skin over the shoulder.

q: How many functional segments does the liver have?
why: Each has its own portal venous, arterial and biliary supply, so it can be removed alone.

q: Which liver segment is the caudate lobe?
why: It drains straight into the IVC, so it is spared and enlarges in Budd–Chiari syndrome.

q: What lies between the liver segments?
hint: Which vessels are not in the portal triads?
why: Portal triads run in the centre of segments, hepatic veins between them.

q: Which vein divides the functional right and left livers?
why: The line runs from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC.

q: Which two nuclei make up the striatum?
hint: The C-shaped nucleus and the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.
why: It is the input nucleus of the basal ganglia.

q: Which neurotransmitter is lost from the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease?
why: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine causes bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.

q: A lesion of which nucleus causes hemiballismus?
why: Usually a small stroke; the opposite limbs fling wildly.

q: Atrophy of which nucleus is typical of Huntington's disease?
hint: It bulges into the lateral ventricle.
why: It causes chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric problems.

q: Through which thalamic nuclei do the basal ganglia project to the motor cortex?
acc: va / vl / ventral anterior / ventral lateral
model: The ventral anterior and ventral lateral (VA/VL) nuclei.
why: The basal ganglia have no direct spinal output.

q: Does the direct pathway of the basal ganglia facilitate or suppress movement?
hint: The opposite of the indirect pathway.
why: The indirect pathway, via the subthalamic nucleus, suppresses movement.

q: Which thalamic nucleus relays vision?
why: The medial geniculate relays hearing.

q: Which thalamic nucleus relays sensation from the face?
why: VPL relays sensation from the body.

q: Which sense does not relay through the thalamus first?
why: Olfactory fibres reach the cortex directly.

q: What is Dejerine–Roussy syndrome?
model: Thalamic pain syndrome after a thalamic stroke.
hint: A syndrome after a stroke in a sensory relay.
why: Severe burning pain on the opposite side of the body.

q: Which thalamic nucleus relays hearing?
why: "M for music".

q: Which limbic structure forms new declarative memories?
why: It is affected early in Alzheimer's disease.

q: Which limbic structure processes fear?
why: Bilateral damage causes Klüver–Bucy syndrome (no fear, hyperorality).

q: Damage to the mammillary bodies in thiamine deficiency causes what?
why: The mammillary bodies are part of the Papez memory circuit.

q: What is the main output tract of the hippocampus?
why: It runs to the mammillary bodies in the Papez circuit.

q: Put the start of the Papez circuit in order: after the hippocampus comes which tract?
model: The fornix, then mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus and back to the hippocampus.
hint: An arched tract under the corpus callosum.
why: It links memory and emotion.

q: Which limbic structure links emotion to autonomic and hormonal responses?
why: It drives the heart rate, sweating and stress hormone responses to emotion.

q: In which part of the brainstem are the pyramids?
why: The corticospinal tracts decussate at their lower end.

q: Damage to which tract causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia?
hint: It links the eye movement nuclei.
why: It links the VI nucleus on one side with the III nucleus on the other; MS is a common cause in young people.

q: In the "rule of 4s", what do the four midline structures of the brainstem begin with?
model: M (motor tract, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor nuclei).
why: The four lateral structures begin with S.

q: Which sensory tract runs near the midline throughout the brainstem?
why: It carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception after crossing in the medulla.

q: Where in the internal capsule do corticospinal fibres to the limbs run?
why: A small lacunar infarct here causes a dense hemiplegia of face, arm and leg.

q: Name two upper motor neuron signs.
acc: spastic / hyperreflexi / brisk / babinski / upgoing / clonus
why: LMN lesions cause wasting, fasciculations and hyporeflexia instead.

q: A brainstem lesion causing an ipsilateral III palsy with contralateral hemiplegia is called what?
why: A midbrain lesion hits the III fascicles and the cerebral peduncle.

q: A cord lesion of the corticospinal tract causes weakness on which side?
why: The tract has already crossed in the medulla.

q: Which name describes the pattern of weakness in a UMN lesion?
why: Arm extensors and leg flexors are weaker than their antagonists.

q: Where do the dorsal column fibres cross?
hint: The lowest part of the brainstem.
why: After synapsing in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, they cross as internal arcuate fibres.

q: Where do spinothalamic fibres cross?
acc: anterior white commissure / spinal cord / within / 1 2 segment
model: In the spinal cord within 1–2 segments of entry (anterior white commissure).
why: So cord lesions cause opposite-side loss of pain and temperature.

q: Which thalamic nucleus relays both sensory pathways from the body?
why: It projects to the postcentral gyrus.

q: Which fasciculus carries fine touch from the legs?
why: The cuneate fasciculus carries it from the arms and lies lateral.

q: A positive Romberg's test points to loss of which pathway?
hint: The pathway for joint position sense.
why: Patients rely on vision for balance, so they sway with eyes shut.

q: In which gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex?
why: It lies behind the central sulcus in the parietal lobe.

q: Which imaging is best for the posterior fossa?
why: Bone artefact from the petrous bones obscures the brainstem on CT.

q: Why is a large cerebellar haemorrhage a neurosurgical emergency?
acc: hydrocephalus / 4th ventricle / fourth ventricle / brainstem / coning
model: It compresses the 4th ventricle and brainstem.
hint: Think of what lies in front of the cerebellum.
why: It causes obstructive hydrocephalus and coning.

q: Which tumour sits at the cerebellopontine angle?
hint: A tumour of the nerve sheath of VIII.
why: It causes unilateral deafness and tinnitus, then V and VII signs.

q: In a Chiari I malformation, what lies below the foramen magnum?
why: More than 5 mm below the foramen magnum; it can cause headache and syringomyelia.

q: Which imaging sequence shows an acute posterior circulation stroke?
hint: An MRI sequence that detects restricted water movement.
why: Early infarcts show as bright; CT often misses posterior fossa strokes.

q: Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium. Which nerve can it compress?
model: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome).
hint: It hooks under the aortic arch.
why: The large atrium and pulmonary artery stretch the nerve under the aortic arch, causing hoarseness.

q: Which way is the trachea pushed in a tension pneumothorax?
hint: Air under pressure in one side of the chest.
why: Air under pressure pushes the mediastinum across and kinks the great veins.

q: A pleural effusion and a lobar collapse both cause dullness. How does the trachea help tell them apart?
model: A large effusion pushes it away; collapse pulls it towards the affected side.
hint: Which one adds volume and which removes it?
why: Effusion adds volume to that side; collapse removes it.

q: A Pancoast tumour at the lung apex can cause which syndrome affecting the eye?
why: It invades the sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion.

q: Why does coarctation of the aorta cause rib notching?
model: Enlarged intercostal collateral arteries erode the rib undersides.
hint: Bypass vessels run in the grooves under the ribs.
why: Blood bypasses the narrowing through internal thoracic and intercostal arteries.

q: Why does an inhaled foreign body usually enter the right main bronchus?
model: It is wider, shorter and more vertical.
hint: Compare its shape with the left.
why: Aspiration pneumonia also favours the right lower lobe.

q: Right heart failure causes liver enlargement. Why?
acc: hepatic vein / ivc / back pressure / congestion
model: Raised pressure backs up through the IVC into the hepatic veins.
hint: Follow the venous return from the liver.
why: The liver becomes congested and tender.

q: A lung cancer at the hilum compressing the SVC causes what?
acc: svc obstruction / superior vena cava / facial swelling / swelling
model: SVC obstruction: facial and arm swelling with dilated chest veins.
hint: Venous return from the head and arms is blocked.
why: Headache worse on bending forward; treat with a stent and steroids.

q: Why does a large left atrium cause difficulty swallowing?
model: It presses on the oesophagus behind it.
hint: What lies directly behind the left atrium?
why: The oesophagus lies directly behind the left atrium.

q: Which artery can bleed from a posterior duodenal ulcer?
hint: A branch of the common hepatic artery.
why: It runs behind the 1st part of the duodenum.

q: Which watershed area of the colon is most prone to ischaemia?
why: It lies between the SMA and IMA territories.

q: In large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve, which part is most likely to perforate?
hint: The widest part of the colon.
why: It has the widest diameter, so wall tension is highest (law of Laplace).

q: Why is sigmoid volvulus possible?
model: The sigmoid has a long mesentery.
hint: It is mobile on a long fold of peritoneum.
why: It can twist on itself, giving a "coffee-bean" sign on X-ray.

q: Where do diverticula form in the colon wall?
acc: vessel / blood vessels / vasa recta / weak
model: Where blood vessels pierce the muscle wall.
hint: Where something passes through the muscle layer.
why: Mostly in the sigmoid, which has the highest pressure.

q: Why are internal haemorrhoids painless?
model: They arise above the pectinate line, which has visceral nerve supply.
hint: Think about the nerve supply above the dentate line.
why: Below the line, somatic pudendal fibres make lesions painful.

q: Through which vein do colorectal cancers reach the liver?
why: Gut venous blood drains to the liver first, so it is the commonest site of metastasis.

q: How can small bowel be told from large bowel on an abdominal X-ray?
model: Small bowel has valvulae conniventes crossing the full width; large bowel has haustra that don't.
why: Small bowel is central; large bowel is peripheral.

q: Stomach cancer spreading to the left supraclavicular node is called what sign?
why: Lymph reaches it via the thoracic duct.

q: Why can cervical cancer cause renal failure?
model: It spreads to the parametrium and blocks the ureters.
why: The ureters lie about 2 cm lateral to the cervix.

q: Why can a left renal tumour cause a left varicocele?
acc: renal vein / left renal / testicular vein / gonadal vein
model: It blocks the left renal vein, into which the left testicular vein drains.
hint: Left and right veins from the testes end in different places.
why: The right testicular vein drains straight into the IVC.

q: Which sign of BPH can damage both kidneys?
hint: The obstruction is below both ureters.
why: High bladder pressure is transmitted up both ureters.

q: Where is a horseshoe kidney trapped during ascent?
why: The fused lower poles catch on it.

q: Why does testicular cancer spread to para-aortic nodes rather than inguinal nodes?
acc: develop / descen / kidney / posterior abdominal / retroperitone
model: The testis develops near the kidneys and keeps its lymph drainage when it descends.
why: Scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to the inguinal nodes.

q: Through which venous plexus does prostate cancer spread to the spine?
why: It is valveless and connects the prostatic and vertebral veins.

q: Where does blood collect after a ruptured ectopic pregnancy in a standing woman?
hint: Between the uterus and the rectum.
why: It is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity when upright.

q: Why can ovarian pathology cause medial thigh pain?
model: The obturator nerve lies beside the ovary.
why: It runs on the lateral pelvic wall next to the ovarian fossa.

q: Which supports, weakened by childbirth, allow uterovaginal prolapse?
acc: levator / pelvic floor + fascia / cardinal / uterosacral
model: Levator ani and the endopelvic fascia (cardinal and uterosacral ligaments).
hint: A muscle sheet and condensed connective tissue.
why: Stretching of the pudendal nerve adds to the weakness.

q: What protein forms neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease?
why: Tangles are intracellular; amyloid plaques are extracellular.

q: What forms the plaques in Alzheimer's disease?
why: Plaques are extracellular; amyloid also deposits in vessel walls (amyloid angiopathy).

q: Which part of the brain atrophies earliest in Alzheimer's disease?
why: That is why new memory is lost first.

q: What protein forms Lewy bodies?
hint: The same protein builds up in Parkinson's disease.
why: Lewy bodies are round eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions with a pale halo.

q: Which midbrain structure looks pale in Parkinson's and Lewy body disease?
why: Dopaminergic, pigmented neurons are lost.

q: Name a histological feature of vascular dementia.
acc: infarct / lacun / arteriolosclerosis / white matter / hyaline / gliosis
model: Multiple small infarcts (lacunes), arteriolosclerosis and white matter rarefaction.
why: It causes a stepwise decline with focal signs.

q: Which stain shows amyloid with apple-green birefringence?
hint: A red dye named after an African country.
why: Viewed under polarised light.

q: Which dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism?
why: Patients are very sensitive to antipsychotics.

q: From which embryonic tissue do the kidneys develop?
hint: The mesoderm between the somites and the lateral plate.
why: It forms the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros in turn.

q: Which kidney system becomes the permanent kidney?
hint: The third and most caudal system.
why: The pronephros regresses and the mesonephros works only temporarily.

q: Which tissue forms the nephrons?
acc: metanephric blastema / metanephric mesenchyme / blastema / mesenchyme
why: The ureteric bud forms the collecting system; each induces the other.

q: Bilateral renal agenesis leads to oligohydramnios and which sequence?
hint: Named after the pathologist who described the facial features.
why: Without fetal urine there is little amniotic fluid, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and facial compression.

q: What does the allantois become in the adult?
model: The urachus, then the median umbilical ligament.
hint: A ligament running from the bladder apex to the umbilicus.
why: A patent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus.

q: What does the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct form in males?
model: The epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory duct.
why: Testosterone from Leydig cells keeps it from regressing.

q: What do the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts form in females?
acc: uterine tube / fallopian / uterus / cervix / vagina
model: The uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina.
why: Without AMH they persist; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus.

q: What does the genital tubercle become in each sex?
why: DHT drives the male pathway.

q: Which enzyme converts testosterone to DHT for male external genitalia?
why: Deficiency gives ambiguous genitalia in a 46,XY baby that virilise at puberty.

q: Incomplete fusion of the urogenital folds causes what?
hint: The meatus opens on the ventral surface.
why: The urethral opening lies on the underside of the penis.

q: What structure guides the testis into the scrotum?
why: In females it becomes the ovarian and round ligaments.

q: What forms the floor of the oral cavity?
model: The mylohyoid (oral diaphragm), with geniohyoid and the tongue.
hint: A muscular sheet from the mandible to the hyoid.
why: The submandibular gland wraps round its posterior border.

q: What is the space between the lips and cheeks and the teeth called?
hint: The entrance hall of the mouth.
why: The parotid duct opens into it opposite the upper 2nd molar.

q: Which nerve gives sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and oropharynx?
why: It is the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the hard palate behind the incisors?
hint: It runs down the nasal septum first.
why: The greater palatine nerve supplies the rest of the hard palate.

q: Which ganglion relays the parasympathetic supply to the parotid gland?
why: Fibres from IX reach it via the tympanic and lesser petrosal nerves, then travel with the auriculotemporal nerve.

q: Which nerve crosses the submandibular duct in the floor of the mouth?
hint: It supplies sensation to the front of the tongue.
why: It loops under the duct and is at risk when removing a duct stone.

q: What type of saliva does the parotid gland make?
why: The sublingual gland makes mainly mucous saliva; the submandibular makes mixed.

q: Why is mumps so painful?
model: The swollen parotid is enclosed by tight parotid fascia.
hint: Think about what surrounds the gland.
why: The fascia comes from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

q: What effect does parasympathetic stimulation have on saliva?
why: Sympathetic stimulation produces scanty, thick saliva.

q: Why are stones more common in the submandibular gland?
acc: viscous / uphill / alkaline / calcium / mucous / long / bend
model: Its saliva is more viscous and alkaline, and its duct is long and runs uphill.
hint: Think about the saliva and the duct's path.
why: About 80–90% of salivary stones form there.

q: Where is the narrowest point of the submandibular duct?
hint: Where it opens beside the frenulum.
why: Stones also impact where the duct bends round mylohyoid.

q: What is the classic symptom of a salivary duct stone?
model: Pain and swelling of the gland at mealtimes.
why: Saliva builds up behind the stone when secretion increases.

q: Which large vein lies within the parotid gland?
why: It forms from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

q: What is the commonest parotid tumour?
why: It is benign; a facial nerve palsy suggests a malignant tumour instead.

q: What is Frey's syndrome?
hint: Something happens to the cheek skin when eating.
why: Parasympathetic fibres in the auriculotemporal nerve regrow into sweat glands.

q: What does the facial nerve divide the parotid gland into?
why: It is the surgical plane for a superficial parotidectomy.

q: What V-shaped groove divides the tongue into its anterior two-thirds and posterior third?
why: The foramen caecum at its apex marks where the thyroid began to develop.

q: Which papillae lie in a V just in front of the sulcus terminalis?
why: They are large, surrounded by a trench, and have many taste buds.

q: Which artery supplies the tongue?
model: The lingual artery (from the external carotid).
why: It runs deep to hyoglossus.

q: Why can cancer of the back of the tongue spread to nodes on both sides of the neck?
model: Lymph near the midline drains to both sides.
hint: Think about where the posterior third sits and where its lymph goes.
why: The posterior third drains to the deep cervical nodes.

q: Which extrinsic tongue muscle protrudes the tongue?
hint: Attached to the inside of the chin.
why: A jaw thrust pulls it forwards and opens the airway.

q: Do the intrinsic muscles of the tongue change its shape or position?
why: The extrinsic muscles, attached to bone, change its position.

q: Which nerve supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus?
why: Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus.

q: Which tongue muscle runs from the styloid process?
why: It retracts and elevates the tongue in swallowing.

q: Which nerve carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
why: Taste from the same area travels with it in the chorda tympani.

q: Which nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue?
hint: It also gives the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
why: It carries both taste and general sensation there, including the circumvallate papillae.

q: In which brainstem nucleus do taste fibres end?
model: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
why: From there taste goes to the VPM of the thalamus and the insula.

q: Why can removing a lower third molar cause loss of taste on the front of the tongue?
model: The lingual nerve, carrying chorda tympani fibres, lies close to the tooth.
hint: A nerve runs just inside the jaw beside the wisdom tooth.
why: Injury causes numbness and taste loss on the anterior two-thirds.

q: Which muscle's weakness makes the tongue deviate on protrusion?
why: The working muscle on the other side pushes the tongue towards the weak side.

q: Wasting and fasciculation of the tongue suggest an upper or lower motor neuron lesion?
why: For example motor neurone disease (bulbar palsy).

q: What is the difference between bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy in the tongue?
model: Bulbar: wasted, fasciculating tongue (LMN). Pseudobulbar: small, stiff, spastic tongue (UMN).
why: Pseudobulbar palsy also has a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability.

q: Where is the otic ganglion?
model: In the infratemporal fossa, just below the foramen ovale.
hint: Just below the opening for V3.
why: It lies medial to the mandibular nerve.

q: Which nerve carries fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland?
hint: It runs up in front of the ear.
why: Damage to it after parotidectomy can cause Frey's syndrome.

q: Through which plexus in the middle ear do the parotid's parasympathetic fibres pass?
hint: On the promontory of the middle ear.
why: From IX via the tympanic nerve, then out as the lesser petrosal nerve.

q: Which artery supplies the caecum, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon?
why: Its ileocolic, right colic and middle colic branches supply the midgut part of the colon.

q: What is the arterial arcade running along the inner margin of the colon called?
hint: An eponymous artery at the edge of the colon.
why: It links the colic arteries, so the colon can survive if one feeding artery is tied.

q: Which parts of the colon are retroperitoneal?
why: The transverse and sigmoid colon have mesenteries and are mobile.

q: Midgut pain is felt around the umbilicus. Where is hindgut pain felt?
why: Visceral afferents follow sympathetic supply from about L1.

q: Lymph from the colon drains to nodes along which vessels?
model: Along the colic and mesenteric arteries (to superior and inferior mesenteric nodes).
