why: Cancer surgery removes the artery with its mesentery and nodes.

q: Which artery supplies the appendix?
why: It is an end artery, so inflammation can cause gangrene and perforation.

q: How can the base of the appendix be found at surgery?
model: Follow the taeniae coli down the caecum: they converge at its base.
hint: The three longitudinal bands of the colon.
why: The tip varies in position but the base is constant.

q: Why does a pelvic appendicitis cause urinary or rectal symptoms?
acc: bladder / rectum / pelvis / adjacent / next to
model: The inflamed tip lies against the bladder or rectum.
hint: Think about which organs touch its tip.
why: Abdominal signs can be minimal; a rectal exam may be tender.

q: Why does early appendicitis pain start around the umbilicus?
model: It is visceral pain from a midgut organ (T10).
hint: Which part of the gut does the appendix come from?
why: Once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed, the pain localises to the right iliac fossa.

q: What are the boundaries of the ischioanal fossa?
model: Lateral: obturator internus; medial: levator ani and external anal sphincter; floor: perianal skin.
hint: A wedge between the pelvic wall muscle and the pelvic floor.
why: It is filled with fat and lets the anal canal distend.

q: What is a horseshoe abscess?
model: Pus spreading from one ischioanal fossa to the other behind the anal canal.
hint: It wraps round the back of the anus.
why: The two fossae communicate posteriorly.

q: Where do most anal fissures occur?
why: Blood supply is poorest there; anterior fissures are more common after childbirth.

q: Infection of which glands causes most perianal abscesses and fistulas?
model: The anal glands (in the anal crypts at the dentate line).
hint: Small glands at the dentate line.
why: Infection tracks through the sphincters into the ischioanal fossa.

q: At which vertebral level does the sigmoid colon become the rectum?
why: Here the taeniae spread out and the mesentery ends.

q: What lies behind the rectum?
model: The sacrum and coccyx (with the sacral plexus and median sacral vessels).
hint: Bones at the back of the pelvis.
why: Rectal cancer can invade the sacral nerves, causing pain.

q: What lies in front of the rectum in a man?
model: The bladder, seminal vesicles and prostate (with the rectovesical pouch).
hint: What do you feel on a male rectal exam?
why: The prostate is felt through the anterior rectal wall.

q: What happens to the taeniae coli at the rectum?
model: They spread out into a continuous longitudinal muscle coat.
hint: The three bands no longer stay separate.
why: The rectum also has no haustra or appendices epiploicae.

q: Which muscle forms the anorectal angle by looping behind the anorectal junction?
hint: A muscle from the pubis around the rectum.
why: Its sling pulls the junction forwards; relaxing it straightens the angle for defecation.

q: What is the internal anal sphincter made of?
model: Smooth muscle (thickened circular muscle of the gut).
hint: Continuous with the circular muscle of the rectum.
why: It is involuntary and sympathetically maintained; the external sphincter is skeletal.

q: Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
hint: The nerve to the perineum, S2–4.
why: It is under voluntary control; damage in childbirth contributes to incontinence.

q: Is the external anal sphincter under voluntary or involuntary control?
why: It contracts to defer defecation; the internal sphincter is involuntary.

q: What is the rectoanal inhibitory reflex?
model: Relaxation of the internal sphincter when the rectum distends.
hint: Distension of the rectum triggers one sphincter to open.
why: It lets the anal canal sample the contents (gas versus stool) while the external sphincter holds.

q: Which three structures maintain faecal continence?
model: The internal sphincter, external sphincter and puborectalis (plus the anal cushions).
why: Sphincter injury in childbirth is a common cause of incontinence.

q: Which line marks the junction between the gut-derived and skin-derived parts of the anal canal?
why: Above it: visceral nerves, IMA supply, portal venous drainage; below it: somatic nerves, pudendal supply, systemic drainage.

q: To which nodes does the anal canal below the pectinate line drain?
why: Above the line lymph goes to internal iliac and mesenteric nodes.

q: Why are lesions below the pectinate line painful?
model: They have somatic sensory supply (inferior rectal nerve, from the pudendal).
hint: Which kind of nerves supply skin?
why: Above the line, visceral nerves only sense stretch.

q: From which artery does the superior rectal artery arise?
why: It is the main supply to the rectum.

q: From which artery does the inferior rectal artery arise?
why: It supplies only the anal canal below the pectinate line.

q: Into which vein does the superior rectal vein drain?
why: The middle and inferior rectal veins drain systemically, forming a portosystemic anastomosis.

q: From which artery does the middle rectal artery arise?
hint: The main artery of the pelvis.
why: It supplies the lower rectum and anastomoses with the superior and inferior rectal arteries.

q: What do the anal cushions contribute to continence?
model: They seal the anal canal for fine control of fluid and gas.
hint: They act like a soft plug.
why: They provide about 15–20% of resting pressure.

q: What are haemorrhoids?
why: Straining and constipation stretch their supporting tissue; they bleed bright red blood.

q: Are internal haemorrhoids above or below the pectinate line?
why: That is why they are painless.

q: What do haustra look like on an abdominal X-ray?
acc: do not cross / partial / don't cross / not cross
model: Folds that don't cross the full width of the bowel.
why: Small bowel valvulae conniventes cross the whole width.

q: Above what diameter is the caecum considered dangerously dilated?
why: The caecum is at risk of perforation in large bowel obstruction.

q: Which colon part appears as a "coffee bean" on X-ray when twisted?
why: Its long mesentery lets it twist.

q: What are the wings around the nostrils called?
why: They flare in respiratory distress (nasal flaring).

q: Which part of the external nose is made of bone?
model: The upper part (bridge), formed by the nasal bones and maxillae.
why: The lower part is cartilage, so nasal fractures affect the bridge.

q: What separates the two nostrils?
model: The columella (lower edge of the septum).
why: Septal haematoma after trauma must be drained to prevent cartilage necrosis.

q: Which bones form the nasal septum?
model: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer (plus septal cartilage).
hint: A perpendicular plate and a ploughshare-shaped bone.
why: A deviated septum can block airflow.

q: Which bone forms the inferior concha?
model: It is a separate bone (the inferior nasal concha).
hint: Unlike the other two, it is a bone of its own.
why: The superior and middle conchae belong to the ethmoid.

q: Which bone carries the superior and middle conchae?
why: Its labyrinth contains the ethmoid air cells.

q: Which arteries form Kiesselbach's plexus?
acc: sphenopalatine / greater palatine / anterior ethmoidal / superior labial / facial
model: The sphenopalatine, greater palatine, anterior ethmoidal and superior labial arteries.
hint: Four arteries meeting on the front of the septum.
why: It sits on the anterior septum (Little's area) and causes most nosebleeds.

q: Where do dangerous posterior nosebleeds come from?
hint: The main artery of the nasal cavity.
why: They occur in older people and may need packing or endoscopic ligation.

q: Which branch of the internal carotid system supplies the upper nasal cavity?
model: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic).
hint: Named after the bone they pass through.
why: Bleeding from them may need ligation through the orbit.

q: What lies above the superior concha?
why: The sphenoid sinus drains into it.

q: What is the space under each concha called?
why: The sinuses and nasolacrimal duct drain into them.

q: What function do the conchae serve?
model: They increase surface area to warm, humidify and filter air.
why: They create turbulence so particles hit the mucus.

q: Which paranasal sinus is present at birth and lies between the orbits?
why: Infection can spread through the thin lamina papyracea, causing orbital cellulitis.

q: Which paranasal sinus lies in the body of the sphenoid, below the pituitary?
why: It is the route for transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.

q: Which sinus develops last, often not until about age 7?
why: It is often asymmetric or absent.

q: Into which meatus do the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain?
why: They drain into the hiatus semilunaris; blockage of this area (osteomeatal complex) causes sinusitis.

q: Why does the maxillary sinus drain poorly?
model: Its opening is high on its medial wall.
hint: Where is its exit compared with its floor?
why: It drains well only when lying on the other side.

q: Where do the posterior ethmoid air cells drain?
why: The anterior and middle cells drain into the middle meatus.

q: Which nerve supplies the frontal sinus?
model: The ophthalmic division (V1), via the supraorbital nerve.
why: Frontal sinusitis causes forehead pain.

q: Which nerve supplies the maxillary sinus?
model: The maxillary division (V2), via the superior alveolar and infraorbital nerves.
why: These also supply the upper teeth, so maxillary sinusitis can mimic toothache.

q: Where can sphenoid sinusitis refer pain?
acc: vertex / occiput / back of head / behind the eyes / top of the head
model: The vertex, occiput or behind the eyes.
why: It is supplied by branches of V1 and V2.

q: Which part of the nasal cavity has olfactory epithelium?
model: The roof and upper septum, under the cribriform plate.
why: Head injury can tear the olfactory nerves, causing anosmia.

q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the anterior and upper nasal cavity?
model: The ophthalmic division (V1) via the anterior ethmoidal nerve.
why: The maxillary division supplies the rest via the pterygopalatine ganglion.

q: Which ganglion relays parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the nasal glands?
hint: In the fossa between the pterygoid plates and the palatine bone.
why: Fibres come from the facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve.

q: What finding in a maxillary sinus suggests acute sinusitis on X-ray?
model: An air–fluid level or an opaque sinus.
hint: A horizontal line in the sinus.
why: After trauma, fluid in the sinus suggests a fracture.

q: Which imaging is used to plan sinus surgery?
why: It shows the bony anatomy of the osteomeatal complex.

q: Which pharyngeal arch forms the muscles of mastication?
why: Its nerve is the mandibular division of the trigeminal (V3); it also forms the malleus and incus.

q: Which pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear cavity and auditory tube?
why: The 1st cleft forms the external acoustic meatus; the membrane between becomes the eardrum.

q: Which arch's nerve is the glossopharyngeal nerve?
why: It forms stylopharyngeus and part of the hyoid.

q: A persistent neck lump in front of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult may be a remnant of which pharyngeal structure?
why: Branchial cysts lie at the anterior border of SCM.

q: Which part of the auricle is not supported by cartilage?
why: The rest is elastic cartilage, which can form a "cauliflower ear" after a haematoma.

q: What is the small flap in front of the external acoustic meatus called?
hint: It covers the ear canal opening.
why: Pain on pressing it suggests otitis externa.

q: How long is the adult external acoustic meatus?
why: The outer third is cartilage and the inner two-thirds bone; pull the auricle up and back to straighten it for otoscopy.

q: Which ossicle attaches to the tympanic membrane?
why: Its handle is seen through the eardrum on otoscopy.

q: Which ossicle sits in the oval window?
why: Otosclerosis fixes it, causing conductive deafness.

q: Which muscle damps movement of the stapes?
why: It is supplied by the facial nerve; loss causes hyperacusis.

q: What lies on the anterior wall of the middle ear?
acc: internal carotid / carotid / auditory tube / tensor tympani
model: The internal carotid artery (and the auditory tube opening).
hint: A major artery heading for the cavernous sinus.
why: The jugular bulb lies in the floor; the facial nerve on the medial wall.

q: Where does the chorda tympani cross the middle ear?
model: Across the inner surface of the tympanic membrane, between the malleus and incus.
hint: Between the hammer and the anvil.
why: It can be damaged in middle ear surgery, altering taste.

q: From which nerve does the chorda tympani branch?
model: The facial nerve (in the facial canal, above the stylomastoid foramen).
hint: It goes on to leave the skull at the stylomastoid foramen.
why: A lesion above this branch loses taste on the front of the tongue.

q: Where is the tympanic plexus?
model: On the promontory of the medial wall of the middle ear.
hint: Over the bulge made by the basal turn of the cochlea.
why: It is formed by the tympanic branch of IX and sympathetic fibres.

q: Which nerve leaves the tympanic plexus to reach the otic ganglion?
why: It carries parasympathetic fibres for the parotid gland.

q: Why can throat cancer cause earache?
acc: ix / glossopharyngeal / tympanic / x / vagus / referred
model: Referred pain: IX (tympanic branch) and X also supply the ear.
why: Unexplained otalgia with a normal ear needs the throat examining.

q: Which muscle opens the auditory tube?
model: Tensor veli palatini (with levator veli palatini).
hint: It also tenses the soft palate.
why: It opens on swallowing and yawning to equalise pressure.

q: Which part of the auditory tube is bony?
model: The lateral (posterior) third, next to the middle ear.
why: The medial two-thirds is cartilage, opening into the nasopharynx.

q: Which paranasal sinuses are present at birth?
why: The sphenoid and frontal sinuses develop later in childhood.

q: How do the paranasal sinuses form?
model: As outgrowths of the nasal cavity lining into the surrounding bones.
hint: They bud out from the nose.
why: That is why they all drain into the nose.

q: Why do the sinuses enlarge most at puberty and with the adult teeth?
model: The facial bones grow and the permanent teeth erupt.
hint: Think about what happens to the skull through childhood.
why: The maxillary sinus expands into the space left as teeth move down.

q: How does the auditory tube change from childhood to adulthood?
model: It becomes longer and more steeply angled.
hint: Compare a child's tube with an adult's.
why: This improves drainage and reduces middle ear infections.

q: Why do enlarged adenoids cause glue ear?
model: They block the nasopharyngeal opening of the auditory tube.
why: The middle ear can't ventilate, so fluid collects.

q: Which bone forms the lamina papyracea?
hint: The bone with air cells between the orbits.
why: It forms most of the medial orbital wall.

q: Why does ethmoid sinusitis spread to the orbit easily?
why: Orbital cellulitis threatens sight and needs urgent treatment.

q: What lies lateral to the ethmoid air cells?
why: The ethmoid labyrinth sits between the nasal cavity and orbits.

q: Which structure protects the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen in adults?
hint: A bony projection behind the ear.
why: In infants it is undeveloped, so the nerve is superficial and at risk with forceps or post-auricular incisions.

q: Why is the facial nerve vulnerable in newborns?
model: The mastoid process hasn't developed yet.
hint: Think about the bony protection behind the ear.
why: The nerve emerges just under the skin.

q: In which part of its course does the facial nerve run through the temporal bone?
model: The intratemporal segment, in the facial canal.
why: Swelling here (Bell's palsy) compresses the nerve.

q: Through which opening does the facial nerve enter the temporal bone?
why: It travels with the vestibulocochlear nerve.

q: Which branch of the facial nerve carries fibres to the lacrimal gland?
why: It synapses in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

q: Which branch of the facial nerve supplies frontalis?
hint: Crosses the zygomatic arch to the temple.
why: Damage stops the eyebrow rising.

q: Which parotid operation risks the facial nerve?
why: The nerve divides within the gland; surgeons identify the trunk first.

q: Why can a mastoidectomy damage the facial nerve?
model: The nerve runs down through the mastoid (vertical) segment of the facial canal.
hint: Where does the nerve run after the middle ear?
why: Surgeons use nerve monitoring.

q: What is the commonest cause of an acute lower motor neuron facial palsy?
why: Idiopathic swelling in the facial canal; treat with prednisolone within 72 hours and protect the eye.

q: Which tumour at the cerebellopontine angle can affect the facial nerve?
hint: A tumour of the nerve beside VII.
why: Hearing loss usually comes first.

q: Which middle ear disease can erode the facial canal?
hint: A destructive skin cyst in the middle ear.
why: The tympanic segment's bony covering can be thin or absent.

q: What is the main job of the middle ear?
model: To match impedance between air and the fluid-filled inner ear.
hint: Sound passes from air into fluid.
why: The eardrum-to-oval-window area ratio and the ossicle lever boost pressure about 20 times.

q: Which part of the ear converts sound into nerve signals?
model: The cochlea (organ of Corti, inner ear).
why: Hair cells on the basilar membrane respond to different frequencies along its length.

q: What type of hearing loss does a perforated eardrum cause?
hint: Sound can't be passed on efficiently.
why: Rinne's test is negative (bone conduction better than air) on that side.

q: What are the crystals in the macula called?
why: Displaced crystals in a semicircular canal cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

q: Which sense organs are in the utricle and saccule?
why: They detect gravity and linear acceleration.

q: Where are the cristae ampullaris found?
model: In the ampullae of the semicircular canals.
hint: At the swollen end of each canal.
why: Their cupula is bent by fluid movement during head rotation.

q: What does the vestibulo-ocular reflex do?
model: Keeps the eyes fixed on a target when the head moves.
hint: Stops the world blurring when you walk.
why: Eyes move equally and opposite to head movement.

q: Which tract carries vestibular signals to the eye movement nuclei?
why: It links the vestibular nuclei to III, IV and VI.

q: Which bedside test checks the vestibulo-ocular reflex?
acc: head impulse / head thrust / halmagyi / doll
hint: Turn the head quickly while they look at your nose.
why: A catch-up saccade shows a peripheral vestibular problem (part of HINTS).

q: Which artery do the two vertebral arteries join to form?
hint: It runs on the front of the pons.
why: They join at the lower border of the pons.

q: Through which opening do the vertebral arteries enter the skull?
why: They first ascend through the foramina transversaria of C6–C1.

q: What is the first intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery?
why: ICA disease can cause amaurosis fugax (temporary monocular blindness).

q: Which sinus does the internal carotid artery pass through?
why: Aneurysms here compress VI first; a tear causes a carotid–cavernous fistula.

q: Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery causes weakness of which body parts most?
model: The contralateral face and arm (more than the leg).
why: The MCA supplies the lateral cortex where face and arm are represented.

q: Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery gives which visual problem?
hint: Half the visual field in both eyes.
why: It supplies the occipital lobe.

q: Which artery supplies the lateral medulla?
model: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (or vertebral).
why: Occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

q: Expressive dysphasia from a stroke points to which artery?
hint: The artery to the lateral hemisphere.
why: It supplies Broca's area in the frontal lobe.

q: Which artery supplies the upper surface of the cerebellum?
why: It arises near the top of the basilar artery; III passes between it and the PCA.

q: Which basilar branch supplies the front of the lower cerebellum?
hint: The middle of the three cerebellar arteries.
why: It often gives the labyrinthine artery; occlusion can cause deafness and vertigo.

q: Which basilar branches supply the pons?
hint: Named after the part they supply.
why: Their occlusion causes lacunar strokes; basilar occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome.

q: Which arteries join the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral arteries?
why: PCom aneurysms compress III, causing a dilated pupil.

q: Where do most berry aneurysms arise?
model: At junctions of the circle of Willis, most often the anterior communicating artery.
why: Rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage ("thunderclap headache").

q: Which artery gives rise to the two posterior cerebral arteries?
why: It divides at the top of the midbrain.

q: From which artery does the middle meningeal artery arise?
hint: A terminal branch of the ECA.
why: It enters through the foramen spinosum.

q: Between which layers does an extradural haematoma collect?
model: Between the skull and the dura.
why: Arterial bleeding strips the dura off the bone; it is limited by the sutures.

q: What is the treatment for an expanding extradural haematoma?
why: Delay causes uncal herniation and death.

q: Into which vein does the sigmoid sinus drain?
hint: The large vein in the neck.
why: At the jugular foramen.

q: What are the typical features of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?
model: Headache, seizures, focal deficits and signs of raised ICP (papilloedema).
hint: Think of raised pressure plus irritation of the cortex.
why: Risk factors: pregnancy, the pill, dehydration, thrombophilia.

q: Which sinus runs in the attached edge of the falx cerebri?
hint: The top sinus in the midline.
why: Thrombosis here causes raised ICP and bilateral signs.

q: Where do the straight and superior sagittal sinuses meet?
model: At the confluence of sinuses (torcular Herophili).
why: Blood then flows into the transverse sinuses.

q: Why are older people and alcoholics prone to subdural haemorrhage?
model: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins.
hint: The brain shrinks away from the skull.
why: Minor trauma can tear them.

q: Why does a subdural haemorrhage develop slowly?
why: Symptoms may appear days or weeks after a minor injury (chronic subdural).

q: Why does an extradural haematoma often have a lucid interval?
model: Arterial blood takes time to strip the dura from the skull.
hint: The outer meningeal layer must be peeled away first.
why: The patient recovers from the initial concussion before the haematoma grows big enough to cause coning.

q: What shape is an extradural haematoma on CT?
why: The dura is stuck at the sutures, so the blood can't spread past them.

q: What shape is an acute subdural haematoma on CT?
why: It spreads along the brain surface and crosses sutures.

q: Does a subdural haematoma cross suture lines?
why: Extradural haematomas don't cross sutures, where the dura is firmly attached.

q: How does a chronic subdural haematoma look on CT compared with an acute one?
why: Blood becomes less dense as it breaks down; acute blood is bright.

q: Which muscle attaches to the greater trochanter?
acc: gluteus medius / gluteus minimus / piriformis / obturator / gemell
model: Gluteus medius and minimus (plus piriformis and the short lateral rotators).
why: The hip abductors pull on it.

q: Which muscle attaches to the lesser trochanter?
why: An isolated lesser trochanter fracture in an adult suggests a pathological (tumour) fracture.

q: What angle does the femoral neck make with the shaft in adults?
why: A smaller angle is coxa vara, a larger one coxa valga.

q: Which ridge on the back of the femur receives muscle attachments?
why: The adductors and parts of the quadriceps and hamstrings attach to it.

q: Why do displaced intracapsular neck of femur fractures often need a hip replacement?
acc: blood supply / avascular / avn / necrosis / medial circumflex
model: They cut the blood supply to the femoral head, risking avascular necrosis.
hint: Think about how blood reaches the head.
why: The retinacular vessels from the medial circumflex run up the neck inside the capsule.

q: How does the leg lie in a posterior hip dislocation?
model: Shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated.
why: A neck of femur fracture causes external rotation instead.

q: Which fracture classification is used for intracapsular neck of femur fractures?
why: Grades I–II (undisplaced) are fixed with screws; III–IV are replaced.

q: Which band of fascia lata runs down the lateral thigh?
hint: From the ilium to the tibia.
why: It inserts on Gerdy's tubercle; friction over the lateral femoral condyle causes ITB syndrome.

q: Which structure in the femoral triangle lies outside the femoral sheath?
why: The sheath holds the artery, vein and femoral canal.

q: Which compartment of the thigh is supplied by the obturator nerve?
why: Femoral supplies the anterior, sciatic the posterior.

q: Through which opening in the fascia lata does the great saphenous vein pass?
model: The saphenous opening (covered by cribriform fascia).
why: It lies about 3 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; the vein then joins the femoral vein.

q: Weak big toe extension and numbness on the top of the foot suggest which root?
hint: The root tested by extensor hallucis longus.
why: Usually from an L4/5 disc prolapse; the ankle jerk is preserved.

q: A lost ankle jerk with weak plantarflexion suggests which root?
why: Usually from an L5/S1 disc prolapse.

q: Which nerve root lesion reduces the knee jerk and weakens knee extension?
why: Quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve from L2–4.

q: How can you tell a common fibular nerve palsy from an L5 root lesion?
model: Inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) and hip abduction are spared in a fibular palsy but weak in an L5 lesion.
hint: Test muscles supplied by L5 but not by the fibular nerve.
why: Both cause foot drop.

q: Which nerve root trunk joins the sacral plexus from the lumbar plexus?
why: It crosses the pelvic brim to join S1–3 on piriformis.

q: Which sacral plexus branch supplies the perineum?
why: It leaves through the greater sciatic foramen and returns through the lesser.

q: On which muscle does the sacral plexus lie?
why: Branches leave the pelvis above or below it.

q: Between which two bony landmarks does the sciatic nerve run in the buttock?
model: Midway between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity.
hint: A bump on the femur and the bone you sit on.
why: It is the largest nerve in the body; injections go in the upper outer quadrant to avoid it.

q: Into which two nerves does the sciatic nerve divide?
model: The tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves.
hint: One goes to the calf, one round the fibular neck.
why: Usually at the top of the popliteal fossa, but sometimes higher.

q: Which hamstring is supplied by the common fibular part of the sciatic nerve?
model: The short head of biceps femoris.
hint: The only hamstring not crossing the hip.
why: All the other hamstrings come from the tibial part.

q: From which roots does the coccygeal plexus arise?
why: It supplies coccygeus, part of levator ani and the skin over the coccyx.

q: What area of skin does the coccygeal plexus supply?
model: The skin over the coccyx (anococcygeal nerves).
hint: At the very bottom of the spine.
why: Coccydynia is felt here.

q: Which roots form the obturator nerve?
hint: The same roots as the femoral nerve.
why: It comes from the anterior divisions of the lumbar plexus.

q: Why can an obturator hernia present with medial knee or thigh pain?
model: It compresses the obturator nerve (Howship–Romberg sign).
why: Usually in thin elderly women.

q: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas?
why: The femoral nerve emerges laterally.

q: Where does the great saphenous vein run at the knee?
model: Behind the medial condyle of the femur.
hint: On the inner side, at the back.
why: It runs up the medial leg and thigh.

q: Which nerve runs with the small saphenous vein?
why: It is at risk in varicose vein surgery.

q: Which deep vein lies in the popliteal fossa?
why: Popliteal and femoral DVTs carry the highest risk of pulmonary embolism.

q: What makes a perforator vein incompetent?
why: Blood flows from deep to superficial veins, causing varicose veins and venous ulcers.

q: Where do venous ulcers usually occur?
model: In the gaiter area, over the medial malleolus.
why: Perforators and the great saphenous vein are under high pressure here.

q: Which test checks whether varicose veins come from the saphenofemoral junction?
model: The tourniquet (Trendelenburg) test, or duplex ultrasound.
why: Duplex is now the standard test.

q: Which muscle forms the main calf pump?
hint: The flat muscle deep in the back of the leg.
why: Contraction squeezes the deep veins; valves stop backflow.

q: Why does prolonged immobility increase DVT risk?
model: The calf muscle pump stops, causing venous stasis.
why: Stasis is part of Virchow's triad.

q: Name one mechanism of venous return other than the muscle pump.
acc: valve / respiratory / thoracic / breathing / arterial pulsation / vis a tergo / pressure
model: Valves, the respiratory pump (negative chest pressure) or pulsation of adjacent arteries.
hint: Think of what happens in the chest when you breathe in.
why: Together they return blood against gravity.

q: Which structure lies medial to the femoral vein in the femoral triangle?
why: Femoral hernias pass through it.

q: Where should a femoral artery puncture be made?
acc: below the inguinal ligament / below / mid inguinal / midinguinal
model: At the midinguinal point, just below the inguinal ligament.
why: Too high risks retroperitoneal bleeding; too low hits the bifurcation.

q: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle?
why: The medial border is adductor longus.

q: Which artery is the main supply to the thigh muscles?
hint: The deep artery of the thigh.
why: Its perforating branches supply the posterior compartment.

q: Where does the femoral artery become the popliteal artery?
why: It passes through adductor magnus into the popliteal fossa.

q: Which artery continues as the dorsalis pedis?
hint: The artery of the front of the leg.
why: It becomes dorsalis pedis in front of the ankle.

q: Which arteries supply the gluteal region?
model: The superior and inferior gluteal arteries (from the internal iliac).
why: They leave above and below piriformis.

q: Name the anastomosis around the knee.
why: It keeps the leg alive after slow popliteal occlusion but not after acute injury.

q: Why can a slowly blocked superficial femoral artery cause only claudication?
model: Collaterals from the profunda femoris and genicular arteries develop.
why: Sudden occlusion doesn't allow time for this, so acute ischaemia follows.

q: Where is the femoral pulse felt?
model: At the midinguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis).
why: Below the inguinal ligament.

q: Why is the popliteal pulse hard to feel?
model: It lies deep in the fossa.
hint: Think about what lies on top of it.
why: Feel it with the knee flexed to relax the fascia; an easily felt one suggests an aneurysm.

q: What are the six Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
acc: pain + pallor + pulseless + paraesthesia + paralysis + perishing / poikilothermia / cold
model: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold.
why: Paralysis and paraesthesia are late, limb-threatening signs.

q: To which nodes does the superficial lymph of most of the lower limb drain?
why: They also drain the lower abdominal wall, perineum and buttock.

q: Lymph from the lateral heel follows which vein first?
model: The small saphenous vein, to the popliteal nodes.
why: Melanoma on the heel can spread to popliteal nodes.

q: Where does lymph from the inguinal nodes drain next?
hint: Along the main pelvic artery to the leg.
why: Then the common iliac and para-aortic nodes.

q: What is Shenton's line used to assess?
acc: neck of femur / hip / femur / dislocation
model: Hip fractures and dislocation on an AP pelvis X-ray.
hint: An arc on the AP pelvis film.
why: It runs along the underside of the femoral neck and the top of the obturator foramen.

q: Which X-ray views are needed for a suspected hip fracture?
model: AP pelvis and a lateral of the hip.
why: Fractures can be invisible on one view; MRI if still suspected.

q: What is the commonest site of a femoral shaft stress fracture in runners?
why: Compression-side fractures are usually managed conservatively.

q: What type of joint is the superior tibiofibular joint?
hint: The upper one has a joint cavity.
why: The inferior joint is a fibrous syndesmosis; both allow only slight movement.

q: What injury happens when the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis is torn?
hint: A sprain above the usual lateral ligaments.
why: The ankle mortise widens and may need fixation.

q: Which calf muscle crosses both the knee and the ankle?
why: It flexes the knee and plantarflexes the ankle; soleus crosses only the ankle.

q: Name the deep posterior compartment muscles.
acc: tibialis posterior / flexor digitorum longus / flexor hallucis longus / popliteus
model: Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus (and popliteus).
why: "Tom, Dick and Harry" pass behind the medial malleolus.

q: Which tendon forms from gastrocnemius and soleus?
hint: Named after a Greek hero's weak spot.
why: Simmonds' (Thompson's) test checks for rupture.

q: Which nerve supplies the calf muscles?
hint: The larger branch of the sciatic nerve.
why: It runs with the posterior tibial artery in the deep posterior compartment.

q: How many fascial compartments does the leg have?
model: Four: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior.
why: Each has its own nerve.

q: Which nerve supplies the lateral compartment of the leg?
hint: A branch of the common fibular nerve.
why: It supplies fibularis longus and brevis (eversion).

q: Which artery runs in the anterior compartment of the leg?
hint: Named after the compartment and the bone.
why: It reaches the compartment through the interosseous membrane and becomes dorsalis pedis.

q: What is the earliest symptom of compartment syndrome?
model: Pain out of proportion, worse on passive stretch.
why: Pulses are usually present until late.

q: What is the treatment for acute compartment syndrome?
why: Raised pressure in a closed compartment kills muscle and nerve within hours.

q: Why does compartment syndrome occur in the leg?
acc: fascia / closed / non expandable / inelastic / bone / swelling
model: Muscles lie in closed compartments bounded by tough fascia and bone that can't expand.
why: Swelling after fractures, crush or reperfusion raises the pressure.

q: Which bones form the ankle mortise?
model: The tibia and fibula (malleoli), holding the talus.
hint: Two leg bones gripping one foot bone.
why: The talus is wider in front, so the joint is most stable in dorsiflexion.

q: Name the three parts of the lateral ankle ligament.
hint: Named after the bones each one joins.
why: The anterior talofibular is the weakest and most often torn.

q: Which rules decide whether an ankle injury needs an X-ray?
why: Bone tenderness at the back of either malleolus or inability to bear weight.

q: What is the largest tarsal bone?
why: Falls from height fracture it, often with a spinal fracture.

q: Which nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the leg?
hint: A branch of the common fibular nerve.
why: Injury causes foot drop and numbness of the 1st web space.

q: Which anterior compartment muscle extends the big toe?
why: Weakness is an early sign of an L5 root lesion.

q: Which artery supplies the anterior compartment of the leg?
why: It continues as dorsalis pedis.

q: Why is the ankle less stable in plantarflexion?
model: The narrower back of the talus sits in the mortise.
hint: The bone in the mortise is wider at the front.
why: That is why most sprains happen with the foot pointed down and turned in.

q: What is the usual mechanism of a lateral ankle sprain?
why: It tears the anterior talofibular ligament first.

q: Which ligament is torn with an eversion injury?
hint: A triangular ligament on the inner ankle.
why: It is strong, so eversion injuries often fracture the medial malleolus instead.

q: Name the arches of the foot.
model: Medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal and transverse arches.
why: They spread weight, absorb shock and act as a spring in walking.

q: Which tendon supports the medial longitudinal arch?
why: Its dysfunction causes acquired flat foot in adults.

q: What is the windlass mechanism?
acc: plantar aponeurosis / plantar fascia / toe extension / big toe
model: Extending the toes tightens the plantar aponeurosis and raises the arch.
hint: Like winding a rope round a drum.
why: It stiffens the foot for push-off.

q: Which arch is the highest?
hint: On the inner side of the foot.
why: It is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms and medial three metatarsals.

q: At which joint do inversion and eversion mainly occur?
model: The subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint (with the midtarsal joints).
why: The ankle joint only dorsiflexes and plantarflexes.

q: Name the main invertors of the foot.
why: Tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve, tibialis anterior by the deep fibular nerve.

q: Where does fibularis longus insert?
model: The base of the 1st metatarsal and the medial cuneiform.
hint: On the opposite side of the foot from where it starts.
why: Its tendon crosses the sole and supports the arches.

q: Which nerve supplies the abductor hallucis and flexor hallucis brevis?
hint: The plantar equivalent of the median nerve.
why: Like the median nerve in the hand, it supplies a few muscles and much of the skin.

q: Where does the tibial nerve divide into the plantar nerves?
model: In the tarsal tunnel, behind the medial malleolus.
hint: A tunnel on the inner ankle.
why: Compression here causes tarsal tunnel syndrome.

q: Which skin does the medial plantar nerve supply?
model: The medial sole and medial 3½ toes.
hint: Compare with the median nerve in the hand.
why: Like the median nerve in the palm.

q: Which artery forms the deep plantar arch?
model: The lateral plantar artery (with the deep plantar branch of dorsalis pedis).
why: Like the deep palmar arch in the hand.

q: Which skin does the lateral plantar nerve supply?
acc: lateral 1 / lateral one / lateral sole / lateral
model: The lateral sole and lateral 1½ toes.
why: It is the plantar equivalent of the ulnar nerve.

q: Which nerve supplies the interossei of the foot?
hint: The plantar equivalent of the ulnar nerve.
why: Like the ulnar nerve supplying the hand interossei.

q: From which bone does the plantar aponeurosis arise?
why: Plantar fasciitis causes pain at this attachment.

q: What is the function of the plantar aponeurosis?
model: It supports the longitudinal arches and protects the sole.
why: It tightens with toe extension (windlass mechanism).

q: Which muscle lies in the first (superficial) layer of the sole?
acc: abductor hallucis / flexor digitorum brevis / abductor digiti minimi
model: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis or abductor digiti minimi.
hint: The most superficial layer under the plantar aponeurosis.
why: The sole has four muscle layers.

q: Which tendons run in the second layer of the sole?
acc: flexor digitorum longus / flexor hallucis longus / quadratus plantae / lumbrical
model: Flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus tendons (with quadratus plantae and lumbricals).
why: These are the long flexor tendons from the calf.

q: Which tendons cross the deepest layer of the sole?
acc: fibularis longus / peroneus longus / tibialis posterior
hint: Two tendons crossing from the leg.
why: They support the arches from below.

q: Which bones form each hip bone?
why: They meet at the acetabulum.

q: Which part of the pelvis holds the pelvic organs?
why: The greater (false) pelvis is part of the abdomen.

q: What is the projection at the front of the upper sacrum called?
hint: It juts forward like a headland.
why: It forms the back of the pelvic inlet.

q: Which landmark do you sit on?
why: The hamstrings and sacrotuberous ligament attach to it.

q: What surface landmark marks the posterior superior iliac spines?
hint: Small skin depressions above the buttocks.
why: They mark the sacroiliac joints.

q: Which bony landmark is the guide for a pudendal nerve block?
why: The pudendal nerve passes just behind it.

q: What type of joint is the sacroiliac joint?
model: A synovial (plane) joint, reinforced by strong ligaments.
hint: It has a joint cavity at the front.
why: Little movement; inflamed in ankylosing spondylitis.

q: Which ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity?
why: With the sacrospinous ligament it forms the sciatic foramina.

q: Why does the pubic symphysis widen in pregnancy?
hint: Its name describes what it does to ligaments.
why: This helps delivery but can cause symphysis pubis dysfunction.

q: Which structure forms the back of the pelvic inlet?
hint: The front of the top of the sacrum.
why: The inlet runs round the pelvic brim to the pubic symphysis.

q: Which pelvic diameter is longest at the inlet in a female pelvis?
why: At the outlet the anteroposterior diameter is longest, so the head rotates during labour.

q: At which pelvic level is the fetal head said to be "engaged"?
model: When its widest part has passed through the pelvic inlet (brim).
why: Station 0 is the head at the ischial spines.

q: What shape is the typical female pelvic inlet?
why: The male inlet is heart-shaped (android).

q: How do the ischial spines differ in the female pelvis?
model: They project less inwards and are further apart.
hint: Think about room for the baby's head.
why: This widens the midpelvis for childbirth.

q: Which pelvis has a wider, shallower greater sciatic notch?
why: A useful sexing feature in skeletons.

q: What line divides the perineum into urogenital and anal triangles?
model: A line between the ischial tuberosities.
hint: Between the bones you sit on.
why: The urogenital triangle is in front, the anal triangle behind.

q: What are the boundaries of the perineum?
model: Pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx.
hint: A diamond shape below the pelvic floor.
why: It is diamond-shaped below the pelvic floor.

q: Which fossa lies on each side of the anal canal in the anal triangle?
hint: Between the ischium and the anus.
why: Fat here lets the anal canal distend; abscesses can form.

q: Which muscle covers the lateral pelvic wall?
why: Levator ani arises from its fascia.

q: Which muscle forms part of the posterior pelvic wall with the sacrum?
why: The sacral plexus lies on it.

q: Which parts make up levator ani?
why: With coccygeus they form the pelvic diaphragm.

q: From which ligament do the abdominal obliques gain their lower attachment?
why: It runs from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.

q: Where does levator ani attach at the back?
why: The two sides meet in the midline.

q: Where does rectus abdominis attach below?
model: The pubic crest and pubic symphysis.
hint: The front of the pubic bone.
why: It runs up to the xiphoid and costal cartilages 5–7.

q: Name a function of the pelvic floor.
acc: support / continence / intra abdominal / childbirth / sexual
model: Supports pelvic organs, maintains continence, resists rises in abdominal pressure, guides the fetal head in labour.
why: Damage leads to prolapse and incontinence.

q: What is the midline raphe of levator ani called behind the anus?
why: It links the anal canal to the coccyx.

q: Which muscle forms a sling around the anorectal junction?
hint: From the pubis around the rectum.
why: It maintains the anorectal angle for continence.

q: What is the perineal membrane?
model: A strong fibrous sheet across the urogenital triangle.
why: It separates the deep and superficial perineal pouches and anchors the external genitalia.

q: Why does damage to the perineal body matter?
model: It weakens pelvic floor support, causing prolapse and incontinence.
why: Many perineal muscles attach to it; it is cut in an episiotomy.

q: Which surgical cut in childbirth is made through the perineum?
hint: A cut to enlarge the vaginal opening.
why: Usually mediolateral to avoid extending into the anal sphincter.

q: In which ligament does the uterine artery run to reach the uterus?
model: The base of the broad ligament (with the cardinal ligament).
why: It arises from the internal iliac artery and crosses over the ureter beside the cervix.

q: Where do the uterine and ovarian arteries anastomose?
acc: broad ligament / uterine tube / cornu / mesosalpinx
model: In the broad ligament near the uterine tube.
hint: At the top corner of the uterus.
why: This dual supply matters in hysterectomy and uterine artery embolisation.

q: In which ligament does the ovarian artery reach the ovary?
hint: It suspends the ovary from the pelvic wall.
why: It is tied during oophorectomy.

q: Through which foramen does the pudendal nerve leave the pelvis?
model: The greater sciatic foramen (then re-enters through the lesser).
why: It hooks round the ischial spine.

q: In which canal does the pudendal nerve run?
why: It runs in the obturator internus fascia on the side of the ischioanal fossa.

q: What does a pudendal block numb?
model: The perineum, vulva and lower vagina.
hint: The area supplied by the nerve.
why: Used for instrumental deliveries and perineal repair.

q: Where do Bartholin's glands open?
model: Posterolaterally into the vestibule (about 4 and 8 o'clock).
why: Blocked ducts form cysts or abscesses.

q: What is the male homologue of Bartholin's glands?
hint: Glands near the bulb of the penis.
why: Both lubricate during arousal.

q: Which pouch lies between the bladder and uterus?
why: It is shallow; the rectouterine pouch behind is deeper.

q: Through which vaginal fornix can the pouch of Douglas be reached?
why: Fluid or pus can be sampled (culdocentesis).

q: To which nodes does lymph from the uterine body and cervix drain?
model: The internal and external iliac nodes (and sacral nodes).
why: The fundus also drains to para-aortic nodes.

q: Which pelvic organ's lymph can reach the superficial inguinal nodes via the round ligament?
hint: The organ the round ligament is attached to.
why: Lymph runs with the round ligament through the inguinal canal.

q: To which nodes does the lower anal canal drain?
why: Below the pectinate line.

q: Which imaging is first-line for most gynaecological pelvic problems?
why: MRI is used for staging cancers and complex masses.

q: On an AP pelvis X-ray, what should you check after trauma?
model: That the pelvic ring is intact: rami, sacroiliac joints and symphysis.
hint: Think of breaking a polo mint.
why: A ring usually breaks in two places.

q: Which imaging stages cervical and endometrial cancer?
why: It shows soft tissue planes and parametrial spread.

q: Where does a DVT embolus usually lodge?
hint: The first capillary bed it meets.
why: It travels through the right heart; a large one blocks the main pulmonary arteries (saddle embolus).

q: Where does an embolus from the left atrium in AF usually lodge?
model: In the systemic arteries, especially the brain (stroke).
hint: Clots from the left heart enter which circulation?
why: Left heart clots enter the arterial circulation.

q: What is a saddle embolus?
model: A large embolus straddling the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk.
why: It can cause sudden collapse and death.

q: What supplies each bronchopulmonary segment?
model: Its own segmental bronchus and branch of the pulmonary artery.
why: Veins run between segments.

q: How many bronchopulmonary segments are in the left lung?
why: The right lung has 10.

q: Why does aspiration in a supine patient affect the apical segment of the right lower lobe?
model: It is the most dependent segment when lying on the back.
hint: Which segment is lowest when lying on your back?
why: The right main bronchus is also wider and more vertical.

q: Which fetal remnant joins the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch?
hint: The remnant of a fetal duct.
why: It is the remains of the ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks round it.

q: Which pulmonary artery passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC?
why: The left is shorter and passes in front of the descending aorta.

q: How many pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium?
why: Two from each lung.

q: Which circulation supplies the lung tissue itself?
why: The pulmonary circulation carries blood for gas exchange.

q: Where do the bronchial veins drain?
model: Mostly to the azygos and hemiazygos veins; some to the pulmonary veins.
hint: A vein system on the back of the thorax.
why: The part draining to pulmonary veins causes a small physiological shunt.

q: What is the pressure in the pulmonary circulation compared with the systemic?
why: Thin-walled vessels; pulmonary hypertension strains the right ventricle.

q: Why is pulmonary infarction uncommon after a PE?
model: The lung has a dual blood supply (bronchial as well as pulmonary).
hint: Think about the second blood supply.
why: Infarction is more likely if the bronchial circulation is also poor (e.g. heart failure).

q: What does hypoxia do to pulmonary arteries?
why: This diverts blood to ventilated areas; systemic arteries dilate instead.

q: What treatment controls massive haemoptysis from the bronchial arteries?
why: Most massive haemoptysis comes from the high-pressure bronchial arteries.

q: Which part of Virchow's triad does immobility cause?
why: The calf muscle pump stops.

q: Which part of Virchow's triad does the combined pill affect?
hint: A change in the blood itself.
why: Oestrogen increases clotting factors.

q: Which part of Virchow's triad does surgery or trauma cause?
model: Endothelial (vessel wall) injury (plus stasis and hypercoagulability).
why: Major surgery hits all three.

q: What is the classic triad of fat embolism syndrome?
model: Respiratory distress, neurological symptoms and a petechial rash.
why: It occurs 1–3 days after long bone fractures.

q: Which embolism can occur during childbirth?
why: It causes sudden collapse and DIC.

q: How can air embolism happen during central line insertion?
acc: sitting / upright / negative pressure / head up / open
model: Air is sucked into an open vein when the patient is upright (negative venous pressure).
why: Lines are inserted head-down and the patient holds their breath on removal.

q: What makes the alveolar–capillary barrier so thin?
model: Type I pneumocytes and capillary endothelium share a fused basement membrane.
why: About 0.5 µm thick, for fast diffusion.

q: Which cells in the alveoli remove debris?
why: In heart failure they contain haemosiderin ("heart failure cells").

q: What do the pores of Kohn do?
model: They connect neighbouring alveoli for collateral ventilation.
why: They also let infection spread between alveoli.

q: Where do the muscles of facial expression attach, since the face has no deep fascia?
why: That is how they move the skin to make expressions.

q: Which external carotid branch supplies the scalp behind the ear?
hint: Named after its position relative to the ear.
why: The occipital artery supplies the back of the scalp further back.

q: Which nerve supplies the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis?
model: The posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve.
hint: A branch given off just after the stylomastoid foramen.
why: The frontal belly gets the temporal branch.

q: Which X-ray shows the whole mandible and teeth on one film?
hint: A dental film that sweeps round the head.
why: Used for mandibular fractures and dental problems.

q: Which artery's branches join the scapular anastomosis from the subclavian side?
model: The suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries.
hint: Named after the bone they run over.
why: They link with the subscapular branches of the axillary artery.

q: Why is the radial pulse used for an arterial blood gas?
model: It is superficial over bone, easy to compress, and the ulnar artery gives collateral supply.
hint: Think about pressing it afterwards and what else supplies the hand.
why: Check collateral flow first (Allen's test).

q: Which vein in the antecubital fossa is most used for blood tests?
hint: It crosses the elbow crease diagonally.
why: It joins the cephalic and basilic veins and lies on the bicipital aponeurosis.

q: Which elbow ligament holds the radial head against the ulna?
why: In toddlers the head can slip out of it (pulled elbow).

q: Epworth score that means excessive daytime sleepiness?
why: The Epworth score adds up the chance of dozing in 8 everyday situations (0–3 each, total 24); above 10 means excessive daytime sleepiness.

q: Biggest risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea?
why: Fat around the neck and pharynx narrows the upper airway, which collapses when muscles relax in sleep; a collar over 17 inches in men is a red flag.

q: Sleepiness with cataplexy suggests?
why: Narcolepsy is loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons; cataplexy, sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion, is specific to it.

q: Name a non-OSA cause of tiredness to screen for in bloods.
acc: hypothyroid / thyroid / tft / anaemia / fbc / diabetes / glucose / hba1c
why: Tiredness has many medical causes; checking thyroid function, FBC and glucose finds treatable ones before attributing it to sleep apnoea.

q: High pH, high HCO₃⁻, compensatory high PaCO₂: what disorder?
hint: The primary problem is the bicarbonate.
why: Raised pH with raised bicarbonate means a primary metabolic alkalosis; the lungs compensate by hypoventilating, so CO₂ rises.

q: Low pH, high PaCO₂, high HCO₃⁻: what pattern?
acc: acute on chronic / partially compensated / partly compensated
hint: The kidneys have started to compensate.
why: Acidosis with high CO₂ is respiratory; a raised bicarbonate shows the kidneys have had days to compensate (chronic), but the low pH shows an acute rise on top.

q: Name a neuromuscular cause of hypoventilation.
acc: mnd / motor neurone / guillain / gbs / myasthenia / muscular dystrophy / duchenne
model: MND, Guillain–Barré, myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy.
hint: Anywhere from anterior horn cell to muscle.
why: Weak respiratory muscles from nerve or muscle disease can't move enough air, so CO₂ builds up (type 2 failure) even with healthy lungs.

q: Bedside test to monitor ventilation in Guillain–Barré?
why: FVC reflects respiratory muscle strength and falls before oxygen sats; serial FVC below about 20 mL/kg calls for ICU assessment.

q: Define type 2 respiratory failure.
acc: hypoxi / pao2 / low oxygen / low o2 / o2 + hypercapni / paco2 / co2 / carbon dioxide
why: Type 2 failure is hypoxaemia with hypercapnia, from inadequate ventilation (pump failure); type 1 is hypoxaemia with normal or low CO₂.

q: Target sats in a CO₂ retainer?
why: Patients who retain CO₂ rely partly on hypoxic drive and get worse V/Q matching with high oxygen, so aiming for 88–92% avoids worsening hypercapnia.

q: First-line treatment for moderate–severe OSA?
why: CPAP splints the upper airway open during sleep, abolishing apnoeas; it improves sleepiness, blood pressure and quality of life.

q: When is NIV started in a COPD exacerbation?
model: Respiratory acidosis: pH <7.35 and PaCO₂ >6.5 despite treatment.
hint: Check the gas after an hour of optimal treatment.
why: NIV is offered if pH stays below 7.35 with PaCO₂ above 6.5 after an hour of optimal treatment, because it lowers CO₂ and reduces the need for intubation.

q: Which mode of support is NIV (BiPAP) and what does it treat?
model: Bilevel pressure support for hypercapnic (type 2) failure.
why: BiPAP gives a higher inspiratory pressure to boost ventilation and blow off CO₂, and a lower expiratory pressure to keep airways open.

q: Name a consequence of an ageing population.
acc: multimorbidity / polypharmacy / dependency / dementia / social care / frailty
model: More multimorbidity, frailty, dementia, social care need, higher dependency ratio.
why: People live longer with chronic disease, so there's more multimorbidity, frailty and dementia, more demand for social care, and fewer working-age people per older person.

q: Name a Kübler-Ross stage of grief.
why: Kübler-Ross described denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance; people don't move through them in a fixed order.

q: Name a part of the external nose.
acc: root / bridge / dorsum / apex / tip / ala / alae / nares / nostril / columella
model: Root, dorsum, apex, alae, nares, columella.
hint: Look in a mirror, top to bottom.
why: The external nose has a root between the eyes, a bridge and dorsum, an apex (tip), alae around the nostrils (nares) and a columella between them.

q: Which bone forms the roof of the nasal cavity?
why: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid forms the roof; it's thin and perforated, so fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhoea and loss of smell.

q: Name a bone forming the nasal floor.
model: Palatine process of the maxilla, horizontal plate of the palatine.
hint: It's also the roof of the mouth.
why: The palatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone form both the nasal floor and the hard palate.

q: Where do most anterior nosebleeds arise?
hint: An area on the front of the septum.
why: Little's area on the front of the septum is where several arteries meet (Kiesselbach's plexus); it's easily traumatised, causing most nosebleeds.

q: Main artery supplying the nasal cavity?
hint: A branch of the maxillary artery.
why: The sphenopalatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, supplies most of the nasal cavity and is the main source of posterior bleeds.

q: Where does the nasolacrimal duct drain?
why: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the inferior meatus, which is why your nose runs when you cry.

q: Which paranasal sinus is the largest?
why: The maxillary sinus fills the cheek; its opening is high on its medial wall, so it drains poorly and often gets infected.

q: Where does the maxillary sinus drain?
why: The maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain into the middle meatus via the hiatus semilunaris (the osteomeatal complex).

q: Where does the sphenoid sinus drain?
why: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess, above the superior concha.

q: Where is maxillary sinusitis pain often referred?
why: The maxillary sinus and upper teeth share V2 innervation, and the molar roots sit next to the sinus floor, so sinusitis can feel like toothache.

q: Through which structure do the olfactory nerves pass?
why: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the holes of the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, so fractures here can cause anosmia.

q: Which divisions of the trigeminal nerve give general sensation to the nasal cavity?
why: V1 (via the anterior ethmoidal nerve) supplies the front and roof, V2 the rest; this explains referred pain from the nose.

q: Standard X-ray view for the paranasal sinuses?
why: The occipitomental view tilts the head back so the petrous bones are projected below the maxillary sinuses, showing them clearly (CT has largely replaced it).

q: Rinne result in conductive hearing loss?
hint: Which conducts better on that side?
why: In conductive loss sound reaches the cochlea better through bone than through the blocked middle ear, so bone conduction beats air (Rinne negative).

q: Weber lateralises to which ear in conductive loss?
hint: Plug your own ear and hum.
why: In conductive loss the affected ear hears bone-conducted sound louder because background noise is masked (block your own ear and hum to try it).

q: Weber lateralises to which ear in sensorineural loss?
why: In sensorineural loss the damaged cochlea or nerve can't detect sound well, so it's heard louder in the better ear.

q: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss needs which scan?
why: Unexplained asymmetrical sensorineural loss or unilateral tinnitus could be a vestibular schwannoma, which MRI of the internal acoustic meatus detects.

q: Emergency treatment for sudden sensorineural hearing loss?
model: High-dose oral steroids; urgent ENT within 24 h.
why: Sudden sensorineural loss has a better chance of recovery with early high-dose steroids, so it needs urgent ENT review within 24 hours.

q: Foul discharge with attic retraction suggests?
hint: Skin growing in the middle ear.
why: Cholesteatoma is skin trapped in the middle ear from a retraction pocket; it erodes bone and can cause hearing loss, facial palsy and intracranial infection.

q: Test that diagnoses BPPV?
hint: Lie back with the head turned.
why: Dix–Hallpike moves the posterior canal into the plane of gravity; loose otoconia then cause torsional nystagmus after a short delay.

q: Manoeuvre that treats BPPV?
why: The Epley manoeuvre rotates the head so the otoconia roll out of the posterior canal into the utricle, curing most BPPV.

q: Vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness?
why: Excess endolymph distorts the inner ear, causing episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.

q: Vertigo for days without hearing loss after a cold?
why: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve causes days of constant vertigo without hearing loss; labyrinthitis also affects hearing.

q: Commonest cause of hearing loss in children?
acc: glue ear / otitis media with effusion / ome
why: Glue ear is fluid in the middle ear without infection, often after colds, damping sound conduction in young children.

q: Surgical treatment for persistent glue ear?
why: Grommets ventilate the middle ear so fluid clears and hearing improves; they fall out on their own after 6–12 months.

q: Which pharyngeal arch forms the muscles of facial expression?
why: The second arch's nerve is the facial nerve, which supplies its muscles: the muscles of facial expression, stapedius and posterior digastric.

q: Which pouch forms the inferior parathyroids and thymus?
hint: Inferior glands come from the higher number.
why: The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroids and thymus; they migrate downwards, ending up below the superior parathyroids from the fourth pouch.

q: Nerve of the first pharyngeal arch?
hint: It supplies the muscles of mastication.
why: The first arch forms the muscles of mastication, supplied by V3, plus the malleus, incus and parts of the jaw.

q: Name a normal function of the nose.
acc: warm / humidify / filter / smell / olfaction / resonance
why: The nose warms, humidifies and filters inspired air, provides smell and adds resonance to the voice.

q: Rhinosinusitis lasting how long is chronic?
why: Symptoms lasting under 12 weeks are acute; 12 weeks or more is chronic and suggests structural or inflammatory disease such as polyps.

q: First-line treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps?
acc: nasal steroid / intranasal / steroid spray / topical steroid
why: Intranasal steroids reduce mucosal inflammation and polyp size, and saline irrigation clears mucus; surgery is for failed treatment.

q: Commonest head and neck cancer histology?
why: Most head and neck cancers arise from the squamous epithelium lining the upper aerodigestive tract; smoking, alcohol and HPV are the main risks.

q: Virus linked to oropharyngeal cancer?
why: HPV-16 causes a rising number of oropharyngeal (tonsil, tongue base) cancers in younger non-smokers; they respond better to treatment.

q: Sore throat, trismus and uvula deviation?
why: Pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles pushes the tonsil and uvula across and irritates the pterygoids (trismus).

q: Why must a nasal septal haematoma be drained urgently?
why: Septal cartilage gets its nutrition from the overlying perichondrium; a haematoma lifts it off, and the cartilage dies within days, causing a saddle nose.

q: Which ingested foreign body is an ENT emergency?
why: A button battery stuck in the oesophagus causes rapid electrical and chemical burns within hours, risking perforation and fistula; it needs urgent removal.

q: First aid for epistaxis?
model: Pinch the soft nose 10–15 min, lean forward.
hint: The soft part of the nose, lean...
why: Pinching the soft part of the nose compresses Little's area; leaning forward stops blood being swallowed or inhaled.

q: What is a systematic review?
acc: systematic / comprehensive / reproducible / all studies / predefined
model: A comprehensive, reproducible search and appraisal of all studies on a defined question.
hint: Explicit methods to find and appraise all the evidence.
why: A systematic review uses a predefined, comprehensive and reproducible search with explicit inclusion criteria and quality appraisal, reducing bias.

q: Which way does a tonsillar abscess push the uvula?
why: A peritonsillar abscess swells on one side, pushing the soft palate and uvula towards the healthy side.

q: Why do you pull the pinna up and back in adults for otoscopy?
why: The adult ear canal is S-shaped; pulling the pinna up and back straightens it to see the drum (down and back in young children).

q: Where is the cone of light on a normal right eardrum?
why: The cone of light reflects from the anteroinferior drum, at 5 o'clock on the right and 7 o'clock on the left; loss suggests a bulging or retracted drum.

q: Red bulging drum with fever and pain?
why: Acute otitis media is bacterial or viral infection of the middle ear; pus under pressure makes the drum red and bulging, with pain and fever.

q: Name a way to adapt communication for a deaf patient.
acc: face / lip / bsl / interpreter / write / quiet / loop
model: Face them, good lighting, BSL interpreter, writing, hearing loop.
why: Deaf patients may lip-read or sign, so face them in good light, check their preferred method, and book a BSL interpreter when needed.

q: Should you shout or exaggerate lip movements with a lip-reader?
model: No: speak clearly at normal pace.
why: Shouting and exaggerated lip movements distort mouth shapes and make lip-reading harder; speak clearly at a normal pace.

q: Name a barrier to healthcare for deaf patients.
model: Phone-only booking, no interpreter, inaccessible information.
why: Phone-only booking, no interpreters and inaccessible information stop deaf people accessing care, leading to missed diagnoses and poorer health.

q: Name a source for confirming a drug history.
acc: patient / gp / summary care / pharmacy / community pharmacist / medicines / mar / carer
model: Patient, GP record, community pharmacy, the medicines themselves.
why: Using at least two sources (patient, GP record, pharmacy, the medicines themselves) catches errors in the drug history, which are common on admission.

q: Medicines reconciliation should be done within how many hours of admission?
why: NICE recommends reconciliation within 24 hours of admission because unintended omissions or changes cause harm.

q: Name a drug class that commonly causes admission.
acc: nsaid / anticoagulant / warfarin / antiplatelet / diuretic / opioid / insulin / digoxin / antihypertensive
why: NSAIDs (GI bleeds, AKI), anticoagulants and antiplatelets (bleeding), diuretics (dehydration, electrolytes) and opioids (falls, constipation) are common causes of drug-related admissions.

q: Name a medication often needed on admission.
acc: vte / thromboprophylaxis / enoxaparin / heparin / analgesia / laxative
why: Admission adds new risks: VTE from immobility, pain, and constipation from opioids and reduced activity, so these are often prescribed.

q: Name a part of the auricle.
acc: helix / antihelix / tragus / antitragus / concha / lobule
hint: The outer rim and the flap at the front.
why: The auricle has a helix (outer rim), antihelix, tragus and antitragus, concha (bowl) and lobule; it collects and funnels sound.

q: Name the three ossicles.
why: The malleus, incus and stapes transmit vibration from the drum to the oval window and amplify pressure.

q: Which nerve does the chorda tympani join?
hint: A branch of V3 in the floor of the mouth.
why: The chorda tympani crosses the middle ear and joins the lingual nerve to supply taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

q: Which glands get parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani?
hint: The ones under the tongue and jaw.
why: Parasympathetic fibres travel with the chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion, then to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

q: Which cranial nerve forms the tympanic plexus?
why: The tympanic branch of IX (Jacobson's nerve) forms the tympanic plexus on the promontory, supplying middle ear sensation and parotid parasympathetic fibres.

q: What does the auditory tube connect?
why: The auditory tube equalises middle ear pressure with the atmosphere and drains secretions into the nasopharynx.

q: Which paranasal sinus develops last?
why: Maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth; the frontal sinus develops last, appearing in childhood and fully formed after puberty.

q: Why are children prone to otitis media?
model: Shorter, wider, more horizontal auditory tube.
why: In children the auditory tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, so nasopharyngeal secretions and bacteria reach the middle ear easily.

q: Orbital cellulitis often spreads from which sinus?
model: The ethmoid sinus, through the lamina papyracea.
why: The lamina papyracea between the ethmoid sinus and orbit is paper-thin, so ethmoid infection spreads easily into the orbit.

q: Where does the facial nerve leave the skull?
hint: Between the styloid and the mastoid.
why: The facial nerve exits through the stylomastoid foramen, protected in adults by the mastoid process; in babies it's superficial and easily injured.

q: Name the three segments of the facial nerve.
hint: Inside the skull, within the bone, outside.
why: The facial nerve runs intracranially from the pons to the internal acoustic meatus, through the temporal bone (intratemporal), and then out to the face (extratemporal).

q: Name the five terminal branches of the facial nerve.
model: Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical.
why: In the parotid, the facial nerve divides into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches to the muscles of facial expression.

q: Loss of the nerve to stapedius causes?
why: Stapedius damps ossicle movement to protect the ear from loud sounds; losing it makes normal sounds seem uncomfortably loud.

q: Which surgery risks the marginal mandibular nerve?
why: The marginal mandibular branch runs just below the jaw near the submandibular gland, so surgery there can weaken the lower lip.

q: Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear?
why: Reactivated VZV in the geniculate ganglion causes facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal; it has a worse prognosis than Bell's palsy.

q: Which part of the ear is the impedance matcher?
why: Sound passes from air to fluid; the middle ear overcomes the mismatch by concentrating force from the large drum onto the small footplate and by the ossicle lever.

q: What does the macula detect?
why: The utricle and saccule maculae have otoliths that move hair cells with linear acceleration and gravity, sensing head tilt.

q: What does the crista ampullaris detect?
why: The cristae in the semicircular canal ampullae detect fluid movement during head rotation (angular acceleration).

q: Head turns right: which way do the eyes move in the VOR?
why: The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes equally and oppositely to head movement to keep the image stable on the retina.

q: Commonest cause of dementia?
why: Alzheimer's causes about 60% of dementia: gradual memory loss from amyloid plaques and tau tangles starting in medial temporal structures.

q: Visual hallucinations, fluctuation and parkinsonism suggest?
why: Dementia with Lewy bodies has fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder, from α-synuclein deposits.

q: Disinhibition and personality change in a 55-year-old suggest?
why: Frontotemporal dementia affects frontal and temporal lobes, causing early personality change, disinhibition or language problems, often before 65, with memory relatively spared.

q: ACE-III is scored out of what?
why: ACE-III is scored out of 100 across attention, memory, fluency, language and visuospatial domains; below about 82–88 suggests cognitive impairment.

q: Name a blood test to exclude reversible causes of dementia.
acc: b12 / folate / tft / thyroid / calcium / glucose / fbc / u&e / lft
model: B12, folate, TFTs, calcium, glucose, FBC, U&E, LFTs.
why: Treatable mimics include B12 and folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia and glucose problems, so these are checked before diagnosing dementia.

q: Who should be told if a patient with dementia drives?
model: The DVLA (the patient must inform them).
why: Dementia can impair driving, so patients must tell the DVLA; if they won't and are unsafe, doctors may break confidentiality.

q: Legal tool for future decisions while capacity remains?
model: Lasting power of attorney (or advance decision).
why: An LPA appoints someone to decide about health and welfare or finances if capacity is lost, while the person can still choose who.

q: Name a delirium screening tool.
why: The 4AT is a quick test of alertness, orientation (AMT4), attention (months backwards) and acute change that screens for delirium.

q: Where does tau pathology start in Alzheimer's?
why: Tau tangles start in the entorhinal cortex and spread to the hippocampus (Braak stages), explaining why memory is affected first.

q: Two hallmark lesions of Alzheimer's?
why: Extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau are the defining pathology.

q: Protein in Lewy bodies?
why: Lewy bodies are aggregates of α-synuclein, also found in Parkinson's disease.

q: Name an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.
why: AChE inhibitors stop acetylcholine being broken down, boosting cholinergic transmission lost in Alzheimer's; they help mild–moderate disease.

q: Mechanism of memantine?
why: Memantine blocks NMDA receptors, reducing glutamate excitotoxicity; it's used for moderate–severe Alzheimer's.

q: Cardiac side effect of AChE inhibitors?
why: Raising acetylcholine increases vagal tone on the heart, causing bradycardia and heart block, so check pulse and ECG.

q: Why avoid antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia?
why: Up to half of patients with Lewy body dementia have severe reactions to antipsychotics (rigidity, falls, confusion, even death) because of their dopamine deficit.

q: Which article protects liberty (relevant to DoLS)?
hint: Between the ban on torture (3) and the right to a fair trial (6).
why: Article 5 protects liberty; depriving someone who lacks capacity of their liberty needs legal authorisation (DoLS).

q: Which article protects private and family life?
why: Article 8 protects private and family life, including confidentiality and bodily autonomy.

q: Name a social theory of ageing.
hint: Withdraw, stay active, or carry on as before.
why: Disengagement theory says older people withdraw, activity theory says staying active matters, and continuity theory says people keep their habits.

q: Name a document supporting person-centred dementia care in hospital.
why: "This is me" records a person's preferences, routines and background so staff can give care that fits them.

q: Name a differential for memory loss.
acc: depression / delirium / b12 / hypothyroid / normal pressure / nph / subdural / alcohol
model: Depression, delirium, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, NPH, subdural.
why: Depression, delirium, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, normal pressure hydrocephalus and subdural haematoma can all mimic dementia and many are reversible.

q: Triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
acc: gait + incontinence / urinary + cognitive / dementia / confusion
why: NPH causes gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and dementia from enlarged ventricles; it may improve after CSF drainage.

q: Why take a third-party history in dementia?
model: The patient may lack insight; an informant gives the timeline and function.
hint: The patient may not notice the changes.
why: People with dementia often lack insight, so a relative or carer gives the timeline, functional decline and risks.

q: Name an ACE-III domain.
why: ACE-III tests attention, memory, verbal fluency, language and visuospatial skills, building a cognitive profile.

q: Name a risk to assess in dementia.
acc: driving / falls / wandering / fire / cooking / medication / financial / abuse / self-neglect
model: Driving, falls, wandering, cooking/fire, medication, finances.
why: Risk assessment covers driving, falls, wandering, cooking and fire, medication errors, finances and vulnerability to exploitation.

q: Test for lumbar flexion in suspected ankylosing spondylitis?
hint: Mark 10 cm above the dimples of Venus.
why: Modified Schober's marks points on the lumbar spine; less than 5 cm increase on forward flexion suggests restricted movement, as in ankylosing spondylitis.

q: Name a cauda equina red flag.
acc: saddle / retention / incontinence / bilateral sciatica / anal tone
model: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral sciatica, reduced anal tone.
why: Compression of the sacral roots causes saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, bilateral sciatica and reduced anal tone, needing emergency MRI.

q: Painful arc between which angles suggests subacromial impingement?
why: Between 60° and 120° of abduction the inflamed supraspinatus tendon is squeezed under the acromion, causing pain.

q: Name the rotator cuff muscles.
why: SITS: supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (external rotation), subscapularis (internal rotation).

q: Loss of passive external rotation of the shoulder suggests?
why: Frozen shoulder is capsular inflammation and fibrosis that restricts active and passive movement, especially external rotation.

q: Painful shoulder in an older patient with a weak empty can test: likely diagnosis?
why: The empty can test isolates supraspinatus; weakness suggests a tear, common in older people with degenerative tendons.

q: Order of a musculoskeletal exam?
why: Look, feel, move (then special tests) ensures nothing is missed and the most painful parts come last.

q: On CT, what density is acute blood?
why: Fresh clot is dense from packed red cells and protein, so it looks bright (hyperdense) compared with brain.

q: Lentiform haematoma that doesn't cross sutures?
why: Extradural bleeding is usually arterial (middle meningeal); it's lens-shaped because dura is stuck to the skull at sutures, so blood can't cross them.

q: Crescent-shaped bleed crossing sutures?
why: Subdurals come from torn bridging veins; blood spreads along the brain under the dura, crossing sutures but not the falx.

q: Name a sign of mass effect.
acc: midline shift / effacement / herniation / compressed ventricle
model: Midline shift, sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, herniation.
why: A mass pushes brain structures: midline shift, effaced sulci, compressed ventricles and eventually herniation.

q: What density is a chronic subdural on CT?
hint: Compare it with brain tissue as the blood ages.
why: As blood breaks down over weeks, it becomes less dense than brain (hypodense).

q: Name a cause of a ring-enhancing lesion.
acc: abscess / metastasis / metastases / glioblastoma / gbm / toxoplasm / lymphoma
