why: Ring enhancement means a lesion with a leaky rim around a necrotic or purulent centre: abscesses, metastases and high-grade gliomas.

q: First scan in suspected stroke and why?
why: Non-contrast CT is fast and shows haemorrhage, which must be excluded before thrombolysis.

q: Time window for thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke?
why: Alteplase is licensed within 4.5 hours of onset because benefit falls and bleeding risk rises over time; thrombectomy windows are longer.

q: Which finding rules out thrombolysis?
why: Thrombolysis breaks clots, so it would worsen an intracranial bleed; haemorrhage is an absolute contraindication.

q: Through which foramina do the vertebral arteries ascend?
why: The vertebral arteries rise through the transverse foramina of C6–C1, enter the skull through the foramen magnum and join to form the basilar.

q: How does the ICA enter the skull?
why: The internal carotid enters through the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone, then runs through the cavernous sinus.

q: Which artery's occlusion gives contralateral leg weakness?
why: The ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, where the leg area of the motor cortex lies.

q: Which basilar branch supplies the inner ear?
why: The labyrinthine artery supplies the inner ear, so its occlusion causes sudden vertigo and hearing loss.

q: Which artery connects the two ACAs?
why: The anterior communicating artery joins the two ACAs; it's the commonest site of berry aneurysms.

q: Middle meningeal artery lies under which skull point?
why: The middle meningeal artery runs beneath the pterion, where the skull is thinnest, so a blow there can tear it, causing an extradural haematoma.

q: Through which foramen does the middle meningeal artery enter?
hint: A small hole in the sphenoid.
why: It enters through the foramen spinosum in the greater wing of the sphenoid.

q: Name a cranial nerve in the cavernous sinus.
acc: iii / oculomotor / iv / trochlear / v1 / v2 / ophthalmic / maxillary / vi / abducens
hint: Eye movers and two branches of V.
why: The cavernous sinus contains III, IV, V1, V2 and VI plus the internal carotid; thrombosis or a mass causes painful ophthalmoplegia.

q: Investigation for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?
why: CT or MR venography shows a filling defect in the venous sinuses; plain CT is often normal.

q: Which veins tear in subdural haemorrhage?
hint: They cross from cortex to sinus.
why: Bridging veins cross from the brain surface to the dural sinuses; brain atrophy (in older people and with alcohol) stretches them, so they tear easily.

q: Extradural or subdural: which classically has a lucid interval?
why: Arterial extradural bleeding may be followed by a lucid interval before the haematoma expands and consciousness falls rapidly.

q: Leading cause of lower limb amputation in the UK?
why: Diabetes and peripheral arterial disease together cause most non-traumatic amputations, through ischaemia, neuropathy and infection.

q: Main process causing PAD?
why: PAD is atherosclerosis in leg arteries, narrowing them so muscles become ischaemic on exertion.

q: Strongest modifiable risk factor for PAD?
why: Smoking damages endothelium and accelerates atherosclerosis; stopping is the most effective intervention for PAD.

q: ABPI value diagnostic of PAD?
why: ABPI compares ankle with arm systolic pressure; below 0.9 indicates arterial narrowing.

q: First-line treatment for intermittent claudication?
why: Supervised exercise improves collateral circulation and walking distance; statins and clopidogrel reduce cardiovascular events.

q: Antiplatelet for symptomatic PAD?
why: NICE recommends clopidogrel for symptomatic PAD because it reduces cardiovascular events more than aspirin.

q: Name a feature of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
acc: rest pain / ulcer / gangrene / tissue loss
why: When blood flow can't meet resting demand, patients get rest pain, ulcers and gangrene, threatening the limb.

q: Why do patients hang their leg out of bed at night?
model: Gravity improves perfusion and eases rest pain.
why: Hanging the leg down uses gravity to increase arterial pressure and perfusion, easing ischaemic rest pain.

q: Name an indication for amputation.
acc: dead / dangerous / damn nuisance / gangrene / sepsis / unreconstructable / non-salvageable
why: Amputation is indicated for a dead limb (gangrene), a dangerous one (spreading sepsis), or a "damn nuisance" (useless and painful).

q: Name the six Ps of acute limb ischaemia.
acc: pain + pallor + pulseless + paraesthesia + perishing / poikilothermia / cold + paralysis
model: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, perishing cold, paralysis.
why: Acute ischaemia causes pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, perishing cold and paralysis; paralysis and paraesthesia mean the limb is at immediate risk.

q: Sudden ischaemia in a patient in AF suggests what cause?
why: AF causes clots in the left atrium that can embolise to the leg, causing sudden ischaemia without previous claudication.

q: Which wall component is lost in AAA?
hint: The stretchy component, degraded by MMPs.
why: AAAs form when matrix metalloproteinases break down elastin and collagen in the media, so the wall weakens and dilates.

q: Who is offered AAA screening?
model: Men in the year they turn 65.
why: Men are offered a one-off ultrasound at 65 because AAA is much commoner in older men, and screening reduces deaths from rupture.

q: Size threshold for AAA repair?
hint: The same as the referral threshold.
why: Rupture risk rises sharply above 5.5 cm, outweighing surgical risk; rapid growth or symptoms also prompt repair.

q: Name the two types of AAA repair.
hint: One through the groin, one through the abdomen.
why: EVAR places a stent graft through the femoral arteries, while open repair replaces the aneurysm with a graft through the abdomen.

q: What fails in varicose veins?
why: Incompetent valves let blood flow back into superficial veins, raising pressure and dilating them.

q: Name a skin change of chronic venous disease.
acc: haemosiderin / lipodermatosclerosis / eczema / atrophie blanche / ulcer
model: Haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, venous eczema, atrophie blanche.
why: Chronic venous hypertension leaks red cells (haemosiderin staining), causes fibrosis (lipodermatosclerosis), eczema and white scars (atrophie blanche).

q: Where do venous ulcers typically occur?
hint: Above the ankle, on the inside.
why: Venous pressure is highest above the medial malleolus (the gaiter area), where perforators connect deep and superficial veins.

q: Name an impact of venous ulcers on patients.
acc: pain / odour / smell / isolation / sleep / mobility / dressings / cost
model: Pain, odour, social isolation, poor sleep, reduced mobility.
why: Venous ulcers cause pain, odour, leakage and poor sleep, leading to social isolation and depression.

q: First-line intervention for symptomatic varicose veins (NICE)?
why: NICE recommends endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or laser) first because it's effective, done under local anaesthetic and has quick recovery.

q: Which substances cross capillaries through clefts?
why: Water and small water-soluble molecules pass through clefts between endothelial cells, while proteins stay in the plasma.

q: Which Starling force pulls fluid back into capillaries?
why: Plasma proteins create oncotic pressure that draws fluid back into capillaries, opposing hydrostatic pressure.

q: Where does excess filtered fluid return?
why: Slightly more fluid filters out than returns, and the lymphatics carry the excess back to the circulation.

q: Name a theory of venous ulceration.
acc: fibrin cuff / white cell trapping / leucocyte trapping / growth factor trapping
model: Fibrin cuff, white cell trapping, growth factor trapping.
why: Proposed mechanisms include fibrin cuffs blocking oxygen diffusion, white cells trapped in capillaries releasing toxins, and growth factors trapped away from tissues.

q: Name a reason diabetic feet ulcerate.
why: Neuropathy removes protective pain, ischaemia slows healing, and high glucose impairs immunity, so small injuries become ulcers.

q: Punched-out painful ulcer on the toes?
why: Arterial ulcers occur where perfusion is poorest (toes, pressure points); they look punched out and are painful.

q: Painless ulcer over the metatarsal heads?
why: Neuropathic ulcers form under pressure points like the metatarsal heads where sensation is lost, so they're painless.

q: Name a role of podiatry.
acc: foot / screening / nail / callus / footwear / offloading / education
model: Foot screening, nail and callus care, footwear, offloading, education.
why: Podiatrists screen and treat diabetic feet, manage nails and calluses, advise on footwear and offload pressure, preventing ulcers.

q: Tool to test protective foot sensation?
why: Failing to feel a 10 g monofilament on the sole means loss of protective sensation and high ulcer risk.

q: Where does the great saphenous vein join the femoral vein?
why: The great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein through the saphenous opening, about 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

q: NICE: name an indication for vascular referral with varicose veins.
acc: symptom / skin change / bleed / ulcer / thrombophlebitis
model: Symptoms, skin changes, bleeding, ulcer, superficial thrombophlebitis.
why: Refer if varicose veins cause symptoms, skin changes, bleeding, ulceration or superficial thrombophlebitis.

q: What must be checked before compression bandaging?
why: Compression can cause ischaemia if arterial supply is poor, so check ABPI; full compression is generally safe at 0.8 or above.

q: Where does lymph from the leg mostly drain?
why: Most leg lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, then deep inguinal nodes, so groin nodes enlarge with leg infections or tumours.

q: Commonest cause of lymphoedema worldwide?
why: Filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, spread by mosquitoes) blocks lymphatics and causes elephantiasis.

q: Commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema in the UK?
why: Removing lymph nodes or irradiating them for cancer damages lymphatic drainage, causing secondary lymphoedema.

q: Name the sign where you can't pinch the skin at the base of the 2nd toe.
why: Lymphoedema thickens the skin, so a fold at the base of the second toe can't be pinched (positive Stemmer's sign).

q: Main treatment of lymphoedema?
acc: decongestive / compression / manual lymphatic drainage / mld
model: Decongestive lymphatic therapy (compression, MLD, skin care, exercise).
why: Decongestive therapy combines manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, skin care and exercise to reduce swelling.

q: Classic leg position in hip fracture?
why: Muscles pull the distal fragment up (shortening) and iliopsoas rotates it outwards.

q: Fixation for an extracapsular hip fracture?
acc: dhs / dynamic hip screw / sliding hip screw / nail
why: Extracapsular fractures have good blood supply and heal, so a dynamic hip screw fixes them and allows compression at the fracture.

q: Treatment of a displaced intracapsular fracture?
why: Displaced intracapsular fractures disrupt the blood supply to the femoral head, so replacing it avoids non-union and AVN.

q: Why do displaced intracapsular fractures need replacement?
acc: avn / avascular / blood supply / medial circumflex
why: The femoral head's blood mainly comes from retinacular vessels of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which tear in displaced intracapsular fractures.

q: Name a common cause of falls in the elderly.
acc: postural hypotension / drugs / medication / vision / syncope / arrhythmia / weakness / cognitive / environment
model: Postural hypotension, drugs, poor vision, weakness, syncope, cognitive impairment.
why: Falls often have several causes: postural hypotension, drugs (antihypertensives, sedatives), poor vision, weakness, syncope and cognitive impairment.

q: Name a falls prevention intervention.
acc: strength / balance / medication review / home hazard / vision / exercise
model: Strength and balance training, medication review, home hazard assessment.
why: Strength and balance training, medication review, home hazard assessment and vision correction reduce falls.

q: Hip fracture surgery should happen within how many hours?
hint: The day of or after admission.
why: Surgery within 36 hours (day of or after admission) reduces mortality and complications such as pneumonia and pressure sores.

q: Rule of twos for fracture X-rays?
model: Two views, two joints (two occasions, two sides in kids).
why: Two views (fractures can hide on one), two joints (above and below), two occasions (some only show later) and, in children, comparison views.

q: Key sign of compartment syndrome?
model: Pain on passive stretch (out of proportion).
hint: Pain out of proportion, worse when...
why: Rising compartment pressure makes muscles ischaemic; pain out of proportion and on passive stretch are early signs, before pulses are lost.

q: Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to which landmark?
hint: A bony point on the pubis.
why: Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle, femoral hernias below and lateral.

q: Feel of BPH on DRE?
hint: Classically like the tip of your nose.
why: BPH enlarges the prostate symmetrically, keeping it smooth and rubbery with a preserved median sulcus; cancer feels hard and irregular.

q: A scrotal lump you can't get above?
hint: It came down from the abdomen.
why: If you can't get above a scrotal lump, it comes from the abdomen through the inguinal canal (an inguinoscrotal hernia).

q: "Bag of worms" in the scrotum?
why: A varicocele is dilated pampiniform veins, usually left-sided because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle.

q: Absent cremasteric reflex + high-riding testis?
why: Torsion twists the cord, pulling the testis up and cutting off blood supply; it needs surgery within about 6 hours.

q: Pulse in aortic stenosis?
why: A narrowed aortic valve slows ejection, so the pulse rises slowly and has a small volume.

q: Murmur of aortic regurgitation?
model: Early diastolic, left sternal edge, sitting forward in expiration.
why: Blood flows back from the aorta into the ventricle in early diastole; leaning forward in expiration brings the heart closer to the chest wall.

q: Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla?
why: A leaky mitral valve lets blood flow back into the left atrium throughout systole; the sound radiates towards the axilla.

q: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids?
why: Turbulent flow across a narrowed aortic valve during ejection radiates up into the carotids.

q: Test where the leg goes pale on elevation and red on dependency?
why: In severe PAD, raising the leg empties arterial blood (pallor), and hanging it down brings reactive hyperaemia (red); a low Buerger's angle means severe ischaemia.

q: How do you calculate ABPI?
model: Highest ankle pressure ÷ highest brachial pressure.
why: ABPI divides the highest ankle systolic pressure by the highest brachial pressure; a normal leg pressure is equal to or a little above the arm's.

q: Why is ABPI falsely high in diabetes?
why: Calcified arteries (common in diabetes and CKD) can't be compressed by the cuff, so the ankle pressure reads falsely high; use toe pressures instead.

q: Fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation?
why: A fall on an outstretched hand angulates the distal radius dorsally, giving a dinner-fork deformity.

q: Fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck?
why: Punching with a closed fist drives force through the 5th metacarpal, fracturing its neck (boxer's fracture).

q: Name a normal variant that mimics a fracture.
acc: epiphys / growth plate / accessory ossicle / sesamoid / bipartite
model: Unfused epiphyses, accessory ossicles, sesamoids, bipartite patella.
why: Children's growth plates and accessory bones look like fracture lines, so know normal variants and compare with the other side.

q: Fracture with more than two fragments?
why: A comminuted fracture has more than two fragments, usually from high-energy injury.

q: Elbow X-ray sign of an occult fracture?
why: An effusion lifts the posterior fat pad out of the olecranon fossa so it becomes visible; with trauma this suggests an occult fracture (radial head in adults, supracondylar in children).

q: Fat–fluid level in the knee means?
why: Fat from the marrow leaking into the joint floats on blood, so a fat–fluid level means a fracture extends into the joint.

q: "Lightbulb" humeral head suggests which dislocation?
why: In posterior dislocation the humeral head is internally rotated, so it looks round like a lightbulb on an AP film; it follows seizures or electric shocks.

q: Commonest shoulder dislocation?
why: About 95% of shoulder dislocations are anterior, from forced abduction and external rotation.

q: Scaphoid fracture complication?
model: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
why: Blood enters the scaphoid distally and flows backwards, so a waist fracture can leave the proximal pole without supply (AVN).

q: Name a part of fracture description.
acc: site / bone / pattern / type / displacement / angulation / open / closed / comminution
model: Bone, site, pattern, displacement, angulation, open/closed.
why: A structured description (bone, site, pattern, displacement, angulation, open or closed) communicates the injury clearly and guides management.

q: Name an emergency fracture finding.
acc: open / neurovascular / pelvic / compartment / spinal / cervical
model: Open fracture, neurovascular compromise, unstable pelvic fracture.
why: Open fractures risk infection, neurovascular compromise threatens the limb, and unstable pelvic fractures can cause major bleeding.

q: On which side of the femur is the linea aspera?
why: The linea aspera is a ridge on the back of the femur where many thigh muscles attach.

q: Main artery to the femoral head?
why: The medial circumflex femoral artery gives the retinacular vessels that supply most of the femoral head.

q: Which nerve is at risk in posterior hip dislocation?
why: The sciatic nerve lies directly behind the hip, so posterior dislocation can stretch or injure it, causing foot drop.

q: Where is the great saphenous vein at the ankle?
hint: In front of a bony bump.
why: The great saphenous vein lies just in front of the medial malleolus, a reliable site for venous cut-down.

q: Root value of the knee jerk?
why: The knee jerk tests the femoral nerve, roots L3–4.

q: Root value of the ankle jerk?
why: The ankle jerk tests S1 via the tibial nerve; it's lost in S1 radiculopathy.

q: Foot drop after a fibular neck fracture: which nerve?
hint: It wraps around the fibular neck.
why: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, so fractures there can damage it, weakening dorsiflexion and eversion.

q: Which sacral plexus nerve injury gives a Trendelenburg gait?
why: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus; without them the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg.

q: Through which foramen does the sciatic nerve leave the pelvis?
why: The sciatic nerve leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, entering the buttock.

q: Muscle supplied by the coccygeal plexus?
why: The coccygeal plexus (S4–Co1) supplies coccygeus and part of levator ani, and the skin around the coccyx.

q: Through which opening does the obturator nerve reach the thigh?
why: The obturator nerve runs along the pelvic wall and passes through the obturator canal into the medial thigh.

q: Main muscle group supplied by the obturator nerve?
why: The obturator nerve supplies the adductors of the thigh, so injury weakens adduction.

q: Where does the small saphenous vein drain?
why: The small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus and up the calf to join the popliteal vein.

q: Which way do perforator veins carry blood?
why: Valves in the perforators direct blood from superficial to deep veins; when they fail, blood flows outwards, causing varicose veins.

q: Main mechanism of venous return from the leg?
why: Contracting calf muscles squeeze deep veins, and valves stop backflow, pumping blood towards the heart.

q: Name the boundaries of the femoral triangle.
why: The femoral triangle lies between the inguinal ligament (above), sartorius (lateral) and adductor longus (medial).

q: Order of femoral structures, lateral to medial?
why: From lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, then lymphatics in the femoral canal (NAVY); the nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

q: Continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee?
hint: Through the hiatus in adductor magnus.
why: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery behind the knee.

q: Name the anastomosis around the hip.
why: The cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses connect branches of the internal iliac and femoral arteries, providing collateral flow around the hip.

q: Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse felt?
model: Lateral to the EHL tendon on the dorsum of the foot.
hint: Next to the big toe's extensor tendon.
why: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

q: Where is the posterior tibial pulse felt?
why: The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, where it can be felt.

q: Nodes enlarged by a melanoma on the heel?
model: Popliteal (lateral heel) or superficial inguinal nodes.
why: The lateral heel drains with the small saphenous vein to the popliteal nodes; most of the foot drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

q: Line disrupted on a pelvis X-ray in a neck of femur fracture?
why: Shenton's line runs along the inferior femoral neck and the superior pubic ramus; a break suggests a displaced neck of femur fracture.

q: Name a symptom of left heart failure.
hint: Worse lying flat or at night.
why: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing breathlessness that's worse lying flat (orthopnoea) or waking the patient at night (PND).

q: Heart sound in heart failure?
why: An S3 is rapid filling into a stiff or overloaded ventricle in early diastole; in adults over 40 it suggests heart failure.

q: First blood test in suspected chronic heart failure?
why: NT-proBNP is released when ventricles are stretched; a normal level makes heart failure unlikely, and high levels prompt urgent echo.

q: Investigation that confirms heart failure?
hint: A bedside scan that measures ejection fraction.
why: Echo shows ejection fraction, valve disease and structure, confirming the type of heart failure and guiding treatment.

q: EF cut-off for HFrEF?
hint: The same as the lower bound of "mildly reduced".
why: HFrEF is EF 40% or below, the group with proven mortality benefit from ACEi/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i.

q: Mechanism of sacubitril?
hint: Stops natriuretic peptides being broken down.
why: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, which breaks down natriuretic peptides; higher levels cause vasodilation and natriuresis.

q: How long must ACEi be stopped before sacubitril/valsartan?
why: Neprilysin also breaks down bradykinin, so combining sacubitril with an ACE inhibitor greatly raises angioedema risk; a 36-hour washout is needed.

q: Name an SGLT2 inhibitor used in heart failure.
why: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin reduce death and heart failure admissions in heart failure, with or without diabetes.

q: Which drug treats congestion but doesn't improve survival?
why: Loop diuretics relieve fluid overload and symptoms but haven't been shown to improve survival.

q: Name a non-drug measure in heart failure.
acc: weight / salt / fluid / rehab / vaccin / smoking / exercise
model: Daily weights, rehab, flu/pneumococcal vaccines, salt advice, smoking cessation.
why: Daily weights catch fluid build-up early; cardiac rehab, vaccinations, salt advice and smoking cessation improve outcomes.

q: Name a neurohormonal system activated in heart failure.
model: RAAS and the sympathetic nervous system.
why: Low cardiac output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system, which retain salt and water and constrict vessels; useful short term, harmful long term, which is why blocking them helps.

q: Which law links ventricular size to wall stress?
why: Laplace: wall stress is proportional to pressure × radius ÷ wall thickness.

q: Why does dilation worsen function?
model: Higher wall stress raises oxygen demand.
hint: A bigger radius means more tension.
why: A dilated ventricle has a bigger radius, so wall stress and oxygen demand rise, worsening ischaemia and remodelling.

q: Name a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure.
why: Bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol reduce mortality in HFrEF by blocking harmful sympathetic activation; start low and increase slowly.

q: Drug added for HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥75 despite β-blocker?
why: Ivabradine blocks the funny current in the SA node, lowering heart rate without lowering blood pressure, only in sinus rhythm.

q: Device for HFrEF with LBBB and wide QRS?
why: In LBBB the ventricles contract out of sync; biventricular pacing (CRT) resynchronises them, improving output and survival.

q: Name a surgical option in heart failure.
acc: cabg / valve / lvad / transplant / crt / icd
why: Revascularisation (CABG), valve repair or replacement, ventricular assist devices and transplant treat underlying causes or support failing hearts.

q: Type of joint at the inferior tibiofibular joint?
why: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis held by strong ligaments; injury (high ankle sprain) widens the ankle mortise.

q: Name a superficial calf muscle.
why: The superficial calf muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris) join to form the Achilles tendon and plantarflex the foot.

q: Nerve of the anterior compartment of the leg?
hint: A branch of the common fibular.
why: The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior compartment muscles (dorsiflexors) and the skin between the first and second toes.

q: Commonest compartment for compartment syndrome in the leg?
why: The anterior compartment has tight fascia and bone boundaries, so swelling after tibial fractures raises pressure quickly.

q: Which ankle ligament is most often sprained?
why: Inversion injuries in plantarflexion stress the anterior talofibular ligament first, as it is the weakest lateral ligament.

q: Medial ankle ligament?
why: The deltoid ligament is a strong fan-shaped ligament on the medial side that resists eversion.

q: Main dorsiflexor of the ankle?
hint: The muscle at the front of the shin.
why: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot; weakness causes foot drop.

q: Which ankle position is least stable?
why: The talus is wider at the front, so it fits tightly in dorsiflexion but loosely in plantarflexion, making sprains likelier then.

q: Ligament supporting the medial longitudinal arch?
hint: Runs from the calcaneus to the navicular.
why: The spring ligament supports the head of the talus, holding up the medial arch; failure contributes to flat foot.

q: Main evertors of the foot?
why: Fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment evert the foot.

q: Nerve to the evertors?
why: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the lateral compartment (evertors) and most of the dorsum of the foot.

q: The medial plantar nerve is equivalent to which hand nerve?
why: Like the median nerve in the hand, the medial plantar nerve supplies a few intrinsic muscles and sensation to the medial 3½ digits.

q: The lateral plantar nerve is equivalent to which hand nerve?
why: Like the ulnar nerve, the lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic foot muscles and the lateral 1½ digits.

q: Heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning?
why: Plantar fasciitis is degeneration of the plantar fascia at its calcaneal attachment; pain is worst with the first steps after rest.

q: How many layers of muscle are in the sole?
why: The sole has four layers of muscles, from superficial (abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis) to deep (interossei).

q: Most effective first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding?
why: The LNG-IUS releases progestogen locally, thinning the endometrium; it reduces blood loss more than other medical options and lasts years.

q: Mechanism of tranexamic acid?
why: Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen activation, reducing breakdown of clots in the endometrium and cutting menstrual blood loss.

q: Blood test confirming ovulation?
why: Progesterone made by the corpus luteum peaks about 7 days before the period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle); a high level confirms ovulation.

q: Test of tubal patency?
why: HSG or HyCoSy pushes contrast through the uterus and tubes; spillage into the pelvis shows patency.

q: First-line drug for ovulation induction in PCOS?
why: Letrozole blocks oestrogen synthesis, increasing FSH to stimulate follicles; it gives higher live birth rates than clomifene in PCOS.

q: Pain, bleeding and a positive test with an empty uterus: suspect?
why: A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound suggests an ectopic, which can rupture and bleed.

q: Drug used for medical management of ectopic pregnancy?
why: Methotrexate stops trophoblast cells dividing (it's a folate antagonist), so a small, unruptured ectopic resolves without surgery.

q: Hormone that makes fibroids grow?
why: Fibroids are oestrogen-sensitive: they grow in pregnancy and shrink after menopause; GnRH agonists shrink them before surgery.

q: Fibroid surgery that preserves fertility?
why: Myomectomy removes fibroids while keeping the uterus, so fertility is preserved.

q: Commonest ovarian tumour in young women at risk of torsion?
why: Mature cystic teratomas contain hair, fat and teeth; they're heavy, which makes torsion likely.

q: Tumour marker in the RMI?
hint: A serum marker of ovarian cancer.
why: The RMI multiplies ultrasound features, menopausal status and CA-125 to estimate cancer risk and decide referral.

q: Commonest bacterial STI in the UK?
why: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI, often asymptomatic, which is why young people are screened.

q: Treatment of gonorrhoea?
why: Gonorrhoea has developed resistance to many antibiotics, so a single high dose of IM ceftriaxone is used, with a test of cure.

q: Treatment of uncomplicated chlamydia?
why: A week of doxycycline cures chlamydia more reliably than single-dose azithromycin.

q: Which body regulates IVF in the UK?
why: The Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority licenses and regulates fertility clinics and embryo research.

q: Muscles forming the pelvic floor?
hint: One big sheet plus a small posterior muscle.
why: Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus form the pelvic diaphragm that supports the pelvic organs.

q: Name the screening criteria.
why: Wilson and Jungner's criteria (1968) set out when screening is worthwhile: an important condition, a suitable test, an early stage and effective treatment.

q: First test in cervical screening?
why: Persistent high-risk HPV causes nearly all cervical cancer, so HPV is tested first; only HPV-positive samples go on to cytology.

q: What is the age range for breast screening in Wales?
hint: Every three years in middle age.
why: Breast Test Wales invites women aged 50–70 every three years for mammography.

q: Leading cause of infant death in the UK?
why: Most infant deaths in the UK follow preterm birth and congenital anomalies, ahead of infection and SIDS.

q: Menopause is diagnosed after how long without periods?
why: Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without periods, reflecting loss of ovarian follicles.

q: Name a vasomotor symptom.
why: Falling oestrogen unsettles the hypothalamic thermostat, causing hot flushes and night sweats.

q: Premature ovarian insufficiency is menopause before what age?
why: Menopause before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency; it needs hormone replacement to protect bones and heart.

q: Name a cause of premature ovarian insufficiency.
acc: chemo / radiotherapy / oophorectomy / surgery / autoimmune / turner / fragile x / idiopathic
model: Idiopathic, chemo/radiotherapy, surgery, autoimmune, Turner, fragile X.
why: POI can follow chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery, or be autoimmune or genetic (Turner, fragile X premutation); many cases are unexplained.

q: Name a long-term health risk after menopause.
why: Oestrogen protects bone and blood vessels, so after menopause osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease become more common.

q: Why add a progestogen to HRT in women with a uterus?
model: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
why: Oestrogen alone stimulates the endometrium, risking hyperplasia and cancer; a progestogen protects it in women with a uterus.

q: Which HRT route doesn't increase VTE risk?
why: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first-pass liver metabolism, so it doesn't raise clotting factors or VTE risk like oral oestrogen.

q: Name a contraindication to HRT.
acc: breast cancer / oestrogen-dependent / undiagnosed bleeding / vte / liver / pregnancy
model: Breast cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active VTE, liver disease, pregnancy.
why: Hormone-sensitive cancers, undiagnosed bleeding, active VTE and liver disease can be worsened by HRT, so it's avoided in them.

q: Name a psychological symptom of menopause.
acc: low mood / anxiety / irritab / brain fog / memory / concentration / sleep
model: Low mood, anxiety, irritability, brain fog.
why: Fluctuating oestrogen affects mood and cognition, causing low mood, anxiety, irritability and "brain fog".

q: Name a key question in a gynae history.
acc: lmp / cycle / intermenstrual / postcoital / postmenopausal / smear / screening / contraception / obstetric
model: LMP, cycle, IMB/PCB/PMB, smear history, contraception, obstetric history.
why: Menstrual history (LMP, cycle, abnormal bleeding), screening history, contraception and obstetric history narrow the differential.

q: Which speculum is used for routine cervical visualisation?
why: Cusco's bivalve speculum holds the vaginal walls apart to show the cervix for smears and inspection.

q: Framework for structured handover?
why: SBAR structures handover (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) so information isn't lost.

q: Unilateral pelvic pain + positive pregnancy test: what must you exclude first?
why: An ectopic pregnancy can rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding, so it's excluded first with ultrasound and serum hCG.

q: Organisms usually causing PID?
why: PID is usually ascending infection by chlamydia or gonorrhoea, often with anaerobes, which is why treatment covers all three.

q: Name a long-term complication of PID.
model: Infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.
why: Tubal scarring after PID causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain; risk rises with each episode.

q: Perihepatitis in PID?
why: Infection spreads to the liver capsule, causing right upper quadrant pain and "violin-string" adhesions (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis).

q: Outpatient PID regimen (BASHH)?
model: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days.
hint: An IM injection plus two oral drugs for 14 days.
why: Ceftriaxone covers gonorrhoea, doxycycline covers chlamydia and metronidazole covers anaerobes; 14 days treats upper genital tract infection.

q: Device for endometrial biopsy in clinic?
why: A pipelle is a thin flexible tube that sucks out an endometrial sample in clinic, without anaesthesia.

q: Speculum used to examine prolapse?
why: A Sims speculum retracts one vaginal wall at a time, so the opposite wall can be inspected for prolapse.

q: Instrument for an assisted vaginal birth with suction?
why: A ventouse applies a suction cup to the baby's head to help delivery; forceps grip the head instead.

q: Name a differential for pelvic pain in a woman of reproductive age.
acc: ectopic / pid / endometriosis / ovarian torsion / cyst / appendicitis / uti
model: Ectopic, PID, endometriosis, torsion, ruptured cyst, appendicitis.
why: Gynaecological (ectopic, PID, endometriosis, torsion, cysts) and surgical (appendicitis) causes overlap, so pregnancy testing and imaging are key.

q: Loading dose of aspirin in STEMI?
why: 300 mg of aspirin gives rapid, near-complete platelet inhibition in acute coronary syndromes.

q: How long is dual antiplatelet therapy given after MI?
why: Dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months after MI prevents stent thrombosis and recurrent events, balanced against bleeding.

q: Statin and dose after MI?
why: High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg lowers LDL and stabilises plaques after ACS, reducing further events.

q: Antidepressant of choice after MI?
hint: The SSRI from the SADHART trial.
why: Sertraline is safe after MI: no significant QT effect or hypotension, and the SADHART trial showed it was safe in cardiac patients.

q: Antidepressant class to avoid after MI?
why: Tricyclics prolong QRS and QT, cause arrhythmias and postural hypotension, so they're avoided after MI.

q: Name a discharge advice point after MI.
acc: driving / dvla / rehab / gtn / smoking / sex / work
model: Driving rules, cardiac rehab, GTN use, smoking cessation, return to work.
hint: What they can and can't do in the next few weeks.
why: After MI, patients need advice on driving (DVLA rules), cardiac rehab, GTN use, smoking cessation and returning to work and exercise.

q: A neck lump that moves with tongue protrusion?
why: A thyroglossal cyst is a remnant of the duct the thyroid travelled down, still tethered to the tongue base, so it rises when the tongue is stuck out.

q: Eye sign specific to Graves' disease?
why: Thyroid eye disease (exophthalmos, lid retraction) is caused by TSH-receptor antibodies acting on orbital tissue, so it's specific to Graves'.

q: How do you show a goitre moves on swallowing?
model: Ask the patient to swallow water.
why: The thyroid is wrapped in pretracheal fascia attached to the larynx, so it moves up with swallowing.

q: Line separating the greater and lesser pelvis?
acc: pelvic brim / linea terminalis / pelvic inlet
why: The pelvic brim (linea terminalis) separates the greater (false) pelvis above from the lesser (true) pelvis below.

q: Name a palpable pelvic landmark.
acc: asis / iliac crest / pubic tubercle / ischial tuberosity / psis / pubic symphysis
model: ASIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle, ischial tuberosity, PSIS.
why: Palpable landmarks (ASIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle, ischial tuberosity, PSIS) guide examination and procedures.

q: Which ligaments create the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
why: Sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.

q: Type of joint at the pubic symphysis?
why: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilage disc; it loosens slightly in pregnancy.

q: Name a boundary of the pelvic outlet.
acc: ischial tuberosit / coccyx / pubic arch / sacrotuberous / pubic symphysis
model: Pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, coccyx.
why: The outlet is diamond-shaped: pubic symphysis at the front, ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities at the sides, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx at the back.

q: Female pelvis subpubic angle compared with male?
why: A wider subpubic angle (about 90°) and rounder inlet give more room for the baby's head during birth.

q: The perineum divides into which two triangles?
why: A line between the ischial tuberosities divides the diamond-shaped perineum into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.

q: Main nerve supplying the pelvic floor?
acc: pudendal / s4 / nerve to levator ani
model: S4 (nerve to levator ani) and pudendal nerve.
why: The nerve to levator ani (S4) supplies the muscle from above and the pudendal nerve (S2–4) from below.

q: From which structure does levator ani arise laterally?
acc: tendinous arch / obturator fascia / arcus tendineus
model: Tendinous arch of the obturator fascia.
hint: A thickening of the obturator internus fascia.
why: Iliococcygeus arises from the tendinous arch, a thickening of obturator internus fascia on the pelvic side wall.

q: Name a structure passing through the female pelvic floor.
why: In women the urethra, vagina and anal canal pass through the pelvic floor, which is why childbirth can weaken it.

q: What is the perineal body?
model: The central tendon of the perineum.
hint: A central meeting point for muscles.
why: The perineal body is a fibromuscular node where perineal muscles meet; it's important for pelvic floor support and is cut in an episiotomy.

q: Which structure passes under the uterine artery?
why: The ureter runs under the uterine artery near the cervix ("water under the bridge"), so it's at risk of being clamped during hysterectomy.

q: Origin of the ovarian artery?
why: The ovarian arteries come straight off the abdominal aorta because the gonads develop high up and descend.

q: Pudendal nerve roots?
hint: The same roots as the pelvic splanchnics.
why: The pudendal nerve arises from S2–4 and supplies the perineum, external sphincters and genitalia.

q: Landmark for a pudendal nerve block?
why: The pudendal nerve passes around the ischial spine, which can be felt vaginally, so local anaesthetic is injected there.

q: Function of Bartholin's glands?
why: Bartholin's glands secrete mucus to lubricate the vulva; a blocked duct forms a cyst or abscess at 4 or 8 o'clock.

q: Lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity?
why: The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity, so fluid, blood or pus collects there.

q: Lymph drainage of the ovaries?
why: Ovarian lymph follows the ovarian vessels up to the para-aortic nodes, because the ovaries developed near the kidneys.

q: Lymph drainage of the vulva?
why: The vulva drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so vulval cancers spread to the groin.

q: First imaging for most pelvic gynae pathology?
why: Transvaginal ultrasound gives detailed views of the uterus and ovaries without radiation, so it's the first test for most pelvic problems.

q: Name a cause of haemoptysis.
acc: lung cancer / cancer / tb / tuberculosis / pe / bronchiectasis / pneumonia / vasculitis / mitral stenosis
model: Lung cancer, TB, PE, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, vasculitis.
why: Haemoptysis can come from infection (pneumonia, TB), bronchiectasis, cancer, PE or vasculitis; age, smoking and travel history narrow it.

q: How do you position a patient with massive haemoptysis?
why: Lying on the bleeding side keeps blood out of the healthy lung, protecting gas exchange while the source is treated.

q: Wells score at which PE is "likely"?
why: A Wells score over 4 makes PE likely, so go straight to CTPA; 4 or below, check a D-dimer first.

q: Imaging for suspected PE?
why: CT pulmonary angiography shows clots in the pulmonary arteries directly; V/Q scanning is used if contrast is contraindicated.

q: Commonest ECG finding in PE?
why: Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding in PE; the classic S1Q3T3 pattern is uncommon.

q: Commonest inherited thrombophilia?
why: Factor V Leiden resists inactivation by activated protein C, so clotting continues, raising VTE risk.

q: Name a VTE risk factor.
acc: surgery / immobility / cancer / pregnancy / pill / cocp / hrt / previous / obesity / travel
model: Surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogens, previous VTE.
why: Surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogens and previous VTE all act through Virchow's triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability).

q: How do DVTs reach the lung?
acc: ivc / right heart / venous / vena cava
model: Via the venous return (IVC) through the right heart.
hint: Through the right side of the heart.
why: A DVT breaks off, travels up the IVC, through the right heart and into the pulmonary arteries.

q: Mean PAP threshold for pulmonary hypertension?
why: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg at rest (lowered from 25 in 2022).

q: Mechanism of pulmonary hypertension in chronic lung disease?
why: Alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles to match perfusion to ventilation; when chronic, the vessel walls thicken and pressure rises.

q: Right heart failure caused by lung disease?
why: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular failure from lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, causing raised JVP and oedema.

q: Name a drug class for pulmonary arterial hypertension.
acc: endothelin / bosentan / ambrisentan / pde5 / sildenafil / prostacyclin / prostanoid / epoprostenol
why: PAH treatments target three pathways: block endothelin, boost nitric oxide (PDE5 inhibitors) and add prostacyclin.

q: Treatment of massive PE with shock?
why: Massive PE with shock causes right heart failure, so the clot is broken down quickly with thrombolysis.

q: Minimum anticoagulation for a provoked PE?
why: A provoked PE (e.g. after surgery) has low recurrence risk once the trigger is gone, so 3 months is usually enough.

q: Anticoagulant in antiphospholipid syndrome?
why: DOACs perform worse than warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome (especially high risk), so warfarin is used.

q: Name the three steps of Very Brief Advice.
why: Very Brief Advice: Ask about smoking, Advise that the best way to stop is medication plus support, and Act by referring or prescribing.

q: Mechanism of varenicline?
why: Varenicline partially activates nicotinic receptors to ease cravings and blocks nicotine from binding, reducing the reward from smoking.

q: Who sets "Outcomes for graduates"?
why: The GMC's "Outcomes for graduates" sets what newly qualified doctors must know and be able to do.

q: Which of the four ethical principles concerns fair distribution of resources?
why: Justice is about fair distribution of resources and treating people equally.

q: What should you do at the limits of your competence?
why: Patient safety requires recognising your limits and asking for help early.

q: Name a protected characteristic (Equality Act).
acc: age / disability / gender reassignment / marriage / pregnancy / race / religion / sex / sexual orientation
model: Age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, pregnancy, marriage.
why: The Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics, including age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, pregnancy and marriage.

q: FEV1/FVC ratio diagnostic of COPD?
why: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 shows persistent airflow obstruction, confirming COPD.

q: COPD in a young non-smoker suggests?
why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes, even without much smoking.

q: What does OARS stand for in MI?
why: OARS (open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries) are the core skills of motivational interviewing.

q: Low pH, high PaCO₂, normal HCO₃⁻?
why: High CO₂ with low pH and normal bicarbonate means acute respiratory acidosis; the kidneys haven't had time to compensate.

q: Low PaO₂, low PaCO₂ in an asthmatic?
why: A low PaO₂ with low CO₂ means type 1 failure; the patient is hyperventilating, typical of acute asthma before they tire.

q: Name a key symptom in a cardiorespiratory history.
acc: chest pain / breathless / cough / haemoptysis / palpitations / wheeze / orthopnoea / syncope / oedema
model: Chest pain, breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis, palpitations, syncope.
why: Chest pain, breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis, palpitations and syncope are the core cardiorespiratory symptoms to explore.

q: Pleural plaques suggest exposure to?
why: Pleural plaques are benign markers of asbestos exposure, common in shipyard, construction and insulation workers.

q: Farmer's lung is which type of disease?
acc: hypersensitivity pneumonitis / extrinsic allergic alveolitis / eaa
why: Inhaled antigens from mouldy hay trigger a hypersensitivity reaction in the alveoli (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

q: Name a sign of right heart strain on examination.
acc: raised jvp / jvp / parasternal heave / rv heave / loud p2 / oedema
model: Raised JVP, RV heave, loud P2, peripheral oedema.
why: Pulmonary hypertension strains the right ventricle: raised JVP, a parasternal heave, a loud P2 and peripheral oedema.

q: How can a venous clot cause a stroke?
acc: paradoxical / pfo / patent foramen ovale / asd
why: A venous clot can pass through a patent foramen ovale from right to left atrium and reach the brain (paradoxical embolism).

q: Why are bronchopulmonary segments surgically important?
model: Each has its own bronchus and artery: resectable alone.
why: Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own bronchus and artery, so it can be removed without affecting neighbouring segments.

q: How many segments in the right lung?
why: The right lung has 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left has 8–10, depending on how they're counted.

q: Where does the pulmonary trunk divide?
acc: t4 / t5 / sternal angle / under the aortic arch / concavity
model: Under the aortic arch, at about T4–5.
hint: The same level as the second costal cartilage.
why: The pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries under the aortic arch, at about T4–5 (the level of the sternal angle).

q: Name the two blood supplies of the lung.
hint: One for gas exchange, one systemic.
why: The pulmonary circulation brings blood for gas exchange; the bronchial circulation (systemic) supplies the airways and lung tissue.

q: Bronchial arteries usually arise from?
why: Bronchial arteries usually arise from the descending thoracic aorta, so they carry blood at systemic pressure.

q: Which circulation causes most massive haemoptysis?
why: Bronchial arteries are at systemic pressure, so when they bleed (e.g. in bronchiectasis or TB) bleeding can be massive; they can be embolised.

q: Name the three parts of Virchow's triad.
why: Virchow's triad: stasis (immobility), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma) and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, thrombophilia).

q: Embolus type after a long bone fracture?
why: Fat from marrow enters veins after long bone fractures, causing fat embolism syndrome (hypoxia, confusion, petechial rash).

q: Name a non-thrombotic embolus.
acc: fat / air / amniotic / tumour / septic / cholesterol / foreign
model: Fat, air, amniotic fluid, tumour, septic.
why: Emboli can be fat, air, amniotic fluid, tumour or septic material, not just thrombus.

q: Which cells make surfactant?
acc: type ii / type 2 / pneumocyte ii / type two
why: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant and can divide to replace type I cells after injury.

q: Which cells line most of the alveolar surface?
why: Type I pneumocytes are thin and flat, covering about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange.
